Section 1
Introduction


1.1. About This Manual
1.1.1.   Purpose
         This manual provides detailed information about how to convert your COBOL source
         program into an executable object module. This manual is the companion to the
         OS 2200 Universal Compiling System (UCS) COBOL Programming Reference Manual
         Volume 1, COBOL Statements. Use Volume 1 as a reference source for topics relating
         to the language. Use Volume 2 for procedural information about using the features and
         capabilities of UCS COBOL. Both volumes give examples to emphasize and clarify the
         accompanying text instructions.

         This manual describes how to compile, link, execute, and debug your UCS COBOL
         source program. In addition, it shows the necessary steps required to make your
         program interact with other system software, such as relational databases and
         Executive requests.

1.1.2.   Scope
         This manual presents Unisys specific information to help you convert your UCS
         COBOL program source code into a fully executable program. This volume does not
         provide information about writing your initial UCS COBOL source program. The
         companion volume, Volume 1, presents this information.

         Each section in this manual discusses a particular task or group of related tasks. One
         section is devoted entirely to providing the steps required to compile your UCS
         COBOL source program. This section also discusses compiler listings and provides
         examples of various listing capabilities.

         Later sections give an overview of how to link, execute, and debug your compiled
         program using the Programmers Advanced Debugging System (PADS). Other sections
         provide enough information so that your program can interact with other system
         software, for example:

         ∩é╖   Relational databases
         ∩é╖   Executive requests
         ∩é╖   DMS 2200 databases




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 1ΓÇô1
Introduction




         Appendixes A and B contain numerical listings of compilation-time and execution-time
         diagnostic messages. Where necessary, brief explanations provide supplementary
         information.

1.1.3.   Audience
         This manual is intended for systems and applications programmers and analysts who
         are already familiar with the UCS COBOL programming language and need specific
         information about how to use UCS COBOL.

1.1.4.   Prerequisites
         To use this manual effectively, you should have knowledge of the UCS COBOL
         programming language as well as familiarity with basic OS 2200 job control language
         concepts.

1.1.5.   How to Use This Manual
         Use this manual as a tutorial document by following the directions provided in the
         applicable sections. The tasks described are organized in a logical sequence for easy
         referencing. Many sections present the information using a step-by-step format that is
         easy to use as a learning tool. You can read the manual through to become familiar
         with the processes described or you can refer to selected sections or pages to learn
         about one topic in detail.

         The following points apply throughout this manual:

         ∩é╖   The term ΓÇ£COBOLΓÇ¥ refers to the COBOL language generally or to standard COBOL.
             ΓÇ£UCS COBOLΓÇ¥ refers to this implementation of COBOL.
         ∩é╖   Text with yellow color highlighting indicates where technical information has been
             added or modified for this release of the programming reference manual. This
             material is different from the previous level of UCS COBOL.

1.1.6.   Conventions
         This manual uses the following conventions to illustrate COBOL syntax:

         ∩é╖   UPPERCASE represents COBOL keywords that are required in the syntax.
             Keywords must be spelled exactly as shown.
         ∩é╖   [ UPPERCASE in brackets ] represents keywords that you can optionally use to
             make your program more readable. Keywords must be spelled exactly as shown.

         Change bars in the margins indicate where technical information has been added or
         modified for this release of the reference manual.




1ΓÇô2                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                                   Introduction




1.2. Documentation Updates
         This document contains all the information that was available at the time of
         publication. Changes identified after release of this document are included in problem
         list entry (PLE) 19248828. To obtain a copy of the PLE, contact your Unisys
         representative or access the current PLE from the Unisys Product Support website:

             http://www.support.unisys.com/all/ple/19248828

         Note: If you are not logged into the Product Support site, you will be asked to do
         so.


1.3. UCS COBOL Overview
         Common Business Oriented Language (COBOL) is a high-level programming language
         that is procedure-oriented. The language is designed for organizational data
         processing applications that typically use large files and extensive input and output to
         produce large formatted reports. The language commands are derived from English
         grammar, consisting of language components such as

         ∩é╖   Clauses
         ∩é╖   Sentences
         ∩é╖   Paragraphs
         ∩é╖   Word order

         Universal Compiling System (UCS) COBOL is the implementation of COBOL for your
         system. UCS COBOL includes all of the required features of the following standards:

         ∩é╖   American National Standard COBOL, X3.23-1985
         ∩é╖   Federal Information Processing Standards Publication 21-2 (FIPS PUB 21-2)

         The UCS COBOL implementation contains some extensions that are additions or
         enhancements to American National Standard COBOL. In addition, this implementation
         includes compatibility features for migrating ASCII COBOL programs to UCS COBOL.

         The UCS COBOL compiler uses the American Standard Code for Information
         Interchange (ASCII) and International Standards Organization (ISO) character sets, and,
         optionally, the kanji character set, in processing source text and execution-time
         character data. The UCS COBOL compiler is fully reentrant and produces optimized
         reentrant code usable in multibanked applications, shared subsystems, or transaction
         programs.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 1ΓÇô3
Introduction




1.4. The Universal Compiling System
        UCS COBOL is a component of the Universal Compiling System (UCS). UCS consists of

        ∩é╖   A set of independent front-end language processors (for languages such as C and
            COBOL)
        ∩é╖   The Language Support System (LSS), which is a code generator used in common
            by all front-end language processors
        ∩é╖   The UCS Runtime System, which sets up the run-time environment for a program

        For more information about UCS, refer to the UCS Conceptual Overview.


1.5. Developing UCS COBOL Programs
        UCS COBOL belongs to a suite of software products specifically designed to execute
        on the extended mode architecture that is featured on Unisys systems. This hardware
        and software combination enhances your program development environment with the
        following benefits:

        ∩é╖   Latest programming language standards
        ∩é╖   Easier methods of constructing, executing, debugging and maintaining programs
        ∩é╖   Better control over sharing data between different parts of the system
        ∩é╖   Better protection of programs
        ∩é╖   Standard calling sequence across programming languages and the operating
            system
        ∩é╖   Dynamic replacement of processors
        ∩é╖   Automatic support of multiple user data banks
        ∩é╖   Use of a single command interface for compiling and interactive debugging
        ∩é╖   Dramatically enlarged data access through extended mode hardware addressing

        Such software includes the following:

        ∩é╖   Universal Compiling System
        ∩é╖   Linking System
        ∩é╖   Service Library
        ∩é╖   Programmers Advanced Debugging System (PADS)
        ∩é╖   Software subsystems (shared banks)
        ∩é╖   Executive system support

        Figure 1ΓÇô1 illustrates the extended mode software products hierarchy.

                                                                                Introduction




                   Figure 1ΓÇô1. Extended Mode Software Products

         You use this suite of products to compile, link, execute, and debug programs. Figure
         1ΓÇô2 illustrates the different software components involved in compiling, linking,
         executing, and debugging a program.




                Figure 1ΓÇô2. Developing Programs in Extended Mode

Introduction




         The following subsections give an overview of how to develop UCS COBOL programs.

1.5.1.   Compiling a UCS COBOL Program
         Program compilation occurs in the following steps:

         1.    The user calls the UCS COBOL compiler with the compiler call (@UCOB).
         2.    The front-end processor takes the text of the source program and translates it
               into an intermediate form that is independent of the language being used.
         3.    LSS translates the intermediate, language-independent information into
               machine-dependent code, producing an object module element that is ready to be
               executed on your extended mode system.

         See Section 2 for specific information about compiling your program.

1.5.2. Executing and Linking a UCS COBOL Program
         Immediately after compilation, you can execute a UCS COBOL object module element
         with an @XQT statement. For example,

              @XQT qual*file.om

         The execution statement causes the Linking System to load the object module into
         main storage. If required, the Linking System links the object module to any other
         object modules that are referenced (called) by the executed object module. Such
         references can be to any of the following:

         ∩é╖     External routines
         ∩é╖     External data items
         ∩é╖     Global constants
         ∩é╖     Common blocks

         Once loaded into main storage, the object module is executed by the Exec.

         You can choose when linking takes place. The Linking System can dynamically link a
         called object module to its caller after the caller has been loaded and execution has
         begun. Alternatively, you can link object modules before loading into main storage; this
         causes efficient execution because linking does not interrupt execution.

         The UCS Runtime System aids program execution by setting up the environment in
         which your program executes. The UCS Runtime System also provides interfaces to
         other UCS programs needed at run time. The UCS Runtime System includes both

         ∩é╖     Routines that are common to all of the UCS languages
         ∩é╖     Routines that are unique to one language




1ΓÇô6                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                                 Introduction




         UCS Runtime System routines include the following:

         ∩é╖   Environment control routines that
             ∩Ç¡   Manage main storage
             ∩Ç¡   Handle interrupts, contingencies, and interlanguage calls
         ∩é╖   Data manipulation routines that handle
             ∩Ç¡   Intrinsic functions
             ∩Ç¡   Conversions
             ∩Ç¡   Comparisons too complicated to do with generated code
         ∩é╖   Debugging routines that interface with the PADS
         ∩é╖   System interface modules that handle machine-dependent features
         ∩é╖   Processor interface modules for
             ∩Ç¡   Communications
             ∩Ç¡   Data Management System (DMS 2200)
             ∩Ç¡   Relational Data Management System (RDMS 2200)
             ∩Ç¡   Sort/Merge
             ∩Ç¡   Transaction programming environments (TIP and HVTIP)
         ∩é╖   Interfaces for the Processor Common Input/Output System (PCIOS), allowing all
             UCS languages to read or write from the same physical file
         ∩é╖   Run-time message routines that produce diagnostic messages when run-time
             errors occur (see Appendix B)

         See Section 3 for specific information about linking and executing your program.

1.5.3. Debugging a UCS COBOL Program
         A symbolic debugging tool called the Programmers Advanced Debugging System
         (PADS) is available to help you debug your UCS COBOL programs. PADS is a high-level
         interactive debugging tool that is common to all of the UCS languages. You can turn
         PADS on or off at the start of program execution without having to recompile the
         program each time. It has a simple interactive command language that lets you stop
         programs at desired places, examine or modify the values of program variables, and
         resume program execution. PADS is automatically called if your program fails; there is
         no overhead due to PADS if your program does not fail.

         See Section 3 for specific information about debugging your program with PADS.

Introduction




1.6. Creating Shared Subsystems (Common Banks)
        Extended mode shared subsystems are the functional equivalent of basic mode
        common banks. A shared subsystem is a group of one or more object modules that
        multiple programs can access at the same time. Each program accessing a shared
        bank accesses the same copy of the bank.

        Shared banks help limit the amount of main storage required by a system because
        multiple users can all use the same main storage space represented by the bank. A
        shared subsystem is partitioned off from the rest of the system by a combination of
        hardware and software mechanisms so that access to the shared subsystem can be
        controlled.

        Shared subsystems begin as ordinary object modules (compiled code). For information
        about how to create shared subsystems from ordinary object modules, refer to the
        Linking System Subsystems Programming Guide.


1.7. Organization of UCS COBOL Documentation
        This manual is Volume 2 of a two-volume set of reference manuals. It contains
        information about the following:

        ∩é╖    Compiling, linking, executing, and debugging a program
        ∩é╖    Interfacing with other system software

        Volume 1 is titled OS 2200 Universal Compiling Systems (UCS) COBOL Programming
        Reference Manual Volume 1, COBOL Statements (7831 0448). It contains information
        about COBOL language statements

        The overall structure of UCS documentation is designed in a logical order of
        introductory and technical information. This logical order is as follows:

        1.   The UCS Conceptual Overview (7831 0802) introduces the reader to UCS. It
             describes UCS software components and discusses how they are used to develop
             user applications in a high-level programming language. It is intended for data
             processing managers and potential UCS users.
        2.   The UCS Evaluation Overview (7833 0792) provides a more detailed description of
             UCS software. It describes specific programming statements and commands
             available and gives examples of their use. It is intended for managers and technical
             specialists who are evaluating whether to acquire or increase use of UCS.
        3.   The Application Development Programming Guide (7831 4077) is intended for
             programmers. It also introduces the reader to UCS. It is intended to give enough
             detailed programming instructions and guidelines concerning UCS so that a
             programmer can in many cases use it to create, compile, link, and execute
             programs, without necessarily having to reference other UCS documentation.
             Programmers should read this document first.

                    The language documentation is described in two volumes. Volume 1, which

Section 2
Compiling Your Program

         This section describes the compiler call you use to compile your UCS COBOL program.
         It also describes options that control compilation and compiler listings.


2.1. Calling the UCS COBOL Compiler (@UCOB)
         To compile your program, call the UCS COBOL compiler by using the @UCOB
         statement. The @UCOB statement

         ∩é╖     Specifies the location of your program source statements
         ∩é╖     Specifies the location (name) of the compiled object module to be created
         ∩é╖     Specifies compiler call options (see 2.2), which control the compilation

         Examples
             @UCOB       qual*file.source,qual*file.om
             @UCOB,I    ,qual*file.om
             @UCOB       qual*file.source,qual*file.om,,,WARNING,DOUBLESPACE
             @UCOB       qual*file.source,qual*file.om,,qual*file.keywords

         General Format
             @UCOB[,letter-options] [source-program][,[object-program]
                  [,,[keyword-option-element][,keyword-option]...]]

         where:

         [ ]

               Brackets mean the enclosed syntax unit is optional. Brackets are notational
               symbols only; do not actually specify them.

         letter-options

               Letter options control the compilation and are described in Table 2ΓÇô2. In case of
               conflict, keyword options take precedence over letter options; letter options take
               precedence over keyword options listed in keyword-option-element.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 2ΓÇô1
Compiling Your Program




        source-program

             Source-program is the name of the program file symbolic source element
             containing the program to be compiled. If you omit the source program name, the
             following conditions must be met:

             ∩é╖   You must use the I option.
             ∩é╖   The source program must immediately follow the compiler call in the
                 runstream.
             ∩é╖   The @EOF statement (or another system statement) must follow the source
                 program runstream to signal termination of the source program.

             If you use the I option and specify source-program, the source program from the
             runstream is saved in source-program.

             If source-program does not have a file name, the system uses the file TPF$.

        object-program

             Object-program is the name of the program file object module element in which
             the compiled program will be stored. If you omit the object program name

             ∩é╖   The compiled object module receives the file and element name of
                 source-program.
             ∩é╖   If you also omit source-program, the compiled object module receives the file
                 and element name TPF$.NAME$.

        ,,

             The two commas preceding keyword-option-element denote an unused field. If
             you specify anything beyond the object-program field, you must specify these
             commas.

        keyword-option-element

             keyword-option-element is the name of the symbolic element containing keyword
             options used to control this compilation. Compiler keyword options are described
             in 2.2.4 through 2.2.8.

             A keyword option element lets you store commonly used sets of keyword
             options so that you do not have to specify the same keywords over and over in
             different compilations.

             This element contains one or more lines containing one or more keywords per
             line, separated by commas. You can also include a comment on any line by
             preceding it with the sequence space-period-space (ΓÇÖ . ΓÇÖ). The Language Support
             System (LSS) processes everything on the line up to this sequence and ignores
             everything after it. A comment on one line does not affect the next line in the
             element.




2ΓÇô2                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                     Compiling Your Program




         Example
               NO-CODE,                      . No object module - syntax check only
               SOURCE,REMARK

                  Note: You can include comments only within the keyword option element,
                  not on the compiler call line.

                In case of conflict, keyword options and letter options take precedence over
                keyword options listed in keyword option element.

         keyword-option

                Keyword options control the compilation and are described in this section. In case
                of conflict, keyword options take precedence over letter options and keyword
                options listed in keyword option element.

         ...

                The ellipsis means you can list more than one keyword option, separating them by
                commas. The ellipsis is a notational symbol only; do not actually specify it.

         Note: In the following examples, qual*file.source is a symbolic element containing
         the source program and qual*file.om is the object module to be created. (In actual
         usage, the source program and object module need not be in the same file.)

         Example
         Source program in a symbolic element, default options:

               @UCOB     qual*file.source,qual*file.om

         Example
         Source program from the runstream (the letter option I is required):

               @UCOB,I    ,qual*file.om
                 .
                 . { language statements }
                 .
               @EOF

         Example
         Compilation using keyword options WARNING and DOUBLESPACE:

               @UCOB     qual*file.source,qual*file.om,,,WARNING,DOUBLESPACE




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  2ΓÇô3
Compiling Your Program




        Example
        Compilation using keyword options listed in the symbolic element qual*file.keywords:

            @UCOB      qual*file.source,qual*file.om,,qual*file.keywords

        In case of conflict, keyword options and letter options take precedence over keyword
        options listed in keyword-option-element.

        Example
        Compilation using

        ∩é╖    The letter options D and E
        ∩é╖    The keyword options listed in the symbolic element qual*file.keywords
        ∩é╖    The additional keyword option XREF
            @UCOB,DE     qual*file.source,qual*file.om,,qual*file.keywords,XREF

        Example
        Compilation using

        ∩é╖    No object program name (the object module receives the source program name)
        ∩é╖    The keyword options WARNING and DOUBLESPACE
            @UCOB      qual*file.source,,,,WARNING,DOUBLESPACE

        Additional Rules
        ∩é╖    When you omit fields in the compiler call, use commas to indicate the missing
             fields.
        ∩é╖    Compiler call lines are limited to 80 characters. Use a semicolon ( ; ) at the end of a
             line to continue the compiler call on another line, for example:
            @UCOB      qual*file.source,qual*file.om,,,WARNING,DOUBLESPACE,;
                       NO-CODE

             Use of the semicolon as a continuation marker is subject to various rules. See the
             ECL End Use and Programming Reference Manual for more information.
        ∩é╖    Since UCS compilers use the Service Library (SLIB) symbolic read and symbolic
             write routines for input and output, correction lines are not accepted. You must
             apply correction lines using the ELT processor before to compiling the source
             program.

                                                                          Compiling Your Program




2.2. Specifying Compiler Call Options
         You can control the compilation of your source program using options on the compiler
         call in any of the following ways:

         ∩é╖      Specify letter options on the compiler call (see 2.2.1 and 2.2.2).
                 @UCOB,SR qual*file.source,qual*file.om

         ∩é╖      Specify keyword options on the compiler call (see 2.2.1 and 2.2.3).
                 @UCOB qual*file.source,qual*file.om,,,CODE,FULL-DEBUG,OPTIONS,WARNING

         ∩é╖      Specify an element name that contains keyword options (see 2.2.1 and 2.2.3).
                 @UCOB qual*file.source,qual*file.om,,qual*file.keywords

         If a conflict occurs between letter options, keyword options on the compiler call, or
         keyword options in an element, the compiler assigns priority in the following order:

         1.     Keyword options on the compiler call (highest priority)
         2.     Letter options
         3.     Keyword options in the element

2.2.1. Commonly Used Sets of Options
         Keyword and letter options give you considerable flexibility in controlling the
         compilation. However, certain sets of keyword or letter options are typically used for
         certain types of compilations. Table 2ΓÇô1 gives examples of such compilations and the
         options typically used to perform them. The compilation types and corresponding
         options are meant as examples only and are not intended to limit your choice. Note
         that default values are not listed, since the compiler applies them automatically.


                Table 2ΓÇô1. Typical Compilations and the Options to Perform Them


                        Compilation Type                                 Options Used

             Checking for syntax errors (no object       NO-CODE, SOURCE, REMARK
             module)
             Program development and debugging           CLEAR, DEBUG/FULL, DEBUG/MONITOR,
                                                         MONITOR, NO-OPTIM, RUNCHECK, PARMCHECK
             Optimal execution                           COMPAT/ARGUMENTS, OPTIM/option
             Optimal compilation (wall time) for large   CACHE
             programs
             Displaying nonstandard features             LEVEL/STANDARD
             Providing compatibility with ASCII COBOL    CLEAR, COMPAT
             Providing compatibility with C programs     CALIGN

                        Compilation Type                               Options Used

            Producing the least information (output)   N option (implies NO-WARNING)
            about the compilation
            Producing the most information (output)    L option (implies LISTCOPY, ALLOC, OBJECT,
            about the compilation                      OPTIONS, SOURCE, XREF, LEVEL/STANDARD,
                                                       REMARK)
            Producing the least information (output)   N option (implies NO-WARNING)

        The Linker Information Listing specifies linker information for the object module. It is
        produced by the LINKINFO keyword option. (LINKINFO is the default if you have
        specified OBJECT or OBJECT-ONLY.) The compiler produces a Linker Information
        Listing for each object module produced. Linker Information Listing is composed of
        the following sections:

        ∩é╖      Header
        ∩é╖      EXTERNAL REFERENCES
        ∩é╖      EXTERNAL DEFINITIONS
        ∩é╖      COMMON BLOCKS
        ∩é╖      ALS INFORMATION
        ∩é╖      LOGICAL BANK

        Header Section
        The header specifies the

        ∩é╖      Object module name
        ∩é╖      Bank group name for this compilation
               Bank group names are created by appending the suffix $ to the object module
               name.

        EXTERNAL REFERENCES Section
        This section lists the names of all external references (calls) made in the object
        module. Only the first 12 characters of the names are printed. Typical UCS object
        modules contain external references to the following, in addition to references to user
        subprograms:

        ∩é╖      Entry points with the prefix RTS$, which are UCS Runtime System entry points
        ∩é╖      TCA$$$, a UCS Runtime System entry point for the task control area



2ΓÇô6                                                                                    7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                        Compiling Your Program




         EXTERNAL DEFINITIONS Section
         This section lists all external definitions (entry points) contained in the object module
         and their addresses. Each entry starts on a new line and has four subfields when the
         NARROW option is in effect. If the WIDE option is used, the entries contain the fifth
         field ΓÇÖLINE NUMBERΓÇÖ. External definitions include

         ∩é╖   Internal Name
             This is the entry point name as defined in the source program. It is truncated at 32
             characters.
         ∩é╖   External Name
             This is the entry point name used for LINK resolution.
         ∩é╖   LC
             This is the location counter of the defined entry point.
         ∩é╖   Offset
             This is the address of the definition, relative to the start of the given location
             counter.
         ∩é╖   Line Number
             This is the line number in the source program where the definition occurred. It is
             truncated at 53 characters.

         COMMON BLOCKS Section
         This section lists all common blocks contained in the object module. Each entry starts
         on a new line and has two subfields:

         ∩é╖   Common block name
             ∩Ç¡    All EXTERNAL user names appear in this section.
             ∩Ç¡    All names listed in the COMMON-STORAGE section appear under the single
                  name $BLANK$COMMON$.
         ∩é╖   Logical bank number of the bank containing the common block

         ALS INFORMATION Section
         This section lists the sizes of the activity local stack (ALS) for each procedure in the
         source program. Each entry starts on a new line and has the following three subfields:

         ∩é╖   Internal name
             The procedure name found in the source program.
         ∩é╖   External name
             The EXTERNAL name of the procedure used for linker resolution.
         ∩é╖   Size
             The number of words needed for the procedureΓÇÖs ALS.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                     2ΓÇô7
Compiling Your Program




        LOGICAL BANK Section
        This section describes the logical banks created by the compilation. It includes the
        following subfields:

        ∩é╖   Logical bank name
            Logical bank names are created by appending the logical bank number as a suffix
            to the bank group name.
        ∩é╖   Location counter number allocated for the bank
            This is the same as the logical bank number.
        ∩é╖   Size
            This gives the size of the bank in words, in both octal and decimal values.
            The compiler allocates one extra word for each common block and each data bank
            declared in the program. This permits the compiler to generate more efficient
            coding sequences in some cases. Thus the size of the common storage is larger
            than both of the following:
            ∩Ç¡   The size of the corresponding common block declared in the program
            ∩Ç¡   The size of the corresponding common block in the Allocation and Cross-
                Reference Listings
        ∩é╖   Bank
            Bank types are code, data, link vector, and so forth. See the Linking System
            Programming Reference Manual for all possible values.
        ∩é╖   Bank mode
            Bank modes are EM (extended mode). See the Linking System Programming
            Reference Manual for all possible values.
        ∩é╖   Storage class
            This gives the type of storage the bank is loaded into. MSU means ordinary main
            storage. See the Linking System Programming Reference Manual for all possible
            values.

2.2.2. Specifying Letter Options
        Letter options are a convenient way to briefly specify compiler options and listings
        produced during compilation. They also let you control

        ∩é╖   Whether warning and remark messages are produced during compilation
        ∩é╖   Whether source input is being provided from the runstream
        ∩é╖   Whether the compilation should terminate in error if major errors are encountered




2ΓÇô8                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                          Compiling Your Program




         Table 2ΓÇô2 lists letter options.


                               Table 2ΓÇô2. Compiler Call Letter Options


           Letter                                        Description

             D      Prints the Allocation Listing. This is a listing of all program symbols for which
                    storage is allocated, including information about data types, storage allocation, and
                    line number where a symbol is declared.
                    Same as keyword option ALLOC.
             E      Prints warning and remark messages.
                    Same as keyword options WARNING and REMARK.
                I   Specifies that source input is from the runstream.
                    If you specify the I option, the source program must directly follow the compiler
                    call. If you also specify a source element in the compiler call, the source program is
                    saved in a file assigned that source element name. @EOF or some other system
                    statement must follow the source to signal its termination.
                L   Specifies all of the listing keyword options. Same as specifying the keyword
                    options ALLOC, LINKINFO, LITERAL, OBJECT, OBJ-PKT, OPTIONS, REMARK,
                    SOURCE, and XREF.
             N      Specifies no listing options are to take effect. Same as specifying the keyword
                    options
                    NO-ALLOC, NO-LINKINFO, NO-LITERAL, NO-OBJECT, NO-OBJ-PKT, NO-OPTIONS,
                    NO-REMARK, NO-SOURCE, NO-WARNING, and NO-XREF.
                    The N option is the opposite of L.
                    If D, E, O, R, or S (which conflict with N) are specified with N, they take precedence
                    over N.
             O      Prints the Object Code Listing. This is a listing of the generated object code with
                    related source lines interspersed.
                    Same as keyword option OBJECT.
             R      Prints the Cross-Reference Listing. This is an alphabetized list of symbols defined in
                    the program and the line numbers of statements that reference the symbols.
                    Same as the keyword option XREF.
             S      Prints a listing of the source program.
                    Same as the keyword options SOURCE and REMARK.
                    If you also specify WARNING, the default diagnostic control option, warning
                    messages are printed.
             X      Specifies that the termination routine checks for major errors at the end of
                    compilation; if any have occurred, it terminates the compilation in error.
                    Same as the keyword option ERREXIT.

2.2.3. Specifying Keyword Options
        Keyword options give you more control over compilation than letter options. The
        following categories of keyword options exist:

        ∩é╖     Source control
              Controls how the compiler searches for copied source text. See 2.2.4.
        ∩é╖     Compilation control
              Primarily controls how errors affect the compilation and whether an object module
              should be produced. See 2.2.5.
        ∩é╖     Listing control
              Controls which compiler listings are produced. See 2.2.6.
        ∩é╖     Program control
              Controls the nature of the object program code generated by the compiler. These
              keyword options are extremely important because they let you create code that is
              designed for special purposes or situations; for example, code that
              ∩Ç¡     Provides the best compilation or execution performance
              ∩Ç¡     Can efficiently handle large programs
              ∩Ç¡     Is specifically designed for debugging or production
              See 2.2.7.
        ∩é╖     Diagnostics control
              Controls whether the compiler issues warning, remark, and level diagnostic
              messages during compilation. See 2.2.8.

        Table 2ΓÇô3 alphabetically lists each keyword option and the subsection containing
        detailed information. (Note that only one keyword option name of a set of related

2.2.4. Compiler Call Keyword Options for Source Control
         Table 2ΓÇô4 summarizes the source control keyword options.


                        Table 2ΓÇô4. Source Control Compiler Keyword Options


              Keyword Option                                Description

             MULTI-PF          Determines whether you can have multiple special program files of
                               copied source text.
             SEARCH-order      Determines the search order for copied source text.



MULTI-PF
         Format
              MULTI-PF
              NO-MULTI-PF

         Default: MULTI-PF

         These keyword options determine whether you can have multiple special program
         files of copied source text, used by the COPY statement.

         MULTI-PF means you can have multiple special program files, with a maximum of 51.
         These files must have an actual file name or an @USE name of the following format:

         COB$PF, COB$PF1, COB$PF2, ... COB$PF50

         The compiler searches all such files for copied source text, until one of the following
         occurs:

         ∩é╖     COB$PF50 is searched.
         ∩é╖     A gap in the sequence of files occurs.

         For example, in both of the following cases, COB$PF3 is the last file searched:

         COB$PF, COBPF1, COB$PF2, COB$PF3

         COB$PF, COB$PF1, COB$PF2, COB$PF3, COB$PF5

         If these files are not assigned, the compiler dynamically assigns them to the run and
         frees them at the end of compilation (provided the files exist).

         NO-MULTI-PF means the compiler searches only the single file COB$PF for copied
         source text (provided it exists).




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                      2ΓÇô13
Compiling Your Program




SEARCH-order
        Format
             SEARCH-PF-SI
             SEARCH-SI-PF

        Default: SEARCH-PF-SI

        These keyword options determine which files are searched by the compiler for COPY
        libraries when you have not specified the file containing the library. (These options
        have no effect when you do specify the file.)

        In these options, PF stands for program file, meaning the special program file COB$PF.
        SI stands for source input (that is, the file specified in source-program on the compiler
        call). SEARCH-PF-SI searches the special program file first; SEARCH-SI-PF searches the
        source input file first.

        Other files are also searched if the copied text is not found in these files. The
        complete search order is as follows for SEARCH-PF-SI:

        1.    The special program file COB$PF is searched. (This can be the actual file name or
              an @USE name.) If the file is not assigned, the compiler dynamically assigns it to
              the run and frees it at the end of compilation (provided the file exists).
        If you use the MULTI-PF keyword option, you can use up to 51 such files.
        2.    The file specified in source-program on the compiler call (source input) is searched
              (provided you do not use the I option).
              If you do use the I option, the file specified in object-program on the compiler call
              (object module output) is searched.
        3.    The program file TPF$ is searched.
        4. The system library file SYS$LIB$*PROC$ is searched.
        5.    If the proc or element is not found in any of these files, the compiler issues an
              error message; compilation continues as if the COPY statement is not present.

        SEARCH-SI-PF reverses the order of the first two files.

2.2.5. Compiler Call Keyword Options for Compilation Control
         Table 2ΓÇô5 summarizes the compilation control keyword options.


                  Table 2ΓÇô5. Compilation Control Compiler Keyword Options


          Keyword Option                                  Description

          CODE             Determines whether the compiler produces an object module or merely
                           checks syntax.
          ERRCHECK         Determines whether an object module is produced if there are major
                           errors.
          ERREXIT          Determines whether the compilation is terminated if there are major
                           errors.
          LISTCOPY         Determines whether text of included files or copied source lines is listed.
          MAXERRORS/n      Terminates compilation after n major errors.
          TRIM-CRLF        Causes CR and/or LF (carriage-return line-feed) characters at the end of a
                           source input line to be ignored. Only one of each will be ignored.



CODE
         Format
           CODE
           NO-CODE

         Default: CODE

         CODE causes the compiler to produce an object module. NO-CODE means the
         compiler does not produce an object module or generate the Allocation,
         Cross-Reference, or Object Code listings. However, the compiler does check syntax
         and semantics and generates the Source Listing if requested. NO-CODE is useful for
         syntax checking when you first compile your program. It prevents you from wasting
         system resources by trying to produce an object module when your program has
         errors.

ERRCHECK
         Format
           ERRCHECK
           NO-ERRCHECK
           STD-ERRCHECK

         ERRCHECK means an object module and most listings are not produced if the source
         element has any major errors. This effectively cancels the ALLOC, LINKINFO, and
         OBJECT options.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                      2ΓÇô15
Compiling Your Program




        NO-ERRCHECK causes the compiler to produce an object module even if the source
        element has major errors, unless ERREXIT is specified. (Fatal or internal errors,
        however, are nonrecoverable and prevent generation of an object module, even with
        NO-ERRCHECK.)

        Note that ERREXIT has precedence over NO-ERRCHECK and can suppress the
        generation of an object module.

        STD-ERRCHECK has the same effect as ERRCHECK, but it also changes the default of
        the LEVEL option to LEVEL/STANDARD and produces no object module if the program
        contains any nonstandard features (extensions).

ERREXIT
        Format
          ERREXIT
          NO-ERREXIT

        Default: NO-ERREXIT

        ERREXIT causes the compiler to check for major errors. If it finds any, the compiler
        calls the termination routine to terminate the compilation in error. For ERREXIT,
        ERRCHECK is in effect unless you specify STD-ERRCHECK.

        NO-ERREXIT means the compiler does not terminate the compilation in error.

        If you use NO-ERREXIT and NO-ERRCHECK, and your object module has major errors,
        there is no guarantee that the object module will execute correctly.

        Neither ERREXIT nor NO-ERREXIT has an effect if other conditions cause premature
        error termination.

LISTCOPY
        Format
          LISTCOPY
          NO-LISTCOPY

        Default: NO-LISTCOPY

        LISTCOPY lists the text of all included files or copied source lines. NO-LISTCOPY
        prevents the copied source from being included in the source listing.

        These options are subordinate to the SOURCE option and the S letter option; SOURCE
        specifies LISTCOPY and NO-SOURCE specifies NO-LISTCOPY.




2ΓÇô16                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                   Compiling Your Program




MAXERRORS/n
         Format
           MAXERRORS/n

         MAXERRORS/n specifies that the compilation terminates immediately if more than n
         major errors occur in the compilation. If you specify MAXERRORS, you must specify
         /n, with no spaces on either side of the slash.

         If you do not specify MAXERRORS, the default for n is 100,000.

         Since UCS compilers are multiple-pass compilers, the order in which the system lists
         error messages is not necessarily the order in which it detected them. Therefore, after
         the compilation terminates as a result of reaching the MAXERRORS limit, additional
         error messages can appear in the listing because they were detected in an earlier
         pass of the compilation.

TRIM-CRLF
         Formats
           TRIM-CRLF
           NO-TRIM-CRLF

         Default: TRIM-CRLF

         TRIM-CRLF automatically strips a CR and/or LF from the end of a source line when a
         program is compiled. Only one CR and/or one LF is stripped, and they must be at the
         very end of the line (or followed only by blanks).

         When source programs are edited or created on workstations, there are usually CR-LF
         (Carriage-Return Line-Feed) characters at the end of each line to signal the end of a
         line. When these programs are copied to OS 2200 files with products such as cpFTP or
         TAS, these trailing sequences are usually removed when the OS 2200 SDF images are
         created for the lines. If the sequences are NOT removed, the UCS compilers usually
         give errors or warnings during compilation when they encounter the ΓÇÿextraΓÇÖ CR or LF
         characters at the ends of the lines.

         In addition, one can edit OS 2200 files directly from workstations using a mapped drive
         handled by CIFS. CIFS removes a line feed character and terminates the SDF image for
         a line at that point. It does NOT remove the carriage return if one is there. You must
         manually run a utility to remove the extra CR that CIFS leaves at the end of the images.
         (You must do a @CIFSUT cp command with the ΓÇôw option.) For more information on
         this, see the CIFS for ClearPath OS 2200 User, Programmer, and Administrator
         Reference Manual. Using the TRIM-CRLF option means that you do not have to
         manually remove these trailing CR characters.

         NO-TRIM-CRLF will not strip the CR and/or LF from the end of the source lines.

         ∩é╖     The repository in which cross-reference relationships are created when the
               UREP-XREF option is in effect.
         ∩é╖     The repository used for embedded SQL commands for both compile-time and
               run-time actions.

         APPLICATION/alias specifies an alias for the name to be used for the same functions.

         Both the name and alias consist of 1 to 12 characters. If you do not specify
         APPLICATION, the default is (in order of precedence)

         ∩é╖     The application name on an optional DMS 2200 INVOKE statement
         ∩é╖     The application name UDSSRC
         See Section 7 for more information about RDMS and programs containing embedded
         SQL statements. See Section 8 for more information about UREP.

AUXPROLOG/n
        Format
            AUXPROLOG/n
            NO-AUXPROLOG

        Default: NO-AUXPROLOG
        AUXPROLOG/n generates additional prologue and epilogue code for each user routine
        in a compilation unit. This generated code determines if user-supplied auxiliary
        prologue (USER$PROLOG) and epilogue (USER$EPILOG) subprograms should be called
        during the execution of the prologue and epilogue code for a program or subprogram.
        The calling of these subprograms is governed by a flag that is set at program
        execution time by calling the service subprogram UCS$ACTAUX and cleared by calling
        the service subprogram UCS$DEACTAUX.
        AUXPROLOG/n also creates an auxiliary stack frame on the activity-local stack (ALS)
        with a size of n words, with a minimum size of two words. The first two words of the
        stack frame are reserved. The first word contains the virtual address (VA) of the
        previous auxiliary stack frame (if one is active on the stack frame) or zero. The second
        word contains the virtual address of the entry point of the routine that called the
        user-supplied USER$PROLOG or USER$EPILOG routine. These two reserved words
        can be accessed by the user-supplied USER$PROLOG and USER$EPILOG routines but
        should not be modified by them. The remaining words can be used and modified.
        USER$PROLOG and USER$EPILOG are the external names of the user-supplied
        routines that are called from the auxiliary prologue and epilogue code generated by
        the compiler. They each have one parameter, which is the auxiliary stack frame. These
        subprograms are usually written in a system software language such as UCS C, which
        can manipulate virtual addresses. See the keyword AUXPROLOG/n in the C Compiler
        Programming Reference Manual Volume 2 for an example of a user-supplied auxiliary
        prologue and epilogue subprogram.
        NO-AUXPROLOG inhibits the generation of additional auxiliary prologue and epilogue
        code by the compiler. It also inhibits the creation of the auxiliary stack frame.

CACHE/spec
        Formats
            CACHE/D0
            CACHE/Dn
            CACHE/Sn
            CACHE/n

        Default: CACHE/D0.
        The purpose of CACHE is to improve wall-time compilation performance by using the
        available real memory on the system to reduce the number of I/O CACHE/Dn requests.
        (Real memory is much faster than issuing I/O requests to peripheral devices.) You may
        want to use this option in the following circumstances:

        ∩é╖    You have a very large program. (Cache storage is especially useful for very large
             programs.)



2ΓÇô26                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                   Compiling Your Program




         ∩é╖    Compilation is unacceptably slow.
         ∩é╖    Your system has extra memory that you can use during compilation.

         The compiler's storage manager has an internal paging area that holds the
         intermediate form of your program. (This internal paging area is approximately 15
         million words.) When this paging area overflows, the compiler's storage manager uses
         peripheral I/O storage to manage this space.

         When the CACHE/n option is used, the storage manager uses up to n 262,144 word
         cache banks as intermediate buffers to manage its paging area. It only uses peripheral
         I/O if it runs out of space in the cache banks. (The CACHE option is probably
         unnecessary on most compilations on current 2200 systems due to their large
         memories.)

         If the system gives you the memory to hold the cache banks, cache storage
         decreases wall time and I/O SUPs. If real memory is not available or the operating
         system does not give your run the space the cache banks needed, the compilation
         wall time increases, system swap file activity increases, and general system
         throughput can suffer. If your system is short on memory, heavy use of the CACHE
         option should be reserved for batch runs at off-peak times.

         CACHE/D0 (the default) means cache storage is not used during compilation; the
         compilation uses a mass storage file, if needed.

         For CACHE/Dn or CACHE/n, n represents an upper limit on the number of banks that
         can be used in the compilation. (The absolute upper limit is 256.) The compiler
         allocates only as many banks as it needs. The larger the program, the greater the value
         for n. You should use one cache bank for every 1000 to 2000 lines of code.

         CACHE/Sn is similar to CACHE/Dn except that some required memory is obtained
         immediately, instead of only as needed. This method decreases ER SUPS for large
         compilations, but also can allocate more memory than needed for your compilation.

CALIGN
         Format
             CALIGN
             NO-CALIGN

         Default: NO-CALIGN

         CALIGN assures that all data names with the following definitions and group items
         containing such data names will be word-aligned:

         ∩é╖    USAGE COMP-1
         ∩é╖    USAGE COMP-2
         ∩é╖    USAGE COMP-5 PIC S9(y) or PIC 9(y); where y = 5 through 10
