Compiling Your Program




        CALIGN assures that all data names with the definition USAGE COMP-5 PIC S9(z) or
        PIC 9(z) (where z = 1 through 4) will be half-word-aligned. Group items containing such
        data names will be word-aligned.

CLEAR
        Format
          CLEAR
          NO-CLEAR

        Default: NO-CLEAR

        CLEAR sets any static variables (that have no initial value specified) to zero.

        NO-CLEAR does not specify an initial value for these variables.

CODE-LVE
        Format
          CODE-LVE
          NO-CODE-LVE

        Default: NO-CODE-LVE

        CODE-LVE eliminates the need for a subsystem creator to define fixed gates for
        routines (entry points) internal to the subsystem. It generates a one-word link vector
        entry in the code bank for each imported procedure, in addition to the normal
        two-word link vector entry in the link vector bank.

        When the subsystem creator splits subsystem code from data during static linking
        with @LINK,Y, the Linking System uses the appropriate link vector entry to resolve the
        call to the internal entry point.

        NO-CODE-LVE suppresses generation of the one-word link vector entry in the bank;
        subsystems using @LINK,Y must still define fixed gates for internal entry points.

        For complete information on use of this feature, see the Linking System Subsystems
        Programming Guide.

COMPAT
        Format
          COMPAT
          COMPAT/FULL
          COMPAT/FULLHV377
          COMPAT/HV177
          NO-COMPAT
          COMPAT/ARGUMENTS

        Default: NO-COMPAT



2ΓÇô28                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                       Compiling Your Program




         COMPAT makes the following features compatible with ASCII COBOL:

         ∩é╖    HIGH-VALUE is octal 0177 (all bits set for a 7-bit machine).
         ∩é╖    The SYNCHRONIZED clause allocates compatible data.
         ∩é╖    Word alignment for COMP-1 and COMP-2 data items is compatible.
         ∩é╖    COMP data items are allocated as binary.
         ∩é╖    COMP-3 data items are allocated as PACKED-DECIMAL. COMP-3 requires
              COMPAT or COMP-BIN.
         ∩é╖    Exact binary items can be described the same. For example, PIC 1 without a
              USAGE BINARY-1 clause defines an exact binary item.
         ∩é╖    PROGRAM-ID can be an integer.
         ∩é╖    No decimal truncation occurs when the value of the sender contains more
              significant digits than the receiver, if the receiver is a binary, character numeric,
              edited or packed-decimal item.
         ∩é╖    Moving a floating-point item or performing an arithmetic calculation done in
              floating point where the receiver is a binary, character numeric, edited or
              packed-decimal item will produce the same results as ASCII COBOL.

         COMPAT/FULL is the same as COMPAT, except that all static variables are allocated,
         whether or not they are ever referenced. Also, all static variables are placed in one
         bank except for DMCA (DML), which is defined in working storage section or common
         storage section depending on the specifications you specified in the INVOKE clause. In
         addition, database data names (USAGE DATABASE-KEY, AREA-NAME,
         RECORD-NAME ΓÇª) will be placed in a separate bank. COMPAT/FULL sets COMP-BIN.

         COMPAT/FULLHV377 is the same as COMPAT, except that HIGH-VALUES is set to
         octal 0377 (all bits set for an 8-bit machine). COMPAT/FULLHV377 sets COMP-BIN.

         COMPAT/HV177 sets HIGH-VALUES to octal 0177. It does nothing else. It does not set
         COMP-BIN.

         NO-COMPAT performs no compatibility actions.

         COMPAT/ARGUMENTS restricts parameters passed BY REFERENCE to 01 and 77 level
         item. This allows the compiler to assume that all incoming parameters are word
         aligned and thus allows better code to be generated for parameter references.

COMP-BIN
         Format
             COMP-BIN
             NO-COMP-BIN

         Default: NO-COMP-BIN

         COMP-BIN promotes compatibility between ASCII COBOL and UCS COBOL source
         programs.



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                    2ΓÇô29
Compiling Your Program




        COMP-BIN causes an item declared as USAGE COMP to be treated as though it was
        declared USAGE BINARY. COMP-BIN also causes items declared as USAGE COMP-3 to
        be allocated as USAGE PACKED-DECIMAL. The COMPAT, COMPAT/FULL, and
        COMPAT/FULLHV377 options set this option. Programs that use the COMPAT,
        COMPAT/FULL, and COMPAT/FULLHV377 options cannot override COMP-BIN during
        compilation.

        NO-COMP-BIN does not cause any difference in treatment of COMP data items.

D$WORK-WS
        Format
            D$WORK-WS

            NO-D$WORK-WS

        Default: NO-D$WORK-WS

        This option is for use by DMS programs. When a DMS program places the DMCA into
        COMMON using the INVOKE clause, the UCS COBOL compiler normally puts the DMS
        D$WORK data structure at the end of COMMON-STORAGE, after all the user
        variables. If COMMON-STORAGE layout is not the same in all program units in an
        executable program, user variables can overlay the D$WORK data structure and
        problems can occur. The D$WORK-WS keyword option causes the compiler to put the
        DMS D$WORK data structure into WORKING-STORAGE, thereby eliminating any
        potential problems.

        It is recommended that all COBOL programs that use DMS use this keyword option in
        their compilations since it eliminates the potential problems that results if D$WORK
        overlays user variables in COMMON-STORAGE. The option is not on by default.

DEBUG/option
        Format
            DEBUG
            DEBUG/option
            NO-DEBUG

        DEBUG generates a PADS symbolic debugging dictionary (SDD) that eliminates all
        information about variables that are declared but not referenced in the program.
        However, if any member of a group is referenced, information on all group members
        and any REDEFINES of the group are included in the SDD. This is useful when using
        PADS to debug programs that copy source code but actually use only a few of the
        shared items declared in the copied text.

        DEBUG/option controls the amount and type of debugging information available for a
        program. The following options are available:

        ∩é╖    DEBUG/FULL
        ∩é╖    DEBUG/MONITOR



2ΓÇô30                                                                          7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                   Compiling Your Program




         ∩é╖    DEBUG/REFERENCE
         ∩é╖    DEBUG/STATEMENT
         ∩é╖    DEBUG/WALKBACK (default)

         DEBUG/FULL generates a PADS symbolic debugging dictionary (SDD) in the object
         module, including declared but unused variables, line numbers, and procedure
         information.

         DEBUG/MONITOR generates information in the symbolic debugging dictionary, in
         addition to the information generated by the DEBUG, DEBUG/REFERENCE, and
         DEBUG/FULL options. This information allows for the monitoring of input and output
         for each line of source code executed during a PADS debugging session. This option
         invokes the DEBUG keyword option if the DEBUG, DEBUG/REFERENCE, or
         DEBUG/FULL keyword options are not specified.

         DEBUG/REFERENCE generates a PADS symbolic debugging dictionary (SDD) similar to
         what is generated for DEBUG, except information on more group members is
         eliminated. Information on variables that are group items or group members is
         included in the SDD when any of the following rules apply:

         1.   An item is included in the SDD when it is referenced in the program.
         2.   A group item is included in the SDD when at least one of its members is
              referenced in the program.
         3.   A group member is included in the SDD when at least one of the group items of
              which it is a member is referenced in the program.
         4. An overlaid item (both redefining and redefined) is included in the SDD when it
            overlays any item that is included in the SDD according to rules 1 through 3.
         Exceptions to these rules include the following:

         ∩é╖    When a group item is only referenced in an APPLY EXDEF/EXREF statement,
              RENAMES clause, or PROCEDURE DIVISION USING statement, the group item is
              included in the SDD but rule 3 does not apply to its group members.
         ∩é╖    The appearance of an item in a DATA RECORD clause is not considered to be a
              reference unless the associated file name is referenced in the program.
         ∩é╖    When a DATA RECORD clause contains more than one record name, these
              records are treated as REDEFINES by the compiler and rule 4 applies.
         ∩é╖    The appearance of an item in a REDEFINES clause is not considered to be a
              reference.
         ∩é╖    When the INITIAL clause is specified on the PROGRAM-ID, all items declared in
              WORKING-STORAGE that contain a VALUE clause are considered to be
              referenced.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 2ΓÇô31
Compiling Your Program




        DEBUG/REFERENCE Example
          01 A.
                  02 B.
                     03 B1 PIC X(2).
                     03 B2 PIC X(2).
                  02 C PIC X(4).
                  02 D.
                     03 D1 PIC 9(4).
                     03 D2 PIC 9(2).
                     03 D3 PIC 9(2).
                  02 E PIC 9(4).
                  02 F PIC X(4).
                  02 G REDEFINES F.
                     03 G1 PIC X(2).
                     03 G2 PIC X(2).
                         .
                         .
                  MOVE 10 TO D2.
                  MOVE ΓÇÖABCDΓÇÖTO F.
                  MOVE F TO B.

        When the DEBUG/REFERENCE keyword option is used to compile this program,
        information on variables A, B, B1, B2, D, D2, F, and G is included in the SDD.
        Information on variables C, D1, D3, E, G1, and G2 is not included in the SDD.

        DEBUG/STATEMENT generates an SDD that contains information about procedures,
        functions, and line numbers. The SDD will not contain any information about variables
        or labels.

        DEBUG/WALKBACK generates an SDD that contains information only about
        procedures and functions, allowing the use of such PADS commands as INQUIRE
        WALKBACK and TRACE ON FOR PROCEDURE. This type of SDD provides the
        minimum level of PADS high-level debugging.

        NO-DEBUG suppresses generation of the SDD and is recommended for production
        programs.

EXTENDED/n
        Format
          EXTENDED
          EXTENDED/n

        Default: EXTENDED.

        Code is targeted for the class of machine that performs the compilation.




2ΓÇô32                                                                           7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                       Compiling Your Program




          EXTENDED/n specifies the machine class of the system where the object module
          produced by the compiler will execute. The parameter n can have one of the following
          values, depending on the machine:

                0      Both XPA and non-XPA systems
                2      1100/90, 2200/400, or 2200/600 system
                4      2200/100, 2200/200 system
                6      2200/XPA machine (CMOS systems)

                8      4000 system and above (SAIL-based
                       systems)

          If you want the most efficient code possible for a particular machine, select the
          appropriate value for n. Code targeted for one class of machine can run on a different
          class. However, it might not be as efficient as code targeted for that class.

          EXTENDED, the default value, means code is targeted for the class of machine that
          performs the compilation.

I18N-IO
          Format
            I18N-IO
            NO-I18N-IO

          Default: NO-I18N-IO

          When the I18N-IO option is specified, processing of CODE TYPE and LOCALE is done
          the same as the original implementation in UCOB 8R1 and 8R1A (i.e., calls to I18NLIB
          routines are generated to get the CODE TYPE number and LOCALE number of the
          locale in force). If the I18N-IO option is not set (NO-I18N-IO) then these calls to I18NLIB
          are not generated, and a CODE TYPE number of 1 (ASCII) and LOCALE number of 0 (no
          locale) are always used.

          The use of the NO-I18N-IO option eliminates the overhead of the I18NLIB calls for
          users who simply want to use the ASCII CODE TYPE and LOCALE number.

MAIN-PROGRAM
          Format
            MAIN-PROGRAM
            SUBPROGRAM

          Default: MAIN-PROGRAM




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                   2ΓÇô33
Compiling Your Program




        These keyword options allow the Linking System to identify which program unit is the
        main program and which are subprograms when it statically links multiple program
        units into a single object module. The Linking System uses these keyword options to
        determine where program execution begins when the statically linked object module
        is executed.

        MAIN-PROGRAM creates an object module that can be executed by @XQT or called
        by another object module as a subprogram.

        SUBPROGRAM creates an object module that can be called as a subprogram by
        another object module only. If the program PROCEDURE DIVISION statement includes
        a USING clause, the compiler assumes SUBPROGRAM.

MAX-SIZE/m and MAXMEM/m
        Format
            MAX-SIZE/m
            MAX-SIZE/mK
            MAX-SIZE/mM
            MAX-SIZE/DEFAULT

            MAXMEM/m
            MAXMEM/mK
            MAXMEM/mM
            MAXMEM/DEFAULT

        Default: MAX-SIZE/DEFAULT or MAXMEM/DEFAULT

        where:

        m

             specifies a memory limit with a granularity of 1 word. The minimum value of m is
             1. The maximum value of m is 16,777,216 (2**24).

        mK

             specifies a memory limit with a granularity of 1,000 decimal words. The minimum
             value of m is 1. The maximum value of m is 16,777.

        mM

             specifies a memory limit with a granularity of 1,000,000 decimal words. The
             minimum value of m is 1. The maximum value of m is 16.

        The MAX-SIZE and MAXMEM keyword options have the same meaning; each can be
        considered an alias of the other. These options can be used to put a limit on the
        amount of memory used by the compilerΓÇÖs internal paging area.




2ΓÇô34                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                     Compiling Your Program




         The compilerΓÇÖs internal paging area is approximately 200,000 words and is in a 262,144
         bank. The paging area is automatically expanded as needed during a compilation. This
         expansion can grow to 16 million words on a large compilation.

         Using the MAX-SIZE or MAXMEM option bypasses these defaults and limits the
         paging area size to the m value. Note that the m value is rounded up to the nearest
         262,144 boundary for expansion purposes (for example, 1 is the same as 262,144 and
         300K is the same as 524,288).

         Using the MAX-SIZE/DEFAULT option nullifies the effect of any previous MAX-SIZE/m
         option (such as one supplied in a keyword options element). The paging area
         maximum size is then determined by the machine type and CACHE/n values as
         described in the previous paragraphs.

         Examples
           @UCOB PROG1,,,,SEGCODE,MAX-SIZE/4000000

           @UCOB PROG2,,,,SEGCODE,CACHE/D100,MAXMEM/1M

         The first compilation limits its paging area size to approximately 4.2 million words.
         Note that this is an upper limit, and the compiler grows to this size only if needed.
         Four million words is a large portion of the available memory if this compilation is
         performed on a non-2200/XPA-class machine. Memory quota limits could abort
         operations if quota limits are in effect.

         The paging area size is limited to approximately 1 million words for the second
         compilation. If you do not use the MAX-SIZE or MAXMEM option, the machine type
         determines the paging area limit. The limit for a 2200/XPA system is 16 million words.
         The maximum paging area for a non-2200/XPA-class machine without the MAX-SIZE or
         MAXMEM option specified is determined as a function of the CACHE/n value and is
         about 3.5 million words for CACHE/D100 ((n/8)*262,144 + 262,144).

         In rare situations, the compiler must expand past the limit dictated by the MAX-SIZE,
         MAXMEM, or CACHE options. Such an expansion is limited to one extra 262,144
         expansion.

         The compilerΓÇÖs paging area is not the only memory the UCS compilers use. There are
         code banks, other D-banks, and up to n 262,144 cache banks if a CACHE/n keyword
         option is specified for the compilation. The cache banks are not used until the main
         paging area is filled up and has expanded to its allowable limit. The size given by an
         @@CONS RC [runid] transparent command is a subset of all these banks. The subset is
         generally the total of the banks currently swapped into memory for your run. On a
         2200/XPA system, this is usually all the banks that your program has used, because
         these machines have a large real memory.

         See also the description of the CACHE/n keyword option in this section.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                    2ΓÇô35
Compiling Your Program




MIN-ALS
        Format
            MIN-ALS
            NO-MIN-ALS

        Default: NO-MIN-ALS

        The program variables in the WORKING-STORAGE section are normally allocated in
        static storage in UCS COBOL. However, if the INITIAL clause is used on the
        PROGRAM-ID statement, then variables in the WORKING-STORAGE section are
        instead allocated on the Activity Local Stack (ALS). (Exception: Those 01 variables
        having the EXTERNAL clause are made into named COMMON blocks, which are
        always allocated in static storage). The ALS stack is a small bank, with a maximum size
        of only 229,376 words (0700000 octal). If you have large buffers in the
        WORKING-STORAGE section that are causing ALS overflows (the ALS might run out of
        space due to nested calls), you can reduce the amount of ALS used in your COBOL
        programs by using the MIN-ALS keyword option on your UCOB compilations. This
        keyword option causes the compiler to allocate those local WORKING-STORAGE
        variables that do not have VALUE clauses on them in static storage instead of
        allocating them on the ALS. If the large buffers causing the overflow problem have
        VALUE clauses on them, remove the VALUE clauses and add code at the beginning of
        your procedures to initialize them. See also the description of the Nested Procedure
        Calls in Appendix C.

        Note: The MIN-ALS keyword option has no effect on programs that do not have
        the INITIAL clause on their PROGRAM-ID statements.

MIN-DBANK
        Format
            MIN-DBANK
            NO-MIN-DBANK

        Default: NO-MIN-DBANK

        MIN-DBANK keyword option causes the compiler to reduce the amount of local static
        D-bank storage that is generated in the output object module. Specifically, it minimizes
        the number of constants and packets that are generated into the $0 location counter.
        The affected items are as follows:

        ∩é╖    Parameter lists are generated on the activity-local stack (ALS) instead of in static
             $0 storage.
        ∩é╖    Some addresses are created by executing extra code, that is AA,U, rather than as
             address constants in $0 storage.
        ∩é╖    Code for Embedded SQL (ESQL) statements will not use writable $0 storage for
             packets.




2ΓÇô36                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                     Compiling Your Program




         Reducing the size of the $0 static storage is at the expense of additional executable
         code. The additional code is larger than the reduction in $0 storage. This can have a
         negative impact on execution time performance.

         The MIN-DBANK option does not affect the location where the WORKING-STORAGE
         variable is allocated. WORKING-STORAGE variables by default are allocated in static
         local location counters, for example $0, $2, $4, and so on, in the compilation.

         If your COBOL program has the INITIAL clause on the PROGRAM-ID statement, then
         the MIN-DBANK keyword option has no effect. The INITIAL clause results in the same
         code for the items listed earlier. The INITIAL clause also causes all variables in
         WORKING-STORAGE variable to be allocated on the ALS instead of in static local
         storage.

         The INITIAL clause is often used when a COBOL application is to be linked into an
         HVTIP transaction. This clause reduces the Dbank size as the WORKING-STORAGE
         variable is reinitialized on each entry to a subprogram. See 3.1.3. The INITIAL clause is
         also used to create fixed-gate subsystems. Due to the INITIAL clause, there is little
         incentive to use the MIN-DBANK keyword option on UCOB compilations.

MONITOR
         Format
             MONITOR
             MONITOR/LABEL
             NO-MONITOR

         Default: NO-MONITOR

         MONITOR helps debug a program by writing the following information to the program
         print file:

         ∩é╖    Each time execution encounters a paragraph or section label, the compiler writes
              the name (label) of the paragraph or section to the print file. This lets you know
              what part of the program is being executed. The monitor output contains:
              ∩Ç¡   The line number of the paragraph or section
              ∩Ç¡   The name of the paragraph or section
              ∩Ç¡   The identifier ΓÇ£PROCΓÇ¥
         ∩é╖    Each time a main program or subprogram is entered, the compiler writes the entry
              point name to the print file. This lets you know what subprogram is currently being
              executed. The monitor output contains
              ∩Ç¡   The line number of the PROGRAM-ID line
              ∩Ç¡   The entry point name
              ∩Ç¡   The identifier "SUBPROGRAM-ENTRY"
              The monitor output for an alternate entry point (a label named in a WITH ENTRY
              POINTS clause on the PROCEDURE DIVISION statement) will NOT have a line
              number.



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 2ΓÇô37
Compiling Your Program




        ∩é╖   Each time a subprogram or main program returns to its caller, the compiler again
            writes the subprogram's entry point name(s) to the print file. This lets you know
            that the subprogram is no longer in execution and that its caller is now again in
            execution. The monitor output contains
            ∩Ç¡   The line number of the last statement in the subprogram
            ∩Ç¡   The entry point name of the subprogram (this is a list of entry point names if
                the subprogram has multiple entry points)
            ∩Ç¡   The identifier ΓÇ£RETURNΓÇ¥
            Note that an EXIT PROGRAM statement executed in a main program does NOT
            cause the main program to stop execution or return to the operating system. You
            can only exit a main program by executing a STOP RUN statement or by branching
            to a label at the end of the program. An EXIT PROGRAM statement in a
            subprogram, however, does cause a return to be done and its caller to resume
            execution.
        ∩é╖   Each time a STOP RUN is executed, the compiler writes a line to the print file. The
            monitor output contains
            ∩Ç¡   The line number of the STOP RUN statement
            ∩Ç¡   The entry point name of the subprogram (this is a list of entry point names if
                the subprogram has multiple entry points, and will be the string
                ΓÇ£(DECLARATIVE)ΓÇ¥ if the STOP RUN is in a DECLARATIVE)
            ∩Ç¡   The identifier "STOP RUN"
        ∩é╖   Each time a data item is referenced, the compiler writes the contents of the data
            item to the print file. This lets you know the value of the data item at a particular
            point in program execution.
            For data references, the monitor output line is printed before the execution of the
            statement containing the reference. When referenced data items are possibly
            changed, as in arithmetic operations, moves, and so forth, monitor output is
            printed both before and after the execution of the statement. For each statement,
            the monitor output contains
            ∩Ç¡   The line number of the statement being executed
            ∩Ç¡   The name of the data item
            ∩Ç¡   The value of the data item
            If reference modification is specified for a data item, the entire data item is
            displayed, not just the portion specified by the reference modifier.
            If a subscripted data item is specified, the subscript is not displayed as part of the
            data item in the monitor output.

        MONITOR/LABEL does not print data item values to the print file. Only output for
        subprogram entries and exits, STOP RUNs, and paragraph and section labels is put into
        the print file.

        NO-MONITOR, which is the default, suppresses the generation of the debugging code.




2ΓÇô38                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                   Compiling Your Program




         Note that all MONITOR output is limited to 76 columns. If a list of entry point names
         causes this limit to be exceeded, the list is truncated.

         MONITOR Example
         The following is an example of a subprogram compiled with the MONITOR keyword
         option:

            1     IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
            2     PROGRAM-ID. subex.
            3     DATA DIVISION.
            4     WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
            5     01 data-item-1 pic s9(10) usage binary value 10.
            6     01 data-item-2 pic s9(10) usage binary value 20.
            7     01 data-item-3 pic s9(10) usage binary value 0.
            8     linkage section.
            9     01 res pic s9(10) usage binary.
           10     01 parm1 pic s9(10) usage binary.
           11      PROCEDURE DIVISION using parm1 res.
           12      ST.
           13          if parm1 is equal to 22
           14              move 2 to res
           15              exit program.
           16      PARA-1.
           17          ADD data-item-1 TO data-item-2 GIVING data-item-3.
           18
           19           compute parm1 = parm1 + data-item-3.
           20           compute res = parm1 + 1.

         The following is an example of the monitor output for this subprogram when called
         with the first parameter having a value of -10 and the second parameter with a value
         of 2:

           2        SUBEX SUBPROGRAM-ENTRY
           12       ST PROC
           13       PARM1 = -0000000010
           16       PARA-1 PROC
           17       DATA-ITEM-1   = +0000000010
                    DATA-ITEM-2   = +0000000020
                    DATA-ITEM-3   = +0000000000
                    DATA-ITEM-3   = +0000000030
           19       PARM1 = -0000000010
                    DATA-ITEM-3   = +0000000030
                    PARM1 = -0000000010
                    PARM1 = +0000000020
           20       PARM1 = +0000000020
                    RES   = +0000000002
                    RES   = +0000000021
           20       SUBEX RETURN




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               2ΓÇô39
Compiling Your Program




        Example Explanation
        First, the line number (2) of the PROGRAM-ID and the name of the subprogram
        (SUBEX) are displayed along with the SUBPROGRAM-ENTRY identifier.

        Next, the line number (12) and label (ST) are displayed for paragraph ST along with the
        identifier PROC. This is the first executable statement in the program.

        Then the line number (13) and value of the PARM1 data item in the IF statement are
        displayed.

        Since PARM1 is not equal to 22, the next output is the line number (16) and label
        (PARA-1) of the next paragraph to be executed along with the identifier PROC.

        The line number (17), each data item specified (DATA-ITEM-1, DATA-ITEM-2,
        DATA-ITEM-3), and the current value of each specified data item in the ADD statement
        are displayed next.

        Next, the values of any data items that are changed as a result of the ADD statement
        (DATA-ITEM-3) are displayed. Note that the line number is displayed only once for all
        data items in a given statement.

        The same is done for the COMPUTE statements for lines 19 and 20. The line number
        and current values are given, followed by the before and after values of the data items
        that have their values changed.

        The subprogram then returns to its caller, and the line number of the last line in the
        subprogram (20) is displayed along with the subprogram's name (SUBEX) and the
        identifier RETURN.

        MCFLAG
        You can dynamically control monitor output by explicitly setting and clearing a data
        item called MCFLAG. MCFLAG lets you selectively turn monitor output on and off
        during the execution of the program; you can produce monitor output for only the part
        of the program you are interested in.

        If MCFLAG has a nonzero value, all monitor output is displayed. If MCFLAG is zero, the
        monitor output is suppressed. It is your responsibility to ensure that the value of
        MCFLAG is properly set.

        You can explicitly define MCFLAG as follows:

          01 MCFLAG PIC 9(10) BINARY.

        If you explicitly define MCFLAG in a program containing nested subprograms, you
        must define it in the main program with the GLOBAL attribute in order for it to be used
        in the subprograms.

        If MCFLAG is present and not defined as shown, UCS COBOL issues a warning and
        monitor output cannot be suppressed by the use of MCFLAG.




2ΓÇô40                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                     Compiling Your Program




         If you do not explicitly define MCFLAG, and you specify the keyword option MONITOR
         or MONITOR/LABEL, the compiler implicitly defines MCFLAG. The compiler gives
         MCFLAG an initial value of 1 (monitor output is displayed).

         Effects of Using MONITOR and MONITOR/LABEL
         MONITOR and MONITOR/LABEL significantly increase the size of the object module
         produced. If the program I-bank becomes larger than 65,535, you must use the
         keyword option SEGCODE. In addition, it is recommended that you use the keyword
         option NO-OPTIM for the compilation of large programs (greater than 10,000 lines) to
         speed up compilation time.

OPTIM
         Format
             OPTIM
             OPTIM/GLOBAL
             OPTIM/LOCAL
             NO-OPTIM

         Default: OPTIM

         OPTIM, OPTIM/GLOBAL, and OPTIM/LOCAL increase the optimizations performed by
         LSS. These optimizations apply a series of transformations to an intermediate form of
         the program in an attempt to eliminate redundant operations and find the most
         efficient way of performing the operations that remain. Optimizations are optional for
         the following reasons:
         ∩é╖    Additional overhead in compilation cost
         ∩é╖    In the generated object code, some operations are moved away from the
              statements that use them, making it more difficult to use the PADS interactive
              debugging system. (Source code is not affected.)

         An example of such an effect is moving load and store operations out of loops. If
         variable X is modified within a loop, it can be kept in a register throughout the loop,
         returning its value to storage only at the end of the loop.

         In such cases, attempts to use PADS to display the value of X within the loop instead
         display the initial value of X and do not reflect any changes made within the loop.

         OPTIM should be used only for well-tested programs in a production environment
         when efficiency takes precedence over debugging capabilities.

         OPTIM/GLOBAL is equivalent to OPTIM.

         OPTIM/LOCAL causes LSS to perform a subset of the optimizations performed for
         OPTIM. The compiler gathers less information and performs optimizations only on
         blocks of straight-line code. (For example, no optimizations are performed between
         code preceding an IF statement and code controlled by the IF statement.) The
         compiler also does not recognize loops in the code and cannot move invariant
         calculations out of loops, as occurs for OPTIM.



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  2ΓÇô41
Compiling Your Program




        OPTIM/LOCAL has the following advantages:
        ∩é╖    For some programs, OPTIM requires a large amount of compilation-time overhead.
             OPTIM/LOCAL can reduce this overhead.
        ∩é╖    Code generated by OPTIM/LOCAL is generally more efficient than code generated
             by NO-OPTIM and less efficient than code generated by OPTIM and
             OPTIM/GLOBAL.

        NO-OPTIM causes optimization to be bypassed, producing code that is less efficient
        but easier to debug. Therefore, it is preferable during program development when
        debugging takes precedence over efficiency.

        The NO-OPTIM and TRANSFORM options are incompatible.

PARMCHECK
        Format
            PARMCHECK
            NO-PARMCHECK

        Default: NO-PARMCHECK

        PARMCHECK generates extra code to compare the number of parameters
        (arguments) existing in the called procedure to the number of parameters existing in
        the calling procedure. It issues a warning message when the number of parameters
        does not match.

        When the PARMCHECK option is used in conjunction with the COMPAT/ARGUMENTS
        option, extra code is generated to verify that each incoming parameter is word
        aligned. An error message is issued if a parameter is not word aligned.

        The extra code produced by PARMCHECK has a negative effect on compilation and
        execution performance. PARMCHECK is typically used for program development.

        NO-PARMCHECK suppresses parameter checking. It is typically used for production
        programs, after a program has been tested and debugged (using PARMCHECK).

REL18
        Format
            REL18
            NO-REL18

        Default: NO-REL18

        REL18 causes the code location counters in a compiled object module to be marked as
        having code offset 18 bit relocation, a relocation type introduced in system release
        6.0. NO-REL18 causes the code location counters to be marked as having code offset
        16 bit relocation. The relocation type indicates how the linker handles the relocation of
        JUMP instructions in the code.



2ΓÇô42                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                    Compiling Your Program




         The UCS compilers generate full 18-bit JUMPs, which means that a code location
         counter can be up to 262,144 words in size. When the REL18 option is used, the
         compilers can generate the more efficient bit-map relocation for the JUMPs. When
         the REL18 option is not used, the compilers must use a more general relocation
         mechanism called PCODE to do JUMP relocation since the code offset 16 bit
         mechanism can only handle 16-bit JUMPs. The PCODE mechanism takes more internal
         space in the object module, and a very large static link could even conceivably
         overflow the PCODE table in the resulting ZOOM or object module. Therefore, using
         the REL18 option can be more efficient, and may also prevent the overflow of internal
         tables within a large statically linked object module.

         Another benefit of using REL18 is that the static linker will merge the code banks to be
         after the code banks that result from MASM. (MASM code banks have a relocation
         type of code offset 16 bit, and generally cannot be linked at over 65,535 addresses.)
         This means that MASM object modules from the URTS Service Library (or user
         libraries) will be merged first, and should then not get the truncation errors that occur
         when they are linked at over 65,535. (HVTIP static links often have this problem.)

         Older linkers (prior to Link level 10R1) cannot process an object module having the
         code offset 18-bit relocation type, and for this reason, REL18 is currently not the
         default. You should not use the REL18 keyword option if the resulting object module
         may be used on a system with a Linking system earlier than level 10R1 (system
         release 6.0).

REORDER
         Format
           REORDER
           NO-REORDER

         Default: REORDER on CMOS systems
                  NO-REORDER on SAIL-based systems (EXTENDED/8)

         REORDER causes instruction reordering to be performed. Reordering improves
         program performance by rearranging instructions to better utilize the hardware.

         NO-REORDER suppresses instruction reordering.

         When NO-OPTIM is specified, no instruction reordering is performed unless REORDER
         is specified.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                2ΓÇô43
Compiling Your Program




RUNCHECK
        Format
            RUNCHECK
            NO-RUNCHECK

        Default: NO-RUNCHECK

        RUNCHECK generates extra code to test for the following error conditions and
        terminates program execution when an error condition exists:

        ∩é╖    Range checking for array element references
        ∩é╖    Range checking for reference modifications

        NO-RUNCHECK suppresses error testing.

        Specifying RUNCHECK with OPTIM causes a warning message because the
        restructuring of the program and elimination of statements by optimization can
        suppress the issuing of certain messages. A program compiled with NO-RUNCHECK
        usually runs faster and contains less object code than the same program compiled
        with RUNCHECK. However, it does not contain the advanced error detection
        mechanisms of RUNCHECK and should be used only in a production environment with
        a well-tested program.

SEGCODE
        Format
            SEGCODE
            NO-SEGCODE

        Default: NO-SEGCODE

        By default (NO-SEGCODE), the compiler generates one instruction bank (I-bank) for a
        compilation unit. The size of an I-bank produced by the compiler can be up to 262,143
        words. If you are using EXTENDED/0, EXTENDED/2, or EXTENDED/4 options to target
        your code for a non-XPA system, the size of an I-bank produced by the compiler can
        be up to 65,535 words.

        Non-XPA systems include all systems released before the 2200/900 such as the
        2200/600 and 2200/400. XPA systems include the 2200/900, 2200/500 and all
        subsequent systems. Be aware that Unisys no longer supports non-XPA systems.

        If you reach these limits, you can split the program into smaller, separate program
        units or use the SEGCODE option. The SEGCODE option causes the compiler to
        generate separate I-banks for each program unit group and selected program
        segments, up to a maximum of 99 I-banks. If you compile more than 99 program units
        or program segments, the compiler cycles back to the first I-bank and combines the
        generated code for additional program units or program segments into existing
        I-banks.




2ΓÇô44                                                                           7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                     Compiling Your Program




         The size of each I-bank produced by the compiler when the SEGCODE option is
         present can be up to 262,143 words, or 65,535 words if the EXTENDED/0,
         EXTENDED/2, or EXTENDED/4 keyword options are used.

         If you exceed these limits or the compiler is unable to logically divide a program into a
         code segment that is less than the limit, the compilation terminates in error. You must
         then break the compilation units into smaller units and recompile.

         You can use the Linking System to merge banks. The size of a merged I-bank
         produced by the Linking System can be 262,143 words when merging I-banks that
         were compiled with the SEGCODE option. A special LINK directive, SET
         MERGED_CODE_UL = 262143 is required when merging I-banks over 65,535 words.

         See the Linking System Programming Reference Manual for more information about
         merging banks.

SHIFT
         Format
           SHIFT
           NO-SHIFT

         Default: NO-SHIFT

         SHIFT allows kanji shift code images to be accepted as part of the source input. This
         option is required for programs having kanji symbolic names, kanji literals, or literals
         without the prefix cc.

         NO-SHIFT specifies that kanji shift code images are not part of the source input.

TIPMALLOC
         Formats
           TIPMALLOC
           NO-TIPMALLOC

         Default: NO-TIPMALLOC

         If needed, this option should only be used when compiling the main program.

         The primary purpose of the TIPMALLOC option is to prevent URTS$TABLES from
         expanding to its maximum upper limit in a transaction (TIP) environment, which will
         cause the transaction to create another URTS$TABLES bank and therefore lose its TIP
         sticking.

         This option should be used when a TIP transaction requires more than approximately
         164,000 words of UC memory allocation. Note that the memory allocation request can
         come from the transaction or any subsystem that the transaction calls.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 2ΓÇô45
Compiling Your Program




        This option should not be used if the program is going to execute in an HVTIP
        environment since other means are already in place to handle memory allocation (see
        the Pooled Banks clause of the OUTPUT HVTIP2 link statement in the Linking System
        Programming Reference Manual).

        Batch and demand runs acquire activity level banks dynamically as they are needed
        unless the TIPMALLOC option is specified. The UC malloc, calloc, or realloc functions
        obtain memory allocation from the TIPMALLOC$$$ bank. The TIPMALLOC$$$ bank is
        set to a maximum upper limit of 16,777,216 words with the current upper limit set to
        262,144 words. If memory allocation exceeds 262,144 words and you want to
        preserve TIP sticking, you must expand the current upper limit of the bank by adding
        the SET SIZE statement to your LINK after the RESOLVE statement. The form of the
        statement is SET SIZE = SIZE + xxxxx FOR TIPMALLOC$$$ (where xxxxx is the size
        you wish to expand the bank beyond 262,144 words).

        If the TIPMALLOC$ bank fills up to its limit of 16,777,216 words, the runtime system
        will allocate more banks as needed and allocate memory from them. NO-TIPMALLOC
        causes the UC malloc, calloc, or realloc memory allocation functions to acquire space
        from URTS$TABLES in a transaction (TIP) environment. The URTS$TABLES bank is a
        small bank and cannot be expanded above its maximum upper limit which is 262,144
        words. Once it fills up, another URTS$TABLES bank will be created. and TIP sticking
        will be lost.

TRANSFORM
        Format
          TRANSFORM
          NO-TRANSFORM

        Default: NO-TRANSFORM

        TRANSFORM performs some transformations that cause execution-time
        improvements but can also cause precision differences. For example, some division
        operations are transformed into multiplication with different results due to
        approximation of floating-point numbers.

        NO-TRANSFORM produces program results that are the same for both OPTIM and
        NO-OPTIM compilations.

        The TRANSFORM and NO-OPTIM options are incompatible.




2ΓÇô46                                                                           7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                   Compiling Your Program




UREP-XREF
         Format
             UREP-XREF
             NO-UREP-XREF

         Default: NO-UREP-XREF

         UREP-XREF causes cross-reference information to be stored into UREP. This
         information includes the relationship between the source program and the file names
         and data names that the program introduces with INVOKE or COPY statements. The
         values in the UREP entity UCS OPTIONS determine the type of cross-reference
         information that is stored. See Section 8 for more information.

         Use this option with programs that use the following:

         ∩é╖    INVOKE statements
         ∩é╖    COPY statements
         ∩é╖    Embedded SQL statements

         The keyword option APPLICATION specifies into which repository UREP-XREF stores
         cross-reference information for the UREP-XREF option.

         If you specify NO-UREP-XREF, cross-reference information is not stored into UREP.

URTS$TABLES
         Format
             URTS$TABLES/n

         Default: URTS$TABLES/0

         URTS$TABLES/n can be used to reserve an area in the URTS$TABLES heap bank for
         those things that must be in the same bank (I/O and SORT are the primary users of the
         same bank request). n is an octal number indicating the size (in words) of the reserved
         space. The default value of n is zero, the maximum value is 0500000, and the
         recommended value is 050000. If runtime error 37001 (attempt to expand
         URTS$TABLES beyond its maximum upper limit - all basic mode addressable space
         has been used) persists, try increasing the reserve in increments of 010000 until the
         error goes away. Note that the URTS$TABLES option is only effective when used on
         the compilation of the main program for your executable.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                              2ΓÇô47
Compiling Your Program




        URTS$TABLES is a small bank, and beginning with URTS level 12R1, once the bank is
        filled, another URTS$TABLES heap bank is created. This results in an open-ended size
        for this heavily used space. Several internal data structures are allocated in
        URTS$TABLES, some of which must be in the same bank, and some of which can be
        in different banks. Applications that use several concurrently opened files,
        multitasking, or sorts, may need more than one URTS$TABLES heap bank due to their
        aggregate size requirements. If your application requires more than one
        URTS$TABLES heap bank, this could result in a situation where everything that must
        be in the same bank does not fit in the same URTS$TABLES bank. If the memory
        manager cannot acquire the space from the URTS$TABLES bank that is required, the
        fatal runtime error 37001 (attempt to expand URTS$TABLES beyond its maximum
        upper limit - all basic mode addressable space has been used) is issued. This means
        you must use the URTS$TABLES option to reserve some ΓÇ£same-bankΓÇ¥ space for
        these requests.

        Note: Once a second bank is dynamically acquired, it prevents Checkpoint/Restart
        from working and inhibits TIP sticking for transactions. The default reserve area in
        URTS$TABLES is set to zero to prevent applications from suddenly needing a
        second URTS$TABLES heap bank due to the reserve area. For HVTIP, if a large
        enough pooled bank is available, it is acquired rather than creating a new bank;
        therefore sticking is not inhibited.

        XML/name

        Format

        XML/name
        NO-XML

        Default: NO-XML

        The XML/name keyword option invokes the COBOL to XML (Extensible Markup
        Language) generation tool. The primary purpose of the COBOL to XML generation tool
        is to produce an XML description of a COBOL record layout (sometimes referred to as
        an ΓÇ£01 record layoutΓÇ¥). The XML/name option causes the compiler to create an XML
        document that describes the layout of one or more data records that are defined in
        the program.

        In order to use the XML/name option, a text file must first be created that contains
        one or more 01 data record names that are defined in the COBOL program. This file
        must be placed into the CIFS current working directory (cwd). The name of this file is
        specified in the name portion of the XML/name option. There is one data record per
        line in this text file. In addition to the data record name, each line may contain the CIFS
        location and name of where the resulting XML file (.xsd) will be placed. See Section 18
        XML Generator for additional details of how to create an XML file. An example of the
        contents of this file is as follows:

        cobrec1
        cobrec2 /os2200/bek/xmlwork/xyz
        cobrec3 xmlfile/abc




2ΓÇô48                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                        Compiling Your Program




         In this example, .xsd files for the COBOL record names cobrec1, cobrec2 and cobrec3
         will be generated. Since no CIFS path was specified for cobrec1, by default, the file
         cobrec1.xsd will be placed into the CIFS current working directory. The record name
         cobrec2 has an absolute CIFS path associated with it so, the file xyz.xsd will be
         created in the CIFS path /os2200/bek/xmlwork and will contain the information for the
         COBOL record cobrec2. The record name cobrec3 has a relative CIFS path associated
         with it, so the file abc.xsd will be created and placed into the CIFS current working
         directory in the path xmlfile.

         If the file specified above was given the name recordnames and placed into the CIFS
         current working directory, it can be used in the compilation as follows:

         @ucob qual*file.cobolprog,om,,,XML/recordnames

         The compiler will find the recordnames file in the CIFS current working directory and
         will create the three .xsd files in the specified CIFS locations.

         You must ensure that the CIFS cwd of the run doing the compilations is not at the
         OS 2200 qualifier level. The .xsd extension is applied to the XML files that are created
         and extensions cannot be used on OS 2200 file names. The CIFS cwd should be set to
         either an OS 2200 program file or the CIFS directory created by CIFSUT. The default
         CIFS cwd is the qualifier for the run and that will not allow for the generation of an .xsd
         XML file.

         For additional information about creating XML files, see Section 18 XML File
         Generation.

          Format

            NO-IR-DIFF

          IR-DIFF issues remark messages each time the intermediate result in an arithmetic
          expression assumes maximum precision. Calculations on the intermediate result are
          then performed in floating point. Thus, the higher accuracy of UCS COBOL produces
          results that may differ from the results of the same calculation in ASCII COBOL.
          IR-DIFF also sets the REMARK option.

          NO-IRR-DIFF suppresses remark messages for results that may differ when using
          ASCII COBOL.

2.3. Composition of a Compiler Listing
         When you compile your program, you receive a listing describing the compilation. This
         listing is sent to your terminal or print file, depending on your execution mode, for
         example, demand mode, batch mode, or demand mode controlled by a @BRKPT
         statement.

         A compiler listing is actually composed of many separate listings. Using compiler
         keyword options or letter options, you can control which listings are produced and
         how detailed the listings are. By default, the sign-on line, bank sizes line, and sign-off
         line are produced. (The options listing is produced by default if you are executing in
         batch mode or demand mode controlled by a @BRKPT statement.)

         The following subsections describe the components of a compiler listing. Table 2ΓÇô9
         lists each component, the keyword option that creates it (if applicable), and the
         subsection you can reference for its description.


                               Table 2ΓÇô9. Composition of a Compiler Listing


            Listing Component                     Keyword Option                       Reference

          Sign-on line                SIGNON                                       2.3.1
          Options Listing             OPTIONS                                      2.3.2
          Diagnostic messages         WARNING, REMARK, LEVEL (error messages       2.3.3
                                      always generated)
          Source Listing              SOURCE                                       2.3.4
          Tracecopy Listing           TRACECOPY                                    2.3.5
          Allocation Listing          ALLOC                                        2.3.6
          Cross-Reference Listing     XREF, SHORT-REF                              2.3.7
          Object Code Listing         OBJECT, OBJECT-ONLY, OBJ-PKT                 2.3.8
          Linker Information          LINKINFO                                     2.3.9
          Listing
          Bank sizes line             SIGNON                                       2.3.10
          Sign-off line               SIGNON                                       2.3.11


         The compiler listing is 79 characters wide when you specify the NARROW keyword
         option and 132 characters wide when you specify the WIDE keyword option (see Table
         2ΓÇô6).




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                   2ΓÇô53
Compiling Your Program




        Several listings generated by the compiler (for example, the Allocation Listing,
        Cross-Reference Listing, and Object Code Listing) have headings generated on each
        page when you generate the listings in breakpoint (@BRKPT) mode. The compiler uses
        the system print file defaults to determine where to insert the headings in the listings.
        If the print file is to be printed on a printer that has a page size different from the
        system default page size, you can override these defaults through the use of the
        @HDG command. For example:

          @HDG        heading-text.M,length,top,bottom,lpi

        For information on the @HDG statement, see the ECL End Use and Programming
        Reference Manual.

2.3.1. Sign-On Line
        The system prints the sign-on line at the beginning of each compiler listing,
        immediately after the compiler call. It is produced by the SIGNON keyword option.
        (SIGNON is the default.)

        Example
          UCOB- 12R2 / EM (131127) LSS- 14R4 / EM (131126) 2014 Jul 01 1139:13

        Format
          UCOB- ssRii/genid1 (yymmdd) LSS- lssRii/genid2 (yymmdd) yyyy mmm dd hhmm:ss

        where:

        UCOB-

            identifies the UCS COBOL compiler that performs the compilation.

        ssRii

            is the level number of the compiler, where:
            ∩é╖     ss is the symbolic update number.
            ∩é╖     ii is the incremental update number. A letter after ii can be included to indicate
                  minor modifications to the release level.

        /genid1

            is the COMUS generation identifier, up to 12 characters long. It is present only if a
            COMUS generation of UCS COBOL has been done at your site.

        (yymmdd)

            is the year, month, and day UCS COBOL was created by the development center
            or generated by the user site.




2ΓÇô54                                                                                7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                       Compiling Your Program




         LSS-

             stands for the Language Support System. It is the back-end code generator that
             creates the object module.

         lssRii

             is the level number of LSS, where:

             ∩é╖     lss is the symbolic update number.
             ∩é╖     ii is the incremental update number. A letter after ii can be included to indicate
                   minor modifications to the release level.

         /genid2

             is the COMUS generation identifier, up to 12 characters long. It is present only if a
             COMUS generation of LSS has been done at your site.

         (yymmdd)

             is the year, month, and day LSS was created by the development center or
             generated by the user site.

         yyyy mmm dd

             is the year, month, and day the compilation occurs.

         hhmm:ss

             is the hour, minute, and second the compilation begins.

         The Options Listing follows the sign-on line. It is created by the OPTIONS keyword
         option. The Options Listing displays the compiler keyword options in effect for this
         compilation.

           NO-OBJECT, NO-OBJ-PKT, OPTIM, OPTIONS, NO-PARMCHECK, NO-REMARK,
           REORDER, NO-RUNCHECK, SEARCH-PF-SI, NO-SEGCODE, NO-SHIFT, SIGNON,
           NO-SOURCE, NO-TRACECOPY, NO-TRACEMSG, NO-TRANSFORM, NO-UREP-XREF,
           WARNING, NARROW, NO-XREF

2.3.3. Diagnostic Messages
        The compiler may print diagnostic messages informing you of errors or other
        noteworthy conditions relating to your program or its compilation. The following types
        of messages exist:

        ∩é╖   Error messages
        ∩é╖   Warning messages (includes level messages indicating conformance to language
            standards)
        ∩é╖   Remark messages

        The compiler displays messages according to the following rules:

        ∩é╖   The compiler always displays error messages; there is no keyword or letter option
            to suppress printing of error messages.
        ∩é╖   The compiler displays warning messages if you use the keyword option
            WARNING (which is the default value) or a LEVEL keyword option.
        ∩é╖   The compiler displays remark messages if you use the keyword option REMARK.

        The letter option E also displays warning and remark messages.

        The location of diagnostic messages depends on whether or not you have specified
        production of the Source Listing (SOURCE keyword option or S letter option):

        ∩é╖   If you have specified production of the Source Listing, messages appear in the
            Source Listing, on a line preceding the source line to which they apply.
        ∩é╖   If you have not specified production of the Source Listing, messages appear
            following the Options Listing. (The source line causing the error is also printed.)

        See Appendix A and Appendix B for more information on diagnostic messages,
        including

        ∩é╖   Definitions of message types
        ∩é╖   Information on message subclasses (major, minor, internal, and so forth)
        ∩é╖   A list of all messages and, where appropriate, descriptions of particular messages

2.3.4. Source Listing
        The Source Listing primarily displays your programΓÇÖs source statements. It is produced
        by the SOURCE keyword option. (NO-SOURCE is the default.) When the WIDE
        keyword option is in effect, the Source Listing consists of the following fields:

        ∩é╖   Line number
        ∩é╖   Procedure nesting level number
        ∩é╖   Source lines




2ΓÇô56                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                         Compiling Your Program




           When the NARROW keyword option is in effect, the Source Listing consists of the
           following fields:

           ∩é╖   Line number
           ∩é╖   Source lines

           Fields of the Source Listing
           Line number

               A line number appears in column 1 for each line of source text. If the source input
               element contains CTS or IPF 1100 line numbers, these line numbers appear.
               Otherwise, the compiler uses sequential line numbers (1, 2, 3...).

               If the number is too large to fit in the allotted space, it is printed on a separate line
               preceding the source line.

           Procedure nesting level number

               This field helps you recognize different levels of subprograms. The main program
               is always level 1. This field appears on the line for the Identification Division and all
               lines in the Procedure Division.

           Source lines

               This field displays your programΓÇÖs source statements. If a source line exceeds the
               length of an output line, the compiler prints the remainder of the source line on
               the next line.

               If something in your program is incorrect or noteworthy, the compiler issues an
               error, warning, or remark message informing you (see 2.3.3). If the Source Listing
               is created, such messages appear in the source lines field.

           Examples

      12                                 PRINTER IS PRT.
      13                              INPUT-OUTPUT SECTION.
      14                              FILE-CONTROL.
      15                                 SELECT CARD-FILE ASSIGN TO CARD-READER.

2.3.5. Tracecopy Listing
        The Tracecopy Listing lists the locations of COPY files found during a compilation. The
        location of the Tracecopy Listing line depends on whether or not you have specified
        production of the Source Listing with either the SOURCE keyword option or the S
        letter option.

        If you have specified production of the Source Listing, each Tracecopy Listing line
        appears in the Source Listing on a line preceding the source line to which it applies. If
        you have not specified production of the Source Listing, Tracecopy Listing lines appear
        following the Options Listing.

        Format
            qual*file.elt (proc-name)

        where:

        qual*file.elt

                identifies the name of the element that contains a PROC specified by the COPY
                statement.

        proc-name

                is the name of the PROC specified by the COPY statement.

        Example 2ΓÇô4 shows a Tracecopy Listing when the source code is being produced.

            1                 IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
            2                 PROGRAM-ID. EXAMPLE-PROGRAM.
            3                 PROCEDURE DIVISION.
            4                 PP.



            QUAL*FILE.PROC (MYCOBPROC)
            5                 COPY MYCOBPROC.
            5.C1.2       * This comment is brought into the program via a COPY
            5.C1.3       * statement. The file from which it came is listed above
            5.C1.4       * as the result of using the keyword option TRACECOPY.
            6                 STOP RUN.

                              Example 2ΓÇô4. Tracecopy Listing

2.3.6. Allocation Listing
        The Allocation Listing gives storage information about

        ∩é╖       Variables
        ∩é╖       Labels




2ΓÇô60                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                       Compiling Your Program




         The listing is composed of machine-dependent information. Items described on the
         listing are presented according to the order of their allocation. Within structures,
         subitems are presented according to the order in which they occur in the source input.
         This ordering scheme is most useful for interpreting dumps.

         The compiler generates a single listing for all program units. This listing shows only
         variables for which the compiler has actually allocated storage.

         The Allocation Listing is produced by the ALLOC keyword options. (NO-ALLOC is the
         default.) It consists of the following fields:

         ∩é╖   NAME
         ∩é╖   DECLARED
         ∩é╖   ST/LC
         ∩é╖   OFFSET
         ∩é╖   SB
         ∩é╖   SIZE
         ∩é╖   MACH TYPE
         ∩é╖   DM
         ∩é╖   SPAN SIZE
         ∩é╖   LV
         ∩é╖   ATTRIBUTES

         Fields of the Allocation Listing
         NAME

             This field contains the name of the item defined in the source program. If the
             name is longer than the allotted space, it appears alone on the line; the remainder
             of the information is on the next line.

         DECLARED

             This field contains the line number of the definition of the data item. If the line
             number extends past the end of the field, the next field begins in the appropriate
             position on the next line.
         ST/LC

             This field contains one of the following for the item:
             ∩é╖    Storage type
                  If the itemΓÇÖs storage is dynamically allocated (created at run time), the listing
                  specifies the type of storage containing the item. Possible values are
                  ∩Ç¡   BASED (dynamically allocated storage)
                  ∩Ç¡   AUTO (automatically allocated storage)



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                    2ΓÇô61
Compiling Your Program




                 ∩Ç¡   TEMP (temporary storage)
                 ∩Ç¡   PARM (the item is a parameter for a call)
                 ∩Ç¡   RETURN (the item is a return value from a call)
             ∩é╖   Logical bank number (location counter)
                 If the itemΓÇÖs storage is statically allocated (created at compilation), the listing
                 specifies the logical bank number containing the item.

        OFFSET

             This field identifies where the item is located within the logical bank or
             dynamically-allocated storage described in the ST/LC field. This field contains the
             relative word offset (in octal) of the item within the location counter or
             dynamically-allocated storage.

        SB

             SB stands for ΓÇ£starting bit.ΓÇ¥ This field identifies the number of the bit where the
             itemΓÇÖs storage begins in the word indicated by the OFFSET field. Numbers are
             decimal values and are numbered left to right within a word, beginning with bit
             zero.

        SIZE

             This field contains the itemΓÇÖs storage size in bits (BIT), bytes (BYT), or words
             (WRD). For arrays, only the size of an individual element appears.

        MACH TYPE

             This field contains an abbreviation of the itemΓÇÖs machine type. The machine type
             reflects the internal storage representation of the data. Meanings for most
             abbreviations are self explanatory, for example:
             ∩é╖   CHR_STR means character string.
             ∩é╖   CMN_BLK means common block.
             ∩é╖   BIN_S means binary signed.
             ∩é╖   BFLOT_S means floating binary signed.
        DM

             This field identifies which dimension of an array is being described in the SPAN
             SIZE field. A 1 means the first dimension is being described; a 2 means the second,
             and so forth.

             Each dimension is described on a separate line. If the item is not an array, this field
             is blank.




2ΓÇô62                                                                                  7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                           Compiling Your Program




         SPAN SIZE

              This field contains the amount of internal storage space from the beginning of one
              occurrence of an item to the next occurrence, for the array dimension specified in
              the DM field. That is, it tells how far away in storage is the next array cell, if you
              increment the dimension (specified in the DM field) by one.

              Size is described in one of the following ways:

              ∩é╖   Number of bits (BIT), bytes (BYT), or words (WRD)
              ∩é╖   EXPR (meaning the size is determined by an expression)
              ∩é╖   UNKNOWN (meaning the compiler cannot determine the size)

              Filler bits are included in the size. If the item is not an array, this field is blank.

         LV

              This field contains the logical structure level of a data item:

              ∩é╖   For the most inclusive group items, this field contains a 1. The next most
                  inclusive group (or elementary) items receive a 2 in this field, and so forth.
              ∩é╖   For level 01 elementary items or level 77 items, this field contains SC (meaning
                  scalar).

         ATTRIBUTES

              This field contains declaration information specific to COBOL, such as the
              procedure name and data attributes as expressed by the COBOL language.

              If the information does not fit in this field, it is printed in the same columns of the
              next line. This field appears only when the WIDE keyword option is in effect.

        ∩é╖    If the name is longer than the allotted space, it appears alone on the line; the

2.3.7. Cross-Reference Listing
         The Cross-Reference Listing lets you examine

         ∩é╖   Where identifiers are referenced in your program
         ∩é╖   The nature of the storage containing the identifiers

         It displays all references in your source program to the following items:

         ∩é╖   Statement labels
         ∩é╖   Subprograms
         ∩é╖   Data items

         The Cross-Reference Listing lists them alphabetically. The compiler generates a single
         Cross-Reference Listing for all program units.

         The Cross-Reference Listing is produced by the XREF or SHORT-XREF keyword
         options. (NO-XREF is the default.) It consists of the following fields (which appear with
         both the NARROW and WIDE keyword options):

         ∩é╖   NAME
         ∩é╖   ST/LC
         ∩é╖   OFFSET
         ∩é╖   SB
         ∩é╖   SIZE
         ∩é╖   ATTRIBUTES

         Fields of the Cross-Reference Listing
         NAME

             This field contains the name of the item being cross-referenced. If the name is
             longer than the allotted space, it appears alone on the line; the remainder of the
             information is on the next line.

             Printed beneath the name are the following:

             ∩é╖    DCL
                  DCL stands for ΓÇ£declared.ΓÇ¥ This entry indicates line numbers in the program
                  where the item is declared.
             ∩é╖    SET
                  This entry indicates line numbers where there is a reference that initializes or
                  changes the contents of the item.
                  A label is marked SET when it is used to prefix a statement.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 2ΓÇô65
Compiling Your Program




             ∩é╖   USED
                 This entry indicates line numbers where there is a reference that does not
                 initialize or change the contents of the item.
        ST/LC

             This field contains one of the following for the item:

             ∩é╖   Storage type
                 If the itemΓÇÖs storage is dynamically allocated (created at run time), the listing
                 specifies the type of storage containing the item. Possible values are
                 ∩Ç¡   BASED (dynamically allocated storage)
                 ∩Ç¡   AUTO (automatically allocated storage)
                 ∩Ç¡   TEMP (temporary storage)
                 ∩Ç¡   PARM (the item is a parameter for a call)
                 ∩Ç¡   RETURN (the item is a return value from a call)
             ∩é╖   Logical bank number (location counter)
                 If the itemΓÇÖs storage is statically allocated (created at compilation), the listing
                 specifies the logical bank number containing the item.

        OFFSET

             This field identifies where the item is located within the logical bank or
             dynamically-allocated storage described in the ST/LC field. This field contains the
             relative word offset (in octal) of the item within the location counter or
             dynamically-allocated storage.

        SB

             SB stands for ΓÇ£starting bit.ΓÇ¥ This field identifies the number of the bit where the
             itemΓÇÖs storage begins in the word indicated by the OFFSET field. Numbers are

             ∩é╖   Decimal values
             ∩é╖   Numbered left to right within a word, beginning with bit zero

        SIZE

             This field contains the itemΓÇÖs storage size in bits (BIT), bytes (BYT), or words
             (WRD). For arrays, only the size of an individual element appears.

        ATTRIBUTES

             This field contains declaration information.

             If the information exceeds the length of the line, the excess is printed on the next
             line in the same columns.




2ΓÇô66                                                                                  7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                               Compiling Your Program




         The same Cross-Reference Listing fields appear with the NARROW and WIDE
         keyword options. The NARROW and WIDE keyword options use the same rules for
         overflow of each field. Some fields are narrower with NARROW, however. The DCL,
         SET, and USED line numbers are displayed in the same manner for both keyword
         options.
         Examples
         Example 2ΓÇô6 shows a Cross-Reference Listing with the NARROW keyword option in
         effect.
         C R O S S    R E F E R E N C E       L I S T I N G

         NAME           ST/LC   OFFSET SB             SIZE    ATTRIBUTE
         ALL-DONE           1 00001124 0                      PROCEDURE NAME
               DCL 46
               USED 42
         BEGIN              1 00001045 0                      PROCEDURE NAME
               DCL 38
         CARD-FILE          0 00000012 0             23WRD    FILE NAME
               DCL 19
               USED 15        39        42            47
         CARD-IMAGE    BASED 00000000 0              20WRD    DATA NAME IN FILE SECTION
