2.3.8. Object Code Listing
        The Object Code Listing shows prologue, procedure, and epilogue object code
        (machine--level code) generated by the compiler. The code is shown in octal and
        mnemonic (symbolic) form. This listing is designed to look like an assembly code
        listing.

        The following keyword options control printing of the Object Code Listing:

        ∩é╖   OBJECT or OBJECT-ONLY
        ∩é╖   OBJ-PKT

OBJECT or OBJECT-ONLY Keyword Options
        The Object Code Listing as a whole is produced by the OBJECT or OBJECT-ONLY
        keyword options. (NO-OBJECT is the default.) If you specify OBJECT-ONLY, the listing
        does not contain the programΓÇÖs source statements.

        An Object Code Listing is composed of the following fields:

        ∩é╖   RELATIVE ADDRESS
        ∩é╖   INSTRUCTION SUBFIELDS (F,J,A,X,H,I,B,D)
        ∩é╖   D FLD LC
        ∩é╖   LABEL
        ∩é╖   SYMBOLIC INSTRUCTION (F,J,A,U,X,B)
        ∩é╖   SKELETON NUMBER
        ∩é╖   ACTIVE PROCEDURE

        Fields of the Object Code Listing
        RELATIVE ADDRESS

            This field gives the octal address of the instruction or data word, relative to the
            beginning of the current location counter.

        INSTRUCTION SUBFIELDS

            This field gives the contents of the instruction word, in instruction format. Each
            subfield (F,J,A,X,H,I,B,D) is printed in octal. For data words, this field is printed as a
            single 12-digit octal value preceded by ΓÇ£+ΓÇ¥.




2ΓÇô68                                                                                  7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                      Compiling Your Program




            For a complete description of all of the subfields of instruction format, refer to the
            AIM Programming Reference Manual.

         D FLD LC

            This field gives the following Relocation information:

            ∩é╖    R means the instruction needs relocation by the Linking System.
            ∩é╖    X means the instruction is an external reference requiring resolution by the
                 Linking System.
            ∩é╖    The location counter of the D subfield. It is represented without the usual
                 parentheses and $. For example, $(1) appears as 1.

         LABEL

            This field gives one of the following:

            ∩é╖    The label name used by another instruction to refer to the current instruction
            ∩é╖    The location counter of the instruction itself (for example, $(1))

         SYMBOLIC INSTRUCTION

            This field gives the instruction in mnemonic form as it might appear in an assembly
            language program. Symbolic names for user variables are shown in the mnemonic
            code as follows:

            ∩é╖    ASCII characters are shown in the mnemonic code when the program uses
                 constants.
            ∩é╖    The mnemonic form is separated into instruction format for instructions,
                 parameter format for parameters, and so on. For a complete description of all
                 of the subfields of instruction format, refer to the AIM Programming
                 Reference Manual.
            ∩é╖    Unless you specify OBJECT-ONLY, source lines and line numbers are
                 interspersed in the appropriate place within the listing.
            ∩é╖    Source lines and line numbers corresponding to object code moved for
                 optimization or other reasons are displayed with the moved code.

         SKELETON NUMBER

            This field gives the number of the code generation template used to create the
            sequence of instructions that begins with this instruction. This information is used
            by Unisys for debugging purposes. It is not useful to you.

         ACTIVE PROCEDURE

            This field gives the name of the program, compilation unit, procedure, or function
            that corresponds to this instruction. This information is provided only when the
            WIDE keyword option is in effect.

Compiling Your Program




         If the NARROW keyword option is in effect, the Object Code Listing has the same
         format as with the WIDE keyword option, except for the following:

         ∩é╖    The name of the active procedure is not printed.
         ∩é╖    The listing is compressed.
         ∩é╖    The D FLD LC and LABEL fields are combined into a single field called LC/LABEL.
         ∩é╖    Labels are displayed on a separate line.
         ∩é╖    Variable names in the SYMBOLIC INSTRUCTION field may be truncated.
         ∩é╖    Line numbers and source lines that exceed their field sizes are displayed on
              multiple lines.

OBJ-PKT Keyword Option
         If you use the OBJECT or OBJECT-ONLY keyword options, you can also use the
         OBJ-PKT keyword option. (NO-OBJ-PKT is the default.) The OBJ-PKT keyword option
         produces a more complete Object Code Listing by printing additional information for
         I/O packets, parameter packets, and array descriptors. The following example shows a
         line on the Object Code Listing produced by specifying OBJ-PKT.

         Example
             000007       000000000030          R    0     Input/Output Packet
             INPUT

2.3.9. Linker Information Listing
         The Linker Information Listing specifies linker information for the object module. It is
         produced by the LINKINFO keyword option. (LINKINFO is the default if you have
         specified OBJECT or OBJECT-ONLY.) The compiler produces a Linker Information
         Listing for each object module produced.

         A Linker Information Listing is composed of the following sections:

         ∩é╖    HEADER
         ∩é╖    EXTERNAL REFERENCES
         ∩é╖    EXTERNAL DEFINITIONS
         ∩é╖    COMMON BLOCKS
         ∩é╖    ALS INFORMATION
         ∩é╖    LOGICAL BANK

         HEADER Section
         The header specifies the

         ∩é╖    Object module name
         ∩é╖    Bank group name for this compilation

         Bank group names are created by appending the suffix $ to the object module name.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 2ΓÇô71
Compiling Your Program




        EXTERNAL REFERENCES Section
        This section lists the names of all external references (calls) made in the object
        module. Only the first 12 characters of the names are printed. Typical UCS object
        modules contain external references to the following, in addition to references to user
        subprograms:

        ∩é╖   Entry points with the prefix RTS$, which are UCS Runtime System entry points
        ∩é╖   TCA$$$, a UCS Runtime System entry point for the task control area

        EXTERNAL DEFINITIONS Section
        This section lists all external definitions (entry points) contained in the object module
        and their addresses. Each entry starts on a new line and has four subfields when the
        NARROW option is in effect. If the WIDE option is used, the entries contain the fifth
        field ΓÇÖLINE NUMBERΓÇÖ. External definitions include

        ∩é╖   Internal Name
            This is the entry point name as defined in the source program. It is truncated at 32
            characters.
        ∩é╖   External Name
            This is the entry point name used for LINK resolution.
        ∩é╖   LC
            This is the location counter of the defined entry point.
        ∩é╖   Offset
            This is the address of the definition, relative to the start of the given location
            counter.
        ∩é╖   Line Number
            This is the line number in the source program where the definition occurred. It is
            truncated at 53 characters.

        COMMON BLOCKS Section
        This section lists all common blocks contained in the object module. Each entry starts
        on a new line and has two subfields:

        ∩é╖   Common block name
            ∩Ç¡    All EXTERNAL user names appear in this section.
            ∩Ç¡    All names listed in the COMMON-STORAGE section appear under the single
                 name $BLANK$COMMON$.
        ∩é╖   Logical bank number of the bank containing the common block




2ΓÇô72                                                                                7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                      Compiling Your Program




         ALS INFORMATION Section
         This section lists the sizes of the activity-local stack (ALS) for each procedure in the
         source program. Each new entry starts on a new line and has the following three
         subfields:

         ∩é╖   Internal name
             The procedure name found in the source program.
         ∩é╖   External name
             The EXTERNAL name of the procedure used for linker resolution.
         ∩é╖   Size
             The number of words needed for the procedureΓÇÖs ALS.

         LOGICAL BANK Section
         This section describes the logical banks created by the compilation. It includes the
         following subfields:

         ∩é╖   Logical bank name
             Logical bank names are created by appending the logical bank number as a suffix
             to the bank group name.
         ∩é╖   Location counter number allocated for the bank
             This is the same as the logical bank number.
         ∩é╖   Size
             This gives the size of the bank in words, in both octal and decimal values.
             The compiler allocates one extra word for each common block and each data bank
             declared in the program. This permits the compiler to generate more efficient
             coding sequences in some cases. Thus the size of the common storage is larger
             than both of the following:
             ∩Ç¡   The size of the corresponding common block declared in the program
             ∩Ç¡   The size of the corresponding common block in the Allocation and
                 Cross-Reference Listings
         ∩é╖   Bank Type
             Bank types are code, data, link vector, and so forth. See the Linking System
             Programming Reference Manual for all possible values.
         ∩é╖   Bank Mode
             Bank modes are features such as EM (extended mode). See the Linking System
             Programming Reference Manual for all possible values.
         ∩é╖   Storage Class
             This gives the type of storage the bank is loaded into. MSU means ordinary main
             storage. See the Linking System Programming Reference Manual for all possible
             values.

2.3.10. Bank Sizes Line
         The bank sizes line precedes the sign-off line. It is produced by the SIGNON keyword
         option (SIGNON is the default). The bank sizes line

         ∩é╖    Lists storage usage
         ∩é╖    Identifies the class of machine for which the compiled code has been generated
         Example
             SIZES       CODE(EM2):   117 DATA:   153

         Format
             SIZES: CODE(m):      x   DATA:   y   COMMON:      z

         where:

         m

              represents the mode of the code bank (I-bank). This appears in the form
              EMn

              This means extended mode, where n is a value representing the class of machine
              for which the compiled code has been generated.

              Possible values for n are:


                         Value                       Machine

                     0           Any extended mode machine (generic)
                     2           1100/90, 2200/400, or 2200/600 system
                     4           2200/100 or 2200/200 system
                     6           2200/XPA machine (CMOS systems)
                     8           4000 system and above (SAIL-based systems)
         x

              is the number of words of storage used in the code bank for this mode.

         y

              is the number of words of storage used in the data banks, including link vectors.

         z

              is the number of words of storage used in common blocks. This field only appears
              if your program contains common blocks.
              The compiler allocates one extra word for each common block and each data bank
              declared in the program.



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               2ΓÇô75
Compiling Your Program




2.3.11. Sign-Off Line
        The system prints the sign-off line at the end of each compiler listing. It is produced by
        the SIGNON keyword option. (SIGNON is the default.)

        Example
              END UCOB- 0 ERRORS(MAJOR) 1 ERROR(MINOR) 1 WARNING(USAGE) 1
              WARNING(LEVEL)

        Note: Specific level numbers and dates in the example can differ from the ones at
        your site.

        Format
              END UCOB- n class(subclass)...

        where:

        END UCOB-

               identifies the end of the UCS COBOL compilation.

        n

               is the number of errors or messages for each subclass.

        class

               is the type of error or message: ERROR, WARNING, or REMARK. (See Appendix A
               for descriptions of these types.) If there are no WARNING or REMARK messages,
               no message count appears for that class. The count of WARNING and REMARK
               messages appears even if NO-WARNING and NO-REMARK keyword options
               suppress printing of the messages.

        (subclass)

               is the severity of the error or message: MAJOR, MINOR, USAGE, or LEVEL. (See
               Appendix A for descriptions of these severity types.)

        ...

               means that more than one n class(subclass) group may appear.

2.4. Separate Compilations for a Single Source
     Element (Back-to-Back COBOL Programs)
         Under the new COBOL standard, it is possible for you to pass to the compiler, in one
         source element, a set of separate COBOL programs. The compiler does not determine
         their existence until COPY, REPLACING and the REPLACE directives are resolved,
         which can actually change the position at which separate programs begin and end.

         If the source element (after COPY and REPLACE) looks like this:

           IDENTIFICATION DIVISION
           PROGRAM-ID. A.
              .
              .
              .
           IDENTIFICATION DIVISION
           PROGRAM-ID. B.
              .
              .
              .
           END PROGRAM B.
           END PROGRAM A.

         then program B is nested within program A. The entire source element is considered
         to be one compilation unit. If the source element looks like this:

           IDENTIFICATION DIVISION
           PROGRAM-ID. A.
              .
              .
              .
           END PROGRAM A.
           IDENTIFICATION DIVISION
           PROGRAM-ID. B.
              .
              .
              .
           END PROGRAM B.

         then program A and program B are considered to be separate programs. This means
         there are separate object modules and separate listings for each compilation, with no
         relationship between a definition of an identifier in one program and a reference in
         another, and so forth. The options on the processor call and default options will be the
         same for all compilations, but a new naming convention must be defined since there is
         only one RO field for n object modules. The first program will use the RO field,
         including any version specified; subsequent programs use the element name specified
         in the RO field, with a version ΓÇ£$$$$nn,ΓÇ¥ where nn is incremented by one for each
         separate compile from one up to a maximum of 999.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               2ΓÇô77
Compiling Your Program




         The sign-on line with the newly created object module name, the options in effect (if
         requested), and a separate sign-off line will be displayed for each program. The final
         sign-off line is the same as the sign-off line when there is one compilation per source
         element. The diagnostic totals are for the entire source element. The SIZE information
         will follow each separate compilation sign-off line.

         The separate compilation sign-off line is produced by the SIGNON keyword. (SIGNON
         is the default.) The separate compilation sign-off line is as follows:

         ∩é╖   After first separate compilation
               **OBJECT MODULE ro-name/version GENERATED

         ∩é╖   After second separate compilation
               **OBJECT MODULE ro-name/$$$$1 GENERATED

         ∩é╖   After MAJOR errors in a separate compile with the ERRCHECK option, with
             STD-ERRCHECK and WARNING-LEVEL errors in a separate compilation, or if there
             are any MAJOR errors in tokenization (for example, a missing copy).
               **NO OBJECT MODULE GENERATED

2.4.2. Execution of the Object Modules Produced
         The following example shows the execution statements to execute the preceding
         programs, and the output from them.

           @XQT OM
           *
           XQT OF SEPARATE MAIN PROGRAM MAIN1
           *
           SEPARATE PROGRAM MAIN1 XQTED AS A MAIN PROGRAM
              ELSE THIS IS A FAILURE
           *
           @XQT OM/$$$$1
           *
           MAIN PROGRAM MAIN2 CALLING SUBPROGRAM SUB2
           *
           SUBPROGRAM SUB2 CALLING SEPARATE SUBPROGRAM SUB1
           BECAUSE NESTED SUBPROGRAM SUB1 IS NOT ACCESSIBLE TO SUB2
           *
           SEPARATE PROGRAM MAIN1 CALLED AS SUBPROGRAM SUB1
           *
           MAIN PROGRAM MAIN2 CALLING NESTED SUBPROGRAM SUB1
           *
           ENTRY TO NESTED SUBPROGRAM SUB1

2.5. Using the Run-Condition Word to Detect
     Compilation Errors
         The run-condition word is established by the Executive system. You can use it to
         determine whether your program had severe errors during compilation. This can be
         useful in a batch environment to stop the runstream if a previous step contained this
         type of error.

         The compiler uses bit 9 (numbering from bit 1 on the left) of the run-condition word to
         mean this compilation has an error of subclass MAJOR, FATAL, or INTERNAL. The
         compiler sets bit 9 to 1 at the beginning of the compilation. If it does not detect any of
         these errors during compilation, it sets bit 9 to zero, just before termination. You can
         test the value of this bit when the compilation ends.

         The compiler also uses bit 8 of the run-condition word to mean that some previous
         task in this runstream set bit 9. At the beginning of the compilation, the compiler sets
         bit 8 if either bit 8 or 9 is already set. It then sets bit 9 for this compilation and
         proceeds as in the previous paragraph.

         For more information on the run-condition word, refer to Section 10 and the ER
         Programming Reference Manual.

3.1. Linking Your Program
         Linking is the process of converting a program from the form produced by a compiler
         or assembler into a form that computer hardware can execute. This consists mainly of
         uniting separately compiled subprograms into a whole program.

         Object modules produced by UCS compilers are immediately executable after
         compilation. This means that, unlike the collection process, no explicit linking phase is
         needed. When you execute an object module, the Linking System

         1.   Locates the object module
         2.   Loads it into main storage for execution

         Some programs may consist of more than one object module (compilation unit). If all
         of a programΓÇÖs object modules reside in the same program file, you do not have to do
         anything to link them. When one object module executes a reference (call) to another,
         the following sequence occurs:

         1.   The operating system suspends execution and calls the Linking System.
         2.   The Linking System locates and loads the called object module.
         3.   The operating system executes the called object module.

         This capability to link during execution is called dynamic linking.

         If your programΓÇÖs object modules reside in more than one file, however, you need to
         do one of the following:

         ∩é╖    Copy them into a single file. (See 3.1.1.)
         ∩é╖    Create a LINK$PF.SSDEF$ element so the Linking System can link them during
              execution. (See 3.1.1.)
         ∩é╖    Statically link them. (See 3.1.2.)




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  3ΓÇô1
Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




        The Linking System allows one program to use all three types of linking in a single
        execution, as described in the following table.


                   Linking Type         When It Occurs             Advantages and Typical Use

            Preload linking (also       Before loading    Fast execution, because linking is completed
            called collection, binding,                   before execution. Typically used for production
            or static linking)                            programs.
            Initial load linking       At load time       Can be used in cases where dynamic linking is
                                                          not possible. Typically used to load necessary
                                                          data before a program begins execution. (In
                                                          required cases, compilers specify this type of
                                                          linking.)
            Dynamic linking            During execution   Avoids a separate preload linking phase.
                                                          Typically used during program development
                                                          because linking is not required after each
                                                          recompilation.

        Figure 3ΓÇô1 illustrates how an object module can be

        ∩é╖      Executed immediately after compilation and linked during execution (dynamic
               linking)
        ∩é╖      Explicitly linked before execution to other object modules (static linking)

        Note: In both cases, some references may require initial load linking.




              Figure 3ΓÇô1. Program Development under the Linking System


3ΓÇô2                                                                                       7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                        Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




         The following subsections briefly discuss dynamic and static linking. For complete
         information on the Linking System and static and dynamic linking, see the following
         documents:

         ∩é╖     Linking System Programming Guide
         ∩é╖     Linking System Programming Reference Manual

3.1.1.   Dynamic Linking
         If all of your programΓÇÖs object modules are in the same file, dynamic linking occurs
         automatically. If all of your programΓÇÖs object modules are not in the same file, you
         must create a LINK$PF.SSDEF$ element so that the Linking System can find the
         required object modules during execution. Use the following process:

         1.    Call the Subsystem Definition Processor (part of the Linking System) with the
               @SSDP statement. On the call line, specify the name of the element to be
               produced (preceded by a comma): It can have any file name, but the element name
               must be SSDEF$. For example:
              @SSDP     ,any*file.SSDEF$

         2.    Specify the command DEFINE LSC $LOCAL:
              DEFINE LSC $LOCAL

         3.    In a SEARCH command, list all of the files containing object modules belonging to
               your program, in the order you want the files searched for entry point definitions.
               File names must have periods. Separate file names with commas:
              SEARCH qual*file-1.,qual*file-2.

         4. Use the @EOF statement to exit the Subsystem Definition Processor:
              @EOF

         5.    Give the file specified in the @SSDP statement (step 1) the @USE name LINK$PF:
              @USE LINK$PF,any*file.

         6. Execute the program. During execution, the Linking System searches the files
            listed in the SEARCH command (step 3) for called object modules.

         Note: Initial load linking can be viewed as a special case of dynamic linking.
         Transparently to you, the compiler and Linking System use it as needed. From your
         perspective, references using initial load linking are resolved as if they were linked
         dynamically. However, you can also specifically request initial load linking by using
         static linking commands.

3.1.2. Static Linking
         Static linking means linking together separate object modules before execution. It is
         thus similar to collection. Unlike collection, however, you can subsequently link the
         statically linked object module to another object module.



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                   3ΓÇô3
Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




        Many programs can use the following general static linking runstream to link
        separately compiled object modules into a single object module. See the Linking
        System documentation for more information on static linking.

        1.    Call the LINK Processor (part of the Linking System) with the @LINK statement.
              On the call line, specify the name of the object module to be produced (preceded
              by a comma). For example:
             @LINK     ,my*file.obj-module

        2.    Specify the object modules to be linked in an INCLUDE command. Separate object
              module names with commas:
             INCLUDE qual*file-1.om-1,qual*file-2.om-2

        3.    Resolve references (calls) with a RESOLVE command. (This is especially useful for
              resolving references to system library routines.)
             RESOLVE ALL REFERENCES USING LOCAL_DEFS,LCN

        4. Structure the program for efficient execution with a PROCESS command:
             PROCESS FOR EXTENDED

        5.    Delete all unneeded definitions (entry points) except the program starting address:
             DELETE ALL DEFINITIONS EXCEPT START$

              (This command improves linking and execution performance. However, it means
              other programs cannot link to such entry points because they have been deleted
              from the object module.)
        6. End static linking with the @EOF statement:
             @EOF

        7.    Execute the program:
             @XQT    my*file.obj-module

3.1.3. Creating Fixed-Gate Subsystems
        You can package the code as a subsystem to make it available to other runs and
        transactions without embedding the code in other applications. All applications can
        share the subsystem code using a reference (call) to the subsystem. This results in

        ∩é╖     Applications referring to the subsystem will have lesser code to load.
        ∩é╖     You do not have to relink the applications, when shared libraries are used.

        For information on how to select a subsystem type, for statically linking it, and
        installing the subsystems, refer to the Linking System Subsystems Programming
        Guide.




3ΓÇô4                                                                                7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                      Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




         Most of the COBOL programs are packaged as fast-load (FLSS) or self-contained
         (SCSS) subsystems. These types of subsystems will load thread-local storage for each
         activity. However, it is sometimes possible to package COBOL code as a fully
         application-level fixed-gate subsystem if the code is written to adhere to some rules
         and restrictions.

         A fully application-level fixed-gate subsystem has all the code and data in its object
         modules loaded at application level. The only thread-local storage available is the
         activity local stack (ALS) and any storage obtained through malloc or CREATE$BANK
         calls. By default, the UCS COBOL compiler (UCOB) generates static writable storage
         for WORKING-STORAGE variables and for packets for CALLs, SORT-MERGE, IO, DMS,
         ENTER MASM, and for certain ESQL statements such as FETCH commands. If your
         program is packaged as a fully application-level fixed-gate subsystem, the data being
         loaded at application-level can cause data corruption problems or a write-protect
         violation (IGDM). The following problems might occur:

         ∩é╖   A protected fixed-gate subsystem might experience data corruption; multiple
             execution threads simultaneously access the application-level data if locks are not
             used to protect the data.
         ∩é╖   A chameleon fixed-gate subsystem might experience write-protect violations as
             application-level data is read-only.
         ∩é╖   A chameleon subsystem might also experience the data corruption problem if its
             application-level data is made writable.

         With FLSS or SCSS subsystems, since the data is loaded as thread-local storage for
         the subsystem types, the data corruption or write-protect violation does not occur.

         If you add the INITIAL clause to the PROGRAM-ID statement of a COBOL program, the
         compiler allocates the WORKING-STORAGE variables and parameter packets for CALL
         and ENTER MASM statements on the ALS instead in the static storage. This eliminates
         the possible data corruption and write-protect violation problems when accessing this
         subset of data. The code must be packaged as a fully application-level fixed-gate
         subsystem.

         However, the INITIAL clause by itself is not sufficient to totally eliminate these
         potential subsystem problems. Code generated for IO statements, such as DISPLAY,
         for SORT, MERGE, and for CDML (DMS) statements will be stored in the static storage
         that is generated as part of the output object module. COMMON storage is also
         allocated in static storage. If you want to package COBOL code as a fully
         application-level fixed-gate subsystem you must do the following:

         ∩é╖   Use the INITIAL clause on the PROGRAM-ID statements.
         ∩é╖   Do not do any COBOL IO. You can call C code to execute printf and other IO
             operations.
         ∩é╖   Do not use any COBOL SORT or MERGE statements.
         ∩é╖   Do not use any CDML statements.
         ∩é╖   Do not use any COMMON-STORAGE section (including the EXTERNAL clause for
             01 level variables in the WORKING-STORAGE section).



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  3ΓÇô5
Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




        Since the UCS COBOL system was not designed expecting its data areas to be made
        read-only, there might be more restrictions needed for situations that could cause
        problems but have not yet been encountered at this time. COBOL programs are rarely
        packaged as fully application-level fixed-gate subsystems because of these open
        ended restrictions; they are usually packaged as FLSS or SCSS subsystems, which
        give each activity its own data.


3.2. Executing Your Program
        You can execute an object module immediately after compilation; programs consisting
        of more than one object module may require linking before execution (see 3.1).

        You can execute an object module in the following ways:

        ∩é╖    Ordinary object modules can be executed with the Executive control language
             @XQT statement:
            @XQT    qual*file.obj-module

        ∩é╖    Ordinary object modules developed and executed using the Interactive Processing
             Facility (IPF 1100) can be executed with the following statement:
            XQT    qual*file.obj-module

        You can invoke PADS from your program with the following COBOL statement:

            CALL ΓÇÖPADS$ΓÇÖ.

        When you finish with PADS, control returns to the next statement in your program
        unless, while using PADS, you direct it to cause execution to resume at some other
        point.


3.3. Debugging with PADS
        The Programmers Advanced Debugging System (PADS) is the common debugging
        product for extended mode programs. PADS is a powerful, language-independent,
        interactive debugging tool.

        Note: Although PADS is your primary debugging tool, other compiler keyword
        options can also be useful when the execution of your program results in a storage
        limits violation, unexpected values in the output, or unexpected program flow. Table
        2-1 summarizes the compiler keyword options recommended for debugging.

        Interactive debugging allows you to suspend execution of your program and enter
        PADS commands from a terminal. For example, PADS commands permit you to set
        traps in your program, examine or modify program variables, and resume program
        execution.

        The PADS command set is flexible, making it suitable for users at all levels of skill.
        PADS provides a uniform way to debug programs written in any supported language.
        PADS is independent of the program language it is debugging.




3ΓÇô6                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                       Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




         References to program entities, such as statement labels, procedure names, or
         variables, generally take the same form as in the language used to code the program.

         By compiling with the appropriate compiler keyword option (see 3.3.2), you can debug
         at a symbolic level without having to know the low-level details of the hardware.
         Low-level hardware-dependent debugging is also available with PADS.

         You do not need to include special debugging statements in your program to use
         PADS. A production TIP transaction that wishes to have TIP sticking and RESTART
         should not have PADS as its contingency routine. PADS does a CREATE$BANK call to
         the Exec and this kills TIP sticking and RESTART for the transaction. One way to keep
         PADS out is to name the URTS runtime library in the RESOLVE statement in the static
         link of your transaction. This results in PADS stub object module C$NPADS being
         linked into your program.

             RESOLVE ALL REFERENCES USING L_D,SYS$LIB$*EMOMRTS.,LCN

         Another way is to specifically include the C$NPADS object module from the URTS
         library along with using the LOCAL_DEFS (or L_D) option in the RESOLVE statement in
         your static link:

             INCLUDE SYS$LIB$*EMOMRTS.C$NPADS
             RESOLVE ALL REFERENCES USING L_D,LCN

         For more information on using PADS, see the PADS Programming Guide.

3.3.1. PADS Features
         The following are some of the features provided by PADS:

         ∩é╖    Program component display
              The DISPLAY command displays program constants, variables, or expressions that
              you specify. You can also display all variables in a compilation unit in alphabetical
              order or by program structure order.
              You can use the DUMP command to display storage locations of your program
              that do not correspond to any variables. The storage location is defined by a
              low-level address.
         ∩é╖    Program component modification
              The ASSIGN command changes the contents of program variables.
              The ALTER command changes the contents of a storage location defined by a
              low-level address.
              The SET command changes access permission attributes for a bank in an object
              module.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  3ΓÇô7
Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




        ∩é╖   Program execution control
            You can control program flow by using the STEP command. You can direct PADS
            to execute a specific number of program statements, suspend program
            execution, and then solicit additional commands. Also, you can specify commands
            to be executed when the specified number of program statements have
            executed, by placing the commands in an optional THEN clause.
            You can suspend program execution using the following PADS commands. After
            the program is suspended, you can enter additional debug commands.
            ∩Ç¡   TRAP CONDITION
                This command sets a trap when a program condition (such as a divide fault or
                illegal operation) occurs.
            ∩Ç¡   TRAP EXECUTION
                This command sets a trap at a specific program location. The program location
                can be defined by program label, line number, procedure name, or by a
                low-level address.
            ∩Ç¡   TRAP CHANGE
                This command sets a trap when a specific program variable changes. The
                variable can be defined by program name or by a low-level address. Only
                commands that actually change the program value are trapped.
        Using the optional THEN clause with a TRAP command allows you more debugging
        flexibility.

        ∩é╖   Program execution monitoring
            You can trace program flow using the TRACE command to display a message for
            ∩Ç¡   Each program statement executed.
            ∩Ç¡   Each program label executed. PADS also identifies the calling statement, if
                possible.
            ∩Ç¡   Each procedure or subroutine executed. PADS also identifies the calling
                statement, if possible.
            Tracing can be turned on for an entire program or for specific elements.
            By using the INQUIRE WALKBACK command, you can trace the flow of all
            preceding subprogram calls. You can specify the number of calls to be traced or
            trace all calls back to the main program.
        ∩é╖   PADS procedures
            PADS allows you to define command sequences, which are called procedures.
            PADS procedures can optionally have parameters. You call PADS procedures
            during a debugging session by using a CALL command.
            You can save PADS procedures in a program file by using a PUT command, modify
            them by using a text editor, and retrieve the procedures by using a GET command.




3ΓÇô8                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                     Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




         ∩é╖   PADS control commands
             PADS contains a set of conditional commands that increase the power of the
             command set. These control commands allow
             ∩Ç¡   Conditional execution of blocks of PADS commands (using the IF command)
             ∩Ç¡   Iterative execution of PADS commands (using the DO or DO WHILE
                 commands)
         ∩é╖   PADS variables
             PADS provides internal variables (declare symbols) that you define during the
             debugging session. You can use declare symbols in place of program variables.
             Declare symbols can be arrays and can be local or global.
         ∩é╖   Dump capabilities
             PADS supplies standard dump procedures to produce dumps that closely
             resemble the output of the @PMD processor.
         ∩é╖   Online help
             At any point during a PADS debugging session, you can request help about the
             PADS language by entering the HELP command. The HELP command provides a
             brief description of the definition, usage, and syntax of PADS commands. The
             HELP command can also provide definitions for the terms used in the PADS
             syntax.

3.3.2. Compiler Option Considerations
         The compiler keyword options for debugging provide symbolic support for the
         following high-level program entities:

         ∩é╖   Procedure names
         ∩é╖   Labels
         ∩é╖   Line numbers
         ∩é╖   Variable names

         Symbolic support means that the compiler generates a symbolic debugging dictionary
         (SDD) that enables PADS to locate and refer to program entities during program
         execution. PADS needs an SDD to provide a high-level environment for displaying or
         altering program entities.

         The following are the compiler keyword options that affect debugging with PADS.
         These options are included in 2.2.7.

         ∩é╖   DEBUG
             This option generates a restricted SDD. The SDD does not contain information
             about variables that are not referenced by the program. However, if any member
             of a group is referenced, information on all group members and any overlays of
             the group is included in the SDD.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                3ΓÇô9
Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




        ∩é╖   DEBUG/FULL
            This option generates a PADS SDD in the object module, including declared but
            unused variables, line numbers, and procedure information
        ∩é╖   DEBUG/MONITOR
            This option generates information in the DEBUG/REFERENCE debugging dictionary,
            in addition to the information generated by the DEBUG and DEBUG/FULL options.
            This information allows for the monitoring of input and output for each line of
            source code executed during a PADS debugging session. This option invokes the
            DEBUG keyword option if the DEBUG, DEBUG/REFERENCE, or DEBUG/FULL
            keyword options are not specified.
        ∩é╖   DEBUG/REFERENCE
            This option generates a restricted SDD similar to what is generated for DEBUG,
            except information on more group members is eliminated.
        ∩é╖   DEBUG/STATEMENT
            This option generates an SDD that contains information about procedures,
            functions, and line numbers. The SDD will not contain any information about
            variables or labels.
        ∩é╖   DEBUG/WALKBACK
            This option generates an SDD that contains information only about procedures and
            functions, allowing the use of such PADS commands as INQUIRE WALKBACK and
            TRACE ON FOR PROCEDURE. This type of SDD provides the minimum level of
            PADS high-level debugging.
        ∩é╖   NO-DEBUG
            This option suppresses generation of the SDD and is recommended for production
            programs. PADS is functional, but only in a low-level environment. For example, to
            change the value of a variable, you must know the low-level address of that
            variable. Any PADS commands that refer to high-level entities generate diagnostic
            messages.

        DEBUG generates a symbolic debugging dictionary that eliminates all information
        about variables that are declared but not referenced in the program. This is useful
        when using PADS to debug programs that copy source but actually use only a few of
        the shared items declared in the copied text.

        The various object modules that make up your program can be compiled with different
        compiler keyword options for debugging. This allows the level of symbolic debugging
        to vary from one object module to another.

        PADS uses only the value in the storage area for a variable to determine the value of
        that variable. Program optimization through the use of the OPTIM compiler keyword
        option (which is the default) may affect the debugging of program variables. For
        example, optimization may cause stores to the storage area for a variable to be
        omitted. Optimization may also delete some program statements.




3ΓÇô10                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                      Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




         For these reasons, if you use PADS for debugging, it recommended that you specify
         the NO-OPTIM compiler keyword option until debugging is complete. Otherwise,
         debugging results may be unpredictable.

         Table 2-1 lists the compiler keyword options recommended for program debugging.

3.3.3. Excluding PADS
         For some production application programs it is desirable to exclude PADS in order to
         get the highest performing code. This is especially true for TIP transactions, since you
         cannot get TIP sticking and RESTART when PADS is included in your executable. The
         tradeoff is that PADS cannot be used to debug the application if it has been excluded
         (postmortem debugging using a DIAG$ file can be done). One way to exclude PADS
         from the program is to name the URTS runtime library in the RESOLVE statement in
         the static link of your program. The result is a PADS stub object module, C$NPADS,
         being linked into your program.

         RESOLVE ALL REFERENCES USING L_D, your-libraries., SYS$LIB$*EMOMRTS., LCN

         The SYS$LIB$*EMOMRTS file name should follow the LOCAL_DEFS, and must
         precede LIBCODENAME on the resolve command. If you have library files that you
         want the linker to search, you can put those file names after LOCAL_DEFS.

         Note: Note LOCAL_DEFS can be abbreviated as L_D, and LIBCODENAME can be
         abbreviated as LCN.

         Another way is to specifically include the C$NPADS object module from the URTS
         library along with using the LOCAL_DEFS option in the RESOLVE statement in your
         static link:

         INCLUDE SYS$LIB$*EMOMRTS.C$NPADS
         RESOLVE ALL REFERENCES USING L_D, your-libraries., LCN

3.3.4. Activating PADS
         PADS can be activated by the following methods.

@PADS Activation
         You enter a @PADS ON processor call statement preceding the @XQT statement for
         your program.

         PADS is then activated and accepts command input before any program statements
         are executed. PADS is also activated and accepts command input at program
         termination.

@@X C Activation
         At any time during program execution, you may enter the @@X C statement. If there is
         output coming to your terminal, you must first press the Message Waiting key to
         break the output so you can enter @@X C.



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                3ΓÇô11
Linking, Executing, and Debugging Your Program




        The Exec treats the @@X C statement as a contingency to be handled by the
        contingency handler assigned to your program. The default contingency handler for
        UCS languages is the run-time library. The run-time library stops program execution
        and activates PADS. PADS then solicits your command input.

Compilation-Time Activation
        You can invoke PADS from your program with the following COBOL statement:

          CALL ΓÇÖPADS$ΓÇÖ

        When you finish debugging with PADS, control returns to the next statement in your
        program, unless while using PADS you direct execution to resume at some other
        point in your program.

Postmortem Activation
        You enter a @PADS DIAG or @PADS TIPDIAG processor call statement to debug the
        program state file or the error history file produced by UCS.

        When activated for postmortem debugging, PADS does not accept commands that
        modify the saved program state or control the program flow, since the program is not
        executing.

Error Activation
        The UCS Runtime System calls PADS, if your program causes a contingency.
