Section 4
Changing I/O System Limits and I/O
Optimization


4.1. System I/O Overview
         File input/output for UCS programs uses certain default values. There are several such
         defaults; you can override the defaults at run time using the Define File Processor
         (DFP) if the defaults are not well suited to your application. For information on DFP,
         see the DFP Administration and Programming Reference Manual. This approach lets
         you override defaults without source code changes, recompiling, or relinking.
         However, each time a file is opened, your execution stops and the system calls DFP to
         override the defaults involved. This can degrade performance, perhaps significantly, in
         applications that frequently open files and that need the default I/O values overridden.

         However, you also have the option to change some of the default values used during
         I/O operations. The defaults you can change include

         ∩é╖   Minimum block size (PREPFACTOR)
         ∩é╖   Default block size (BLOCKSIZE)
         ∩é╖   Runtime System heap area size (HEAPSIZE)
         ∩é╖   Conversion table default

         Changing these default values does require relinking. However, you do not have to
         change your source code or recompile your object modules. And you may see
         substantial improvements in performance and reductions in I/O standard units of
         processing (SUP) charges.

         The default values are defined in the UCS Runtime System object module
         URTS$TABLES. URTS$TABLES is an object module residing in the file
         SYS$LIB$*EMOMRTS. It is searched by the Linking System default library search chain
         defined in SYS$*DATA$.SSDEF$.

         The URTS$TABLES element contains the primary data structures for URTS. If you
         generate a custom URTS$TABLES element, it should be regenerated to match the
         URTS level installed on your system before linking the custom URTS$TABLES element
         into your application. Failure to keep the custom URTS$TABLES element up-to-date
         could limit the availability of new features in URTS and the UCOB compiler.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                4ΓÇô1
Changing I/O System Limits and I/O Optimization




        To change the defaults in URTS$TABLES and use the new defaults in your application,
        you must

        1.   Generate an alternate URTS$TABLES object module
        2.   Place the new object module in an alternate file
        3.   Generate an alternate SSDEF$ element that searches the alternate file before it
             searches SYS$*DATA$.SSDEF$
        4. Relink your applicationΓÇÖs object modules so that the new defaults are applied

        A Symbolic Stream Generator (SSG) skeleton has been provided to build an alternate
        URTS$TABLES object module and place the new object module in a file you specify.
        (See 4.2.)

        Changing these values is a part of the process of optimizing I/O in your application.
        Generally, you should modify these default values only if one of the following occurs:

        ∩é╖    Your I/O SUP charges seem excessive for your application
             Changing URTS$TABLES can reduce I/O SUP charges by reducing the I/O needed
             to look up DFP modifications when a file is opened.
        ∩é╖    Your applicationΓÇÖs performance appears to be I/O bound
             If your application is using prep factors or block sizes that are not well matched to
             the data involved in I/O operations, it may result in more I/O operations being
             needed than would otherwise be necessary. This can degrade performance as
             well as drive I/O SUP charges up.
             Since DFP overrides must be retrieved each time a file is opened, changing
             defaults to reduce the number of DFP overrides will also reduce the time spent in
             I/O operations.
        ∩é╖    You find that the URTS$TABLES bank is being expanded automatically as a result
             of an Exec request (ER) issued by the UCS Runtime System
        ∩é╖    Your program fails with error number 37001, indicating that the URTS$TABLES
             bank has no more available space

        The remedies discussed fall into three categories:

        ∩é╖    Optimizing the I/O process so that it is performed most efficiently. This is
             restricted to SDF sequential file I/O. You use the PREPFACTOR and BLOCKSIZE
             SGSs either singly or in combination for I/O optimization.
        ∩é╖    Specifying a larger size for URTS$TABLES so it needs no automatic adjustment.
             This may depend on the amount of main storage available on your system. You
             control the default beginning size for URTS$TABLES with the HEAPSIZE SGS.




4ΓÇô2                                                                                7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                       Changing I/O System Limits and I/O Optimization




         ∩é╖    Reducing the number of files opened concurrently. For example
              ∩Ç¡   Each SDF sequential file requires two buffers in URTS$TABLES, as well as
                  other overhead space.
              ∩Ç¡   Each MSAM file requires five buffers in URTS$TABLES, as well as other
                  overhead space.
              For more information about buffer requirements for various file types, see the
              PCIOS Administration and Programming Reference Manual and the UDS SFS
              Administration and Support Reference Manual.

         You can also modify the default conversion table for IBM tape file I/O using the
         CONVERSION SGS.


4.2. Regenerating the URTS$TABLES Object
     Module
         Use the SSG skeleton, UPDATETABLE, to create or alter an alternate URTS$TABLES
         object module. This skeleton reads stream generation statements (SGS) you enter and
         those contained in the UNITTAB element in SYS$LIB$*URTS. The UNITTAB element
         contains the default SGSs that the skeleton interprets to create an alternate
         URTS$TABLES object module.

         UPDATETABLE reads in those default SGSs, replaces the ones for which you provide
         an alternate SGS in the runstream, and writes a new UNITTAB element on the file you
         specify in the FILE SGS. UPDATETABLE then uses the values in the new UNITTAB
         element to create an alternate URTS$TABLES object module. It then writes this new
         URTS$TABLES on a file with the new UNITTAB. The following example calls the
         skeleton:

         Note: The file name SYS$LIB$*URTS is different if your site uses a different
         name to hold the main UCS Runtime System product file.

             @SSG,L SYS$LIB$*URTS.UPDATETABLE
             SGS
                 .
                 . (Enter SGSs to change the defaults as needed)
                  .
             @EOF
             @EOF




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  4ΓÇô3
Changing I/O System Limits and I/O Optimization




        The following SGSs are allowed. The defaults shown are those Unisys provides when
        the products are shipped. Your site can reconfigure these to different values on
        installation; consult your site administrator for local changes in these defaults.

        ∩é╖   FILE file-name [NEW]
            This SGS is required with each use of UPDATETABLE; file-name is the file where
            the alternate URTS$TABLES object module and UNITTAB element are placed. Thus
            it is this file that you list in the SEARCH command for your SSDEF$ element (see
            4.3, step 2b).
            ∩Ç¡   If you specify NEW, file-name is cataloged, and UPDATETABLE uses the
                UNITTAB element in SYS$LIB$*URTS. Any SGSs you enter replace the
                corresponding SGS in the new UNITTAB that is written to the file you specify.
                UPDATETABLE then uses this new UNITTAB element to create a new
                URTS$TABLES object module in the same file with the new UNITTAB element.
                Specify NEW if this is the first time you have created an alternate
                URTS$TABLES object module or if you wish to use the default UNITTAB
                element as a starting point instead of one you previously created.
            ∩Ç¡   If you do not specify NEW, file-name is assumed to be an alternate
                URTS$TABLES object module and also a UNITTAB element. The new UNITTAB
                element and URTS$TABLES are rewritten to the same file, but with
                incremented cycle numbers.
                Do not specify NEW if you wish to begin your revision of the URTS$TABLES
                object module from the last set of defaults you specified.
        ∩é╖   PREPFACTOR integer
            This SGS is optional. It defines a new value for the SDF sequential prepping factor.
            The prep factor specifies the minimum block size used in an I/O operation on an
            SDF sequential file. All SDF sequential file buffers are a multiple of the SDF
            prepping factor.
            Use PREPFACTOR (along with BLOCKSIZE) to control the amount of buffer space
            allocated for SDF sequential file I/O. Large I/O buffers will usually reduce I/O SUP
            charges because large I/O operations are more efficient than more numerous
            small ones.
            But if too much space is allocated for SDF sequential file I/O buffers, some
            applications can experience a shortage of heap bank space (URTS$TABLES). This
            is a fatal condition marked by error number 37001. (If you need large buffers but
            are running out of heap bank space, try reducing the number of files open
            concurrently.)
            Valid values for integer are 112, 224, 448, 896, 1792, 3584, 7168, and 14336. The
            initial default value for PREPFACTOR is 1792.




4ΓÇô4                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                       Changing I/O System Limits and I/O Optimization




         ∩é╖   BLOCKSIZE integer
             This SGS is optional. BLOCKSIZE defines a new value for the default SDF
             sequential block size used during I/O operations if
             ∩Ç¡    You do not specify a block size when you open an SDF sequential file
             ∩Ç¡    The UCS Runtime System opens an SDF sequential file for its own purposes
             BLOCKSIZE must be larger than PREPFACTOR if you specify both. If you specify
             BLOCKSIZE but do not specify PREPFACTOR, BLOCKSIZE must be larger than the
             system default prepping factor. If you specify a value for BLOCKSIZE that is less
             than or equal to PREPFACTOR or the system default prepping factor (whichever is
             in use), BLOCKSIZE is ignored.
             Valid values for integer are 112, 224, 448, 896, 1792, 3584, 7168, and 14336. The
             initial default value for BLOCKSIZE is 1792.
         ∩é╖   HEAPSIZE integer
             This SGS is optional. HEAPSIZE defines the UCS Runtime System heap area used
             for record and buffer areas, Executive request (ER) packet areas, I/O tables,
             General Syntax Analyzer (GSA) messages, and data staging for other basic mode
             routines.
             The Exec expands the size of URTS$TABLES on receipt of an ER from the UCS
             Runtime System, up to the maximum allowable on your system. However, this ER
             is expensive and degrades performance since execution must be halted while
             URTS$TABLES is expanded. You can reduce costs and improve performance by
             specifying a HEAPSIZE large enough to avoid automatic expansion.
             Determining whether URTS$TABLES has been expanded can be difficult since
             URTS$TABLES can also be reduced in size as well. One method is to use PADS
             entry points at various places in your object module, then use PADS to find the
             current size of URTS$TABLES. One place to try an entry point is immediately after
             a file is opened.
             Depending on system limitations, URTS$TABLES can expand to something over
             170,000 words. If more space is called for than the system can provide, your
             program will fail with error number 37001.
             Valid values for integer are 1000 to 170000. The initial default for HEAPSIZE is
             10000.
             Note: The recommended way to accomplish this task is to add the following to
             the program's static LINK:
                     SET SIZE = SIZE + increased-size FOR URTS$TABLES

             This command must follow the RESOLVE command and precede the PROCESS
             command in the static LINK.
                 @LINK     ,filename. Element
                 INCLUDE   filename.acb
                 INCLUDE   filename.xyz
                 RESOLVE ALL REFERENCES USING LCN
                 SET SIZE = SIZE + increased-size FOR URTS$TABLES
                 PROCESS FOR EXTENDED ZOOM




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                   4ΓÇô5
Changing I/O System Limits and I/O Optimization




        ∩é╖     CONVERSION integer
              This SGS is optional. Use this SGS to set the value for the default conversion table.
              If your application makes extensive use of tapes in EBCDIC in any of the character
              sets shown below, you may find it useful to change the default conversion value.
              (See 14.4.6.). The following integer values are valid.


               Integer value                         Type of Conversion

                 0 (default)   ASCII to/from ISO EBCDIC with the 128 character set
                     1         ASCII to/from ISO EBCDIC with the lowercase alphabetic
                               character set
                     2         ASCII to/from IBM EBCDIC with the KATAKANA character set
                     3         ASCII to/from IBM EBCDIC with the lowercase alphabetic
                               character set
                     4         ASCII to/from ISO EBCDIC with the KATAKANA character set


4.3. Using the Alternate URTS$TABLES Object
     Module
        Note: You must regenerate the URTS$TABLES object module every time a new
        release level of URTS is installed onto your system. You cannot statically link an
        older level of URTS$TABLES with newer levels of the URTS Library. If you have a
        statically linked object module that includes the regenerated URTS$TABLES along
        with the URTS Library from the same release level, it is acceptable to continue
        executing with this object module. However, if you perform a link, you must use the
        regenerated URTS$TABLES object module from the currently installed level along
        with the currently installed level of the URTS library.

        To access the new URTS$TABLES object module generated by UPDATETABLE, you
        must

        1.    Create an alternate subsystem definition element (SSDEF$)
        2.    Place the @USE name of LINK$PF on the file containing the alternate SSDEF$
              element before static links or executions of object modules

        The following describes how to generate and use an alternate SSDEF$ element.

        1.    List the default SSDEF$ element SYS$*DATA$.SSDEF$. Use the @LIST processor
              to produce a symbolic version of the SSDEF$ element. For more information on
              using @LIST with the Linking System, see the Linking System Programming
              Reference Manual. For example
             @LIST,A SYS$*DATA$.SSDEF$




4ΓÇô6                                                                                     7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                           Changing I/O System Limits and I/O Optimization




         2.    Modify the symbolic SSDEF$ element.
               a.   Locate the definition of LSC RTS$EMLIB.
               b. Insert a search of the file which contains the new URTS$TABLES object
                  module before the search of the file SYS$LIB$*EMOMRTS. For example
              DEFINE LSC RTS$EMLIB
              SEARCH qual*file.
              SEARCH SYS$LIB$*EMOMRTS.

                    where qual*file is the file that contains the alternate URTS$TABLES object
                    module.
         3.    Generate an absolute SSDEF$ element from the symbolic input:
              @SSDP    symbolic*file.SSDEF$,absolute*file.SSDEF$

         4. Put the @USE name of LINK$PF on the file which contains the absolute alternate
            SSDEF$ element:
               a.   For static link
              @USE LINK$PF.,absolute*file.
              @LINK qual*file.linksource,qual*file.om
              @XQT qual*file.om

                    where:
                    qual*file.linksource
                      contains static linking commands. (You can also issue static linking
                      commands from the runstream.)
                    qual*file.om
                      is the object module created by static linking. This is the object module
                      being executed for which you want to change the I/O system limits.
               b. For dynamic link
              @USE LINK$PF.,absolute*file.
              @XQT qual*file.om

                    where qual*file.om is the object module being executed for which you want
                    to change the I/O system limits.

4.4. UCS Runtime I/O
         UCOB performs run-time input/output (I/O) operations using the Processor Common
         Input/Output System (PCIOS). PCIOS consists of a number of common bank modules
         that access the various file types and a number of processor interface common bank
         modules for the various UCS compilers such as COBOL, FORTRAN, and C.

         PCIOS is used by the UCS Runtime System for I/O compatibility between the various
         language processors. See the PCIOS Administration and Programming Reference
         Manual for more information.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                     4ΓÇô7
Changing I/O System Limits and I/O Optimization




        A UCOB program accesses sequential, relative, and indexed system data format (SDF)
        files through PCIOS. UCOB handles all formatting and conversions. The actual I/O is
        done in PCIOS. However, a restriction of PCIOS allows I/O processing to be done to
        sector-formatted mass storage only, not to word-addressable mass storage.

        The default block size of 1792 words is used for all PCIOS related files.

        A UCOB program accesses symbiont files through SAR$.




4ΓÇô8                                                                                 7831 0455ΓÇô022
Section 5
Using System Interfaces

         UCS COBOL programs have access to many features available through other products.
         The interfaces described in this section provide the means to do the following:

         ∩é╖    Prepare UCS COBOL libraries
         ∩é╖    Assign and control the attributes of UCS COBOL files
         ∩é╖    Interpret messages that appear on your console

         The following table indicates where this manual describes several additional interfaces
         that are available to UCS COBOL programs.


                                 Interface         Description

                          DMS 2200                     Section 6
                          RDMS 2200                    Section 7
                          UDS UREP                     Section 8
                          PCFP                         Section 9
                          Executive Requests           Section 10
                          Interlanguage Calls          Section 15


5.1. Preparing Your UCS COBOL Library
         To prepare a UCS COBOL library, source images are introduced to the Procedure
         Definition Processor (@PDP). The PDP output produces a UCS COBOL library that
         COBOL programs can access.

         Several procedures (text items) can be grouped together in one element, but each
         separate text name must appear in the label field of a procedure statement (PROC).

         The format for a text item input to PDP is:

             text-name PROC
                  (COBOL statements to be copied)
                  END




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               5ΓÇô1
Using System Interfaces




        The parameter text-name can consist only of the characters A through Z, 0 through 9,
        and -, except that the - cannot appear as the first or last character. The parameter
        text-name must begin in column 1 of the source image and END must begin in column
        2. Library text must conform to the rules for COBOL reference format.


5.2. Assigning a UCS COBOL File
        The purpose of this assignment procedure is to provide a link between the UCS
        COBOL-defined file name and the File Control System name (the actual file facilities).

        The formats given here are specific examples of the @ASG control statements and are
        not intended as samples of general format. Consult the ER Programming Reference
        Manual for general rules and formats. If an @ASG is not present in the runstream for
        executing the object program, an implicit @ASG may be automatically done by the
        run-time system. See the ΓÇ£Availability of a fileΓÇ¥ table in the OPEN statement section
        for the appropriate file type.

5.2.1. Assigning Nonsymbiont Files
        Format
          @ASG,T   DF1,F///200               (disk)

          @ASG,T   TAPE1,HICL,1234           (tape)

          @ASG,T   TAPE3,HICL//////Q,9012    (Information Interchange Tape or IBM Tape)

          @ASG,TJ TAPE3,HICL//////Q,9012     (Information Interchange Tape or IBM Tape)

          @ASG,T   DF2.                      (disk)

        All reel numbers must be specified for input tape files.

        The links between COBOL-defined files and these File Control System files are
        provided in the following COBOL source language statements:

          SELECT PAYROLL ASSIGN TO DISC DF1.

        The COBOL file PAYROLL is now associated with a maximum size of 200 tracks with
        the File Control System name DF1.

          SELECT OLD-MASTER ASSIGN TO TAPE TAPE1.

        The COBOL file OLD-MASTER is now associated with tape number 1234 with the File
        Control System name TAPE1.

          SELECT INTERCHANGE-FILE ASSIGN TO INTERCHANGE TAPE3.

        The Information Interchange file INTERCHANGE-FILE is now associated with tape
        number 9012, which has the File Control System name TAPE3. The second format
        (@ASG,TJ) indicated an unlabeled tape number 9012, in which case LABEL RECORDS
        OMITTED must be stated.


5ΓÇô2                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                      Using System Interfaces




         When an 8-bit prelabeled reel is required for output (files assigned to TAPE or
         INTERCHANGE and LABEL RECORDS ARE STANDARD) and an 8-bit prelabeled reel is
         not mounted, the system issues a console message if the Executive Tape Labeling
         System is not configured to write 8-bit labels on non-J-option reels.

              SELECT IBM TAPE ASSIGN TO TAPE TAPE3.

         If the IBM TAPE is labeled, the system must be set up for EBCDIC tape labeling (see
         Section 13).

         This is an example of element I/O.

              SELECT FILE1 ASSIGN TO DISC ΓÇÖQUAL*DF2.ELEΓÇÖ.

         The COBOL FILE1 is associated with the File Control System QUAL*DF2. This is an
         example of element I/O.

         Device Independency for ANSI Tape Files
         You can assign ANSI tape files (for example, SELECT filename ASSIGN TO TAPE) to a
         mass storage device at execution time. In this case, the system creates an ANSI SDF
         mass storage file that is the same as if the file originally was assigned to DISC in the
         source program.

5.2.2. Assigning Symbiont Files
         Format
         No @ASG control statement is necessary.

         General Rules
         1.    Assignments are handled automatically by the system.
         2.    The COBOL links are
              SELECT file-name ASSIGN TO PRINTER.

              SELECT file-name ASSIGN TO CARD-READER.

              SELECT file-name ASSIGN TO CARD-PUNCH.

               where file-name identifies the file name for use within the COBOL program.

5.2.3. Assigning Alternate Symbiont Files
         Format
              @ASG,CP DF1,F///200

         General Rules
         1.    At the time the file is closed, an @BRKPT statement on that file is issued.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  5ΓÇô3
Using System Interfaces




        2.    In order to control the printing or punching of an alternate file explicitly, that file
              must be assigned by the @ASG statement shown in this subsection and output by
              a @SYM statement.
        3.    For output, if a file is not assigned, the system attempts to assign it dynamically,
              and output and release it at the termination of the run. If the file cannot be
              assigned because of an assignment conflict, the run error terminates with an
              appropriate symbiont message. The automatic @ASG, @FREE, and @SYM are for
              batch runs only.
        4. The COBOL links are
             SELECT file-name ASSIGN TO PRINTER DF1.

             SELECT file-name ASSIGN TO CARD-READER DF1.

             SELECT file-name ASSIGN TO CARD-PUNCH DF1.

              where file-name identifies the file name for use within the COBOL program, and
              DF1 identifies the file name referenced on the @ASG statement.


5.3. Using the Define File Processor (DFP)
        Use the Define File Processor to specify attributes for a file at run time without
        changing the COBOL source statements, recompiling, and relinking.

        You create a define file block (DFB) with the statement @DFP,E. When the system
        opens the file, the UCS Runtime System library accesses the DFB. If a file DFP$ is
        assigned to the run or you gave a file the use (@USE) name DFP$, the UCS Runtime
        System looks in it (through ER PFS$) for an omnibus element that has the same name
        specified as the external name in the ASSIGN clause of the SELECT statement for the
        file in the COBOL source program. The version name must be spaces.

        For more information about the Define File Processor (DFP) call and keyword
        parameters, refer to the DFP Administration and Programming Reference Manual.

5.3.1. Blocking Factors for Non-MSAM Files
        The BLOCK keyword parameter list is as follows:

             BLOCK = bs/bo/bn/bl//bu

        where:

        bs

              is the BLOCK CONTAINS clause value of integer-2. It is an integer in the range 0 ∩éú
              bs ∩éú 131072.

        bo

              is the buffer offset parameter. This parameter is valid only for input tape files
              assigned the INTERCHANGE. It is an integer in the range 0 ∩éú bo ∩éú 99.


5ΓÇô4                                                                                  7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                       Using System Interfaces




         bn

               is the number of buffers parameter. It is an integer in the range of 0 < bn < 64.
               However, values of bn greater than 2 are meaningful only for indexed files.

         bl

               is the replacement for the value of integer-1 in the BLOCK CONTAINS clause. It is
               an integer in the range 0 < bl < 131072. This parameter is meaningful only for files
               that are indexed. Also, this parameter is meaningful only when the bs parameter is
               specified and bl ∩éú bs.

         bu

               is the BLOCK CONTAINS clause RECORDS or CHARACTERS option. It is coded
               either as RECORDS or CHARACTERS.

               In the absence of a bu parameter, CHARACTERS is assumed. This parameter is
               meaningful only when the bs parameter is specified.

5.3.2. Blocking Factors for MSAM Files
         You can use the BLOCK keyword parameter to alter the compiler defaults for buffer
         size and number of buffers for 1974 Standard Indexed files (that is, PCIOS MSAM files).
         Difficulties can occur when running UCS COBOL programs that access MSAM files,
         especially where several MSAM files are accessed simultaneously or where the file
         records are very large. This occurs because the UCS COBOL compiler tries to optimize
         the number of buffers and the size of the buffers so that the PCIOS MSAM processor
         can operate more efficiently.

         You can adjust the current operating environment without recompiling or remapping
         by using the BLOCK keyword parameter to override the compiler generated
         parameters. The BLOCK keyword parameter list is as follows:

              BLOCK = bs//bn/bl/bu

         where:

         bs

               buffer size (see ΓÇ£Specifying the Buffer SizeΓÇ¥ in the following discussion).

         bn

               number of buffer parameters (4 ∩éú bn ∩éú 63); for OUTPUT and I-O mode, bn must be
               ∩é│ 5 (see ΓÇ£Specifying the Number of BuffersΓÇ¥ in the following discussion).

         bl

               block loading factor (see ΓÇ£Specifying the Block Loading FactorΓÇ¥ in the following
               discussion).



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                      5ΓÇô5
Using System Interfaces




        bu

              blocking unit, WORDS, CHARACTERS or RECORDS (ASCII characters are
              assumed).

        Specifying the Buffer Size
        Through DFP, you can alter the compiler generated buffer size by specifying bs or bs
        plus bu. If:

        bu = CHARACTERS or bu parameter absent

              the buffer size used is bs rounded up to words then rounded up again to a
              multiple of 448 words.

        bu = WORDS

              the buffer size used is bs rounded up to a multiple of 448 words.

        bu = RECORDS

              the buffer size used is (rounded up to a multiple of 448 words):

             bs * (mrl + 2 + ndk) + 6

              where:

              mrl

                is the maximum record length (in words)

              ndk

                is the number of keys with duplicates in an indexed file

              This is the same formula that the COBOL compiler uses; however, no minimum
              size check is made. Thus, you can specify fewer than 10 records per block.

        Specifying the Number of Buffers
        Through DFP, you can alter the compiler generated number of buffers by specifying a
        DFP BLOCK bn parameter in the range 5 through 63 for OUTPUT and I-O and 4 through
        63 for INPUT. If bn is less than the compiler generated value, only the top level index
        block for the RECORD key is locked into main storage at run-time. If bn is 4, no index
        blocks are locked into main storage.

        If the BLOCK bn parameter is out of range, the value is ignored. You will obtain the
        default (4 buffers), plus one buffer for each key, plus the number specified on the
        SELECT statement RESERVE n AREAS, minus one.




5ΓÇô6                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                       Using System Interfaces




         Block Loading Factor
         The DFP bl parameter is equivalent to the integer-1 field in a BLOCK CONTAINS
         integer-1 TO integer-2 ... clause.

         The block loading factor is the number of words reserved in a block at file creation
         time and is calculated as

           ((bs - bl) / bs) * buffer size

         If bs is not present, or if bl is not less than bs, the bl parameter is ignored.

5.3.3. Record Formats
         The rf parameter of the RECORD keyword parameter list provided by the DFP is
         allowed for INTERCHANGE and System Data Format (SDF) files only. No validation
         checks on the parameter values specified are made at run time.

           RECORD = /rf

         where rf can be


                    Parameter
                      Value                Meaning        FCB Value

                U               Undefined                 01
                F               Fixed                     02
                D               Variable                  03
                FB              Fixed-blocked             04
                DB              Variable-blocked          05
                FS              Fixed-segmented           06
                DS              Variable-segmented        07
                FBS             Fixed-blocked-segmented   010
                VBS             Variable-blocked-         011
                                segmented

5.3.4. Prep Factors
         The PREP keyword parameter is valid only for mass storage files.

           PREP = pf

         For RELATIVE files (direct access), the pf parameter can be coded as 112, 224, 448,
         896, or 1792.

         Note: Any other values of pf are rounded down to the next value allowed for
         RELATIVE files.

Using System Interfaces




5.3.5. Label Records
        The LABEL keyword parameter list is

          LABEL = lt/li

        lt is the label type parameter. It can be coded as


                Label Type Parameter      FCB Value

             OMITTED                           1
             STANDARD                          3

        Although this parameter is provided via DFP, complete freedom of choice is not
        possible because of the label routine collection requirements. This parameter can
        change the amount of label handling performed on a file only to a lower state than
        was declared in the source program. More precisely:



               Stated Source Program       Allowable lt Value

             STANDARD                   STANDARD,OMITTED
             OMITTED                    OMITTED

        If this parameter is used to change the label processing functions specified in the
        source program, the physical files that are to be processed must conform to the
        ΓÇ£newΓÇ¥ mode of processing stated, where li is the file identifier parameter. It can be
        from 1 to 17 characters in length. It is left justified and space filled.

        Note: The li parameter can only be specified for SDF sequential and relative disk
        files.

5.3.6. EBCDIC Translate
        The OPTIONS keyword parameter is

          OPTIONS = A

        where A indicates that for an EBCDIC file, a 256-character EBCDIC/ASCII translate table
        is used. Absence of the A parameter indicates a 128-character translate is used.




5ΓÇô8                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                          Using System Interfaces




5.3.7. OPEN Parameter
         The OPEN parameter gives the status of the file at open time. It is coded as

           OPEN = os

         where os is the open status and is interpreted as


          Parameter    FCB Value                                  Meaning

         NEW               01      Removes the effect of the OPEN statement EXTEND option if
                                   specified for a standard TAPE file.
         EXTEND            03      If specified for a standard TAPE file opened for output, the action is
                                   the same as if the OPEN statement had the EXTEND option
                                   specified.

5.3.8. CLOSE Parameter
         The CLOSE parameter specifies the disposition of the file at close time. It is coded as:

           CLOSE = cd

         where cd is the close disposition parameter and is interpreted as


          Parameter    FCB Value                                  Meaning

         REWIND            01      If specified for 1974 Standard TAPE or INTERCHANGE file, the file is
                                   rewound regardless of a no rewind option on the CLOSE statement.
         LEAVE             02      Is specified for 1974 Standard TAPE or INTERCHANGE file, the file is
                                   not rewound at close time.
         FREE              03      If specified for 1974 Standard TAPE or INTERCHANGE file, or SDF file,
                                   the file is freed (@FREE) at close time.

5.3.9. SHARE Parameter
         The SHARE keyword parameter specifies that a file is shared (processed by the
         Shared File System). This parameter is only allowed for RELATIVE and INDEXED I-O
         files. The format is

           SHARE = shr

         where the value of shr equals one of the following values:

             YES      the file is to be processed by the Shared File System (SFS).

             NO       the file is to be processed by PCIOS.

         See 5.5 for more information about specifying shared files.

Using System Interfaces




5.3.10. Concatenation of Data Files
        Concatenation of data files allows the system to process separate UCS COBOL
        physical files as one UCS COBOL logical file. Accomplish this by linking the DFB of
        each file. The first and subsequent DFBs must be available through the general
        interface mechanism described at the beginning of this subsection. All DFB keyword
        parameters are interpreted from the first DFB; only LABEL-ID, OPEN, and CLOSE
        parameters are interpreted from each subsequent DFB.

        File concatenation is limited to the input (forward only) mode of ANSI TAPE,
        INTERCHANGE, and SDF sequential DISC files. Concatenation of a set of UCS COBOL
        files is allowed only on component files of the same file format, and uniform labeling
        conventions must exist for all component files. A component file is one of several
        files that compose a concatenated file, and a concatenated file is the entire collection
        of COBOL files that are processed as a single logical file.

        When a data file of the type just mentioned is opened for input, the concatenation
        field of the DFB is checked if a DFB exists for that file. If the field is zero,
        concatenation terminates. If nonzero, the field contains the element name for the DFB
        of the next file in the concatenation chain. All DFBs must be accessible in a file DFP$
        either by assigning the file as DFP$ or by linking it to DFP$ with a @USE statement.

        When an end-of-file is detected on an input file that has a DFB, the concatenation field
        of the DFB is checked. If concatenation is specified, the system automatically closes
        the present file observing the DFB CLOSE parameter, retrieves the next DFB, and
        opens the data file specified in the DFB. If the DFP OPEN parameter for this file is
        OPEN=OLD and the file was cataloged, it is also automatically assigned. Processing of
        the input file continues as if no end-of-file had occurred. A true end-of-file condition is
        not raised until the processing of the last record of the final component file is
        complete.

        The SELECT statement in the COBOL program for the concatenation file can specify
        the OPTIONAL clause but, if the first component file is present, all other component
        files must be present. If the first component file is not present, the entire
        concatenation file is treated as not present.

        The following example shows how to use the Define File Processor to produce the
        define file blocks required to concatenate three component files:

          @DFP,E    F1.,DFP$.FA,DFP$.FB         Keyword parameters describing F1*
          @DFP,E    F2.,DFP$.FB,DFP$.FC         Keyword parameters describing F2*
          @EOF
          @DFP,E    F3.,DFP$.FC                 Keyword parameters describing F3*
          @EOF

        You must assign file DFP$. Files F1, F2, and F3 must be preassigned, or they must be
        cataloged with OPEN parameters of OPEN=OLD, in which case the run dynamically
        assigns them.




5ΓÇô10                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                      Using System Interfaces




         The COBOL source lines to process these files as a single logical file have the form:

             SELECT FA ASSIGN TO implementor-name.
                .
                .
                .
             OPEN INPUT FA.
             READ FA AT END imperative-statement.

         The system does not execute the imperative-statement until it reaches an end-of-file
         on file F3.


5.4. Accessing the Processor Common
     Input/Output System (PCIOS)
         The Processor Common Input/Output System (PCIOS) serves as the default link
         between UCS COBOL programs and data files. For a complete discussion of PCIOS,
         refer to the PCIOS Administration and Programming Reference Manual.


5.5. Accessing the Shared File System (SFS)
         The Shared File System (SFS) can be used for Relative I-O (DSDF) and Indexed I-O
         (MSAM) to serve as a link between UCS COBOL programs and input/output devices.
         For a complete discussion of SFS, refer to the SFS Administration and Support
         Reference Manual.

         This interface allows multithread access to files. These files can be processed singly
         or concurrently in a multithread environment and designated as recoverable. Use one
         of the following methods to designate a file as shared:

         ∩é╖    At compilation time, specify A-SHARED-FILE as the implementor-name-1 on the
              ASSIGN clause in the SELECT clause. This method causes all DFP processing for
              the file to be bypassed.
         ∩é╖    At run time, use the SHARE parameter for DFP. (See 5.3.)

         Rollback and Deadlock Situations
         The Shared File System provides concurrent file access, as well as file recovery. When
         the Shared File System returns a rollback or deadlock status, UCS COBOL takes error
         processing actions, depending on whether the user program has done either or both
         of the following:

         ∩é╖    Specified a FILE STATUS clause in the file control entry of the shared file
         ∩é╖    Defined a USE procedure for the shared file in the declarative portion of the
              Procedure Division

         The UCS COBOL error processing actions are summarized in Table 5ΓÇô1.

               When an internal rollback or deadlock occurs, and the file is declared as
               recoverable, all updates not yet committed are lost.



        If you specify a FILE STATUS to detect rollback or deadlock, it must be defined as
        follows:

          01      F-STATUS
                  02   STATUS-KEY-1 PIC X.
                  02   STATUS-KEY-2 PIC 99 BINARY.

        If STATUS-KEY-1 contains a value of 9, error processing is handled as described in

         procedure name to which the called program requires the calling program to jump.

5.8. Changing the Sort-Merge Main Storage Size
         The execution of a sort or merge requires additional main storage starting at the point
         where the compiler encounters the SORT or MERGE statement. The compiler
         dynamically allocates additional space when it encounters the SORT or MERGE
         statement, and releases the space at the completion of the SORT or MERGE
         statement. Thus, if more than one sort or merge is present in a program, the additional
         space is needed only when a sort or merge is executing.

         You can dynamically change the amount of main storage needed for a sort or merge
         by using the R$CORE feature. Use this feature by doing a mass storage assignment of
         a file called R$CORE. The system uses the maximum granularity on this assign to
         determine the amount of main storage that the sort or merge requires. The UCS
         COBOL library multiplies the maximum granularity on the @ASG,T R$CORE statement
         by 1,000 to determine the actual amount of storage to dynamically assign. For
         example, specify a 14K sort-merge area as follows:

              @ASG,T R$CORE.,f///14

         In the absence of an R$CORE statement, the system uses 30K as the storage
         assignment.


5.9. System Constraints for DENSITY Clause
         The DENSITY clause sets the number of lines per inch for printer output. The value
         specified in the clause is subject to the following system constraints:

         1.    If DENSITY IS identifier clause is specified, identifier can contain only the values
               6, 8, or 12. Any other value causes the printer default to be used.
         2.    Following is a list of rules governing the relationship between DENSITY and
               LINAGE values:
               a.   If the resultant DENSITY is 6, the resultant LINAGE must be a value less than
                    84.
               b. If the resultant DENSITY is 8, the resultant LINAGE must be a value less than
                  109.
               c.   If the resultant DENSITY is 12, the resultant LINAGE must be a value less than
                    167.

         See the UCS COBOL Programming Reference Manual Volume 1 for more information
         about the DENSITY clause.

Using System Interfaces




5.10. Interpreting Operator Console Messages
        Several UCS COBOL statements send messages to the operator console during
        execution. The following subsections list and describe these messages.

5.10.1. ACCEPT . . . FROM CONSOLE
        While running in the batch mode, an ACCEPT command displays a console message

          "ENTER DATA"- - - - -

        for every 50 characters of data that must be entered.

5.10.2. Blank Tape
        A blank tape, assigned without a specified reel number that must have a label, displays
        a console message

          ENTER NUMBER OF BLANK ON /NN

        You can use any 6-character reply.

5.10.3. DISPLAY . . . UPON CONSOLE
        While using batch mode, a DISPLAY command displays a console message for every
        50 characters displayed.

5.10.4. Unlabeled Tape
        When a file is opened, the following message displays on the console if you specify
        label records that are standard for a file assigned to an output tape reel but that are
        not 8-bit labeled:

          LOAD PROPERLY LABELED REEL { llllll } file-name AE

        The llllll specifies the logical device name on which the prelabeled reel is to be
        mounted. The file-name is the external file name specified in the ASSIGN clause for
        the file.

        The operator is given an opportunity to mount a properly labeled tape. The operator
        can then respond with an A or an E. A response of A causes the ER TLBL$ request to
        be issued again. A response of E causes a diagnostic message 36001 to be issued and
        the program to abort.




5ΓÇô16                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                   Using System Interfaces




5.10.5. VALUE OF CARTRIDGE-ID
         If a file has specified a VALUE OF CARTRIDGE-ID clause, execution of either the OPEN
         statement for a nonreport file or the INITIATE statement for a report file can produce
         the following console messages:

           sname xx IN,yy REQUESTED USE IN? YN

           sname MOUNT CARTRIDGE yy A

         A complete description of these messages can be found in the Exec Operations
         Reference Manual Volume 1.

5.10.6. VALUE OF FORMS-REQUEST
         If a file has specified a VALUE OF FORMS-REQUEST clause, execution of either the
         OPEN statement for a nonreport file or the INITIATE statement for a report file
         produces the following console message:

           x - SPECIAL FORMS REQ

         where x is the 24-character alphanumeric field specified in the VALUE OF
         FORMS-REQUEST clause. The field cannot contain any periods.

Section 6
Accessing a DMS Database

         UCS COBOL programs can access a network database through the interface to the
         Data Management System (DMS). This access is possible by inserting COBOL Data
         Manipulation Language (CDML) commands into the Data and Procedure Divisions of
         your COBOL program. The UCS COBOL compiler then syntactically analyzes these
         commands as it compiles your program.

         UCS COBOL also has an interface to the Unisys Repository Manager (UREP), which
         complements the DMS interface. This additional access provides your program with a
         means of
         ∩é╖    Generating UCS COBOL code from schema and subschema definitions that are
              stored in a UREP repository
         ∩é╖    Inserting the generated code into your program

         This section describes the UCS COBOL interface with the Data Management System
         (DMS). See the COBOL Data Manipulation Language Operations and Programming
         Reference Manual for the syntax and examples of the CDML statements. Also, see
         Section 8 for a description of the UCS COBOL interface to UREP, and Section 7 for
         information about accessing a DMS database.


6.1. The UCS COBOL Interface
         To compile and link a UCS COBOL program containing CDML statements, perform the
         following steps:
         1.   Invoke the Data Definition Language (DDL) processor.
              Input to DDL includes your source schema describing the application database
              both physically and logically. DDL and SDDL use internal metaschemas and a
              meta-database to record information needed to define object subschema tables
              for the source schema.
              Output from DDL is the object schema for your application.
         2.   Invoke the Subschema Data Definition Language (SDDL) calling the processor.
              Input to SDDL includes your source subschema, which is a subset of the schema
              giving a logical view of all or part of the database. Again, SDDL uses internal
              metaschemas and the meta-database during processing.
              Output from SDDL consists of the following:
              ∩é╖   Object subschema tables
                  The tables are analogous to the DDL object schema for the application.


7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               6ΓÇô1
Accessing a DMS Database




            ∩é╖   Symbolic element S$PROC/subschema-name
                This element describes the records and database names that you can use in
                CDML statements. It is included automatically in the UCS COBOL compilation.
                See F.2.27 for rules on duplicate names.
            ∩é╖   Object module S$WORK/subschema-name
                Include this module as input to the Linking System.

       3.   Compile the UCS COBOL program with embedded CDML statements. Note that an
            INVOKE clause can appear only in the first program of a series of separately
            compiled programs in a single source element (back-to-back programs). In
            addition, the INVOKE can occur only in the outermost program of nested
            subprograms.
            Input to the UCS COBOL compiler consists of the following:
            ∩é╖   UCS COBOL program
            ∩é╖   Object subschema tables created by the SDDL processor
            ∩é╖   S$PROC/subschema-name, created by the SDDL processor
            Output from the UCS COBOL compiler is an object module that you can execute
            directly or use as input to the Linking System.
            Note: If the schema and subschema source (DDL and SDDL) are processed
            with COBOL85 syntax, then the COMPAT and COMP-BIN keyword options
            cannot be used on the UCOB compilation.
       4. Link the program with information from SDDL.
            Input consists of the following:
            ∩é╖   UCS COBOL output module
            ∩é╖   S$WORK from SDDL
            Output is a statically linked object module Data Manipulation Language (DML)
            program.

       The DML program then executes through the Data Management Routine (DMR), using
       the object schema and subschema to access and update data in the database.

       For more information, see the DMS DDL Administration, Operations, and
       Programming Guide and the DMS SDDL Administration, Operations, and
       Programming Guide.

       Figure 6ΓÇô1 gives a conceptual overview of how a UCS COBOL program interfaces with
       DMS.

6.3. Database Key Usage
         Care should be taken when manipulating values within data items that are declared as
         USAGE DATABASE-KEY. The data type of an item declared as a DATABASE-KEY is the
         same as if it had been declared as PIC 9(10) BINARY. A data item declared as 9(10)
         BINARY is stored internally as 1 word (36 bits).

         Even though a database key is declared as 9(10) BINARY, it can actually hold a value
         that is more than 10 digits in length. As long as the database key is moved to/from
         another database key or data item declared as 9(10) BINARY, the full value is moved
         (no truncation occurs). If you move a data item not declared as 9(10) BINARY (e.g. PIC
         1(36) BINARY-1) to a database key, truncation of the left most digits can occur. This is
         described in F.2.1. If you do not want the decimal truncation to occur, the keyword
         option COMPAT should be used. See COMPAT in 2.2.7 for additional details.

         If a user needs to manipulate various portions of a database key, first move it to a field
         that is declared as 9(10) BINARY and is redefined into the individual fields. Update the
         individual fields as desired and then move the data item declared as 9(10) BINARY back
         to the database key. For example:

            01 DBK1 USAGE DATABASE-KEY.
            01 D1 PIC 9(10) BINARY.
            01 D2 REDEFINES D1.
               02 D2-1 PIC 1(9) BINARY-1.
               02 D2-2 PIC 1(18) BINARY-1.
               02 D2-3 PIC 1(9) BINRAY-1.

           MOVE DBK1 TO D1.
           ADD 5 TO D2-3.
           MOVE D1 TO DBK1.

         The above example works the same whether or not the COMPAT keyword option is
         used. Since the database key was moved to and from a data item declared as 9(10)
         BINARY, no decimal truncation occurs.

Accessing a DMS Database

Section 7
Accessing a Relational Database

         UCS COBOL programs can query, retrieve, and update data from a relational database.
         You accomplish this by inserting Structured Query Language (SQL) commands into
         your UCS COBOL program.

         The UCS COBOL compiler accepts SQL instructions and calls the Relational Data
         Management System (RDMS 2200), which includes the processor that

         1.   Interprets the SQL commands and Unisys SQL extensions in your UCS COBOL
              program
         2.   Performs the requested task

         RDMS is part of the Universal Data System (UDS), which provides a unified system for
         developing, processing, and managing UCS language applications using databases.
         UDS also contains the Unisys Repository (UREP), which you use to create and manage
         the definitions for the relational tables accessed with RDMS (see the Enterprise
         Servers Repository for ClearPath OS 2200 Programming Reference Manual).

         UCS COBOL programs can access a relational database using the following methods:

         ∩é╖    Embedded SQL
              Include SQL commands directly in the program. RDMS parses the embedded SQL
              syntax as each command is compiled. Each command is then executed at run
              time.
         ∩é╖    Interpreted SQL
              Code SQL commands in an ENTER MASM statement. RDMS parses the SQL
              syntax as each command is executed. After parsing the syntax, RDMS processes
              the requested task.

         Figure 7ΓÇô1 illustrates these interfaces. Both methods pass values to and from the
         relational database with UCS COBOL variables that are declared in the UCS COBOL
         program. See 7.3 for the UCS COBOL equivalents to the types that RDMS uses to
         accept or store data. See the SQL Programming Reference Manual for more
         information about using SQL to access an RDMS database.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                7ΓÇô1
Accessing a Relational Database




         Using Interpreted SQL

7.1. Using SQL Commands in a UCS COBOL
     Program
         To use SQL commands in your UCS COBOL program, you must perform the following
         steps:

         1.   Declare any variables needed by SQL commands in your host program.
              See 7.2 for a description of the required variables and how to declare them. See
              7.3 for the correspondence of data types between RDMS and UCS COBOL.
         2.   Code the SQL commands in your program source.
              ∩é╖   For embedded SQL, code the commands directly in your source program
                  (see 7.4).
              ∩é╖   For interpreted SQL, code the commands within ENTER MASM statements in
                  your source program (see 7.5).
         3.   Compile the program (see 7.7). For embedded SQL, use the APPLICATION
              compiler keyword option to specify an application group. The UCS COBOL
              compiler produces an object module that contains your UCS COBOL instructions
              and the processed SQL statements. The processed SQL statements are ready for
              execution, using the same application group specified in the APPLICATION
              keyword option.
         4. Link the program object module with the Linking System, if you want to statically
            link your program (see 7.8).
              Alternatively, you can dynamically link your program.
         5.   Execute your program.

         This section contains an example coded both in embedded SQL. The program accepts
         an employee number as input and displays the information contained in a database
         about the employeeΓÇÖs family. The following tables are used in the example.

Accessing a Relational Database

        INDIVIDUALR

           is a table whose primary key is the individualΓÇÖs employee number
           (INDR-EMP-NUMBER). The table has a secondary index consisting of the
           individualΓÇÖs name
           (indr-last-name, indr-first-name).

        SCHOOL

           is a table whose primary key is the schoolΓÇÖs unique number (SCH-NUMBER).

        CHILD

           is a table whose primary key is the individualΓÇÖs employee number
           (CHILD-EMP-NUMBER) and the sequence of the child within the family
           (CHILD-NUMBER). The table has a secondary index consisting of the childΓÇÖs name
           (child-last-name, child-first-name).

           The childΓÇÖs school number (child-school-number) is a foreign key to the SCHOOL
           table.

7.2. Declaring Variables for SQL Commands
         In most database applications involving programming languages, you need to pass
         information between your program and RDMS. The variables in your program are
         called host program variables. They are UCS COBOL variable names and are declared
         according to their context in the program. They are not part of the SQL statement but
         are used to pass data to and from RDMS, including error information.

         The mechanism and procedure for passing variables depend on the interface, as
         follows:

         ∩é╖    Embedded SQL
              Host program variables are embedded directly in the command string and become
              known as embedded variables. See 7.2.1 and 7.2.2 for the requirements of
              embedded SQL data and error variables.
         ∩é╖    Interpreted SQL
              The command string contains placeholder variables (see 7.2.3) that correspond to
              host program variables, which contain the values to be passed.

         This subsection describes how to declare the necessary variables appropriately. See
         7.4 and 7.5 for the actual coding of embedded and interpreted SQL statements.

7.2.1. Embedded SQL Data Variables
         Any data-item that can be referenced as an identifier in a COBOL statement can be
         referenced in the same manner as an embedded SQL command, subject to the
         restrictions in 7.3.2 and 7.3.3. However, the SQL standard requires you to declare all
         COBOL variables that are used by embedded SQL commands within the
         WORKING-STORAGE SECTION or COMMON-STORAGE SECTION of the host program.
         The format for this declaration section is

                  EXEC SQL BEGIN DECLARE SECTION END-EXEC.

             01   sql-variable                data-description.

                  EXEC SQL END DECLARE SECTION END-EXEC.

         where:

         EXEC SQL BEGIN DECLARE SECTION END-EXEC

              defines the beginning of the SQL declaration section.

         sql-variable

              is a variable data item declared as level 01 or 77. The permitted UCS COBOL types
              are listed in 7.3.2 and 7.3.3.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               7ΓÇô5
Accessing a Relational Database




        data-description

             is the UCS COBOL syntax that defines the data item (for example, PIC S9(9)
             COMP).

        EXEC SQL END DECLARE SECTION END-EXEC

             defines the end of the SQL declaration section.

        In an embedded SQL command, it is nonstandard to reference variables that are not
        declared in the SQL declaration section. The compiler issues warning messages for
        nonstandard syntax or host-variable references within an embedded SQL command
        when you specify the compiler keyword option LEVEL/SQL at compilation time. The
        messages have the following form:

            WARNING(LEVEL-SQL)

        The LEVEL/SQL keyword option is separate from the other LEVEL keyword options.
        LEVEL/SQL can be used in addition to other LEVEL keyword options and does not
        cancel them.

        In compliance with the SQL standard, a program can have multiple DECLARE sections,
        which are limited to the WORKING-STORAGE SECTION or COMMON-STORAGE
        SECTION. However, DECLARE sections cannot be nested and they cannot overlap.

7.2.2. Embedded SQL Error Variables
        RDMS uses special variables to pass information to the program about errors that
        occur during the execution of an embedded SQL command. The only exception is the
        GETERROR command; it does not affect the contents of these variables.

        To be able to use these variables in the Procedure Division to check for errors, you
        must declare them in the Data Division. You can use either of the following data
        structures:

        ∩é╖    SQLSTATE
        ∩é╖    SQLCODE
        ∩é╖    RDMCA variables ERROR-STATUS and AUX-INFO

        If the keyword option LEVEL/SQL is in effect, the absence of the proper declaration of
        either SQLCODE or SQLSTATE will be flagged.

        Refer to the SQL Programming Reference Manual for SQL coding techniques to
        access these variables and for the meaning of the values in them.




7ΓÇô6                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                         Accessing a Relational Database




         Error Code Variable SQLSTATE
         The variable SQLSTATE is always a part of the embedded SQL in your program. RDMS
         uses it to return the status of each embedded SQL command, except the GETERROR
         command. To access the value of SQLSTATE, include either of the following
         definitions in the declaration section for SQL:

             01 SQLSTATE PIC X(5) USAGE DISPLAY.

             77 SQLSTATE PIC X(5) USAGE DISPLAY.

         This declaration conforms to the SQL 92 standard. If SQLSTATE is not declared in this
         way, a MINOR diagnostic error will be produced stating that SQLSTATE will not
         contain the RDMS return status after the execution of an embedded SQL command.

         Error Code Variable SQLCODE
         The variable SQLCODE is always a part of the embedded SQL in your program. RDMS
         uses it to return the status of each embedded SQL command, except the GETERROR
         command. To access the value of SQLCODE, include the following definition in the
         declaration section for SQL:

             01 SQLCODE   PIC S9(9) USAGE COMPUTATIONAL.

         This declaration conforms to the 1989 SQL standard. For efficiency, you can declare
         SQLCODE with a usage of BINARY; however, the compiler flags this usage as
         nonstandard when you specify the LEVEL/SQL compiler keyword option.

         Note: Standard SQL states that SQLSTATE is the preferred status variable and
         SQLCODE will be removed at a later date from a revised version of standard SQL.

         RDMCA Variables ERROR-STATUS and AUX-INFO
         In addition to SQLCODE and SQLSTATE, you can use the variables ERROR-STATUS and
         AUX-INFO in the structure RDMCA. RDMS uses these variables to return the status
         and auxiliary information of each embedded SQL command, except the GETERROR
         command, analogous to the way the interpreter interface uses the second and third
         variables on the ENTER MASM statement (see 7.2.3). You may find them easier to use
         than SQLCODE if you are migrating to embedded SQL from interpreted SQL.

         These variables must be defined to meet the following criteria:

         ∩é╖    Defined with a parent of RDMCA
         ∩é╖    Defined in the SQL declaration section of the program
         ∩é╖    Defined without other clauses




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               7ΓÇô7
Accessing a Relational Database




        Use the following declaration for these variables in your program:
          01     RDMCA.
                 02 ERROR-STATUS PIC 9(4).
                 02 AUX-INFO     PIC S9(9) BINARY.

        where:

        ERROR-STATUS
            is the variable into which RDMS places the status of each command.

        AUX-INFO
            is the variable that receives the column position if RDMS detects an error. It also
            receives auxiliary information for a DELETE, INSERT, LOCATE, REVOKE, UNLOAD,
            or UPDATE command.

        To interpret the values that RDMS assigns to these error variables, see the SQL
        Programming Reference Manual.

7.2.3. Interpreted SQL Variables
        The interpreter interface requires markers, called placeholder variables, in the
        command string for any values that must be passed to or from RDMS. Placeholder
        variables simply mark a place in the command string corresponding to a value the
        command expects. When you call the interpreter interface and pass the command
        string with its placeholder variables, you also pass a list of host program variables
        containing the actual values the command must use. A host program variable must
        correspond to each placeholder variable in the command string.
        The interpreter interface also uses two variables in the statement for reporting the
        command status, including both normal completion and error information.
        Use the ENTER MASM statement to call the interpreter interface. It has the following
        format, where variable names must occur sequentially in the order specified.
        Format
          ENTER MASM ΓÇÖACOB$RDMRΓÇÖ
            USING sql-command
                  error-status
                  auxiliary-information
                [ program-variable-1
                  program-variable-2
                           .
                           .
                           .
                  program-variable-n ] .

        where:

        sql-command
            is a thread control or SQL command. Refer to 7.5.1 for more information on the
            contents of this variable and an example.



7ΓÇô8                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                         Accessing a Relational Database




         error-status

            contains the completion status of the SQL command on exit from the ENTER
            MASM statement. It is the second field in the ENTER MASM statement. It is
            declared as a PIC 9999 DISPLAY or COMP item in the UCS COBOL program. If its
            value is ΓÇÖ0000ΓÇÖ the command completed normally.

         auxiliary-information

            contains useful information about error-status on exit from the ENTER MASM
            statement. It is the third field in the ENTER MASM statement. It is declared as a
            PIC S1(36) BINARY-1 item in the UCS COBOL program.

         program-variable-n

            is a UCS COBOL variable name (a host variable) that is associated with an SQL
            placeholder variable. The number of these host variables must be equal to or
            greater than the number of distinct placeholder variables required for the SQL
            command. The list of host variable names follows auxiliary-information in the
            ENTER MASM statement. You must declare each program-variable-n in your UCS
            COBOL program.

         A value of ΓÇÖ0000ΓÇÖ for error-status means the command completed normally. Refer to
         the SQL Programming Reference Manual for the possible values for error-status and
         the associated values for auxiliary-information, depending on the SQL command
         used.

7.2.4. Binary Large Objects ΓÇô BLOBs
         From a database perspective, a Binary Large Object (BLOB) is a binary string whose
         format is known only to the application that stores or retrieves the value. Typical
         applications may be scanned documents, photographed images, and audio messages.

         BLOB variables can be used in both the embedded and interpreted methods.For both
         methods, the BLOB variable must be declared within the EXEC SQL BEGIN DECLARE
         SECTION described in 7.2.1.

         Program host BLOB variables can be inserted into or fetched from the database. The
         equivalent SQL data type (column definition) is BLOB.

USAGE SQL TYPE IS BLOB
         USAGE SQL is a special USAGE for passing information to and from a relational item
         defined as a BLOB. It can be used to define a COBOL item used as a host-variable in
         either an embedded SQL statement or an interpreted SQL statement. This data type
         may be used wherever a host-variable may be specified, but must be used only on a
         variable declared as a level 01 item and may not be used with any other USAGE clause.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               7ΓÇô9
Accessing a Relational Database




        Format
        Integer n[K | M] is the maximum length for the BLOB host program variable, in bytes.
        The maximum length can be specified as a simple integer representing the number of
        bytes or as an integer followed by one of the following suffixes:

        ∩é╖     K, kilobytes
              210 or 1,024 bytes; 2K is interpreted as 2,048 bytes
        ∩é╖     M, megabytes
              220 or 1,048,576 bytes

             01   blobname USAGE IS SQL      TYPE IS BLOB {(n[K]) }

        or

             01   blobname USAGE IS SQL      TYPE IS BLOB {(n[M]) }

        General Rules:
        If USAGE SQL is specified, the following structure is created by the compiler:

             01 blobname.
                   02   blobname-reserved                  PIC S9(9) BINARY.
                   02   blobname-length                    PIC S9(9) BINARY.
                   02   blobname-data                      PIC X(blob-name-specifier).

        where:

        blob-name-specifier = n

              if only integer specified

        blob-name-specifier = n*1024

              if nK is specified

        blob-name-specifier = n*1048576

              if nM is specified

        The compiler expands the BLOB declaration into a structure that consists of two
        words (8 bytes) of control information and an alphanumeric field that holds the BLOB
        data. The declaration as expanded by the compiler consists of the following items:

        ∩é╖     Structure name, blobname
              The same as the original blobname from the SQL declaration. The generated
              structure tag name in the program can be used as you would with any standard
              UCS COBOL group name. The blobname can be used as a host variable in a SQL
              statement to match the corresponding RDMS column definition of BLOB.




7ΓÇô10                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                           Accessing a Relational Database




         ∩é╖    The structure member, blobname-reserved
              The original blobname with a suffix of -reserved. This is reserved for future use.
              This field must be set to zero when a BLOB is used as an input item to the
              database (for example, used in an INSERT command).
         ∩é╖    Structure member, blobname-length
              The original blobname with a suffix of -length. You are responsible for setting this
              field to the byte length of the alphanumeric field that holds the BLOB data when
              the BLOB is used as an input item in a SQL statement (for example, an INSERT
              command). This size is used by RDMS when transferring the BLOB from the BLOB
              program variable to the database.
              When a BLOB is used as an output item in a SQL statement, (for example, a
              FETCH command) RDMS sets the blobname length field to the byte length of the
              BLOB. This field defines the byte length of the BLOB data, blobname-data. The
              length does not include the 8-byte size of the BLOB control information.
         ∩é╖    Structure member, blobname-data
              The original blobname with a suffix of -data. You are responsible for setting this
              field when the BLOB is used as in input item in an SQL statement. When a BLOB is
              used as an output item in a SQL statement, RDMS sets this field. If truncation
              occurs on output from the database to the host program variable, the BLOB's
              corresponding indicator variable is set to the declared byte length of the BLOB
              column definition.

         Examples
             01 blob1 USAGE IS SQL TYPE IS BLOB (5000).
             01 blob2 USAGE IS SQL TYPE IS BLOB (500K).
             01 blob3 USAGE IS SQL TYPE IS BLOB (200M).

         These declarations result in the following data structures:

             01 blob1.
                02 blob1-reserved          PIC S9(9) BINARY.
                02 blob1-length        PIC S9(9) BINARY.
                02 blob1-data              PIC X(5000).

             01 blob2.
                02 blob2-reserved          PIC S9(9) BINARY.
                02 blob2-length        PIC S9(9) BINARY.
                02 blob2-data             PIC X(512000).

             01 blob3.
                02 blob3-reserved         PIC S9(9) BINARY.
                02 blob3-length        PIC S9(9) BINARY.
                02 blob3-data              PIC X(209715200).




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 7ΓÇô11
Accessing a Relational Database




BLOB Size Limits
        Static BLOBs
        For a BLOB, blob-name-specifier can be in the range 1 to 67,108,852 bytes. The limit is
        based on the largest single object that is addressable by compiler-generated code.
        The largest a single object can be is 224-1 words or 67,108,860 bytes. The actual BLOB
        size allocated by the compiler is blob-name-specifier + 8 where 8 represents control
        information (the reserved word and the length word).

        Automatic BLOBs
        For a BLOB allocated in automatic storage, blob-size-specifier is dependent on how
        many other automatic storage variables are declared in the function. The size of the
        activity level stack (ALS) is 262,143 words. However, the compiler limits the total
        automatic storage size for a given function to 196,608 words or 786,432 bytes. In
        addition to program variables, compiler-generated temporaries are allocated on the
        ALS. The execution flow of the program must also be taken into account since each
        invocation of a function obtains a stack frame on the ALS. Based on these facts, an
        exact limit cannot be documented for BLOBs allocated in automatic storage. As with
        any large object such as an array or structure, you must use your own judgment when
        using automatic storage.

                   IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
                   PROGRAM-ID. cobol-update2.
                   ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.
                   CONFIGURATION SECTION.
                   SOURCE-COMPUTER. Unisys-2200.
                   OBJECT-COMPUTER. Unisys-2200.
                   SPECIAL-NAMES.
                      PRINTER IS PRINTER.

                   DATA DIVISION.

                   WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.

                      01 n-c1                 PIC 9(10) BINARY.
                      01 n-b1                 SQL TYPE IS BLOB(10K).
                      01 n-b2                 SQL TYPE IS BLOB(10K).
                      01 n-b3                 SQL TYPE IS BLOB(10K).
                      01 n-c2                 PIC 9(10) BINARY.
                      01 n-char1              PIC X(20).

                      01 d-b2                 SQL TYPE IS BLOB(10K).
                      01 d-b3                 SQL TYPE IS BLOB(10K).
