7.3. Data Types for Passing Values between RDMS
     and UCS COBOL
        This subsection describes the correspondence of data types for passing values
        between RDMS and a UCS COBOL program.

7.3.1. Equivalent Data Types
        RDMS and UCS COBOL each define specific data types. Some data types require
        conversion when passed; other data types are equivalent and do not require
        conversion. Table 7ΓÇô1 identifies the equivalent data types for UCS COBOL and RDMS.
        To avoid unnecessary conversion and the resulting overhead, use equivalent types for
        corresponding data items.


          Table 7ΓÇô1. Equivalent Data Types for UCS COBOL and RDMS


                RDMS Data Types                 UCS COBOL Data Declarations

         CHARACTER(n)                   X(n)
                                        A(n)
         NCHARACTER(n)                  X(n) usage disp-21
         DECIMAL(d,s)                   S9(d-s-1)v9(s) sign leading separate2
         NUMERIC(d,s)                   S9(d-s)v9(s) usage binary3
         INTEGER                        S9(10) usage binary
                                        S9(9) usage comp-5
                                        S1(36) usage binary-1
         SMALLINT                       S9(5) usage binary
                                        S9(4) usage comp-5
                                        S1(18) usage binary-1
         REAL                           usage comp-1
         DOUBLE PRECISION               usage comp-2
         FLOAT(p)                       usage comp-14
                                        usage comp-24
         DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP          X(n)5
         BLOB                           usage is SQL, type is BLOB.

                                                           Accessing a Relational Database




         Legend
         1.   Kanji characters
         2.   UCS COBOL supports only a value of d ∩éú 19.
         3.   UCS COBOL supports only a value of d ∩éú 18
         4. Depends on the value of p: if p ∩éú 27, use usage comp-1; if p > 27 or not specified,
            use usage comp-2.
         5.   See the Enterprise Relational Database Server for ClearPath OS 2200 SQL
              Programming Reference Manual for appropriate values for n.


7.3.2. Passing Values to RDMS from Program Variables
         If host program variables provide data to RDMS, they can be any of the following data
         types:

         ∩é╖    BINARY (signed or unsigned)
         ∩é╖    BINARY-1 (signed or unsigned)
         ∩é╖    BLOB
         ∩é╖    COMP-1
         ∩é╖    COMP-2
         ∩é╖    COMP-5 (signed)
         ∩é╖    PACKED-DECIMAL (signed or unsigned)
         ∩é╖    Numeric DISPLAY or COMP
              ∩Ç¡   For embedded SQL, these data types can be signed (with any sign position) or
                  unsigned.
              ∩Ç¡   For interpreted SQL, these data types must be signed with the LEADING
                  SEPARATE clause.
         ∩é╖    Alphanumeric (can have the JUSTIFIED attribute)
         ∩é╖    ALPHABETIC (can have the JUSTIFIED attribute)
              This data type is supported for embedded SQL only.
         ∩é╖    Kanji variables

         The following arguments are not supported:
         ∩é╖    Edited numeric program variable arguments
         ∩é╖    Edited alphanumeric arguments
         ∩é╖    Index arguments




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                              7ΓÇô25
Accessing a Relational Database




        An alphabetic program variable argument must correspond to a CHARACTER value;
        that is, a column of type CHARACTER. An alphanumeric program variable argument
        must either correspond to a CHARACTER value, or contain date or time data. If the
        variable contains datetime data, an SQL CAST function must be used. See the
        Enterprise Relational Database Server for ClearPath OS 2200 SQL Programming
        Reference Manual for more information.

        A numeric program variable argument of type BINARY, BINARY-1, COMP-1, COMP-2,
        COMP-5, or PACKED-DECIMAL must correspond to a numeric value of type NUMERIC,
        DECIMAL, INTEGER, REAL, or DOUBLE PRECISION. For numeric variable arguments,
        the UCS Runtime System performs appropriate conversions if the data types are not
        equivalent.

        When used as a host-variable to pass data to RDMS, blobname-data must contain the
        data to be passed and blobname-length must contain the length of the data in bytes.

        Alternate form of qualification:

        If a host variable is declared within a group within the SQL declare section, normal
        UCOB qualification can be used to reference that particular variable. UCOB also allows
        embedded SQL statements to contain a host variable group name followed by a
        period and a data-name. The new name (A.B) is equivalent to using qualification (B of
        A). The alternate qualification method can only be used on two levels of qualification.

        This can be illustrated by the following example:

           IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
           PROGRAM-ID. ESQL-ALT-QUAL.
           ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.
           CONFIGURATION SECTION.
           SOURCE-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
           OBJECT-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
           DATA DIVISION.
           WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
          *****************************************************************
          *     EMBEDDED SQL HOST VARIABLE DECLARATION                    *
          *****************************************************************
                EXEC SQL BEGIN DECLARE SECTION END-EXEC
            01 captain.
                02 qcode                   PIC X(2).
                EXEC SQL END DECLARE SECTION END-EXEC
          *
            PROCEDURE DIVISION.
            BEGIN.
          *
                EXEC SQL DECLARE c9 CURSOR FOR RANDOM FOR
                SELECT * FROM alpha.seed WHERE
                qcode < 'OZ' END-EXEC.
          *
                DISPLAY 'EXEC SQL OPEN c9 END-EXEC'.
                EXEC SQL OPEN c9 END-EXEC.
          *


7ΓÇô26                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                          Accessing a Relational Database




             *****************************************************************
             *    SQL FETCH OF A.B HOST VARIABLE                             *
             *****************************************************************
                  EXEC SQL FETCH FIRST c9 INTO :captain.qcode END-EXEC.
             *****************************************************************
             *    SAME SQL FETCH WITH QUALIFICATION B of A HOST VARIABLE     *
             *****************************************************************
                  EXEC SQL FETCH FIRST c9 INTO :qcode of captain END-EXEC.
                  STOP RUN.

7.3.3. Passing Values from RDMS to Program Variables
         RDMS stores data into the following types of host program variables:

         ∩é╖    BINARY (signed or unsigned)
         ∩é╖    BINARY-1 (signed or unsigned)
         ∩é╖    BLOB
         ∩é╖    COMP-1
         ∩é╖    COMP-2
         ∩é╖    COMP-5 (signed)
         ∩é╖    PACKED-DECIMAL (signed or unsigned)
         ∩é╖    Numeric DISPLAY or COMP
              ∩Ç¡   For embedded SQL, these data types can be signed (with any sign position) or
                  unsigned.
              ∩Ç¡   For interpreted SQL where the receiving data item is signed, the sign must be
                  a separate, leading character.
         ∩é╖    Alphanumeric (can have the JUSTIFIED attribute)
         ∩é╖    ALPHABETIC (can have the JUSTIFIED attribute)
              This data type is supported for embedded SQL only.
         ∩é╖    Kanji variables
         ∩é╖    Edited numeric arguments
              This data type is supported for embedded SQL only.
         ∩é╖    Edited alphanumeric arguments
              This data type is supported for embedded SQL only.

         RDMS does not support any attempt to store into a constant.

         If the host program variable argument is an unsigned numeric item, RDMS strips any
         sign before storing a value into it.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                              7ΓÇô27
Accessing a Relational Database




        You can store any data type in an alphanumeric or edited alphanumeric program
        variable argument. Numeric DISPLAY items are stored as a string with a decimal point
        inserted at the proper position.

        You can store alphanumeric values (RDMS data type CHAR or NCHAR) only in
        alphabetic, alphanumeric, or edited alphanumeric program variable arguments.

        For numeric variable arguments, the UCS Runtime System performs appropriate
        conversions if the data types are not equivalent.

        When used as a host-variable to receive data from RDMS, blobname-data will contain
        the data passed from RDMS and blobname-length will contain the length of the data
        that was passed from RDMS. If the size of blobname-data is not large enough to
        receive the data passed, a truncation error will occur.


7.4. Coding Embedded SQL Commands
        You can place embedded SQL commands directly into your program. The UCS COBOL
        compiler allows RDMS to parse these commands when the program is compiled.

        The two types of embedded SQL commands, static and dynamic, affect the execution
        of your program in different ways. See the Enterprise Relational Database Server for
        ClearPath OS 2200 SQL Programming Reference Manual for a listing of the SQL
        commands you can embed in your program as well as a comparison of the static and
        dynamic commands.

7.4.1. Marking Embedded SQL Commands for the Compiler
        Embedded SQL commands must appear in Area B of the COBOL source line. Except
        for commands that are compiler directives, you can embed SQL commands in the
        Procedure Division wherever a COBOL imperative statement is allowed. The format of
        the embedded commands is the following:

          EXEC SQL sql-command END-EXEC.

        where:

        EXEC SQL

           is the delimiter that defines the beginning of the embedded SQL command.

        sql-command

           is an embedded SQL command.

        END-EXEC

           is the delimiter that terminates the embedded command.




7ΓÇô28                                                                          7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                       Accessing a Relational Database




         You can use the following embedded SQL commands without the beginning and
         ending delimiters:

         ∩é╖    BEGIN THREAD
         ∩é╖    END THREAD
         ∩é╖    COMMIT
         ∩é╖    GETERROR
         ∩é╖    ROLLBACK

         Each of the previous commands must be the only statement in a sentence. Thus, the
         sentence containing one of these commands must end with a period, as follows:

             BEGIN THREAD T1
                FOR APPLICATION APPSVN READ.
             GETERROR INTO T1ERR.

         If you use these commands with the delimiters EXEC SQL and END-EXEC and you
         specify the keyword option LEVEL/SQL at compilation time, the compiler flags the
         statement as nonstandard. If you do not specify the keyword option LEVEL/SQL, the
         compiler does not issue a message.

7.4.2. Example of Using Embedded SQL Commands
         Example 7ΓÇô1 illustrates the use of embedded SQL commands and variables in a UCS
         COBOL program. See 7.1 for a description of the tables used in the program.

              IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
               PROGRAM-ID. DSPFAMESQL.
             ******************************************************************
             ******************************************************************
             *                                                                *
             * SIMPLE BATCH COBOL RDMS EMBEDDED SQL PROGRAM - DSPFAMESQL      *
             *                                                                *
             *         reads the input data                                   *
             *         begins thread with UDS                                 *
             *         retrieves the requested information from the database  *

7.5. Coding Interpreted SQL
         To use the RDMS interpreter interface, embed SQL commands in your UCS COBOL
         program with the ENTER MASM statement. In this method, RDMS parses and
         processes SQL commands as the system encounters them during execution.

7.5.1. Calling the RDMS Interpreter Interface (ENTER MASM)
         Use the following format of the ENTER MASM statement to call the interpreter
         interface, where variable names must occur sequentially in the order specified:

           ENTER MASM ΓÇÖACOB$RDMRΓÇÖ
               USING sql-command
                   error-status
                   auxiliary-information
                 [ program-variable-1
                   program-variable-2
                            .
                            .
                            .
                   program-variable-n ] .

         where:

         sql-command

         is a thread control or SQL command, coded in either of the following ways:

            ∩é╖     As a string constant. This item contains the complete command and any
                  required placeholder variables within apostrophes.
            ∩é╖     As a COBOL variable. This is a nonnumeric DISPLAY item containing the
                  complete command and any required placeholder variables within
                  apostrophes.

         error-status, auxiliary-information, and program-variable-n

            are variables declared in the UCS COBOL program. See 7.2.3 for information on
            declaring these variables.

Accessing a Relational Database




        Example: BEGIN THREAD Command
        To submit a BEGIN THREAD command to the interpreter interface from a UCS COBOL
        program, use the following ENTER MASM statement. The names of the application,
        variables, and thread names are applicable to this example only.

            ENTER MASM ΓÇÖACOB$RDMRΓÇÖ
                USING ΓÇÖBEGIN THREAD T1 FOR APPLICATION APPSVN READ; ΓÇÖ
                    ERRSTAT
                    COLPOS.
            *
                IF ERRSTAT NOT ZERO
                    PERFORM ERRCHK.

        In the previous example,

        ∩é╖    ERRSTAT is the variable declared in the UCS COBOL program to receive the
             completion status.
        ∩é╖    COLPOS is the variable declared in the UCS COBOL program to receive the
             auxiliary information about the outcome of the executed command.
        ∩é╖    If the value of ERRSTAT is not zero, the program branches to an error-handling
             subprogram called ERRCHK.

       Example 7ΓÇô2. UCS COBOL Program Using the Interpreter Interface


7.6. Allocating and Initializing the RDMS Work
     Area (RSA$INIT)
        RDMS provides the subroutine RSA$INIT, which allows you to allocate and initialize all
        the required space for the RDMS work area. Using RSA$INIT reduces the overhead of
        programs that require a large work area. Without the use of RSA$INIT, RDMS initially
        allocates 14,000 words of space for the work area, dynamically acquiring more space
        as it is needed. The overhead incurred to obtain this additional space is expensive and
        should be reduced.

        To specify the size of the RDMS work area, do the following steps:

        1.    Determine the work area size required for your program (see 7.6.1).
        2.    Pass this size to RDMS with the RSA$INIT subroutine (see 7.6.2).

7.6.1. Determining the Work Area Size
        To determine the size of the work area, temporarily code a DEBUG DUMP SIZES
        command (in either embedded or interpreted SQL format) immediately after the
        programΓÇÖs END THREAD command.

        The following code shows the syntax for an embedded SQL DEBUG DUMP SIZES
        command in UCS COBOL:

             EXEC SQL EXECUTE IMMEDIATE
                  ΓÇÖDEBUG DUMP SIZESΓÇÖ
             END-EXEC.

        The following code shows the syntax for an interpreted SQL DEBUG DUMP SIZES
        command in UCS COBOL:

             ENTER MASM ΓÇÖACOB$RDMRΓÇÖ USING
                  ΓÇÖDEBUG DUMP SIZES; ΓÇÖ
                  ERROR-STATUS, AUX-INFO.

        Compile and execute the program and check the output of the DEBUG DUMP SIZES
        command. It has the following format:

        RSA Dbank Size is 13970 words.

        Use the value listed in the call to RSA$INIT (see 7.6.2)

        Note: After determining the work area size, remove the DEBUG DUMP SIZES
        command from the program.




7ΓÇô38                                                                                7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                           Accessing a Relational Database




         See the Enterprise Relational Database Server for ClearPath OS 2200 SQL
         Programming Reference Manual for more information about the DEBUG DUMP SIZES
         command.

7.6.2. Calling RSA$INIT
         Your program should call RSA$INIT only once, and should make the call before calling
         the subroutine ACOB$RDMR. If the default size of the work area (14,000 words) is
         sufficient for your program, no call is necessary in batch or demand mode.

         The call to RDMS has the following format:

         Format
             CALL "RSA$INIT" [ USING work-area-size ]

         where work-area-size specifies the number of words that RDMS allocates and
         initializes for the work area, as determined by the DEBUG DUMP SIZES command. You
         must specify this value as a data item with the following data description:

             PICTURE 1(36) USAGE BINARY-1.

         The value of work-area-size must be within the range 14,000 ∩éú work-area-size ∩éú
         131,000. If you do not specify work-area-size, the default size of the work area is
         14,000 words. If you specify a value less than 14,000, RDMS allocates 14,000 words of
         space. If you specify a value greater than 131,000, RDMS allocates 131,000 words of
         space.


7.7. Compiling Programs That Access RDMS
         Compiling UCS COBOL programs containing SQL is straightforward. The following
         paragraphs describe the minor differences in compiling that exist for the two RDMS
         interfaces:

         ∩é╖    Programs using the interpreter interface (the ENTER MASM statement)
              Simply call the UCS COBOL compiler. No special keyword options or
              preprocessing is necessary.
         ∩é╖    Programs containing embedded SQL
              To access RDMS from the UCOB compilation, RDMS must be installed for the
              default application specified by the APPLICATION keyword option (UDSSRC).
              If your program references table and view definitions contained in an application
              group other than the default (UDSSRC), you must identify the correct application
              group. To do this, specify the APPLICATION keyword option on the compiler call
              (see 2.2.7). The compiler uses the RDMS and repository software located in this
              application group repository when parsing the syntax. Programs with embedded
              SQL do not require any other keyword options or preprocessing.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               7ΓÇô39
Accessing a Relational Database




           The run unit used in any RDMS qualification of SQL names will be the name of the
           UCS COBOL source program.
           Note: You name application groups when you install them, using either the
           default names or others you select. See the UDS Planning and Migration
           Overview for information on installing application groups.

        Example 1
        The following example shows a compiler call for a UCS COBOL program using SQL. If
        the program uses embedded SQL, it runs in the default application group, UDSSRC,
        since no APPLICATION keyword option is specified.

          @UCOB,S qual*file.sql/src,qual*file.sql-prog/om

        This call produces the object module qual*file.sql-prog/om. The run unit used by
        RDMS will be qual*file.sql/src.

        Example 2
        The following example is the same as Example 1, except that it compiles a UCS
        COBOL program using embedded SQL that must run in the application group APPSVN
        (specified by the APPLICATION keyword option).

          @UCOB,S qual*file.sql/src,qual*file.sql-prog/om,,,APPLICATION/APPSVN

        This call produces the object module qual*file.sql-prog/om, which contains the
        processed SQL statements. This object module is in a form ready for execution by
        RDMS at run time.


7.8. Linking Programs That Access RDMS
        You can use either static or dynamic linking to link batch and demand programs
        containing SQL. You must, however, statically link Transaction Processing (TIP) and
        High-Volume Transaction Processing (HVTIP) programs containing SQL. Static linking
        provides better performance for all production environments.

        When you use interpreted or embedded SQL in a program, RDMS uses the UCS C
        malloc function to acquire dynamic memory allocations. In batch/demand, the malloc
        space is acquired by creating an activity-level bank. For TIP, the malloc space is
        acquired from the URTS$TABLES heap bank. This is a small bank and once the bank is
        filled, another URTS$TABLES heap bank is created.

7.8.1. Statically Linking Applications
        The CREATE$BANK call causes your transaction to lose its TIP sticking and TIP restart.
        To prevent this from occurring, the main program must use the keyword option
        TIPMALLOC on the compilation of the program. This results in the TIPMALLOC$$$
        bank being included within your link. The use of the TIPMALLOC option allows TIP
        sticking and restart to function because a dynamic bank creation does not take place.




7ΓÇô40                                                                           7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                           Accessing a Relational Database




         Using the keyword option TIPMALLOC on the compilation of the main program allows
         RDMS and any other subsystem that is called to acquire the memory heap space from
         the TIPMALLOC$$$ heap bank instead of the URTS$TABLES heap bank. A fast load
         zoom cannot be created with the TIPMALLOC option because the total (collective) size
         is more than 262K words. (This is not the actual size, but the potential growth size
         when the program requires more memory.)

         The keyword TIPMALLOC can also be used for batch/demand executions, to eliminate
         a bank from being created at execution time. This would allow TIP sticking and restart
         to function because a dynamic bank creation does not take place.

         TIPMALLOC is not allowed in HVTIP. Under HVTIP, C malloc space is acquired from the
         HVTIP D-bank, program level BDI 5. When heap space runs out, the malloc calls fail,
         returning NULL and the program execution fails. However, if the HVTIP ICP static link
         has an OUTPUT HVTIP2 statement instead of an OUTPUT HVTIP statement, C malloc
         space is then taken from separate activity level banks called "pooled" banks. If your
         static link and VTBUTL VALTAB settings also supply activity level pooled banks, those
         banks are then used for malloc space. If you do not supply any pooled banks,
         CREATE$BANK calls are done to dynamically acquire activity level banks which are
         used for C malloc space. Those system calls result in your transaction losing its TIP
         sticking and restart. See the Transaction Processing Administration and Operations
         Reference Manual for more details on how to supply extra banks to the transaction.
         See the Linking System Programming Reference Manual for a description of the
         OUTPUT HVTIP2 statement.

         See the TIPMALLOC keyword explanation in 2.2.7.

         To identify the library search chain for the application group, include the following
         command in the runstream:

           @USE LINK$PF,SYS$LIB$*APP$n .

         where n is the number of the application group in which the RDMS software resides.

         Example
         The following example is a batch or demand runstream that statically links a program
         containing SQL commands to the application group APP$7. It produces an efficient
         zero overhead object module (ZOOM).

           @USE LINK$PF,SYS$LIB$*APP$7.
           @LINK,S ,qual*file.sql-prog/zm
           INCLUDE qual*file.sql-prog/om
           RESOLVE ALL REFERENCES USING SYS$LIB$*EMOMRTS.,LCN
           PROCESS FOR EXTENDED ZOOM
           DELETE ALL DEFINITIONS EXCEPT START$
           @EOF




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                    7ΓÇô41
Accessing a Relational Database




        Accessing a Relational Database
        The following statements apply to the preceding example:

        ∩é╖    The @USE LINK$PF statement ensures that the program uses the RDMS interface
             for the application group (APP$7 in this example). Any ESQL programs input to this
             static link must have been compiled for this application group using the matching
             APPLICATION/appname keyword option.
        ∩é╖    The @LINK,S statement calls the LINK processor. Notice that the name used for
             the output object module of the static link is different from the compiler output
             object module. Otherwise, the statically linked object module overwrites the
             object module produced by the compiler. This is because standard object modules
             (the compiler output), bound object modules, and ZOOMs are all subtypes of an
             absolute; and the system allows only one version of an absolute to exist per
             name. Giving the statically linked output a unique name assures that the object
             module produced by the compiler remains available for debugging with PADS.
        ∩é╖    The INCLUDE command following the call to the LINK processor specifies the
             object module produced by the compiler, which is the input to the Linking System.
        ∩é╖    The RESOLVE command eliminates references for the Programmers Advanced
             Debugging System (PADS), greatly reducing ZOOM size and aiding performance.
        ∩é╖    The PROCESS command produces the most efficiently banked ZOOM for this
             static link.
        ∩é╖    The DELETE command deletes all unnecessary definitions (entry points), retaining
             only the required entry point, START$. This produces a ZOOM that executes
             efficiently in a production environment.

        For more information about linking and the statements and commands used in this
        runstream, see the Linking System Programming Reference Manual.

7.8.2. Dynamically Linking Applications
        The following runstream dynamically links a program containing SQL commands and
        executes it for the application group APP$7:

            @USE LINK$PF,SYS$LIB$*APP$7.
            @XQT   qual*file.sql-prog/om

        The library search chain for the application group is identified through the @USE
        LINK$PF statement before execution (see 7.8.1). During execution, the Linking System
        dynamically resolves references as they are encountered.

        Note that if any of the programs use Embedded SQL, those programs must have been
        compiled for this application group with a matching APPLICATION/appname keyword
        option. ESQL programs are targeted for a specific application group at compilation
        time.




7ΓÇô42                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                          Accessing a Relational Database




7.9. Compile Time Explain Reports
         RDMS explain reports can be generated adjacent to ESQL DECLARE CURSOR
         statements. The explain report shows the access path chosen by the RDMS optimizer
         for the specified query.

         Compile time explain reports are a subset of the output of the execution time SQL
         EXPLAIN statement.

         You can produce these reports by including the REMARK or SOURCE keyword option,
         or the E, S, or L letter option, on the compiler call. Suppress the reports by including
         the NO-REMARK keyword option or the N option on the compiler call.

Section 8
Accessing the Unisys Repository
Manager (UREP)

         The Unisys Repository Manager (UREP) is the product that you directly use to create,
         update, and store definitions for the following types of Universal Data System (UDS)
         databases:

         ∩é╖   Network (DMS)
         ∩é╖   Relational (RDMS)
         ∩é╖   Conventional file (SFS)

         In addition to creating and storing database definitions, you can use UREP directly
         from your UCS COBOL programs to perform the following functions:

         ∩é╖   Insert code into your UCS COBOL source program with the INVOKE command.
             The INVOKE command causes UREP to generate file descriptions, data
             declarations, arbitrary source code sequences, and screen definitions from
             definitions that you previously created and stored in UREP. UREP places the
             generated code in the source program at the point of the INVOKE command.
         ∩é╖   Store cross-reference information into UREP, using the UREP-XREF keyword
             option, to track definitions that UREP or COPY procedures insert into the UCS
             COBOL source program.

         UCS COBOL provides the following features that allow you to use information from
         and store information into UREP:

         ∩é╖   The INVOKE clause
         ∩é╖   The UREP-XREF compiler keyword option

         The INVOKE clause and UREP-XREF keyword option have interrelated functions. The
         INVOKE clause causes information that you previously defined and stored in UREP to
         be processed, producing source code for your program.

         For example, you create and store the definition for a File Description using UREP.
         During compilation, an INVOKE clause references the definition stored in UREP. At the
         point that the INVOKE clause occurs, UREP generates a File Description from
         information stored in a repository and then inserts it into your source program.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  8ΓÇô1
Accessing the Unisys Repository Manager (UREP)




        The UREP-XREF keyword option has a related function. It processes the source code
        in your program and stores cross-reference information in the repository. This allows
        you to track and control changes to your organizationΓÇÖs common source code. For
        example, when you change the File Description that UREP inserts into your program,
        you can use the UREP-XREF keyword option to store information in UREP about what
        programs reference the stored definition.

        Thus, you can use information stored in UREP to generate source code for your
        program and you can use the UREP-XREF keyword option to track the use of the
        generated code and store it in UREP.

        The type and detail of cross-reference information placed into the repository depend
        on a UREP system-defined entity and its associated attribute values (system-defined
        entity equals Options) that are assigned.

        See the Enterprise Servers Repository for ClearPath OS 2200 Programming
        Reference Manual and the Enterprise Servers Repository for ClearPath OS 2200
        Administration Guide for more information about setting up your code definitions and
        storing cross-reference information.


8.1. Specifying an Application Group
        When creating definitions with UREP, you can store information for a related group of
        programs in the same repository. Each repository is identified by an application name
        that defines which repository contains the information needed for the INVOKE clauses
        in a UCS COBOL source program.

        Designate which repository to use in one of the following ways:

        ∩é╖   Specify the compiler keyword option APPLICATION/name on the call to the
            compiler (see 2.2.7).
        ∩é╖   Do not use an APPLICATION keyword option or a DMS INVOKE statement, causing
            the application name to default to the default repository, UDSSRC.




8ΓÇô2                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                        Accessing the Unisys Repository Manager (UREP)




8.2. Generating Code for Your Source Program
     (INVOKE)
         You can store common attributes of your UCS COBOL applications in UREP entities.
         The INVOKE...FROM REPOSITORY clause uses information that is stored in UREP and
         generates it into UCS COBOL declarations and definitions. UREP places the generated
         code into the source program at the point of the INVOKE clause. The compiler then
         treats the INVOKE clause like a comment line (similar to the treatment of a COPY
         statement).

         The key steps that UREP requires for a program to use the INVOKE clause are as
         follows:

         1.    Create an entity in a UREP repository (using the UREP processor or the FORMGEN
               processor to define DPS forms) that defines the information pertaining to your
               application. The Enterprise Servers Repository for ClearPath OS 2200
               Administration Guide describes this process.
         2.    Use the INVOKE statement in your program. This causes UREP at compilation time
               to generate the stored information into source code that UREP then inserts into
               your program at the point of the INVOKE statement (see 8.2.1, 8.2.2, and 8.2.3).
         3.    At compilation time, specify the APPLICATION keyword option to designate which
               UREP application name to associate with the INVOKE clause (see 8.1).

         The following subsections describe the different types of code that you can generate
         by placing INVOKE statements in a UCS COBOL program.

8.2.1. Inserting SELECT Statement Information with INVOKE
         Function
         You can generate a SELECT statement in the File-Control Paragraph of your source
         program from the definition of a SELECT statement that is stored in UREP. The
         following syntax for the INVOKE clause causes UREP to generate and place this code
         in your source program.

         Format
              INVOKE SELECT [ file-name-2 = ] file-name-1
                   FROM REPOSITORY [ ASSIGN TO { implementor-name-1 }... ] .

         where:

         file-name-1

               is the source code being incorporated into the program. This file must exist in
               UREP.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                    8ΓÇô3
Accessing the Unisys Repository Manager (UREP)




        file-name-2

           provides an optional alias for file-name-1; if you specify file-name-2, use it to
           reference the file in the SELECT statement in the FILE SECTION and the
           PROCEDURE SECTION (including references to a file name in the INVOKE ALL
           FILE...FROM REPOSITORY statement).

        implementor-name-1

           is a file name, 1 to 12 characters long, that corresponds to a file name on an @ASG
           statement. You can use this variable to assign file-name-1 to as many devices as
           needed. The ASSIGN clause must be present on the INVOKE SELECT statement to
           use implementor-name-1.

        Apart from the optional ASSIGN clause, you specify all other information for the
        SELECT statement, including ORGANIZATION, ACCESS, and KEY, when you create the
        definition with UREP.

        Result
        The INVOKE statement generates a SELECT statement, with its appropriate clauses,
        from the associated information in UREP.

        If the compiler keyword option UREP-XREF is in effect for the compilation, UREP
        tracks the use of file-name-2; UREP, however, always stores the information using the
        actual file name, file-name-1.

        Example
        Example 8ΓÇô1 shows the results of generating a SELECT statement with the INVOKE
        statement.

        21             ***********************************************************
        22             * INVOKE SELECT
        23             ***********************************************************
        24             *
        25               invoke select options1-f1 from repository.
        25.C1.1              SELECT OPTIONS1-F1 ASSIGN TO DISC.
        26             *
        27             ***********************************************************
        28             * INVOKE SELECT
        29             ***********************************************************
        30             *
        31               invoke select options1-f1a = options1-f1 from repository.
        31.C1.1              SELECT OPTIONS1-F1 ASSIGN TO DISC.
        32             *
        33             ************************************************************
        34             * INVOKE SELECT
        35             ************************************************************
        36             *
        37               invoke select options1-f2 from repository assign to exfile.
        37.C1.1              SELECT OPTIONS1-F2 ASSIGN TO DISC.
        38             *

8.2.2. Inserting File Descriptions with INVOKE
         Function
         If a file has an INVOKE...FROM REPOSITORY clause in the SELECT statement of the
         source program (see 8.2.1), you must generate its FILE DESCRIPTION in the FILE
         SECTION using the following format. Note that you cannot use any of the other
         clauses associated with a FILE DESCRIPTION if it is generated with the INVOKE ALL
         FILE... FROM REPOSITORY statement.

         Format
           INVOKE ALL FILE file-name-1 FROM REPOSITORY .

         where file-name-1 is the file name or the alias file name if one was given (see 8.2.1)
         that is specified in the INVOKE SELECT clause.

         Result
         The INVOKE statement causes UREP to generate a complete File Description (FD or
         SD) and all Record Descriptions that define the specified file, and place them into the
         source program.

         The following example shows the results of generating a SELECT statement with the
         INVOKE statement.

8.2.3. Inserting Data Descriptions with INVOKE
         Function
         You can use an INVOKE statement to generate descriptions for the following:

         ∩é╖    COBOL data items
         ∩é╖    Relational data
         ∩é╖    Screen definitions

         Use these data descriptions in these sections of the Data Section:

         ∩é╖    WORKING-STORAGE SECTION
         ∩é╖    COMMON-STORAGE SECTION
         ∩é╖    LINKAGE SECTION

         Result
         UREP generates the correct description clauses within the UCS COBOL program for
         the physical location of the INVOKE statement. The line numbering for the new source
         lines is the same as for a COPY statement.

         The INVOKE statement uses the formats described in the following subsections.

Inserting COBOL Data Item Definitions
         Format
             INVOKE   { RECORD [ data-name-2 = ] data-name-1         } FROM REPOSITORY .

         where:

         data-name-1

              must exist as a definition of a level 01 record or a level 77 item in a UREP
              repository. You cannot use the INVOKE RECORD clause if you use an INVOKE ALL
              FILE statement to generate the file description for the file (see 8.2.2).

         data-name-2

              provides an optional alias for data-name-1; if you specify data-name-2, use it for
              references to the data name in the FILE SECTION and the PROCEDURE SECTION of
              the source program. If the compiler keyword option UREP-XREF is in effect for the
              compilation, UREP tracks the use of data-name-2. UREP, however, always stores
              the information using the actual data name, data-name-1.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               8ΓÇô7
Accessing the Unisys Repository Manager (UREP)

        97.C1.3                    03 RECORD-NAME PIC x(12).
        97.C1.4                    03 RECORD-NUMBER PIC 9(6).
        97.C1.5                    03 RPROGRAM-NAME PIC x(12).

Inserting Relational Data Definitions
        Format




        where:

        table-name

           is a user-defined word that identifies a repository definition for a record
           description of an RDMS relational table. You can specify table-name only after the
           TABLE subclause. Underscores and dollar signs are allowed in this name.

        view-name

           is a user-defined word that identifies a repository definition for a record
           description that describes the columns in an RDMS relational view. You can
           specify view-name only after the VIEW subclause. Underscores and dollar signs
           are allowed in this name.




8ΓÇô8                                                                           7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                      Accessing the Unisys Repository Manager (UREP)




         schema-name

            is a user-defined word that identifies the UREP definition of a schema that
            contains the description for the table or view. Underscores and dollar signs are
            allowed in this name.

         Result
         The INVOKE statement generates source variable declarations for all column names
         associated with a table definition. Each column name is assigned a 01 level declaration
         with its associated data type and size assigned as the object. The column name
         defined in the table definition becomes the name of the variable (column underscores
         are consistent with COBOL hyphens).

         The compiler then places these variables into the repository as cross-referenced
         data-items only if they are referenced by embedded SQL statements in the procedure
         division. If they are not referenced by embedded SQL statements, they are not
         cross-referenced (that is, source generation of these variable declarations through the
         INVOKE statement does not generate cross-referencing for the columns brought into
         the source).

         For more information about relational cross-reference information, see the Enterprise
         Servers Repository for ClearPath OS 2200 Administration Guide, the Enterprise
         Relational Database Server for ClearPath OS 2200 Administration Guide, and the
         Enterprise Relational Database Server for ClearPath OS 2200 SQL Programming
         Reference Manual.

      Example 8ΓÇô5. Inserting Screen Definitions with the INVOKE Statement

         Inserting Screen Definitions with Specific Initial Values
         The form in Example 8ΓÇô6 is the same as the previous one, except that it was created
         with specific initial values for the alphabetic and alphanumeric data items. The user
         cannot specify initial values for numeric data items.

         This example is similar to Example 8ΓÇô5, except that the values in the WITH clause are
         reversed to show that order is not important.

         56              *
         57                  invoke form lspi2-2 in formlib forms
         58                              with prefixes values from repository.
         58.C1.1             01 SCREEN-LSPI2-2.
         58.C1.2                 02 SCREEN-LSPI2-2-HEADER.

         three times). Also, the example does not include the WITH clause, causing the
         program to use the default values of VALUES and PREFIXES.

8.2.4. Inserting Source Code with INVOKE
         Function
         You can use an INVOKE statement to bring source code (data declarations or
         executable statements) that are stored in UREP into a program. You can bring this
         source code into any location of the program if the syntax of the code is valid for that
         location.

         Format
           INVOKE {SOURCE source-name} FROM REPOSITORY.

         where source-name is the name associated with a block of UCS COBOL code that
         exists in the UREP repository.

         Result
         The INVOKE SOURCE command causes UREP to place the source code with the
         specified source-name into the source program at the location of the INVOKE. The line
         numbering for the new source lines is the same as for a COPY statement.

         Example
         Example 8ΓÇô8 shows the results of generating a source code sequences with the
         INVOKE statement.

         1                                     invoke source identiv from repository.
         1.C1.1            1                   IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
         1.C1.2                                PROGRAM-ID.     IDDS-TST4.
         2                                     INVOKE SOURCE ENVDIV   FROM REPOSITORY.
         2.C1.1                                ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.
         2.C1.2                                CONFIGURATION SECTION.
         2.C1.3                                SOURCE-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
         2.C1.4                                OBJECT-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
         2.C1.5                                SPECIAL-NAMES.
         2.C1.6                                    PRINTER IS PRT.
         3                                   ***
         4                                     DATA DIVISION.
         5                                   *
         6                                         INVOKE SOURCE WKSTORE    FROM
         REPOSITORY.
         6.C1.1                               WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
         6.C1.2                               01 AA PIC X(3).
         6.C1.3                               01 BB.
         6.C1.4                                   05 CC PIC X(5).
         6.C1.5                                   05 DD PIC S9(9)V9(8).
         6.C1.6                               77 EE       PIC 99.
         7                                   ***
         8                 1                  PROCEDURE DIVISION.
         9                                        INVOKE SOURCE PROCDIV FROM REPOSITORY.
         9.C1.1            1                  BEGIN.
         9.C1.2            1                      DISPLAY "WELCOME TO UREP TESTING."
         UPON PRT.
         9.C1.3            1                       MOVE "XYZ" TO AA.
         9.C1.4            1                       MOVE "STUVW" TO CC.

8.3. Updating UREP (UREP-XREF)
        If the UREP-XREF keyword option is in effect during compilation, UCS COBOL updates
        the repository using program source code. UCS COBOL checks an entity of type
        OPTIONS and name UCS to see how much cross-reference information it should store
        for the following attributes:

        ∩é╖   DMS-LEVEL
            DMS items inserted in the program with the INVOKE statement
        ∩é╖   RDMS-LEVEL
            RDMS relational database items referenced in embedded SQL commands, as well
            as tables and views inserted into the program with the INVOKE statement
        ∩é╖   DPS-LEVEL
            DPS forms inserted in the program with the INVOKE statement
        ∩é╖   INVOKE-LEVEL
            All other items inserted into the program with the INVOKE statement
        ∩é╖   COPY-LEVEL
            All items inserted into the program with the COPY statement

        The amount of information stored in UREP is controlled by the values specified for
        each of these attributes. The possible values for the attributes are NONE, PARTIAL, or
        COMPLETE. Each attribute assumes the default value PARTIAL if either of the
        following is true:

        ∩é╖   You do not specify a value for the attribute.
        ∩é╖   You do not create an OPTIONS UCS entity in UREP (all of the attributes take the
            default value).

        UREP tracks one or more of the following relationships between the UCS COBOL
        source program (MODULE) and individual items, and stores this information in the
        repository for the application:

        ∩é╖   WRITES (changes were made to the contents of an item)
        ∩é╖   REFERENCES (references were made to an item; however, there were no
            changes)
        ∩é╖   CREATES (DMS STORE, RDMS INSERT)




8ΓÇô30                                                                           7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                      Accessing the Unisys Repository Manager (UREP)




         If you specify the value PARTIAL for an attribute, UREP consolidates all of the activity
         that occurs for subitems of a higher-level item named in an INVOKE or COPY
         statement as activity for the higher-level item. Thus, UREP tracks the WRITES and
         REFERENCES relationships to the source program as if they are for the high-level item.

         For example, the UCS COBOL program P1 contains the following statement:

           MOVE 1 TO data-name-a

         where data-name-a is a level 02 subitem of RECORD-B that is updated during
         execution of the program. With PARTIAL in effect, UREP tracks this relationship for the
         high-level item, as follows:

           MODULE P1 WRITES TO RECORD-B

         If you specify the value COMPLETE for an attribute, all of the subitems are tracked
         individually.

         The INVOKE or COPY statement is considered to be a REFERENCES relationship to the
         higher-level named item.

         See the Enterprise Servers Repository for ClearPath OS 2200 Administration Guide
         for more information about storing cross-reference information.

         The compiler stores the UREP-XREF information after successful generation of an
         object module (no major errors during compilation). Errors in the storing process or in
         accessing UREP have no effect on the production of the object module if there are no
         major errors; however, UREP does not store the cross-reference information.

         You can recover this cross-reference information by recompiling the program with the
         NO-CODE compiler keyword option. This keyword causes the compiler to store the
         cross-reference information in UREP for programs that successfully compile, but
         suppresses the creation of an object module.

Section 9
Accessing Program-Callable FURPUR
(PCFP)

         Program-Callable FURPUR (PCFP) performs most of the file and element handling
         functions of the FURPUR statements. It can be called from both user programs and
         system processors. PCFP gives you much more capability in specifying partial names
         than FURPUR does; it can match both single characters or variable length strings by
         using wild card characters.

         To assist you in calling it, PCFP contains definition elements for all the packets that can
         be passed to it, and for all return entries and structures that it returns to the caller.
         There is a set of definition elements for each of the following UCS languages:

         ∩é╖   C
         ∩é╖   COBOL
         ∩é╖   FORTRAN

         For complete information on this product, refer to the PCFP Programming Reference
         Manual.

Section 10
Using Executive Requests

         By using the UCS Runtime System to call Executive requests (ER), your UCS COBOL
         programs can call the Exec to perform functions such as obtain system times, print
         the date, or terminate a program. Figure 10ΓÇô1 illustrates how UCS COBOL programs
         make these calls. The UCS COBOL compiler accepts these calls within your source
         program and the Linking System resolves their references during linking.




                Figure 10ΓÇô1. Using Executive Requests from UCS COBOL

         Accessing the ERs from a UCS COBOL program executing in extended mode is
         nontrivial because ERs execute only in basic mode. This places restrictions on
         overlapping addresses and multiple banks in UCS programs. Most of the complexity in
         accessing the ERs, however, is hidden by the interface in the UCS Runtime System.
         The system accomplishes this for most of the ERs by:

         ∩é╖   Placing all of the data and packets into a bank that is always accessible in basic
             mode
         ∩é╖   Performing ASCII to Fieldata and Fieldata to ASCII conversions where necessary

         Several of the ER calls require you to provide additional information or meet
         constraints (presented later). You should also note the following requirements when
         calling ERs from a UCS COBOL program:

         ∩é╖   You must use the supplied packet building routine UCSSYMBPK$ (see 10.6.1) for
             the FSYMB subroutine.
         ∩é╖   Integer arguments must be declared as PIC 9(10) BINARY to ensure that a full
             word is allocated.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 10ΓÇô1

10.1. Dynamic Control Statement Requests
      (ERACSF, FACSF, FACSF2, IACSF, IACSF2)
        Function
        Permits your program to submit an Exec control statement image (arg1) for
        interpretation and processing during program execution. FACSF, FACSF2, IACSF, and
        IACSF2 all refer to the Executive request function ACSF$.

        Format


               ΓÇ▓FACSF ßç▒
        CALL α╡₧ΓÇ▓FACSF2ßç▒ α╡ó USING ▄╜ΓÇ½▌â▌ÄΓÇ¼1[ , ▄╜ΓÇ½▌â▌ÄΓÇ¼2]
                       ßç▒

               ΓÇ▓IACSF
              ΓÇ▓IACSF2ΓÇ▓

         it should be terminated by the character sequence: blank, period, blank. Otherwise,
         extraneous characters following the actual control statement within the 84 character
         image could cause an Exec error.

         If the length of arg1 is less than the length to be used for the control image, the
         system pads the difference with blanks. For example, the following code passes 84
         characters to the ER with the last 68 being blanks:

         ignores the status returned by the ACSF$ Executive request and continues execution.

10.2. Setting and Retrieving the Condition Word
      (FSETC, FCOND)
        Function
        Provides routines to modify and retrieve the condition word.

        FSETC

            Places (sets) the contents of the lower third (bits 25-36) and bits 8 and 9 of arg in
            the corresponding run condition word. You can use the run condition word as a
            flag that can be tested by the control statement @TEST or retrieved by the COBOL
            call CALL ΓÇÖFCONDΓÇÖ USING arg and then tested (see 2.5). FSETC refers to the ER
            function SETC$. See the ER Programming Reference Manual for more information
            for bit settings. Note that UCS documentation refers to the condition word as bits
            1 to 36 while the Exec documentation refers to 0 to 35.

        FCOND

            Retrieves the condition word and makes it available to you in arg. FCOND refers to
            the Executive request function COND$.

        Formats
          CALL 'FSETC' USING arg.
          CALL 'FCOND' USING arg.

        where arg is an integer scalar expression for FSETC; it is an integer variable or array
        element for FCOND.

        Prior to the execution of the following example, the following command must be
        performed:

          @SETC 7777

          ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.

10.3. Retrieving Date and Time in ASCII (ADATE)
        Function
        Retrieves the time and date in ASCII. ADATE refers to the Executive request function
        DATE$.

        Format

       CALL ΓÇÿADATEΓÇÖ USING arg1, arg2

        where:

        arg1, arg2

            are character variables, contiguous character arrays, or character array elements
            of 6 or more characters in length into which the date and time are stored in ER
            DATE$ format.

            The data in arg1 is the ASCII character form MMDDYY, as follows:

                 ∩é╖   MM represents the month. Values returned are 01 through 12.

                 ∩é╖   DD represents the day. Values returned are 01 through 31.

                 ∩é╖   YY represents the last two digits of the year. Values returned are 00
                     through 99. (00-99).




10ΓÇô8                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                      Using Executive Requests




               The data in arg2 is in the ASCII character form HHMMSS, as follows:

                   ∩é╖   HH represents hours. Values returned are 00 through 23.

                   ∩é╖   MM represents minutes. Values returned are 00 through 59.

                   ∩é╖   SS represents seconds. Values returned are 00 through 59.

               The first six character positions of each variable, array, or array element are filled
               with the ASCII character form of the date and time. The remaining characters are
               space-filled.

         Example
                   01 DATE-1 PIC X(6).
                   01 TIME-1 PIC X(6).
                  *This call supplies the date ('MMDDYY') in DATE-1 and the time
                  *('HHMMSS') in TIME-1.
                       CALL 'ADATE' USING DATE-1 TIME-1.
                       DISPLAY 'DATE' DATE-1 'TIME' TIME-1.

         Note: Timestamp Overflow - The DATE$ format is not a linear format, so overflow
         is not applicable in the same manner as a linear time. However, the DATE$ format
         only provides the last two digits of the year, which might not be sufficient to
         uniquely identify the time.
         For example, 1964-01-01 cannot be distinguished from 2064-01-01. Due to this
         limitation and the local time base used, you might want to consider other timestamp
         formats.

10.4. Retrieving Time and Date (UCSTDATE$)
         Retrieves the time and date in binary. UCSTDATE$ refers to the ER function TDATE$.

         Format


         CALL ΓÇÿUCSDATE$ΓÇÖ USING arg

         where:

         arg

               is a one-word variable or array element into which the binary date and time are
               stored in ER TDATE$ format.

         Note: Timestamp Overflow - The year portion of the TDATE$ timestamp format
         will wrap after 2027-12-31 23:59:59 resulting in times which are ambiguous and
         considered invalid. Unisys strongly recommends that you do not use ER TDATE$
         and the TDATE$ timestamp format within new programs or routines. Further, we
         recommend that you should examine your existing use of the ER and the TDATE$
         timestamp format and consider using other timestamp formats. For more
         information, refer to the Time Considerations for ClearPath OS 2200 Systems.

10.5. Activity Termination (FEXIT, FERR, FABORT,
      FEABT)
        Function
        Provides the following forms of activity termination:

        FEXIT
        Terminates the current activity. Refers to the Executive request function EXIT$.

        FERR
        Terminates the activity in error. One of two entry points for the Executive request
        function ERR$.

        FABORT
        Unconditionally terminates all activities and the run if the run is batch mode. Refers to
        the Executive request function ABORT$.

        FEABT
        Unconditionally terminates all activities but allows error diagnostics. FEABT is similar
        to FABORT except that register dumps are provided and PMD requests are honored.
        One of two entry points for the Executive request function EABT$.

        The following are alternate entry points for the Executive requests ERR$ and EABT$.
        ERERR$
        Performs the same function as FERR. Terminates the activity in error. Refers to the
        Executive request function ERR$.

        EREABT$
        Performs the same function as FEABT. Unconditionally terminates all activities but
        allows error diagnostics. EREABT$ is similar to FABORT except that register dumps
        are provided and PMD requests are honored. Refers to the Executive request function
        EABT$.

        Formats
          CALL 'FEXIT'.
          CALL 'FERR'.
          CALL 'FABORT'.
          CALL 'FEABT'.
          CALL 'ERERR$'.
          CALL 'EREABT$'.

10.6. Input/Output ERs (FIO, FIOW, FSYMB,
      FUNLCK, FWANY, FWST)
         Function
         The following table lists the COBOL I/O Executive requests and their descriptions.


              Executive
               Request                                       Description

          FIO             Requests an operation on an I/O device. Returns control to the executing
                          program without waiting for completion of the I/O operation.
          FIOW            Requests an operation on an I/O device. Returns control upon completion of
                          the I/O operation.
          FSYMB           Provides a means to request certain symbiont Executive request functions,
                          character transfer, and some expanded READ$ capacity.
          FUNLCK          Enables an input/output interrupt activity to reduce its switching priority to the
                          priority of the activity that initiated the input/output request.
          FWANY           Delays execution until any current input/output operation is completed.
          FWST            Delays execution until the I/O operation controlled by the specified I/O packet
                          has completed.


         Formats
              CALL 'FIO' USING pkt.
              CALL 'FIOW' USING pkt.
              CALL 'FSYMB' USING pkt.
              CALL 'FWST' USING pkt.

              CALL 'FUNLCK'.
              CALL 'FWANY'.

         where pkt is a 13-word table filled with input/output packet information. See 10.6.4 for
         examples of these ERs.

         Description
         Two basic steps are necessary when using these routines:

         1.    Use the UCS COBOL subroutine UCSMAKEIOPK$ (see 10.6.2) to construct the
               packets for FIO, FIOW, and FWST. Use the UCSSYMBPK$ subroutine to construct
               the packet for FSYMB (see 10.6.1). You do not need to construct a packet for
               FWANY and FUNLCK.
         2.    Call the I/O Executive request function, passing the I/O packet as the first
               argument of the call.

               Note: If the I/O routines are called from a shared subsystem, the data packets
               and buffers must reside in a data bank with a LOW BDI.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                           10ΓÇô11
Using Executive Requests




             The Executive request is done with register A0 pointing to the program-constructed
             input/output packet. This provides you with full control over the input/output
             operation and complete error analysis capability.

             There are no buffers external to these routines. They are all reentrant at both the
             program and the activity level.

             The following describes the activity that occurs when each procedure is called.

             FIO
             1.       Obtains the parameter pkt, which points to the I/O packet
             2.       References the ER function IO$
             3.       Returns control immediately to the caller

             Construct the I/O packet with UCSMAKEIOPK$ (see 10.6.2). It should contain 125
             words to allow I/O by bank descriptor index (BDI), but it never needs more than 125
             words.

             The I/O packet must be in static storage preceded by at least 128 words, which can
             contain anything other than I/O packets. The following example illustrates a
             constructed I/O packet with 125 words (500 bytes), preceded by 128 words (512
             bytes).

                  *     The following common block declaration declares 125 words of static
                  *     storage preceded by the required 128 words of unused storage:

                      01   XYZ.
                           02 FILLER PIC X(512).
                           02 IOPAK PIC X(500).

             FIOW
             1.       Obtains the parameter pkt, which points to the I/O packet
             2.       References the ER function IOW$
             3.       Waits for completion before returning to the caller

        Construct the I/O packet with UCSMAKEIOPK$ (see 10.6.2). It should contain 125 words
        to allow I/O by bank descriptor index (BDI), but it never needs more than 125 words.
        UCSMAKEIOPK$ tells you the number of words the generated I/O packet actually uses.

        FSYMB
        1.    Obtains the parameter pkt, which points to the I/O packet
        2.    References the ER function SYMB$
        3.    Returns control immediately to the caller

        Construct the symbiont I/O packet with UCSSYMBPK$ (see 10.6.1). It must be 13 words
        long.




10ΓÇô12                                                                                 7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                        Using Executive Requests




      This procedure does not support Fieldata records.

      FUNLCK
      1.     References the ER function UNLCK$, which enables an I/O interrupt activity to
             reduce its switching priority to the priority of the activity that initiated the I/O request
      2.     Returns     control immediately to the caller

      FWANY
      1.     References the ER function WANY$
      2.     Waits for completion of any outstanding input or output activity before returning to
             the caller

      FWST
      1.     Obtains the parameter pkt, which points to the I/O packet
      2.     References the ER function WAIT$
      3.     Waits for completion of any outstanding input or output activity before returning to
             the caller

10.6.1. Building a Symbiont I/O Packet (UCSSYMBPK$)
            Function
            This subroutine builds a SYMB$ packet that can be used for one or more FSYMB calls
            (see 10.6). I/O packets for FSYMB must be created by UCSSYMBPK$.

     Format
        CALL 'UCSSYMBPK$' USING packet, file, function, modes, character count1,
        buffer1
        [ , line spacing [ , character count2, buffer2 ] ]

     where:

     packet

            is a 13-word contiguous array in which the symbiont packet is built.

     file

            is a character scalar expression or contiguous character array that contains the file
            name to be put in the symbiont packet. The standard symbionts (READ$, PRINT$, and
            PUNCH$) are specified as ASCII character strings (for example, ΓÇÖREAD$ΓÇÖ means
            READ$).

Using Executive Requests




        function

           is an integer scalar expression with the following permissible values.


                Value                                       Description

                   8    Write.
                   16   Read.
                   34   Submit print-control or punch-control image. See the ER Programming
                        Reference Manual.
                   37   Write followed by read.
                   45   Submit print-file control image. See the ER Programming Reference Manual.

        modes

           is an integer scalar expression with its value formed as the sum of any of the four
           integers defined as follows:


                Value                                       Description

                   1    ASCII data to be transmitted.
                   2    Truncate if image read is longer than the buffer.
                   8    Used on first write call to an alternate punch file to inform the Executive that
                        the file being written is an alternate punch file and not an alternate print file.
                   16   Special translation information. If you use this, you must fill in the translation
                        table number and the character type in the symbiont packet after the
                        UCSSYMBPK$ call is done.

         character count1, character count2

            are integer scalar expressions that specify the number of characters to be
            transferred. Character count2 is only meaningful when function is FWR; it indicates
            the maximum number of characters accepted for the input buffer.

         buffer1, buffer2

            are character variables, contiguous character arrays, or character array elements (or a
            constant, in the case of buffer1), that contain the image transferred. Buffer2 is only
            meaningful when function is FWR, in which case it is the input buffer.

         line spacing

            is an integer scalar expression that specifies the line spacing. It is meaningful only for
            print files; the default value is 1.

10.6.2. Building an I/O Packet (UCSMAKEIOPK$)
         The UCSMAKEIOPK$ subroutine builds an I/O packet to be used with the I/O ER
         functions described in 10.6. It must be used to build packets for FIO, FIOW, and FWST.

         The I/O packet built can be used for more than one subroutine call. It must not be
         changed for use with I/O Executive requests, except for some fields that can be
         changed for use with FIO and FIOW.

         Format
              CALL 'UCSMAKEIOPK$' USING I/O-packet, file-name, function,
              mass-storage-address, number-of-buffers, directions, word-counts, buffers ,
              number-of-words-used [,MR-functions, MR-flags, MR-data-format ]

         where:

         I/O-packet

               is a contiguous array of 125 words in which the I/O packet is built.

               For UCS COBOL, addressing is a problem when using ERs. The 125-word buffer
               area is used for both the I/O packet and access word pairs, because all read and
               write operations are converted to I/O by BDI. You should not alter any I/O packet
               created by UCSMAKEIOPK$, except to change function, mass-storage-address,
               and MR-data-format for FIO, FIOW, and FWST.

               For FIO, the I/O packet must be in static storage preceded by at least 128 words.

             Example
         *  The following common block declaration produces 125 words of static
         *  storage preceded by 128 words of unused storage.
          01 XYZ.
              02 Filler PIC X(512).
              02 IOPAK PIC X(500).

             To reference individual fields within the I/O packet, you can define IOPAK as a
             structure with the elementary items referenced to match the packet as defined in
             the ER Programming Reference Manual. For example, if the I/O status returned was
             to be referenced, IOPAK could be identified as follows:

                 02    IOPAK
                       03 PIC X(12).
                       03 IOSTAT PIC 1(6) BINARY-1.
                       03 PIC 1(3) BINARY-1.
                       03 PIC X(487).

      file-name

             is a character scalar expression or contiguous character array describing the internal
             file name, as defined in the ER Programming Reference Manual.

          EACQ$ (Extended acquire) You must fill in words 6, 7, and 8 of the I/O packet.      15

                                      I/O Executive Request                                     Value

         mass-storage-address

             an integer scalar expression indicating the mass storage address at which the I/O
             transfer starts. If you use the I/O packet with a tape file, the recommended value
             is 0. You can alter this field (word 5) for use with FIO, FIOW, and FWST.

         number-of-buffers

             is an integer scalar expression indicating the number of buffers to be transferred
             in the I/O operation. It must be greater than 0 and less than 51.

         directions

             is a one-dimensional contiguous integer array whose one-word elements give the
             direction in which addresses are to be changed for each new word going to or
             from the buffer. The number of elements in the array must equal
             number-of-buffers. Each array element is an integer with a value between 0 and
             3, as follows:


            Value                                         Description

                0     Transfer starts with the first word of the buffer and continues in a forward
                      direction. The second word is transferred to or from the second word of the
                      buffer, and so on.
                1     All words are transferred to or from the first word of the buffer.
                      This direction value can be used to clear an area of mass storage.

          Value                                       Description

            2     Transfer starts at the first word of the buffer and continues in a backward direction.
                  The second word is transferred to or from the word before the first word of the
                  buffer; that is, the address of the second word is one lower than the address of the
                  first word. The third word is transferred to or from the word that is two words
                  before the first word of the buffer, and so on.
                  This direction value is normally useful only when reading a tape backwards.
            3     This is the same as a value of 1, except that input operations cannot access
                  storage, depending on how the operating system is configured at your site.


        word-counts

        is a one-dimensional contiguous integer array whose elements give the number of
        words to be transferred to the corresponding buffer. The number of elements in the
        array must equal number-of-buffers. Each array element is an integer greater than
        zero.

           Except for MR$, the total number of words transferred cannot be greater than
           229,376 (which is 128 1792-word tracks). For further information, refer to
           ΓÇ£DescriptionΓÇ¥ in this subsection. For functions that do not allow multiple buffers
           (that is, those other than MR$, BDR$, BDRB$, BDW$, and the functions converted
           to one of these), the value of the first element in the array must be less than
           65,536.

        buffers

        is a one-dimensional contiguous integer array whose elements specify the storage
        address at which each I/O transfer starts. (You can use the LOC$ subroutine to
        retrieve an address located in working storage or common storage (see 10.6.3).) The
        number of elements in the array must equal number-of-buffers.

        Each I/O buffer must start on a word boundary.

        Except for the MR$ function, each call to FIOW or FIO writes one block to or reads
        one block from the external medium, independent of how many buffers were
        specified in the call to UCSMAKEIOPK$. For more information, refer to ΓÇ£DescriptionΓÇ¥ in
        this subsection.

           For MS$, the buffer contains 5 words, as described under function.

        number-of-words-used

        is an integer variable or array element that contains the number of words needed for
        this I/O packet on exit from UCSMAKEIOPK$. The value of this variable is never set
        greater than 125.
