                                                                         Using Executive Requests




         A zero or negative value for this variable indicates an error was discovered in the
         parameters passed, as shown in the following table.


          Value                                            Description

            0     This value can mean any of the following errors:
                  ∩é╖       function contains an invalid code.
                  ∩é╖       number-of-buffers not equal to 1 for ACQ$, EACQ$, MS$, REL$, SM$, or UNL$.
                  ∩é╖       word-counts less than 1 or greater than 65,536 for one ACW.
                  ∩é╖       The wrong data format is used for MR$.
            -1    number-of-buffers is out of range (less than 1 or greater than 50).
            -2    The value of directions is not 0, 1, 2, or 3.
            -3    An element of word-counts exceeds 229,376 and the function is not MR$.
            -4    The buffers specified occupy more banks than can be based at the point of execution
                  of an I/O ER.
            -5    One of the elements of buffers has an address that cannot be expressed in basic
                  mode. It cannot be used with a basic mode ER.
            -6    Automatic buffer splitting has produced more than 50 access-word pairs. For more
                  information, refer to ΓÇ£DescriptionΓÇ¥ in this subsection.


         MR-functions

             is a one-dimensional contiguous integer array of at least number-of-buffers
             integer values that gives the I/O function for each buffer. Refer to the ER
             Programming Reference Manual for the permissible values.

             Pass this argument only if function is MR$.

         MR-flags

             is a one-dimensional contiguous integer array of at least number-of-buffers
             integer values. Bits 31 through 36 of each element, which are numbered as in BITS,
             are used as the MR$ flags for the corresponding buffer. For a description of these
             flags, refer to the ER Programming Reference Manual.

             Pass this argument only if function is MR$.

         MR-data-format

             is an integer scalar expression indicating the data format for all the buffers in the
             MR$ I/O operation.


                  Value            Description

                      1        Quarter-word
                               format
                      3        8-bit packed format



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                   10ΓÇô19
Using Executive Requests




        Any other value causes UCSMAKEIOPK$ to set the error flag. For a description of
        these formats, see the ER Programming Reference Manual.

            Pass this argument only if function is MR$.

        Description
        For functions that support more than one buffer (MR$, BDR$, BDRB$, BDW$, and the
        functions that are converted to these), the buffers are split automatically in order to
        enforce the following I/O restrictions imposed by the operating system:

        ∩é╖   No access-word pair can specify a transfer of more than 65,535 words, because
            the width of the field specifying the data-transfer length to the I/O ER is 16 bits.
        ∩é╖   The set of access-word pairs (for MR$, a single set of data-chained access-word
            pairs) cannot transfer more than 262,143 words. Mass-storage I/O considerations
            reduce this limit to 229,376 words, which is a block of 128 1792-word tracks.
        ∩é╖   The data transfer specified by an access-word pair cannot span the addresses
            associated by more than one BDI.

        Each buffer specified on a call to UCSMAKEIOPK$ is automatically split into two or
        more access-word pairs if it violates any of the previous restrictions. The Exec
        accumulates a running total of words transferred for any sequence of buffers
        specified with data chaining. When the total reaches 229,376, a split occurs with
        command chaining set at the split.

        The maximum number of words that can be specified for the buffers of an MR$
        function depends on various conditions, such as the following:

        ∩é╖   Number of banks containing the buffers
        ∩é╖   Locations of the buffers within the banks
        ∩é╖   Number of buffers

        All the BDIs containing the buffers must be based when either Executive request IO$
        or IOW$ is performed. The required basing is performed automatically by FIO, FIOW,
        or FWST, up to a maximum of eight BDIs. A single BDI describes a maximum of
        262,144 words, so the largest buffer that can be transferred in a single request is
        2,097,152 words (262,144 multiplied by 8).

        You can specify a larger data transfer by, for example, writing a buffer more than
        once. You could write a single 60,000-word buffer 50 times, resulting in the transfer of
        3,000,000 words. This might be useful in initializing a mass-storage file.

        If you write an array of more than 2,097,152 words, split it into multiple calls on
        boundaries that are a multiple of 229,376 words. Alternatively, split a large array into
        multiple records on 131,072-word boundaries. Either approach ensures that automatic
        buffer splitting does not change the record structure in the file. If automatic buffer
        splitting is allowed to create more than one record from a single buffer, you must use
        exactly the same sequence to read the data back in, to avoid altering the assumed
        record sizes.

10.6.3. Retrieving a Buffer Address (LOC$)
         Function
         The LOC$ subroutine provides the capability to retrieve the address of a buffer. It can
         be used in conjunction with UCSMAKEIOPK$ to build an I/O packet. LOC$ can also be
         used to set a pointer to reference based storage. Refer to the UCS COBOL
         Programming Reference Manual Volume 1, COBOL Statements, ΓÇ£The USING
         POINTER ClauseΓÇ¥ for more information.

         The successful completion of LOC$ causes the address of arg1 to be stored in arg2.

         Format
           CALL 'LOC$' USING arg1, arg2

         where:

         arg1

             is the buffer from which the storage address is retrieved. arg1 must be a 01 level
             item. This argument cannot reference an array. Also, you cannot use reference
             modification on this argument.

         arg2

             is the variable into which the address (arg1 address) is stored. arg2 must be a
             one-word binary item defined as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1 or USAGE POINTER. This
             argument cannot reference an array. Also, you cannot use reference modification
             on this argument. The contents of PIC 1(36) BINARY-1 one word VA pointer
             argument can be used by the UCSMAKEIOPK$ subroutine (see 10.6.2).

         Example
         See 10.6.4 for an example.

         Note: All addresses generated by UCS languages are extended mode virtual
         addresses.

10.7. Program File Maintenance Executive Requests
         The program file maintenance Executive requests through UCS COBOL fall into two
         categories: those that require a packet and those that do not.

         The program file maintenance ERs that need a packet are

         ∩é╖        PFD$ - mark element for deletion
         ∩é╖        PFI$ - update element table
         ∩é╖        PFS$ - search table of contents

         Use these Executive request functions in the following manner:

         1.       Prepare a skeleton packet using UCSMAKEPFPK$ (see 10.7.1).
         2.       Fill in the remainder of the packet as described in the ER Programming Reference
                  Manual by using BINARY-1 to define bits.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                10ΓÇô23
Using Executive Requests




        3.     Call the appropriate UCS COBOL subroutine to access the Executive request
               function (see 10.7.2).

        The program file maintenance routines that do not need a packet (see 10.7.3) are

        ∩é╖      PFUWL$ - update next write location
        ∩é╖      PFWL$ - retrieve next write location

10.7.1. Building a Skeleton Packet for Program File
        Maintenance ERs (UCSMAKEPFPK$)
        Function
        This subroutine builds a skeleton packet for the program file maintenance Executive
        request functions that require a packet - PFD$, PFI$, and PFS$ (see 10.7.2).

        Format
             CALL 'UCSMAKEPFPK$' USING packet,file,element,version.

        where:

        packet

               is a one-dimensional contiguous array of one-word items that contains at least 12
               elements; the skeleton packet is built in this parameter.

        file

               is a character scalar expression or contiguous character array giving the internal
               file name of the program file to use; only the first 12 characters are significant.

        element

               is a character scalar expression or contiguous character array specifying the
               element name; only the first 12 characters are significant.

        version

               is a character scalar expression or contiguous character array specifying the
               version of the element; only the first 12 characters are significant.

                      02 PCKT PIC 9(10) BINARY OCCURS 12 TIMES.
            01        FILE-NAME PIC X(12) VALUE '$$$$FILETEST'.
            01        NAME PIC X(12) VALUE 'ELEMENT-NAME'.
            01        VERSION PIC X(12) VALUE 'ELT-VERSION'.

           *     Build a packet for one of these ERs: PFD$, PFI$, PFS$.

                      CALL 'UCSMAKEPFPK$' USING PACKET FILE-NAME NAME VERSION.

10.7.3. Updating and Retrieving Write Limits (UCSPFUWL$,
        UCSPFWL$)
        Function
        The following are program file maintenance Executive request functions that do not
        require a packet:

        UCSPFUWL$

               Updates the next available write limit in a program file to the address given in
               register A1. Refers to the Executive request function PFUWL$.

        UCSPFWL$

               Retrieves the next available write limit in the program file. Refers to the Executive
               request function PFWL$.

        Formats

           CALL 'UCSPFWL$' USING file, current-limit, status.

        where:

        file

               is a character scalar expression or contiguous character array specifying the
               internal file name of the file whose write limit is to be updated or retrieved (only
               the first 12 characters are significant).

        new-limit

               is an integer scalar expression specifying the new write limit for the file.

        current-limit

               is an integer scalar variable or array element into which the current write limit of
               the file is stored.

            is an integer scalar variable or array element into which the status of the Executive
            request is stored. Define status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

         Example
                01   USE-FILE PIC X(12) VALUE 'FILE2T'.
                01   WRITE-LIMIT PIC 9(10) BINARY.
                01   STAT PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.
                01   CONSTANT PIC 9(10) BINARY.

           * Retrieve current limit.

                     CALL 'UCSPFWL$' USING USE-FILE WRITE-LIMIT STAT.
                     ADD CONSTANT TO WRITE-LIMIT.

           * Set new limit.

                      CALL 'UCSPFUWL$' USE-FILE WRITE-LIMIT STAT.

10.9. Retrieving Program Control Table (UCSPCT$)
        Function
        Makes all or specified portions of the information stored in the program control table
        (PCT) available to the requesting program. Refers to Executive request function PCT$.

        Format
          CALL 'UCSPCT$' USING number-of-words, start-word, buffer.

        where:

        number-of-words

           is an integer scalar expression specifying how many words from the PCT are to be
           retrieved.

        start-word

           is an integer scalar expression specifying that word of the PCT at which the
           retrieval is to start; the first word of the PCT is word 0.

           is a contiguous array of one-word elements into which the words copied from the
           PCT are stored. The number of elements in the array must be at least as large as
           number-of-words.

        Example
             01   NUMB PIC 9(10) BINARY.
             01   START-WORD PIC 9(10) BINARY.
             01   BUFR.
                  02 BUFR-1 PIC 1(36) BINARY-1 OCCURS 10 TIMES.

          * Retrieve variable information from the PCT.

10.10. Reading and Writing Tape Label Blocks
      (UCSTLBL$)
         Function
         Reads or writes selected portions of HDR1, HDR2, EOF1, EOF2, EOV1, and EOV2. The
         function also reads and writes user labels before and after each file. Refers to
         Executive request function TLBL$, Version 1. See the ER Programming Reference
         Manual for details.

         Format
            CALL 'UCSTLBL$' USING file, function, buffer-length, buffer, status.

         where:

         file

                is a character scalar expression or contiguous character array specifying the
                internal file name of the tape file for which labels are to be read or written; only
                the first 12 characters are significant.

         function

                is an integer scalar expression specifying the function to be performed. The valid
                function codes are described in the ER Programming Reference Manual.

         buffer-length

                is an integer scalar expression giving the number of elements of buffer.

         buffer

                is a one-dimensional contiguous array of one-word elements. The number of
                elements in the array must be equal to or greater than buffer-length. Buffer
                contains the Read/Write System Label Packet beginning with the fourth word
                (word 3) of the label packet. See the ER Programming Reference Manual for
                details.

         status

                is an integer variable or array element into which the status of the TLBL$
                Executive request is stored. Define status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

         Example
                01   TAPE-FILE PIC X(12) VALUE '$$$TAPE$FILE'.
                01   STAT PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.
                01   BUFFR1 PIC X(80) VALUE 'UHL1 Label to test TLBL$ interface'.

                     CALL 'UCSTLBL$' USING TAPE-FILE 17 20 BUFFR1 STAT.

10.11. Tape File Initialization (UCSTINTL$)
        Function
        Logically rewinds a specified tape file so that a subsequent pass can be made from
        the load point of the first reel. Refers to Executive request function TINTL$.

        Format
           CALL 'UCSTINTL$' USING file, status.

        where:

        file

               is a character scalar expression or contiguous character array specifying the
               internal file name (only the first 12 characters are significant) of the tape file that is
               to be logically rewound, in other words, positioned to the load point of the first
               reel of the file.

        status

               is an integer variable or array element that on execution contains the status
               returned by the TINTL$ Executive request. Define status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

        Example
                 01   TAPE-FILE PIC X(12) VALUE '$$TAPE$FILE'.
                 01   STAT PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

                      CALL 'UCSTINTL$' USING TAPE-FILE STAT.

           *     Rewind tape.


10.12.         Tape Swapping (UCSTSWAP$)
        Function
        Closes access to the current reel of a tape file and requests loading of the next reel of
        the file (unless special action is requested). Refers to the Executive request function
        TSWAP$.

        Format
           CALL 'UCSTSWAP$' USING file, status [ , function, reel ] .

        where:

        file

               is a character scalar expression or contiguous character array indicating the
               internal file name (only the first 12 characters are significant) of the tape file that is
               to have a reel swapped.

                                                                              Using Executive Requests




         status

            is an integer variable or array element indicating the status returned by the
            TSWAP$ Executive request. Define status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

            The next two arguments are optional, but if one is given the other must be
            present.

         function

            is an integer scalar expression specifying the swap function to be performed. The
            permissible values are as follows:


                     Value                                      Description

                  +0 or -0    Standard reel swap. This is the action taken if function and reel are not
                              given; reel is ignored.
                  +1 or -1    Standard reel swap. Returns the reel number of the reel swapped to in
                              reel.
                  +2 or -2    Swap to the reel whose reel number is given in reel.
                  +3 or -3    Swap to the reel whose reel index is given in reel.


            If function is negative, the request is not held on a reel-number conflict.

         reel

            The form of reel varies with the value of function:


                   Function                                   Reel Form

                       0      It can be any valid data item; it is ignored.
                        1     It is a scalar character variable into which the reel number of the new
                              reel is stored.
                       2      It is a character scalar expression giving the reel to swap to; only the
                              first 6 characters of reel are significant.
                       3      It is an integer scalar expression specifying the reel index of the new
                              reel.


         Example
            01      TAPE-FILE PIC X(12) VALUE '$$$TAPE$FILE'.
            01      STAT PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

10.13. Control Statement Listing (UCSCLIST$)
        Function
        Registers a set of control statement names with the Executive. Refers to Executive
        request function CLIST$. The system always returns control statements to you as
        ASCII images.

        Format
          CALL 'UCSCLIST$' USING number-of-names, names, status.

        where:

        number-of-names

            is an integer scalar expression specifying the number of names that are to be
            registered with the EXEC. If this value is zero, CLIST$ mode is terminated and the
            rest of the parameters are ignored; however, they must still be provided.

        names

            is the first item in a one-dimensional contiguous character array. The number of
            elements in the array must be equal to or greater than number-of-names. Only the
            first 6 characters of each element are used; any element of all spaces is ignored
            (and the name count reduced accordingly).

        status

            is an integer scalar variable or array element into which the status of the CLIST$
            Executive request is stored. Define status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

       (UCSINFO$)
         Function
         Retrieves system, run, and program-oriented parameters in a manner independent of
         system level. Refers to the Executive request function INFO$.

         Format
           CALL 'UCSINFO$' USING argument-group1, argument-group2... .

         where:

         argument-group

             pertains to a specific INFO$ Executive request function as described below. The

              where:

                 and briefly described below.

                 INFO$ Executive request is stored as a positive number. If an error has been
                 detected in the argument group, a value of -1 is stored; this means that too few

                 BINARY-1.

        UCSINFO$ Argument Groups
        The following list describes the parameters that UCSINFO$ retrieves and the argument

        1.    Retrieve user-id:

              group).

10.16. General Executive Requests (UCSGENERAL$)
        Function
        Provides access to any Executive request function that satisfies the following criteria:

        ∩é╖   The Executive request always returns to the instruction immediately after the ER
            itself. It can raise a contingency, but it cannot jump.
        ∩é╖   The Executive request does not spin off a new user activity or deactivate an
            existing activity.
        ∩é╖   The Executive request takes all its parameters from A registers, which can either
            contain the value or point to the data items (packets, for example) used by the ER.




10ΓÇô42                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                      Using Executive Requests




         ∩é╖   Addresses in A registers or ER packets are required by the ER to be in basic mode
             format.
             Note: All addresses generated by UCS languages are extended mode virtual
             addresses. You must convert extended mode addresses to basic mode
             addresses for ERs that require basic mode address formats. The UCSEMTOBM$
             service routine is provided for this purpose (see 10.23). If ER requires R1
             register as a parameter, fill-in A13 register with the value in the R1 register.
         ∩é╖   The Executive request delivers its results in A registers or in packets pointed to by
             the A registers used as input parameters.
             Note: If UCSGENERAL$ is called from a shared subsystem, the data packets
             and buffers must reside in a data bank with a LOW BDI.

         The Executive request functions that satisfy these criteria are the following:

         ∩é╖   APRINT$
         ∩é╖   IO$
             Spins off a new activity, but the user does not see it
         ∩é╖   LOG$
         ∩é╖   SYSLOG$
             Needs SSLOGER security privilege and you must convert extended mode
             addresses to basic mode addresses using the UCSEMTOBM$ service routine (see
             10.23).
         ∩é╖   SYMB$

         The Executive request functions that do not satisfy these criteria are the following:

         ∩é╖   AREAD$
             Jumps to the EOF address at the end of the input file
         ∩é╖   FORK$
             Spins off a new activity
         ∩é╖   II$
             Deactivates an activity
         ∩é╖   IOI$
             Temporarily jumps to some out-of-line address
         ∩é╖   TRON$
             Assigns the common bank name section instead of the subsystem name section.
         ∩é╖   Some Transaction Processing (TIP) Executive requests
             Take parameters in R registers

         A UCS COBOL program that calls an Executive request function that requires an
         address of a buffer to be passed as one of its parameters should use the LOC$
         subroutine (see 10.6.3).


7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               10ΓÇô43
Using Executive Requests




        Format
          CALL 'UCSGENERAL$' (ER-code, input-mask, output-mask, input-registers,
          output-registers [,user-D-bank, ER-instruction-word ])

        where:

        ER-code

           is an integer scalar expression (USAGE BINARY) specifying the ER to be
           performed. See the ER Programming Reference Manual for ER codes.

        input-mask

           is a one-word value (normally an integer) specifying which A-registers are to be
           loaded before the ER is performed. Any bits not used in this word must be zero.
           The convention for determining which registers to load is presented in the
           following table.


                     Bit Set                   Register to Load

                        1                             A0
                       2                              A1
                       3                              A2
                       4                              A3
                       5                              A6
                       6                              A5
                       7                              A6
                       8                              A7
                       9                              A8
                       10                             A9
                       11                             A10
                       12                             A11
                       13                             A12
                       14                         A13 and R1
                       15                             A14
                       16                             A15




10ΓÇô44                                                                         7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                    Using Executive Requests




         output-mask

               is a one-word value (normally an integer) specifying which A-registers are to be
               stored to output-registers after the ER. Any bits not used in this word must be
               zero. The convention describing which registers to store is presented in the
               following table.


                        Bit Set                         Register to Store

          1                                   A0
          2                                   A1
          3                                   A2
          4                                   A3
          5                                   A6
          6                                   A5
          7                                   A6
          8                                   A7
          9                                   A8
          10                                  A9
          11                                  A10
          12                                  A11
          13                                  A12
          14                                  A13
          15                                  A14
          16                                  A15


         input-registers

               is a one-dimensional contiguous array of one-word variables. The first element
               contains the value of the first A-register to be loaded, the second element
               contains the value of the second A-register to be loaded, and so forth. For
               example, if the input-mask specifies that A0 and A3 should be loaded, the first
               element of input-registers is loaded into A0 and the second element is loaded into
               A3. The value of A13 register is also moved to the R1 register.

         output-registers

               is a one-dimensional contiguous array of one-word variables. The first A-register
               to be stored is stored in the first element, the second A-register to be stored is
               stored in the second element, and so forth. For example, if the output-mask
               specifies that A1 and A5 are to be stored after the ER, A1 is stored to the first
               element of output-registers and A5 is stored to the second.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                10ΓÇô45
Using Executive Requests




        user-D-bank

           is a variable, array element, or array (except an assumed noncontiguous array
           value) having storage in the same bank as all data used by the ER.

           All data used from memory by the ER must reside in the same bank. This can be
           accomplished by placing all data items used by the ER in the same common block
           or by placing none of the data items in a common block. The UCSGENERAL$
           subroutine bases the bank indicated by the address of this argument as a basic
           mode bank prior to execution of the ER. Basic mode banks reserve the first 128
           words of the address space for use by registers. Thus, the address of any data
           item used from memory by the ER must not fall within the range 0 - 177 octal
           (within the first 128 words). This is usually accomplished by placing the data items
           in a common block with a filler of 128 words preceding it. Note the filler area can
           be used for any data items not used by the ER.

           If the data items are contained in a large bank made up of several small banks, the
           address of the data items used by the ER cannot fall within the first 128 words of
           each small bank.

        ER- instruction- word

           is a required scratch word giving a location in the specified user D-bank written
           into by UCSGENERAL$. It must be a full word, and word-aligned. It must have a
           bank offset greater than 128 (octal 200). Its address must not be within the ER
           packet or other data in use during the ER. The offset must be greater than the
           general register set because the ER is executed in basic mode. You can get the
           correct offset by padding the bank. If you pass an offset of 128 or less, the service
           library ignores the scratch word parameter and prints the following error message:

          19066:   INCORRECT NUMBER OF ARGUMENTS ON SERVICE LIBRARY CALL

           If the ER uses data only from registers and not from memory (for example,
           TIME$), you can omit user D-bank and ER instruction word.

        Note: To ensure that the 128-word offset is allocated, you must allocate its
        variable names or use the COMPAT/FULL keyword option (see 2.2.3).

        Examples
        The following program illustrates the use of UCSGENERAL$. It uses the Executive
        request function MODSWTIME$.

            IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
            PROGRAM-ID. MODSWTIME-EXAMPLE.
            ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.
            CONFIGURATION SECTION.
            SOURCE-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
            OBJECT-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
            DATA DIVISION.
            WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
            01 ER-CODE                             PIC 9(10) BINARY       VALUE 209.



10ΓÇô46                                                                           7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                               Using Executive Requests




             01   INPUT-MASK.
                     02 INPUT-NOUSE-A0-A35       PIC 1(36) BINARY-1 VALUE 0.
              01 OUTPUT-MASK.
                     02 OUTPUT-USE-A0            PIC 1(1) BINARY-1 VALUE 1.
                     02 OUTPUT-NOUSE-A1-A35      PIC 1(35) BINARY-1 VALUE 0.
              01 ER-PACKET                       PIC 1(36) BINARY-1 VALUE 0.
              01 OUTPUT-REG.
                     02 TIME-IS-MODIFIED-SWTIME PIC 1(1) BINARY-1.
                     02 SEASONAL-SHIFT-ON        PIC 1(1) BINARY-1.
                     02 SECONDS-SINCE-1900       PIC 1(34) BINARY-1.
              PROCEDURE DIVISION.
              BEGIN.
                   CALL 'UCSGENERAL$' USING ER-CODE, INPUT-MASK,
                   OUTPUT-MASK, ER-PACKET, OUTPUT-REG.
            * 209 IS THE ER CODE FOR MODSWTIME$
            * Upon successful completion, OUTPUT-REG (A0) contains:
            * TIME-IS-MODIFIED-SWTIME - This is always set to 1. It
            *                             indicates a modified-swtime timestamp.
            * SEASONAL-SHIFT-ON - This is 0 or 1 indicating the seasonal
            *                    offset at the UTC time described in bits 2-35.
            * SECONDS-SINCE-1900 - These 34 bits contain the number of
            *                      seconds since 00:00:00 1899 Dec 31, UTC base.
                   STOP RUN.

         The following program illustrates the use of UCSGENERAL$. It uses the Executive
         request function DATE$.

             01 DATEDOLLAR-ER.
                 02 MMDDYY PIC 9(10) BINARY.
                 02 HHMMSS PIC 9(10) BINARY.
             01 D REDEFINES DATEDOLLAR-ER.
                 02 D1 PIC 1(12) BINARY-1.
                 02 D2 PIC 1(12) BINARY-1.
                 02 D3 PIC 1(12) BINARY-1.
                 02 D4 PIC 1(12) BINARY-1.
                 02 D5 PIC 1(12) BINARY-1.
                 02 D6 PIC 1(12) BINARY-1.
             01 A0-A1.
                 02 BIT1 PIC 1 BINARY-1 VALUE 1.
                 02 BIT2 PIC 1 BINARY-1 VALUE 1.
                 02 BIT3-36 PIC 1(34) BINARY-1 VALUE 0.
             01 ER-CODE PIC 9(10) BINARY VALUE 18.
                                  .
                                  .
                                  .
            * CALL ER DATE$
                 CALL 'UCSGENERAL$' USING ER-CODE, 0, A0-A1, 0, D.
            * 18 is the ER code for DATE$
            * D1 will contain (in Fieldata) the current month
            * D2 will contain (in Fieldata) the current day
            * D3 will contain (in Fieldata) the last two digits of the year




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                          10ΓÇô47
Using Executive Requests




              * D4 will contain (in Fieldata) the hour
              * D5 will contain (in Fieldata) the minutes
              * D6 will contain (in Fieldata) the seconds

        The following example shows the use of UCSGENERAL$ using all 7 parameters.
        This program prints the line ΓÇ£HI THEREΓÇ¥ with single spacing on the standard
        output device using the Executive request function APRINT$.

              IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
              PROGRAM-ID. EXAMPLE.
              ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.
              CONFIGURATION SECTION.
              SOURCE-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
              OBJECT-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
              DATA DIVISION.
              COMMON-STORAGE SECTION.
              01 BANK-OFFSET PIC X(512).
              01 USER-D-BANK PIC X(4).
              01 ER-INSTRUCTION PIC X(4).
              01 CHAR-STRING PIC X(8) VALUE 'HI THERE'.
              01 CHAR-STRING-ADDR PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.
              01 INPUT-MASK.
                  02 INPUT-USE-A0 PIC 1 BINARY-1 VALUE 1.
                  02 INPUT-NOUSE-A1-A36 PIC 1(35) BINARY-1 VALUE 0.
              01 OUTPUT-MASK.
                  02 OUTPUT-NOUSE-A0-A36 PIC 1(36) BINARY-1 VALUE 0.
              01 ER-PACKET.
                  02 PF1 PIC 1(12) BINARY-1 VALUE 1.
                  02 PF2 PIC 1(6) BINARY-1 VALUE 2.
                  02 PF3 PIC 1(18) BINARY-1 VALUE 0.
              01 OUTAR PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.
              PROCEDURE DIVISION.
              BEGIN.
                  CALL 'LOC$' USING CHAR-STRING, CHAR-STRING-ADDR.
                  MOVE CHAR-STRING-ADDR TO PF3.
                  CALL 'UCSGENERAL$'
                          USING 56, INPUT-MASK, OUTPUT-MASK, ER-PACKET, OUTAR,
                                USER-D-BANK, ER-INSTRUCTION.
                  STOP RUN.


10.17. Milliseconds Past Midnight (UCSTIME$)
           Function
           Provides the current local time in milliseconds past midnight, local time base, in
           integer form.

           Format
             CALL 'UCSTIME$' USING t

           where t is a 1-word binary item.



10ΓÇô48                                                                                7831 0455ΓÇô022

         Description

10.18. Retrieving Time (UCSDWTIME$)
         Function
         Provides the current local time in nanoseconds past 00:00:00.000 December 31, 1899,
         in integer form.

         where t is a 2-word binary item.

         Description
         The UCSDWTIME$ subroutine returns the number of nanoseconds past 00:00:00.000
         December 31, 1899, local time base, in the variable t. Because the value is so large,
         two words are required to hold it. Use UCSCNVTIM$ to convert the value in t to a 6-
         character date (see 10.19).

10.19. Converting Time in UCSDWTIME$ Format
       (UCSCNVTIM$)
        Function
        The UCSCNVTIM$ subroutine converts a time in nanoseconds in UCSDWTIME$ format
        to a date in month, day, and year format (mmddyy).

            CALL 'UCSCNVTIM$' USING t, d

        where:
        t
                is a 2-word binary item.

        d
                is an alphanumeric variable with a length of 6.

        The argument t must contain a time in nanoseconds in the format produced by
        UCSDWTIME$. UCSCNVTIM$ converts the value in t to a 6-character month, day, and
        year format (mmddyy). The converted value is returned in argument d.

                CALL 'UCSCNVTIM$' USING TIMEID DATEID.

10.20. Converting Time in UCSDWTIME$ Format to
       a Date (UCSCNVTIM$CC)
         Function
         The UCSCNVTIM$CC subroutine converts a time in nanoseconds in UCSDWTIME$
         format to a date in a format determined by the length of d. It can also return the
         current date in the same formats.

         Format
             CALL 'UCSCNVTIM$CC' USING t, d

         where:

         t
              is a 2-word binary item.

         d
              is an alphanumeric variable with a length of at least 8. The result will be returned
              in d.

         Argument t, if present, must contain a time in nanoseconds in the format produced by
         UCSDWTIME$ (see 10.18). UCSCNVTIM$CC converts this value to an 8 to 17 character
         format holding the 4-digit year, 2-digit month, and 2-digit day and optionally, the 2-digit
         hour, 2-digit minute, 2-digit second, and 3-digit millisecond. The precision is
         determined from the size of the variable d.


                       Size of d           Precision          Format of d
                           8         Day                ccyymmdd

                          10         Hour               ccyymmddhh

                          12         Minute             ccyymmddhhmm

                          14         Second             ccyymmddhhmmss

                          15         1/10 Second        ccyymmddhhmmssm

                          16         1/100 Second       ccyymmddhhmmssmm

                          17         1/1000 Second      ccyymmddhhmmssmmm


         If argument t is not present, the current date-time is returned into argument d.

         The UCSINITREG$ subroutine provides the initial contents of the registers that are set
         up by the Exec when a program begins execution.

10.22. Converting between Fieldata and ASCII
       Characters (UCSASCFD$, UCSFDASC$)
         Function
         These subroutines allow you to convert between Fieldata and ASCII characters, as
         follows:

         ∩é╖   UCSFDASC$
             Converts Fieldata characters to ASCII characters
         ∩é╖   UCSASCFD$
             Converts ASCII characters to Fieldata characters

         Both routines are intended to be used with ER and system service routines only.
         Other uses of UCSASCFD$ are not supported since Fieldata is an obsolete data type.

         Format
                  ßç▒
                   UCSFDASC$ßç▒
         CALL                USING , , 
                  ΓÇ▓UCSASCFD$ΓÇ▓
         where:

         a

             is the source string to be converted. For UCSFDASC$, a is an expression of any
             type. For UCSASCFD$, a is a character expression.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                           10ΓÇô55
Using Executive Requests




        b

             is the target for the converted characters. For UCSFDASC$, b is a character
             variable, character array, character array element, or character substring. For
             UCSASCFD$, b is a variable, array, or array element of any type, or a character
             substring.

        i

             is an integer scalar expression that specifies the number of characters to convert.
             If i = 0, no characters are converted.

        Description
        Note: In the following paragraphs, ASCII characters are assumed to be packed four
        characters per word, starting on a quarter word boundary. Fieldata characters are
        assumed to be packed six characters per word, starting on a half-word boundary
        only. Any other character alignment is not supported and could produce
        unpredictable results.

        UCSFDASC$ converts i Fieldata characters represented by a to ASCII characters and
        places the result into b. If a and b share the same storage, the conversion may fail.

        UCSASCFD$ converts i ASCII characters represented by a to Fieldata characters and
        places the result into b. If a and b share the same storage, the source characters a are
        destroyed.

        The entities a and b cannot be noncontiguous arrays.

        Example
        The following example illustrates the use of UCSFDASC$. The program calls the
        UCSPCT$ service routine to obtain the first word of the program control table (PCT),
        which is the run identifier (RUNID) in Fieldata characters. The program then calls
        UCSFDASC$ to convert the RUNID from Fieldata to ASCII characters.

             IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
             PROGRAM-ID. example.
              ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.
              CONFIGURATION SECTION.
              SOURCE-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
              OBJECT-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
              SPECIAL-NAMES.
                  PRINTER IS PRT.
              DATA DIVISION.
              WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
              01 pct-buffer-runid PIC 9(10) BINARY.
              01 pct-words-to-read PIC 9(10) BINARY VALUE 1.
              01 pct-word-offset PIC 9(10) BINARY VALUE 0.
              01 ascii-runid PIC X(6).
              PROCEDURE DIVISION.
              BEGIN.
            *


10ΓÇô56                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                     Using Executive Requests




           *     Retrieve the Fieldata RUNID from the program control table
           *     (PCT) using the UCSPCT$ Executive Request service routine.
           *     Convert the Fieldata RUNID to ASCII using UCSFDASC$.
           *        CALL 'UCSPCT$'
                           USING pct-words-to-read, pct-word-offset,
                           pct-buffer-runid.
                   CALL 'UCSFDASC$' USING pct-buffer-runid, ascii-runid, 6.
                   DISPLAY ascii-runid UPON PRT.
                   STOP RUN.


10.23. Converting Extended Mode Addresses to
       Basic Mode Addresses (UCSEMTOBM$)
         Function
         UCSEMTOBM$ converts an extended mode address of form

           l, bdi, offset

         to a basic mode address of form

           e, bdi, offset

         Format
           CALL 'UCSEMTOBM$' USING em-addr, bm-addr, status

         where:

         em-addr

               is an integer value representing the extended mode address to be converted.
               em-addr is an extended mode address of form l, bdi, offset. This address is the
               result of the LOC$ service routine (see 10.6.3).

               Note: Most ERs require the packet and data accessed by the ER to be in
               PROGRAM level storage. Common blocks are allocated as PROGRAM level
               storage. em-addr should be the address of an item in a common block; if not,
               you should use the proper @LINK commands to declare the storage as
               PROGRAM level.

         bm-addr

               is an integer scalar variable or array element that contains the result of the
               conversion upon exit from UCSEMTOBM$. bm-addr is a basic mode address of
               form e, bdi, offset. If status is nonzero, bm-addr is returned with a value of zero.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  10ΓÇô57
Using Executive Requests




        status

           is an integer scalar variable or array element that contains the status of the
           conversion on exit from UCSEMTOBM$. status is zero if the conversion was
           successful. status is a nonzero value if the extended mode BDI value is greater
           than 4095 (basic mode limit). Define status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

        Description
        The UCSEMTOBM$ subroutine converts an extended mode address to a basic mode
        address. UCSEMTOBM$ is supported for use with UCSGENERAL$ only, for performing
        ERs that require basic mode addresses for the contents of an A-register or ER packet.

        Example
        The following example illustrates use of UCSEMTOBM$ for performing ER SYSLOG$
        through UCSGENERAL$. ER SYSLOG$ requires a basic mode address in the ER packet
        and in register A0. UCSEMTOBM$ is called to convert extended mode addresses
        (obtained through LOC$) to basic mode addresses.

        Description
        The UCS$ACTAUX subroutine activates the calling of user-supplied auxiliary and

10.25. Subprograms for Performing System
       Level I/O
         The I/O subprograms described in this section provide an interface to the OS 2200
         Executive request ER IOW$ described in the ER Programming Reference Manual. The
         read and write subprograms use the FIOW and UCSMAKEIOPK$ subprograms
         described in the COBOL Compiler Programming Reference Manual Volume 2. Many
         of the status codes returned by the subprograms described in this section (such as
         BULKREAD$ and BULKWRITE$) are the same status codes as those returned by
         FIOW. The advantages of these subprograms compared to FIOW and UCSMAKEIOPK$
         include

         ∩é╖   Ability to transfer larger amounts of data than FIOW
         ∩é╖   Simpler interfaces
         ∩é╖   Files that are assigned and freed through OPEN and CLOSE functions
         ∩é╖   No need to construct an I/O packet by calling UCSMAKEIOPK$

         The input/output ER (FIO, FIOW) subprograms described in the COBOL Compiler
         Programming Reference Manual Volume 2 are limited to reading and writing a
         maximum of 128 tracks (229,376 words) of storage per subprogram call.

         The standard UCS COBOL I/O subprograms are limited to reading and writing a
         maximum of 224-1 (16,777,215) words.

         The UCS COBOL compilers are limited to allocating objects (such as structures and
         arrays) up to 224-1 words in size. The UCS COBOL compilers generate code that can
         address a maximum of 224-1 words for a single object.

         The low-level I/O subprograms described in this subsection provide the capability to
         perform low-level I/O operations of up to 230 (1,073,741,824) words per subprogram
         call.

         Note: The 2200/XPA system (such as the 2200/500, 2200/900, or HMP IX systems)
         supports very large banks up to 233 words. However, the operating system
         currently supports very large banks up to 230 words. A very large bank is made up
         of storage having consecutive bank descriptor indexes (BDI). The system imposes
         limits on the number of BDIs according to the address tree level. See the Internal
         Limits appendix in the Linking System Programming Reference Manual for
         documented limits. For a given program, the Exec and the Linking System may
         allocate a few BDIs at each address tree level for internal use. The actual number of
         BDIs allocated for internal use may vary. In addition, the storage in your program
         requires BDIs. Consequently, the maximum size of a very large bank and the
         maximum number of words performed by one I/O operation is somewhat smaller
         than the limits specified.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                             10ΓÇô61
Using Executive Requests




        The BULKREAD$ and BULKWRITE$ subprograms described in this section use the
        UCSMAKIOPK$ and FIOW subprograms described in the COBOL Compiler
        Programming Reference Manual, Volume 2. The ER IOW$ status codes are defined in
        the ER Programming Reference Manual.

        The functions described in this subsection are limited to FASTRAND-formatted mass
        storage files only. Tape files are not supported. Program files (files containing
        elements) are supported.

        Generally, three function calls are required to perform a simple read or write
        operation:

        ∩é╖    A call to open a file or program file element
        ∩é╖    A call to perform the read or write
        ∩é╖    A call to close the file

        The I/O operation will stop on any I/O error including an I/O error type 5 (read from
        unassigned area of mass storage). A status is returned from the function call indicating
        the I/O status.

        If you call the BULKREAD$ read or BULKWRITE$ routines more than once, it does not
        continue reading or writing from where you left off. Multiple calls will result in the I/O
        operation being performed using the same mass storage address. However, you can
        change the mass storage address using the BULKSETSECTOR$ routine that is
        described in this section.

        All parameters passed to the BULKIO functions must be on word boundaries. If data
        items residing in structures are passed as parameters, you may have to insert FILLER
        items to ensure this.

10.25.1. BULKOPEN$
        Function
        The BULKOPEN$ subprogram opens the OS 2200 file whose name is the string
        referenced by filename. Upon a successful open, the subprogram returns an address
        of a file information packet (FIP) in file-id.

        Format
            CALL ΓÇÖBULKOPEN$ΓÇÖ USING file-id, filename, io-type, open-status

        where:

        file-id

             is an integer variable into which the address of the FIP is returned. The file-id
             variable must be passed as an argument for later read, write, and close
             operations.

             Define file-id as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.



10ΓÇô62                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                            Using Executive Requests




   filename

      is a character string that must represent a valid OS 2200 file name. Qualifiers and file
      cycles are allowed. File names having element and version names are allowed. File
      read/write keys are not allowed. The contents of filename must end with or space.
      Define filename as a quoted string or as PIC X(n). If the file already exists, it must be a
      FASTRAND-formatted mass storage file.

   io-type

      is a character string that consists of a mode specification. The io-type string has three
      fields separated by commas:

      ∩é╖      Read/Write mode indicator

      type string must be terminated by at least one trailing space. If the element subtype
      indicator is specified, it must be preceded by the type indicator.

         If you open a file that is not assigned before the BULKOPEN$ call, the BULKOPEN$
         subprogram attempts to assign the file in the following way:

         ∩é╖     If the file is cataloged, it is assigned.
         ∩é╖     If the file does not exist and the type argument is
               ∩Ç¡   r, r+, then BULKOPEN$ returns a failed indication.
               ∩Ç¡   w, then BULKOPEN$ assigns a temporary file.

         Cataloged files not assigned to the run before the BULKOPEN$ call are freed when
         the file is closed.

         Temporary files assigned during the BULKOPEN$ call remain assigned until the run
         terminates or until you explicitly free the file with the @FREE command.

         All files assigned before the BULKOPEN$ call remain assigned until the run
         terminates or until you explicitly free the file with the @FREE command.

         All use names attached to a file before a BULKOPEN$ call remain attached to the file
         after the file is closed.

         If a given file is opened more than once before being closed, the closes should be
         done in reverse order. If this is not done, the file may not be left in the original
         ΓÇ£assignΓÇ¥ state at the end.

        Element I/O
        The optional element type and subtype are only used if the filename has an element
        specification in it. If you include the optional element type and subtype indicator, they
        are syntactically validated but are ignored if the filename does not have an element
        specification in it. If you include an element name in the filename but do not include an
        element type indicator or element subtype indicator, the default element type is
        SYMBOLIC (1) and subtype is ELT (1). If an element subtype is specified, it must be
        proceeded by an element type specification.

        The values for type-name and type-code are defined in Table 10ΓÇô4.


             Table 10ΓÇô4. Permitted Values for the type-name and type-code on the
                                  BULKOPEN$ Subprogram


                       Element Type                        type-name               type-code

        symbolic                                      SYMBOLIC                          1
                                                      SYM
        assembler procedure                           ASMP                             2
        COBOL procedure                               COBP                             3
        Fortran procedure                             FORP                             4

           Table 10ΓÇô4. Permitted Values for the type-name and type-code on the
                                BULKOPEN$ Subprogram


                       Element Type                  type-name                      type-code

         relocatable                              RELOCATABLE                           5
                                                  REL
                                                  RB
         absolute, object modules,                ABSOLUTE                              6
         ZOOMs, and SSDEF                         ABS
         omnibus                                  OMNIBUS                               7
                                                  OMN


         The subtype-code must be an integer constant. If the integer constant starts with a
         leading zero, it is treated as an octal value. The subtype-code must be a value
         between 0 and 63 (octal 0 through 077). The subtype information is used when
         creating a new program file element (write).

         Read/Write ("r+") is not allowed for element I/O. Elements can only be read or created
         anew (write); they cannot be updated (ΓÇ£R+ΓÇ¥). If you want to update an element, you
         must open it for input, read it in, close it, and then open it for output, write it, and
         close it.

         The bulk I/O routines do not require exclusive access to write to a file. If you want
         exclusive access when writing to a file, you must assign the file yourself exclusively
         before opening the file.

         When you close an element opened for write, it creates a new program file element
         with a new table of contents (TOC) entry. The contents of the new element are not
         available to other programs or activities until the file is closed.

         You must not have more than one element at a time opened for write in a given
         program file. The OS 2200 program file format writes new elements at the end of the
         file, and bad results are ensured if multiple element writes are attempted
         simultaneously. The bulk I/O routines cannot diagnose this error.

         For reads, the ASMP, COBP, and FORP element types are all treated as symbolics
         (SYM).

         Element subtypes are ignored on reads.

         Element subtypes are valid for type SYMBOLIC, ABSOLUTE, and OMNIBUS elements.
         Other element types do not have subtypes.

         You cannot open an ABSOLUTE or RELOCATABLE element for write. Bulk I/O does not
         create the required information needed for the table of contents (TOC) entry.

        When you read file/file-element text, it is read-in in a raw I/O manner. If it consists of
        SDF symbolic images, the SDF information is in the read-in text. If the images are
        cycled, all the cycles are there. It is up to your program to interpret the information. If
        you are working with SDF images with cycle information, you should use regular
        high-level COBOL I/O and not the low-level bulk I/O complex.

        The cycle information for a SYMBOLIC element opened for write is all set to zero. You
        should not have cycling SDF images in the text of the element. If you read in a
        symbolic element having cycling images and write it out to a new symbolic element
        using bulk I/O, the cycling will be at zero and all images with other cycle numbers may
        be ignored by any program or processor that reads the new element. The content of
        any files/file-elements written is your responsibility.

10.25.3. BULKREAD$ Subprogram
        Function
        The BULKREAD$ subprogram reads bytes-to-read number of bytes into the area
        pointed to by buf, from the file pointed by file-id. The BULKREAD$ subprogram
        rounds bytes-to-read up to the next multiple of four bytes, that is, to a whole word
        (bytes-to-read + 3) / 4.

        Format
             CALL ΓÇÖBULKREAD$ΓÇÖ USING file-id, buf, bytes-to-read, bytes-xferred,
             sentinel-flag, sentinel, sentinel-char-offset, read-status

        where:

        file-id

              is an integer variable containing the address of the FIP for the file to be closed.
              file-id is set by a call to BULKOPEN$. Define file-id as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

        bytes-to-read

              contains the size in bytes to be transferred on the read. Define bytes-to-read as
              PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

        buf

              is a word-aligned character string that contains the data read by the subroutine.
              Define buf as PIC X(n), where n is large enough to hold the extraneous bytes
              transferred by BULKREAD$ when the bytes-to-read argument is not a multiple of
              4.



10ΓÇô68                                                                                     7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                    Using Executive Requests




         bytes-xferred

             is set by BULKREAD$ to the number of bytes transferred on the read. It is always
             a multiple of 4. The number of bytes transferred on the read will never be greater
             than the value of bytes-to-read + 3. Define bytes-xferred as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

         sentinel-flag

             is an integer value specifying whether the BULKREAD$ subprogram will or will not
             search for a sentinel character. Define sentinal-flag as a numeric integer or as
             PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

         sentinel

             represents a 1-character variable that contains the value of a sentinel character. If
             the sentinel-flag is nonzero, the BULKREAD$ subprogram performs the read
             operation and then searches the area pointed by buf for a byte containing the
             value of the sentinel argument. The search is performed for bytes-xferred
             number of bytes. Define sentinel as a 1-character nonnumeric literal, a PIC X data
             item OR as a PIC 1(9) BINARY-1 data item for a value not allowed as nonnumeric
             literal. For example, if sentinel is to be octal 0400, the VALUE of the PIC 1 data
             item specified should be 256.

         sentinel-char-offset

             is an integer value returned if sentinel-flag is nonzero. If the search finds the
             sentinel character, the integer pointed to by the sentinel-char-offset argument is
             set to the byte offset of the sentinel in buf. The byte offset starts at zero. If the
             sentinel character is not found, the integer pointed to by the sentinel-char-offset
             argument is set to ΓÇô1. The search operation can be used for objects that are
             greater than the standard UCS limit of 224-1 (16,777,215) words in size. Define
             sentinel-char-offset as PIC S1(36) BINARY-1.

         read-status

             is set to a status constant upon return from a call to BULKREAD$. Define
             read-status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1. The BULKREAD$ subprogram sets read-status
             to the value returned by the Executive request FIOW subprogram.

        Reading to the End of File
        The BULKREAD$ subprogram uses the Executive request IOW and the I/O
        subprogram ΓÇ£read by BDIΓÇ¥ (054). The BULKREAD$ subprogram returns an I/O status
        of 5 when you attempt to read from an unassigned area of the file. The Exec normally
        assigns files with track granularity (1792 words per track). A write of only 1 word to a
        file with no initial tracks reserved results in one track assigned. If you read until you
        encounter an I/O status 5 condition, the number of words transferred includes all the
        words of the last assigned track. If you have a large number of initially reserved tracks,
        you may read many tracks until you encounter an I/O status 5.

        The number of words read depends on the value of the bytes-to-read argument and
        how many tracks are assigned to the file. In general, the extra words read are not part
        of the original data written but are part of the fileΓÇÖs track assigned area and contain
        unpredictable values. You are responsible for interpreting the data read in and
        knowing where the logical end of the file is. The sentinel arguments can help you
        determine the logical end of the file.

        Reading Program Files
        An OS 2200 program file has a table of contents (TOC) at the beginning. There usually
        is a relatively large unassigned area of mass storage between the TOC and the text of
        the first element. If you attempt to read the whole program file in one bulk I/O, you
        will get an I/O Error 5 and will only read the TOC portion. Bulk I/O is low-level I/O so
        you must be careful using it.

10.25.4. BULKWRITE$ Subprogram
        Function
        The BULKWRITE$ subprogram writes bytes-to-write number of bytes from the area
        pointed to by buf to the file pointed to by file-id. The BULKWRITE$ subprogram
        rounds bytes-to-write up to the next multiple of four bytes, that is, to a whole word
        (bytes-to-write + 3) / 4.




10ΓÇô70                                                                                 7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                      Using Executive Requests




         Format
            CALL ΓÇÖBULKWRITE$ΓÇÖ USING file-id, buf, bytes-to-write, bytes-xferred,
            write-status.

         where:

         file-id

               is an integer variable containing the address of the FIP for the file to be closed.
               file-id is set by a call to BULKOPEN$. Define file-id as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

         buf

               is a word-aligned character string that contains the data to be written by the
               subroutine. Define buf as PIC X(n), where n is large enough to hold the number of
               bytes to be written plus any sentinel character to be appended at the end of the
               data.

         bytes-to-write

               is a numeric integer or an integer variable. The integer or the contents of
               bytes-to-write specify how many bytes that BULKWRITE$ should write to the file.
               Define bytes-to-write as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

               If bytes-to-write is negative, the same 4 bytes pointed to by buf are written n
               times to the file referenced by file-id, where n = (ABS(bytes-to-write) + 3 / 4).
               Passing a negative value for bytes-to-write is useful for clearing the contents of a
               file to zero.

         bytes-xferred

               is set by BULKWRITE$ to the number of bytes transferred on the write. It is
               always a multiple of 4. The number of bytes transferred on the write will never be
               greater than the value of bytes-to-write + 3. Define bytes-xferred as PIC 1(36)
               BINARY-1.

         write-status

               is an integer that contains the status returned by BULKWRITE$. BULKWRITE$ will
               set write-status to the status returned by the Executive request IOW function.
               Define open-status a PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

10.25.5. BULKGETFILESIZE$ Subprogram
        Function
        This subprogram determines the size in bytes of a file. The file must be opened. The
        intent of this function is to give a file size that can be used for buffer allocations and
        other approximate uses that do not need an exact byte count. The size will be greater
        than or equal to the size of the program file elementΓÇÖs text.

        Format
           CALL 'BULKGETFILESIZE$' USING file-id, file-size, status.

        where:

        file-id

            is an integer variable containing the address of the FIP for the file for which the
            size is to be determined. The value of file-id is set by a call to BULKOPEN$. Define
            file-id as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1. The file file-id must be associated with a program
            file element opened for input (read). The size is determined by the size in its table
            of contents entry. If file-id is not associated with a program file element opened
            for input, the file-size parameter will be set to zero and a status of 5523 returned.

        file-size

            is set to the size in bytes of the file pointed to by file-id. Define file-size as PIC
            1(36) BINARY-1. file-size is in terms of bytes, but is based on the number of
            sectors, so it will be a multiple of 112.

        status

            is set to a status constant upon return from a call to BULKGETFILESIZE$. Define
            status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

10.25.6. BULKGETSECTOR$ Subprogram
         Function
         The BULKGETSECTOR$ subprogram gets the starting sector address of a file. This
         subprogram can be used in combination with the BULKSETSECTOR$ subprogram to
         perform I/O starting at a specific mass storage address in a file. It can also be used to
         implement a random-access I/O facility.

         Format
            CALL 'BULKGETSECTOR$' USING file-id, file-sector-offset, status.

         where:

         file-id

             is an integer variable containing the address of the FIP for the file for which the
             size is to be determined. file-id is set by a call to BULKOPEN$. Define file-id as
             PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

         file-sector-offset

             Define file-sector-offset as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

                If file-id is associated with a program file element opened for input,
                file-sector-offset will be the sector offset in the file where the element resides.
                If file-id is associated with a program file element opened for output, file-sector-
                offset will be the sector address where the element is to be written.
                If file-id is associated with a data file, the file-sector-offset will be set to zero
                since that is where the I/O is based from.
                File-sector-offset is set to the value as determined at open time. It is not
                affected by BULKSETSECTOR$ calls.

         status

             is set to a status constant upon return from a call to BULKGETSECTOR$. Define
             status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

10.25.7. BULKSETSECTOR$ Subprogram
        Function
        The BULKSETSECTOR$ subprogram sets the sector offset variable in the bulk I/O FIP
        for the associated file. The next I/O call (BULKREAD$ or BULKWRITE$) will be done
        using this value as the mass-storage address for I/O. Normally, the starting
        mass-storage address for bulk I/O is invariant and is set at the open to the beginning
        of the file or element (element if file is associated with a program file element). This
        function allows you to change the mass storage address that is used for the I/O calls
        on the file.

        This routine can be used in combination with the BULKGETSECTOR$ subprogram to be
        able to perform I/O operations starting at a specific mass storage address in a file. It
        can be used to implement a random-access I/O facility.

        Format
           CALL    'BULKSETSECTOR$' USING file-id, file-sector-offset, status.

        where:

        file-id

            is an integer variable containing the address of the FIP for the file for which the
            size is to be determined. file-id is set by a call to BULKOPEN$. Define file-id as
            PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

        file-sector-offset

            Define file-sector-offset as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

        status

            is set to a status constant upon return from a call to BULKSETSECTOR$. Define
            status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

10.25.8. Example of Bulk I/O
         The following example program executes calls to the bulk I/O subprograms and tests
         the results. The program does the following:

         ∩é╖   Initializes 500 bytes of BUF with integer values 1-500.
         ∩é╖   Sets BFCHAR (11) = 'A' (for later search purposes.).
         ∩é╖   Opens file BULKIOTEST1.
         ∩é╖   Writes the contents of BUF to file BULKIOTEST
         ∩é╖   Reads file BULKIOTEST, with search sentinel BYTEINT set to 256
         ∩é╖   Reads file BULKIOTEST, with search sentinel quoted-string 'A'
         ∩é╖   Closes file BULKIOTEST.

         The expected results are:

                          Attempt open
                          Attempt write
                          xfer-count = 0000000500
                          Sent-off should be 255, it is= +0000000255
                          Sent-off should be 10, it is= +0000000010
                          Attempt close

                      IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
                      PROGRAM-ID. BULKIO.
                      ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.
                      CONFIGURATION SECTION.
                      SOURCE-COMPUTER. UNISYS.
                      OBJECT-COMPUTER. UNISYS.
                      INPUT-OUTPUT SECTION.
                      FILE-CONTROL.
                      DATA DIVISION.
                      FILE SECTION.
                      WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
                      01 BUF.

                      02 BFGP OCCURS 1 TO 1000 DEPENDING ON BUFSIZE.

                 01 WS-GRP.
                     02 FILLER PIC X(3).
                      02 PIC 1(9)    BINARY-1 VALUE 256.

                 01 MY-STATUS PIC 1(36)      BINARY-1 VALUE 0.
                 01 SENT-OFF    PIC S1(36) BINARY-1 VALUE 0.
                 01 I           PIC s9(10) BINARY    VALUE 0.

                 PROCEDURE DIVISION.
                 PPPP.
                      PERFORM BUFSIZE TIMES
                        ADD 1 TO I

                      END-PERFORM.

                      DISPLAY 'Attempt open'.

                        STOP RUN.

                        DISPLAY 'status from READ is = ', MY-STATUS STOP RUN.
                      DISPLAY 'sent-off should be 255, it is = ', SENT-OFF.

                      CALL 'BULKREAD$'
                        USING FP, BUF, 500, XFER-COUNT, 1, 'A', SENT-OFF,
                              MY-STATUS.
                      IF MY-STATUS NOT = 0
                        DISPLAY 'status from READ is = ', MY-STATUS STOP RUN.
                      DISPLAY 'sent-off should be 10, it is = ', SENT-OFF.
