Processing IBM Tapes




        General Rules
        1.   The ASSIGN clause specifies the association of the file referenced by file name to
             a storage medium.
        2.   The RESERVE clause allows the user to affect the number of input-output areas
             allocated. If the RESERVE clause is not specified or if integer-1 is specified, two
             input-output areas are allocated. If NO is specified, one input-output area is
             allocated.
        3.   The ORGANIZATION clause specifies the logical structure of a file. The file
             organization is established at the time a file is created and cannot subsequently be
             changed.
        4. Records in the file are accessed in the sequence dictated by the file organization.
           This sequence is specified by predecessor-successor record relationships
           established by the execution of WRITE statements when the file is created.

14.3.3. The I-O-CONTROL Paragraph
        Function
        The I-O-CONTROL paragraph specifies the points at which rerun is to be established
        and the storage area that is to be shared by different files.

        General Format




        Syntax Rules
        1.   The I-O-CONTROL paragraph is optional.
        2.   File-name-1 can be either an input or output file.
        3.   The allowable implementor-names are TAPE and DISC.
        4. More than one RERUN clause can be specified for a given file-name-1, subject to
           the following restrictions:
             a.   When multiple integer-1 RECORDS clauses are specified, no two of them can
                  specify the same file-name-1.
             b. When multiple END OF REEL clauses are specified, no two of them can specify
                the same file-name-1.




14ΓÇô4                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                         Processing IBM Tapes




         5.   The two forms of the SAME clause (SAME AREA, SAME RECORD AREA) are
              considered separately in the following:
              More than one SAME clause can be included in a program. However:
              a.   A file name must not appear in more than one SAME AREA clause.
              b. A file name must not appear in more than one SAME RECORD AREA clause.
              c.   If one or more file names of a SAME AREA clause appear in a SAME RECORD
                   AREA clause, all of the file names in that SAME AREA clause must appear in
                   that SAME RECORD AREA clause. However, additional file names not
                   appearing in that SAME AREA clause can also appear in that SAME RECORD
                   AREA clause. The rule that only one of the files mentioned in a SAME AREA
                   clause can be open at any given time takes precedence over the rule that all
                   files mentioned in a SAME RECORD AREA clause can be open at any given
                   time.
         6. The files referenced in the SAME AREA or SAME RECORD AREA clause need not
            all have the same organization or access.

         General Rules
         1.   The RERUN clause specifies when and where the rerun information is recorded.
         2.   Rerun information is written in a separate file whose file name is RERUN$. The
              two forms of the RERUN clause are based on the following conditions under
              which rerun points can be established:
              a.   When the END OF REEL clause is used. In this case, the rerun information is
                   written whenever the END OF REEL condition occurs on file-name-1.
              b. When the integer-1 RECORDS is used. In this case, the rerun information is
                 written whenever integer-1 records of file-name-1 have been processed.
         3.   The SAME AREA clause specifies that two or more files that do not represent sort
              or merge files are to use the same main storage area during processing. The area
              being shared includes all storage areas assigned to the files specified; therefore, it
              is not valid to have more than one of the files open at the same time. (See the
              UCS COBOL Programming Reference Manual Volume 1 for more information.)
         4. The SAME RECORD AREA clause specifies that two or more files are to use the
            same storage area for processing the current logical record. All of the files can be
            open at the same time. A logical record in the SAME RECORD AREA is considered
            a logical record of each opened output file whose file name appears in this SAME
            RECORD AREA clause and of the most recently read input file whose file name
            appears in this SAME RECORD AREA clause. This is equivalent to an implicit
            redefinition of the area; that is, records are aligned on the leftmost character
            position.

        In a COBOL program, the File Description (FD) entry represents the highest level of
        organization in the File Section. The File Section header is followed by a file description
        entry consisting of a level indicator (FD), a file name, and a series of independent
        clauses. The FD clauses specify the size of the logical and physical records, the
        presence or absence of label records, the value of label items defined by Unisys, and
        the names of the data records that comprise the file. The entry itself is terminated by
        a period.

14.4.2. The BLOCK CONTAINS Clause
         Function
         The BLOCK CONTAINS clause specifies the size of a physical record.

         General Format




         General Rules
         1.   This clause is required except when:
              a.   A physical record contains only one complete logical record.
              b. RECORDING MODE U is specified.
         2.   The size of the physical record can be stated in terms of RECORDS, unless one of
              the following situations exists, in which case the RECORDS phrase must not be
              used.
              a.   The physical record contains padding (area not contained in a logical record).
              b. Logical records are grouped in such a manner that an inaccurate physical
                 record size would be implied.
         3.   When the word CHARACTERS is specified, the physical record size is specified in
              terms of the number of ASCII character positions required to store the physical
              record, regardless of the types of characters used to represent the items within
              the physical record.
         4. If only integer-2 is shown, it represents the exact size of the physical record.
              If integer-1 and integer-2 are both shown, they refer to the minimum and
              maximum size of the physical record.

14.4.3. The DATA RECORDS Clause
         Function
         The DATA RECORDS clause serves only as documentation for the names of data
         records with their associated file.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  14ΓÇô7
Processing IBM Tapes




        General Format




        Syntax Rule
        Data-name-1 represents the names of the data records and must have
        01-level-number record descriptions, with the same names associated with them.

        General Rules
        1.    The presence of more than one data-name indicates that the file contains more
              than one type of data record. These records can be of different sizes, different
              formats, and so forth. The order in which they are listed is not significant.
        2.    Conceptually, all data records within a file share the same area. This is in no way
              altered by the presence of more than one type of data record within the file.

14.4.4. The LABEL RECORDS Clause
        Function
        The LABEL RECORDS clause specifies whether labels are present.

        General Format

                RECORD  IS 
        LABEL )               *          
               RECORDS  ARE 
                                 STANDARD
                                  OMITTED

        Syntax Rule
        This clause is required when STANDARD is used.

        General Rules
        1.    OMITTED specifies that no explicit labels exist for the file or the device to which
              the file is assigned.
        2.    STANDARD specifies that EBCDIC labels exist for the file or the device to which
              the file is assigned. (See 5.2.1)

14.4.5. The RECORD Clause
        Function
        The RECORD clause specifies the number of character positions in a fixed-length
        record, or specifies the range of character positions in a variable-length record. If the
        number of character positions does vary, the clause specifies the minimum and
        maximum number of character positions.

        Format 1
             RECORD CONTAINS integer-1 CHARACTERS

         Format 2
              RECORD IS VARYING IN SIZE [ [FROM integer-2][TO integer-3] CHARACTERS]

                  [DEPENDING ON data-name-1]

         Format 3
              RECORD CONTAINS integer-4 TO integer-5 CHARACTERS

         Syntax Rules
         The following is a list of the syntax rules.

         Format 1
         The following syntax rule applies to format 1:

         1.    Format 1 is used to specify fixed length records; no other record description entry
               for the file can specify a number of character positions other than integer-1.
         Format 2
         The following syntax rules applies to format 2:

         1.    Record descriptions for the file must not describe records that contain a lesser
               number of character positions than that specified by integer-2, nor records that
               contain a greater number of character positions than that specified by integer-3.
         2.    Integer-3 must be greater than integer-2.
         3.    Data-name-1 must describe an elementary unsigned integer in the
               Working-Storage or Linkage Section.

         General Rules
         The following is a list of general rules.

         All Formats
         The following general rules apply to all formats:

         1.    If the RECORD clause is not specified, the size of each data record is completely
               defined in the record description entry.
         2.    If the associated file connector is an external file connector, all file description
               entries in the run unit that are associated with that file connector must specify the
               same values for integer-1 or integer-2 and integer-3. If the RECORD clause is not
               specified, all record description entries associated with this file connector must be
               the same length.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  14ΓÇô9
Processing IBM Tapes




        Format 2
        The following general rules apply to format 2:

        1.   Format 2 is used to specify variable-length records. Integer-2 specifies the
             minimum number of character positions to be contained in any record of the file.
             Integer-3 specifies the maximum number of character positions in any record of
             the file.
        2.   The number of character positions associated with a record description is
             determined by the sum of the number of character positions in all elementary data
             items excluding redefinitions and renamings, plus any implicit FILLER due to
             synchronization. If a table is specified
             a.   The minimum number of table elements described in the record is used in the
                  previous summation to determine the minimum number of character positions
                  associated with the record description.
             b. The maximum number of table elements described in the record is used in the
                previous summation to determine the maximum number of character
                positions associated with the record description.
        3.   If integer-2 is not specified, the minimum number of character positions to be
             contained in any record of the file is equal to the least number of character
             positions described for a record in that file.
        4. If integer-3 is not specified, the maximum number of character positions to be
           contained in any record of the file is equal to the greatest number of character
           positions described for a record in that file.
        5.   If data-name-1 is specified, the results of a READ or WRITE are unpredictable,
             unless the AN option is used on the RECORDING MODE clause.
        6. If data-name-1 is specified, the number of character positions in the record must
           be placed into the data item referred to by data-name-1 before any WRITE
           statement is executed for the file.
        7.   If data-name-1 is specified, the execution of a WRITE statement or the
             unsuccessful execution of a READ statement does not alter the contents of the
             data item referred to by data-name-1.
        8. During the execution of a WRITE statement, the number of character positions in
           the record is determined by the following conditions:
             a.   If data-name-1 is specified, by the content of the data item referred to by
                  data-name-1.
             b. If data-name-1 is not specified and the record does not contain a
                variable-occurrence data item, by the number of character positions in the
                record.
             c.   If data-name-1 is not specified and the record does contain a
                  variable-occurrence data item, by the sum of the fixed portion and that portion
                  of the table described by the number of occurrences at the time of execution
                  of the output statement.
        9. If data-name-1 is specified, after the successful execution of a READ statement
           for the file, the contents of the data item referred to by data-name-1 indicate the
           number of character positions in the record just read.


14ΓÇô10                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                         Processing IBM Tapes




         10. If the INTO phrase is specified in the READ statement, the number of character
             positions in the current record that participate as the sending data items in the
             implicit MOVE statement is determined by the following conditions:
              a.   If data-name-1 is specified, by the content of the data item referred to by
                   data-name-1.
              b. If data-name-1 is not specified, by the value that would have been moved into
                 the data item referred to by data-name-1 had data-name-1 been specified.

         Format 3
         The following general rules apply to format 3:

         1.   When format 3 of the RECORD clause is used, integer-4 and integer-5 refer to the
              minimum number of characters in the smallest size data record and the maximum
              number of characters in the largest size data record, respectively. However, in this
              case, the size of each data record is completely defined in the record description
              entry.
         2.   The size of each data record is specified in terms of the number of character
              positions required to store the logical record, regardless of the types of characters
              used to represent the items within the logical record. The size of a record is
              determined by the sum of the number of characters in all fixed-length elementary
              items plus the sum of the maximum number of characters in any variable-length
              item subordinate to the record. This sum can be different from the actual size of
              the record. (See 3.5.15 and 3.5.16.)

14.4.6. The RECORDING MODE Clause
         Function
         The RECORDING MODE clause is required to specify IBM OS/360 9-track tape
         compatibility.

         General Format

         RECORDING  MODE IS  + U ,  AN 
                                 F

                                 V

         General Rules
         1.   The structure of the physical data blocks can be defined by one of the following
              forms:
              a.   The F phrase specifies fixed blocked records.
              b. The U phrase specifies variable-length unblocked records.
              c.   The V phrase specifies variable-length blocked records.
         2.   When the AN option is specified, the records are assumed to consist entirely of
              ASCII characters internally and of EBCDIC characters on magnetic tape.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                    14ΓÇô11
Processing IBM Tapes




        3.   When the AN option is not specified, the following data conversions are
             performed:
             a.   On input, all DISPLAY data items are converted from EBCDIC to ASCII.
             b. On output, all DISPLAY data items are converted from ASCII to EBCDIC.
             c.   When a record is read from tape, leading blanks are converted to leading zeros
                  in every numeric DISPLAY field.
             d. Signed numeric DISPLAY fields are written to tape with an overpunched sign
                on the low-order digit.
             e. On input, all COMPUTATIONAL and PACKED-DECIMAL data items are
                converted from IBM OS/360 format to UCS COBOL internal format.
             f.   On output, all COMPUTATIONAL and PACKED-DECIMAL data items are
                  converted from UCS COBOL internal format to IBM OS/360 format.
             g. Records written to tape are adjusted such that slack bytes are inserted where
                necessary to ensure proper IBM OS/360 alignment.
             h.   For RECORDING MODES U and V files, format 2 of the OCCURS clause is
                  allowed in the record description and the following processing is performed:
                  1.   A data item whose size is variable is expanded on input using the value of
                       the data item referenced by data-name-1 of the OCCURS clause.
                  2.   A data item whose size is variable is compressed on output using the
                       value of the data item referenced by data-name-1 of the OCCURS clause.
             i.   If a REDEFINES clause is used within a record description, then the original
                  definition is used rather than the redefinition for the purposes of record
                  conversion.
        4. If AN is not specified and the file contains multiple record descriptions, then a
           record selector field within each record description is required. (See 14.4.9)

14.4.8. The Record DescriptionΓÇöComplete Entry Skeleton
         A record description consists of a set of data description entries describing the
         characteristics of a particular record. Each data description entry consists of a level
         number followed by a data name, if required, followed by a series of independent
         clauses as required. A record description has a hierarchical structure and therefore the
         clauses used with an entry can vary considerably, depending on whether or not they
         are followed by subordinate entries. The structure of a record description is defined in
         the UCS COBOL Programming Reference Manual Volume 1.

        Syntax Rules

         General Rules
         Format 1
         1.    A PICTURE character-string containing one or more 1s is not allowed.

               described in the remainder of this subsection.

         Formats 2 and 3
         See the UCS COBOL Programming Reference Manual Volume 1.

The RANK Clause
         Function
         The RANK clause increases the efficiency of the process of record selection.

         General Format
              RANK IS integer-1

         Syntax Rules
         1.    The RANK clause is optional.
         2.    The RANK clause can be used only in the description of a record selector. Record
               selectors are described in 14.4.9.
         3.    Integer-1 is an unsigned integer in the range 1 through 63.

         General Rules
         1.    When the RANK clause is omitted, a value of 63 is assumed for the record
               selector.
         2.    When two or more record selectors in the same record description have the same
               RANK, the textual order determines the order in which the selectors are tested.
         3.    When a record description contains multiple record selectors, the value of the
               RANK assigned to each record selector need not be consecutive.
         4. When a record description contains more than one record selector, the order in
            which the record selectors are tested is determined by the RANK of each selector.
            Record selectors of rank n are tested before any record selector of rank n + 1; for
            example, RANK 1 has a higher precedence than a record selector of RANK 2.
         5.    When a record description contains only one record selector, the RANK clause is
               permitted but it has no meaning.

The SYNCHRONIZED Clause
         Function
         The SYNCHRONIZED clause specifies the alignment of an elementary item on the
         natural boundaries of the computer main storage when IBM OS/360 allocation and
         alignment rules apply.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                               14ΓÇô15
Processing IBM Tapes




        General Format




        Syntax Rules
        1.   This clause can appear only with an elementary item.
        2.   SYNC is an abbreviation for SYNCHRONIZED.

        General Rules
        1.   A full description of data allocation and alignment can be found in the UCS COBOL
             Programming Reference Manual Volume 1.
        2.   This clause specifies that the subject data item is to be aligned in the computer
             such that no other data item occupies any of the character positions between the
             leftmost and rightmost natural boundaries delimiting this data item. If the number
             of character positions required to store this data item is less than the number of
             character positions between those natural boundaries, the unused character
             positions (or portions thereof) must not be used for any other data item. Such
             unused character positions, however, are included in:
             a.   The size of any group items to which the elementary item belongs.
             b. The character positions redefined when this data item is the object of a
                REDEFINES clause.
        3.   The LEFT and RIGHT phrases serve for documentation only.
        4. Whenever a SYNCHRONIZED item is referenced in the source program, the
           original size of the item, as shown in the PICTURE clause, is used in determining
           any action that depends on size, such as justification, truncation, or overflow.
        5.   If the data description of an item contains the SYNCHRONIZED clause and an
             operational sign, the sign of the item appears in the normal operational sign
             position, regardless of whether the item is SYNCHRONIZED LEFT or
             SYNCHRONIZED RIGHT.
        6. When the SYNCHRONIZED clause is specified in a data description entry of a data
           item that also contains an OCCURS clause or in a data description entry of a data
           item subordinate to a data description entry that contains an OCCURS clause, then:
             a.   Each occurrence of the data item is SYNCHRONIZED.
             b. Any implicit FILLER generated for other data items within that same table is
                generated for each occurrence of those data items.
        7.   The elementary items associated with this clause are handled as follows:
             Any necessary generation of implicit FILLER, if the elementary item immediately
             preceding an item containing the SYNCHRONIZED clause does not terminate at a
             word boundary, is not included as part of the elementary item. Such automatically
             generated FILLER positions are included in:
             a.   The size of any group to which the FILLER item belongs.
             b. The number of character positions allocated when the group item of which the
                FILLER item is a part appears as the object of a REDEFINES clause.


14ΓÇô16                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                       Processing IBM Tapes




         8. The presence of the SYNCHRONIZED clause has no effect on the alignment of
            data items.

         Syntax Rules
         1.   The PICTURE character-string of a COMPUTATIONAL, and PACKED-DECIMAL item
              can contain only 9s, the operational sign character S, the implied decimal point
              character V, and one or more Ps.
         2.   COMP, COMP-n, and DISP are abbreviations for COMPUTATIONAL,
              COMPUTATIONAL-n, and DISPLAY, respectively.
         3.   COMPUTATIONAL-1 and COMPUTATIONAL-2 usage specifications cannot appear
              in a data description that has a PICTURE clause, because the computer storage
              format of these items is fixed.

         1.   A full description of data allocation and alignment can be found in the UCS COBOL
              Programming Reference Manual Volume 1.
         2.   The USAGE clause can be written at any level. If the USAGE clause is written at a
              group level, it applies to each group or elementary item in the group. The USAGE
              clause of an elementary item cannot contradict the USAGE clause of a group to
              which the item belongs.
         3.   If the group usage is DISPLAY or COMPUTATIONAL, the group is considered to be
              an alphanumeric string of ASCII characters.
         4. If the USAGE clause is not specified on a group item, the group is considered to be
            an alphanumeric string of ASCII characters. If the USAGE clause is not specified for
            an elementary item or for any group to which the item belongs, the usage is
            implicitly DISPLAY.

Processing IBM Tapes




        5.   This clause specifies the manner in which a data item is represented in the storage
             of a computer. It does not affect the use of the data item, although the
             specifications for some statements in the Procedure Division can restrict the
             USAGE clause of the operands referred to. The USAGE clause can affect the radix
             or type of character representation of the item.
        6. A COMPUTATIONAL or COMPUTATIONAL-n item is capable of representing a
           value to be used in computations and must be numeric. If a group item is
           described as COMPUTATIONAL or COMPUTATIONAL-n, the elementary items in
           the group are COMPUTATIONAL or COMPUTATIONAL-n. The group item itself is
           not COMPUTATIONAL or COMPUTATIONAL-n (cannot be used in computations).
        7.   The USAGE IS DISPLAY clause indicates that the format of the data is a standard
             data format.
        8. The USAGE IS PACKED-DECIMAL clause specifies that the data item is
           represented in the storage of the computer with a radix of 10. PACKED-DECIMAL
           usage is equivalent to ASCII COBOL COMPUTATIONAL-3 usage.

The VALUE Clause
        Function
        The VALUE clause is used to specify a record selector. (See 14.4.9)

        General Format




        Syntax Rules
        1.   The words THRU and THROUGH are equivalent.
        2.   The VALUE clause cannot be stated for any item whose size is variable.
        3.   A signed numeric literal must be associated with a signed numeric PICTURE
             character-string.
        4. All numeric literals in a VALUE clause of an item must have a value that is within
           the range of values indicated by the PICTURE clause, and not have a value that
           would require truncation of nonzero digits. Nonnumeric literals in a VALUE clause
           of an item must not exceed the size indicated by the PICTURE clause.

        General Rules
        1.   The VALUE clause must not conflict with other clauses in the data description of
             the item or in the data description within the hierarchy of the item. The following
             rules apply:
             a.   If the category of the item is numeric, all literals in the VALUE clause must be
                  numeric. The literal is aligned according to the standard alignment rules.




14ΓÇô18                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                         Processing IBM Tapes




              b. If the category of the item is alphabetic, alphanumeric, alphanumeric edited, or
                 numeric edited, all literals in the VALUE clause must be nonnumeric literals.
                 The literal is aligned as if the data item had been described as alphanumeric. If
                 the THRU phrase is used, the native EBCDIC collating sequence is used for
                 record selection comparison.
         2.   A figurative constant can be substituted wherever a literal is specified.
         3.   Wherever the THRU phrase is used, literal-1 must be less than literal-2.
         4. The VALUE clause must not be stated in a data description entry that contains an
            OCCURS clause or in an entry that is subordinate to an entry containing an
            OCCURS clause.
         5.   The VALUE clause must not be stated in a data description entry that contains a
              REDEFINES clause or in an entry that is subordinate to an entry containing a
              REDEFINES clause.
         6. If the VALUE clause is used in an entry at the group level, the literal must be a
            figurative constant or a nonnumeric literal, and the group area is initialized without
            consideration for the individual elementary or group items contained within this
            group. The VALUE clause cannot be stated at the subordinate levels within this
            group.
         7.   The VALUE clause must not be written for a group containing items with
              descriptions including JUSTIFIED, SYNCHRONIZED, or USAGE (other than USAGE IS
              DISPLAY).

14.4.9. Record Selector Fields
         A record selector field is identified to the compiler by the appearance of a VALUE
         clause in the record description. (See the VALUE clause in 14.4.8.)

         When the file is read, the record selectors are tested to determine which record
         conversion must be performed. The record selectors in the first record are tested; if
         any of the selectors fail, the next record is considered. If all the record selectors
         match, the first record description is chosen. This process is repeated for all the data
         descriptions until a record description is encountered, all of whose selectors match. If
         no record description can be chosen, a diagnostic is issued.

         In any given record description, the record selectors are listed in their textual order.
         This ordering can be changed by using the RANK clause. (See the RANK clause in
         14.4.8.)

         The RANK clause does not affect the record description chosen; its purpose is to
         increase the efficiency of the record selection process.

         The number of record selectors in any single record description must not exceed 63.
         Each record description in a given file description need not contain the same number
         of selectors. In addition, the selectors need not be in the same position (internal or
         external) in each record description, and they need not have the same USAGE or
         PICTURE. However, it is the userΓÇÖs responsibility to ensure that this does not lead to
         inadvertent record selection.

Processing IBM Tapes




14.5. Procedure Division
        The Procedure Division contains declarative procedures when the USE statement from
        the Sequential I-O module is present in a COBOL source program.

14.5.1. The CLOSE Statement
        Function
        The CLOSE statement terminates the processing of reels/units and files with optional
        rewind and/or lock where applicable.

        General Format




        Syntax Rule
        The files referenced in the CLOSE statement need not all have the same organization
        or access.

        General Rules
        Except where otherwise stated in the general rules that follow, the terms ΓÇ£reelΓÇ¥ and
        ΓÇ£unitΓÇ¥ are synonymous and completely interchangeable in the CLOSE statement.

        1.   A CLOSE statement can be executed only for a file in an open mode.
        2.   For the purpose of showing the effect of various types of CLOSE statements as
             applied to various storage media, all files are divided into the following categories:
             a.   Sequential single-reel (a sequential file that is entirely contained on one reel).
             b. Sequential multi-reel (a sequential file that is contained on more than one reel).
        3.   The results of executing each type of CLOSE for each category of file are
             summarized in Table 14ΓÇô1.




14ΓÇô20                                                                                 7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                               Processing IBM Tapes




                   Table 14ΓÇô1. CLOSE Statement File Categories and Formats


                                                                            File Category


                                                                Sequential            Sequential
                        CLOSE Statement Format                  Single-Reel           Multi-Reel

                CLOSE                                                  F                    C,F,A
                CLOSE WITH LOCK                                       F,D               C,F,E,A
                CLOSE WITH NO REWIND                                  C,B               C,B,A
                CLOSE REEL/UNIT                                       X                      E,F
                CLOSE REEL/UNIT WITH NO REWIND                        X                      E


            The definitions of the symbols in the table follow. Where the definition depends
            on whether the file is an input or output file, alternate definitions are given;
            otherwise, a definition applies to input and output files.
            A
                  Previous Reels (Units) Unaffected
                  Input Files:
                  All reels in the file prior to the current reel are processed according to the
                  standard reel swap procedure, except those reels controlled by a prior CLOSE
                  REEL/UNIT statement. If the current reel is not the last in the file, the reels in
                  the file following the current one are not processed.
                  Output Files:
                  All reels in the file prior to the current reel are processed according to the
                  standard reel swap procedure, except those reels controlled by a prior CLOSE
                  REEL/UNIT statement.
            B
                  No Rewind of Current Reel (Unit)
                  The current reel is left in its current position.
            C
                  Close File
                  Input Files:
                  If the file is positioned at its end and label records are specified for the file, the
                  labels are processed according to the standard label convention. The behavior
                  of the CLOSE statement when label records are specified but not present, or
                  when label records are not specified but are present, is undefined. Closing
                  operations are executed. If the file is positioned at its end and label records
                  are not specified for the file, label processing does not take place, but other
                  closing operations are executed. If the file is positioned other than at its end,
                  the closing operations are executed, but there is no ending label processing.

Processing IBM Tapes




               Output Files:
               If label records are specified for the file, the labels are processed according to
               the standard label convention. The behavior of the CLOSE statement when
               label records are specified but not present, or when label records are not
               specified but are present, is undefined. Closing operations are executed. If
               label records are not specified for the file, label processing does not take
               place, but other closing operations are executed.
           D
               File Lock
               This file cannot be opened again during this execution of this run unit.
           E
               Close Reel (Unit)
               Input Files:
               The following operations take place:
               1.   A reel swap.
               2.   The standard beginning reel label procedure is executed.
                    The next executed READ statement for that file makes available the next
                    data record on the new reel.
               Output Files:
               The following operations take place:
               1.   The standard ending reel label procedure is executed.
               2.   A reel is swapped.
               3.   The standard beginning reel label procedure is executed.
               The next executed WRITE statement that references that file directs the next
               logical data record to the next reel of the file.
           F
               Rewind
               The current reel is positioned at its physical beginning.
           X
               Illegal
               This is an illegal combination of a CLOSE option and a file category. The results
               at object time are undefined.
        4. The action taken if the file is in the open mode when a STOP RUN statement is
           executed or the action taken for a file that has been opened in a called program
           and not closed in that program prior to the execution of a CANCEL statement for
           that program are undefined. No implicit CLOSE procedures will be initiated. This
           could cause the file to be unusable on subsequent accesses to it.




14ΓÇô22                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                          Processing IBM Tapes




         5.   If the OPTIONAL phrase has been specified for the file in the FILE-CONTROL
              paragraph of the Environment Division and the file is not present, the standard
              end-of-file processing is not performed for that file.
         6. If a CLOSE statement without the REEL or UNIT phrase has been executed for a
            file, no other statement (except the SORT or MERGE statements with the USING
            or GIVING phrases) can be executed that references that file, either explicitly or
            implicitly, unless an intervening OPEN statement for that file is executed.
         7.   Following the successful execution of a CLOSE statement without the REEL or
              UNIT phrase, the record area associated with the file name is no longer available.
              The unsuccessful execution of such a CLOSE statement leaves the availability of
              the record area undefined.

14.5.2. The OPEN Statement
         Function
         The OPEN statement initiates the processing of files. It also performs checking and
         writing of labels and other input-output operations.

         General Format




         Rule
         The files referenced in the OPEN statement need not all have the same organization or
         access.

         General Rules
         1.   The successful execution of an OPEN statement determines the availability of the
              file and results in the file being in an open mode.
         2.   The successful execution of an OPEN statement makes the associated record
              area available to the program.
         3.   Prior to the successful execution of an OPEN statement for a given file, no
              statement (except for a SORT or MERGE statement with the USING or GIVING
              phrases) can be executed that references that file, either explicitly or implicitly.
         4. An OPEN statement must be successfully executed prior to the execution of any
            of the permissible input-output statements. In Table 14ΓÇô2, an X at an intersection
            indicates that the specified statement, used in the sequential access mode, can be
            used with the sequential file organization and open mode given at the top of the
            column.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                   14ΓÇô23
Processing IBM Tapes




                       Table 14ΓÇô2. Permissible Statements


                     Statement                   Open Mode

                                         Input               Output
                   READ                     X
                   WRITE                                       X


        5.   A file can be opened with the INPUT and OUTPUT phrases in the same program.
             Following the initial execution of an OPEN statement for a file, each subsequent
             OPEN statement execution for that same file must be preceded by the execution
             of a CLOSE statement, without the REEL, UNIT, or LOCK phrase, for that file.
        6. Execution of the OPEN statement does not obtain or release the first data record.
        7.   If label records are specified for the file, the beginning labels are processed as
             follows:
             a.   When the INPUT phrase is specified, the execution of the OPEN statement
                  causes the labels to be checked in accordance with the conventions for input
                  label checking.
             b. When the OUTPUT phrase is specified, the execution of the OPEN statement
                causes the labels to be written in accordance with the conventions for output
                label writing.
             The behavior of the OPEN statement when label records are specified but not
             present, or when label records are not specified but are present, is undefined.
        8. The file description entry for file-name-1 or file-name-2 must be equivalent to that
           used when this file was created.
        9. If an input file is designated with the OPTIONAL phrase in its SELECT clause, the
           object program causes an interrogation for the presence or absence of this file. If
           the file is not present, the first READ statement for this file causes the at-end
           condition to occur. (See 14.5.3.)
        10. The NO REWIND phrase can be used only with sequential single reel files. (See
            14.5.1.)
        11. Since the storage medium for the file permits rewinding, the following rules apply:
             a.   When the NO REWIND phrase is not specified, execution of the OPEN
                  statement causes the file to be positioned at its beginning.
             b. When the NO REWIND phrase is specified, execution of the OPEN statement
                does not cause the file to be repositioned; the file must be already positioned
                at its beginning prior to execution of the OPEN statement.
        12. For files being opened with the INPUT phrase, the OPEN statement sets the file
            position indicator to the first record currently existing within the file. If no record
            exists in the file, the file position indicator is set such that the next executed READ
            statement for the file will result in an at-end condition.




14ΓÇô24                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                          Processing IBM Tapes




         13. Upon successful execution of an OPEN statement with the OUTPUT phrase
             specified, a file is created. At that time, the associated file contains no data
             records.

14.5.3. The READ Statement
         Function
         The READ statement makes available the next logical record from a file.

         General Format
              READ file-name [ RECORD ] [ INTO identifier ] [ AT ] END imperative-statement

         Syntax Rule
         The INTO phrase must not be used when the input file contains logical records of
         various sizes, as indicated by their record descriptions. The storage area associated
         with identifier and the record area associated with file-name must not be the same
         storage area.

         General Rules
         1.    The associated file must be open in the INPUT mode at the time this statement is
               executed. (See 14.5.2)
         2.    The record to be made available by the READ statement is determined as follows:
               a.   If the file position indicator was positioned by the execution of the OPEN
                    statement, the record pointed to by the file position indicator is made
                    available.
               b. If the file position indicator was positioned by the execution of a previous
                  READ statement, the file position indicator is updated to point to the next
                  existing record in the file and then that record is made available.
         3.    Regardless of the method used to overlap access time with processing time, the
               concept of the READ statement is unchanged in that a record is available to the
               object program prior to the execution of any statement following the READ
               statement.
         4. When the logical records of a file are described with more than one record
            description, these records share the same storage area. This is equivalent to an
            implicit redefinition of the area. The contents of any data items that lie beyond the
            range of the current data record are undefined at the completion of the execution
            of the READ statement.
         5.    If the INTO phrase is specified, the record being read is moved from the record
               area to the area specified by identifier according to the rules specified for the
               MOVE statement without the CORRESPONDING phrase. The implied MOVE does
               not occur if the execution of the READ statement was unsuccessful. Any
               subscripting or indexing associated with the identifier is evaluated after the record
               has been read and immediately before it is moved to the data item.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                    14ΓÇô25
Processing IBM Tapes




        6. When the INTO phrase is used, the record being read is available in both the input
           record area and the data area associated with identifier.
        7.    If, at the time of execution of a READ statement, the position of the file position
              indicator for that file is undefined, the execution of that READ statement is
              unsuccessful.
        8. If the end of a reel is recognized during execution of a READ statement and the
           logical end of the file has not been reached, the following operations are executed:
              a.   The standard ending reel label procedure is executed.
              b. A reel is swapped.
              c.   The standard beginning reel label procedure is executed.
              d. The first data record of the new reel is made available.
        9. If a file described with the OPTIONAL phrase is not present at the time the file is
           opened, then at the time of execution of the first READ statement for the file, the
           AT END condition occurs and the execution of the READ statement is
           unsuccessful. The standard end-of-file procedures are not performed. (See 14.3.1
           and 14.5.2) Execution of the program then proceeds as specified in general rule 11.
        10. If, at the time of the execution of a READ statement, no next logical record exists
            in the file, the at-end condition occurs and the execution of the READ statement is
            considered unsuccessful.
        11. When the at-end condition is recognized, control is transferred to the AT END
            imperative-statement.
              When the at-end condition occurs, execution of the input-output statement that
              caused the condition is unsuccessful.
        12. Following the unsuccessful execution of any READ statement, the contents of the
            associated record area and the position of the file position indicator are undefined.
        13. When the at-end condition has been recognized, a READ statement for that file
            must not be executed without first executing a successful CLOSE statement
            followed by the execution of a successful OPEN statement for that file.

14.5.4. The WRITE Statement
        Function
        The WRITE statement releases a logical record for an output file.

        General Format
             WRITE record-name [ FROM identifier ]

        Syntax Rules
        1.    Record-name and identifier must not reference the same storage area.
        2.    Record-name is the name of a logical record in the File Section of the Data Division
              and can be qualified.




14ΓÇô26                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                           Processing IBM Tapes




         General Rules
         1.    The associated file must be open in the OUTPUT mode at the time of the
               execution of this statement. (See 14.5.2)
         2.    The logical record released by the execution of the WRITE statement is no longer
               available in the record area unless the associated file is named in a SAME RECORD
               AREA clause or the execution of the WRITE statement was unsuccessful due to a
               boundary violation. The logical record is also available to the program as a record
               of other files referenced in the same SAME RECORD AREA clause as the
               associated output file, as well as to the file associated with record-name.
         3.    The results of the execution of the WRITE statement with the FROM phrase are
               equivalent to the execution of the statement

              MOVE identifier TO record-name

               according to the rules specified for the MOVE statement, followed by the same
               WRITE statement without the FROM phrase.
               The contents of the record area prior to the execution of the implicit MOVE
               statement have no effect on the execution of this WRITE statement.
               After execution of the WRITE statement is complete, the information in the area
               referenced by identifier is available, even though the information in the area
               referenced by record-name cannot be. (See general rule 2.)
         4. The file position indicator is unaffected by the execution of a WRITE statement.
         5.    The maximum record size for a file is established at the time the file is created and
               must not subsequently be changed.
         6. The execution of the WRITE statement releases a logical record to the operating
            system.
         7.    After the recognition of an end-of-reel or an end-of-unit of an output file that is
               contained on more than one physical reel, the WRITE statement performs the
               following operations:
               a.   The standard ending reel label procedure is executed.
               b. A reel is swapped.
               c.   The standard beginning reel label procedure is executed.

Section 15
Interlanguage Calls

         Procedures written in one UCS language (currently UCS C, UCS COBOL, and UCS
         FORTRAN) can be called from any of the others. However, differences among the
         languages require certain restrictions for handling the following items:

         ∩é╖   Data types
         ∩é╖   Data alignments
         ∩é╖   Data sizes
         ∩é╖   Passing modes used by the languages
             ∩Ç¡   Pass by value (PBV)
                 PBV is the convention of passing a parameter value directly as an immediate
                 value.
                 In the UCS standard calling sequence (SCS), the value can be immediate if its
                 size is two words or less. If the language requires PBV and the parameter size
                 is greater than two words, the compiler uses the pass-by-reference-value
                 passing mode.
             ∩Ç¡   Pass by reference (PBR)
                 PBR is the convention of passing the address of an object, which allows the
                 called program to change the parameter, if the language rules allow it.
             ∩Ç¡   Pass by reference value (PBRV)
                 PBRV is the convention that allows the compiler to automatically copy an
                 object to a temporary variable and pass the address of the temporary variable.
                 The called program cannot change the value of the object, only the value of
                 the copy. This method is used by the compiler when the parameter to be
                 passed is greater than two words in size (that is, it does not fit into the SCS
                 packet as an immediate value).
         ∩é╖   Contingency handling
             Each UCS language handles contingencies according to its own standard.
             However, once C signal handling is initialized, it takes precedence over the
             contingency handling method of any other language. This occurs whether C is the
             language of the main program or a called function. In a multilanguage environment,
             therefore, C signal handling can effectively disable the contingency handling
             routines of UCS COBOL, and UCS FORTRAN.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  15ΓÇô1
Interlanguage Calls




             Each UCS language handles contingencies according to its own standard.
             However, once C signal handling is initialized, it takes precedence over the
             contingency handling method of any other language. This occurs whether C is the
             language of the main program or a called function. In a multilanguage environment,
             therefore, C signal handling can effectively disable the contingency handling
             routines of UCS COBOL.
             If C signal handling does not provide a routine for a given contingency, the default
             action prints a message and aborts the program.


                                                Caution
              In a multilanguage environment, differences among language definitions,
              defaults, and control mechanisms can produce unpredictable results from
              contingencies.

        You should be aware of the following considerations when calling a FORTRAN
        program from a COBOL program:

        ∩é╖      I/O files
               Mass-storage and tape I/O files can be shared between different UCS languages,
               but they must be closed by the language that opened them before they can be
               accessed by the other language.
        ∩é╖      Length of identifiers
               FORTRAN identifiers must begin with a letter and cannot contain a hyphen ( - ).
        ∩é╖      Alignment of data
               FORTRAN expects all noncharacter arguments to be word-aligned.
        ∩é╖      Character data
               COBOL cannot pass character data to FORTRAN variables declared with an
               asterisk length.
        ∩é╖      Structures
               FORTRAN does not have structures.
        ∩é╖      Functions
               A FORTRAN function cannot be called.
        ∩é╖      Arrays
               FORTRAN arrays are allocated storage in column-major order. UCS COBOL
               allocates arrays in row-major order. If a COBOL array is passed as an argument to
               UCS FORTRAN, the FORTRAN program must declare and reference the array with
               the array subscripts in reverse order as compared to the array in COBOL.




15ΓÇô4                                                                                   7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                           Interlanguage Calls




         ∩é╖    Assumed-shape arrays
              COBOL cannot pass arrays to FORTRAN assumed-shape arrays.
         ∩é╖    Standard print file
              FORTRAN output to the standard print file operates in the reverse order of the
              COBOL DISPLAY statement. FORTRAN performs a line feed and then writes the
              items in the output list. By default, the COBOL DISPLAY statement first writes the
              items in the output list and then performs a line feed. Therefore, you may need
              special logic to avoid overprinting if both the main COBOL program and the
              FORTRAN subprogram print output. The example at the end of this subsection
              demonstrates this consideration.

         Example
         Example 15ΓÇô1 and Example 15ΓÇô2 demonstrate a call from a COBOL main program to a
         FORTRAN subprogram, with the following actions by the main program and
         subprogram:

         1.   The COBOL main program initializes an integer variable, a character string, and a
              one-dimensional floating-point array.
         2.   The contents of the COBOL data items are displayed to verify initialization.
         3.   The COBOL main program calls the FORTRAN subprogram, passing the three data
              items as actual arguments.
         4. The FORTRAN subprogram displays the incoming dummy arguments to
            demonstrate that the dummy arguments were received correctly and that the
            subprogram interprets them correctly.
         5.   The subprogram updates the contents of the dummy arguments and returns
              control to the main program. The changes to the dummy arguments are
              straightforward.
         6. The main program again displays the contents of the arguments to verify that the
            FORTRAN subprogram updated them correctly.

        You should be aware of the following considerations when calling a C program from a
        COBOL program:

        ∩é╖    Parameter passing
             C passes arguments by value. However, applying the #pragma interface to a C
             function being called from COBOL will cause the compiler to convert reference
             parameters into CΓÇÖs pointer format. The C program must define all of its
             parameters as being pointers.
        ∩é╖    Alignment of data
             When a parameter is passed by reference to a C function with the interface
             pragma applied, the parameterΓÇÖs alignment must match UCS CΓÇÖs alignment rules.
             When the C formal parameter is a pointer to a char, the data passed must be byte
             aligned. When the C formal parameter is a pointer to short, the data passed must
             be half-word aligned. When the C formal parameter is any other type of pointer,
             the data passed must be word aligned. If the compiler keyword option CALIGN is
             in effect, the compiler will assure that data items with USAGE COMP-1, COMP-2,
             and COMP-5 are aligned on the proper boundare (see 2.2.7).
        ∩é╖    I/O files
             Mass-storage and tape I/O files can be shared between different UCS languages,
             but they must be closed by the language that opened them before they can be
             accessed by the other language.
        ∩é╖    C run-time environment
             To ensure the proper C runtime environment, including I/O and contingency
             handling within URTS, any language transition from another UCS language to UCS
             C requires the compilation unit containing the called C function to be compiled
             with the AFA/FULL keyword option when the C function does not have the
             #pragma interface applied.
        ∩é╖    Case sensitivity of names
             Since the C language is case-sensitive and COBOL converts external names to
             uppercase letters, be sure the external names of all C subprograms are declared in
             uppercase characters.
        ∩é╖    Function names
             The names of C functions called from a COBOL program must start with a letter
             and cannot contain a hyphen ( - ).




15ΓÇô8                                                                                7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                            Interlanguage Calls




         ∩é╖    Functions
              COBOL does not support function calls and should not call a function written in C.
              In other words, COBOL cannot receive the return value from a C function. You
              must use arguments to pass a returned value from C to COBOL.
         ∩é╖    Character strings
              The C convention for indicating the end of a character string (which C maintains as
              a single-dimension array) is to use a null character, which is a byte containing all
              binary zeros. C string functions, as well as the %s format descriptor, require the
              null character to terminate the string.
              If a COBOL program passes a character string to a C function, it must insert a null
              character in the appropriate place in the string. If a COBOL program receives a
              character string from a C program, the COBOL program should consider the length
              of the string to be the length of the text preceding the null character in the string,
              not the declared length of the string.

         Example
         Example 15ΓÇô4 and Example 15ΓÇô5 demonstrate a call from a COBOL main program to a
         C subprogram, with the following actions by the main program and subprogram:

         1.   The COBOL main program initializes an integer variable, a character string, and a
              one-dimensional floating-point array.
         2.   The contents of the COBOL data items are displayed to verify initialization.
         3.   The COBOL main program calls the C subprogram, passing the three data items as
              actual arguments.
              The second argument is a structure that represents a C character string, which has
              a terminating null character.
         4. The C subprogram displays the incoming dummy arguments to demonstrate that
            the dummy arguments were received correctly and that the subprogram
            interprets them correctly.
         5.   The subprogram updates the contents of the dummy arguments and returns
              control to the main program. The changes to the dummy arguments are
              straightforward.
         6. The main program again displays the contents of the arguments to verify that the
            C subprogram updated them correctly.

           #include <stdio.h>

           #pragma interface CSUB
           void CSUB(int *iptr,char *cptr,float (*fptr)[3])
           {
             int i;

            printf("\n");
            printf("*Inside C      Parm1 =%d \n",*iptr);
            printf("               Parm2 =%s \n",cptr);
            for (i=0;i<3;i++)
              printf("               Parm3(%i) = %f\n",i+1,(*fptr)[i]) ;
            printf("\n") ;

            *iptr =456 ;
            strcpy(cptr,"CHANGE");
            (*fptr)[0] = (*fptr)[1] = (*fptr)[2] = 5.0 ;
           }

Section 16
Internationalization

         Internationalization (I18N) refers to the Unisys software features that enable you to
         develop and run applications that can be customized to meet the needs of a specific
         language, culture, or business environment. The internationalization features provide
         support for numerous character sets and locales.


16.1. I18NLIB Components
         The Internationalization Library (I18NLIB) product forms the basis for the operating
         systemΓÇÖs internationalization capabilities and provides services for system software
         and application programs to use when working with non-US-English operating
         environments.

         I18NLIB has the following major parts:

         1.   Exec Environment Variables - The environment variables convey information
              between the application program and the service routines.
         2.   Locale definition files - These files define the processing rules for a region. Their
              related CHARMAP files define the allowable characters for the regionΓÇÖs
              language(s). The locale definition files are provide by Unisys.
         3.   UREP entities and relationships - UREP is used to keep track of and report on
              locale, CHARMAP, translation, and other information available to the service
              routines and available to the system software and application programs.
         4. Service Routines - These routines process data passed by the system software or
            application program according to the rules supplied by the locale definition.
         5.   COPY procs for PLUS, C, and COBOL which provide the declarations for the
              service routines and define templates for the structures used by the service
              routines.


16.2. Internationalization of Programs
         In order to internationalize a UCS COBOL program, a user must insert CALL
         statements to the desired I18NLIB service routine (i.e. UCOB$SETLOC,
         UCOB$STRCOLL, UCOB$TOUPPER ...) and/or use the new data types defined by the
         USAGE DISP-I18N and USAGE BYTE-I18N clauses. The Internationalization Planning
         and Implementation Overview provides complete details on how to call each of the
         I18NLIB service routines.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                    16ΓÇô1
Internationalization




         The USAGE DISP-I18N data type has been added to allow the UCS COBOL compiler to
         do comparisons in a culturally sensitive manner. When a DISP-I18N data item is
         explicitly used in a comparison (i.e. IF, EVALUATE, SEARCH) the compiler will generate
         a call to the I18NLIB service routine string_collate in order to do the comparison based
         upon the locale that is currently in force. The use of this data type can eliminate the
         need for the user to insert CALL statements to the string_collate service routine.

         The USAGE BYTE-I18N data type will be used to declare a string of bits that are
         obtained by calling the I18NLIB service routine string_transform (UCOB$STRXFRM).
         This string of bits can be compared to another string of bits obtained from another call
         to string_transform to determine the collating order of the items that are being
         compared. The two BYTE-I18N data items are compared as bit strings with no
         conversion being done. If the BYTE-I18N data items are of unequal length, then the
         shorter one will be padded with binary zeroes on the right until it is of equal size to the
         larger one.

         Code type and locale information can be stored and retrieved from data files through
         the CODE TYPE and LOCALE clauses. These clauses allow you to store information
         about the data at the time the file is created and to retrieve the information about the
         data at the time the file is input. The setting and retrieving of CODE TYPE and LOCALE
         information is controlled by the use of the I18N-IO compiler option.

         The Internationalization Planning and Implementation Overview provides complete
         details about all of the locales and service routines that can be used. Please refer to
         that document for questions concerning the internationalization of your UCS COBOL
         program.




16ΓÇô2                                                                                7831 0455ΓÇô022
Section 17
CIFS COBOL Program Interface

         CIFS for ClearPath OS 2200, is an implementation of the Common Internet File System
         (CIFS) specification that allows access to OS 2200 files via standard Internet protocols.
         For complete details about CIFS, see CIFS for ClearPath OS 2200 User, Programmer,
         and Administrator Reference Manual.

         CIFS permits direct access to files stored in OS 2200 through SMB clients like
         Windows Explorer. You can move, copy, delete, and display properties of their
         OS 2200 files. You can also edit files with Notepad, Word, image processors, and so
         on, and save changes to the files. Using Windows drag-and-drop functions, you can
         copy or move files between your workstation and OS 2200.

         COBOL programmers can access CIFS services and application program interfaces
         (APIs) by calling them as subprograms from a COBOL program. See the CIFS for
         ClearPath OS 2200 User, Programmer, and Administrator Reference Manual for
         complete details and descriptions of all the available APIs.


17.1. CIFS Copy Procedures
         The following table lists the UCOB COPY PROCs that are available to CIFS programs.
         These PROCs are in the element CIFS-DEF in the file SYS$LIB$*CIFS$LIB. These COPY
         PROCs should be used in programs that call the CIFS APIs.


                Proc Name                              Description

           CIFS-AMODE            Contains definitions for CIFS$ACCESS
           CIFS-API              Contains definitions for the CIFS status definitions
           CIFS-DIR              Contains definitions for a DIR variable for directory
                                 service subprograms
           CIFS-FCNTL            Contains definitions for the cifs-flock-struct variable
                                 for file locking and cifs-fcntl-cmd variable for file
                                 control operations
           CIFS-FILE             Contains definitions for a FILE variable for stream
                                 service subprograms
           CIFS-FPOS             Contains definitions for the cifs-fpos variable for file
                                 positioning
           CIFS-MODE             Contains definitions for the cifs-mode variable for
                                 CIFS$OPEN, CIFS$CHMOD, and so on

17.3. Example Program
         The following example program can be used to list the contents of a file/directory that
         resides on the 2200 or it can be use to copy a file/directory from one location to
         another. It uses many of the service programs that were discussed earlier in this
         section. First, compile the program. Be sure to perform the following command prior
         to the compilation:

           @use cob$pf.,sys$lib$*cifs$lib.

            IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
            PROGRAM-ID.
                CIFS-TEST.
            ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.
            CONFIGURATION SECTION.
            SOURCE-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.
            OBJECT-COMPUTER. UNISYS-2200.

           *    Control characters commonly used in C strings.
           *
            SPECIAL-NAMES.
                SYMBOLIC nul, lf IS 1, 11.
            DATA DIVISION.
            WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.

           *    General CIFS definitions.
           *
             COPY CIFS-API.
           *
           * Definitions for OFLAG bits used on open() calls.
           *
             COPY CIFS-OFLAG.
           *
           * Definitions for MODE bits used when creating files.
           *
             COPY CIFS-MODE.
           *
           * Space for a pointer to the standard output and standard error stream
           * control structures.
           *
             COPY CIFS-FILE REPLACING CIFS-FILE BY CIFS-STDERR-FILE.
             COPY CIFS-FILE REPLACING CIFS-FILE BY CIFS-STDOUT-FILE.

           * Command parsing control string, result fields, and error messages.

               03 FILLER                    PIC X(7) VALUE " %4095s".
               03 FILLER                    PIC X(7) VALUE " %4095s".
               03 FILLER                    PIC X(4) VALUE " %1s".

          *

           PROCEDURE DIVISION.

          *   Retrieve the FILE struct pointers for use on normal and

                CALL "CIFS$STDOUT" USING CIFS-STDOUT-FILE.

          *
          *   Main loop to read, parse, and dispatch commands.
          *
                PERFORM TEST AFTER UNTIL COMMAND-BYTES = 0
          *
          *   Read a command line from standard input.
          *
                    CALL "CIFS$READ" USING CIFS-STDIN-FD,
                                           DATA-BUFFER,
                                           131071,
                                           COMMAND-BYTES,
                                           CIFS-STATUS
                    IF BYTES-READ < 0
                        CALL "CIFS$PERROR" USING CIFS-STATUS,
                                                 COMMAND-ERROR-MESSAGE
                        STOP RUN
                    END-IF
          *
          *   Insure the image is nul terminated for sscanf().
          *
                    IF COMMAND-BYTES > 0 AND DATA-BYTE(COMMAND-BYTES) = lf
                         MOVE nul to DATA-BYTE(COMMAND-BYTES)
                    ELSE
                         MOVE nul TO DATA-BYTE(COMMAND-BYTES + 1)
                    END-IF
          *
          *   Clear command field before parsing into it.
          *
                    MOVE SPACES TO COMMAND-LINE
                    CALL "CIFS$SSCANF" USING FIELD-COUNT,
                                             DATA-BUFFER,
                                             COMMAND-FORMAT,
                                             COMMAND-START,
                                             COMMAND-LINE,
                                             COMMAND-STOP,
                                             ARGUMENT-1,
                                             ARGUMENT-2,
                                             ARGUMENT-3

           *     allow COBOL comparisons to work, then branch to the proper handler.

                           SUBTRACT COMMAND-START FROM COMMAND-STOP GIVING
                              COMMAND-BYTES
                           MOVE SPACE TO COMMAND-BYTE(COMMAND-BYTES + 1)
                           EVALUATE COMMAND-LINE ALSO FIELD-COUNT
                                WHEN "cp" ALSO 3 PERFORM COPY-FILE
                                WHEN "ls" ALSO 2 PERFORM LIST-DIRECTORY
                                WHEN OTHER PERFORM SYNTAX-ERROR

           *
           *     Section to copy a file to a new location.

               COPY-FILE SECTION.
           *
           *     Open the source file read-only. Display an error message and give
           *     up if the open() fails.
           *
               OPEN-INPUT-FILE.
                   MOVE 0 TO CIFS-OFLAG.
                   MOVE 1 TO CIFS-OFLAG-RDONLY.
                   MOVE 0 TO CIFS-MODE.
                   CALL "CIFS$OPEN" USING ARGUMENT-1,
                                          CIFS-OFLAG,
                                          CIFS-MODE,
                                          READ-FD,
                                          CIFS-STATUS.
                   IF READ-FD < 0
                       CALL "CIFS$FPRINTF" USING BYTES-WRITTEN,
                                                 CIFS-STDERR-FILE,
                                                 OPEN-ERROR-FORMAT,
                                                 ARGUMENT-1
                       CALL "CIFS$PERROR" USING CIFS-STATUS
                       GO TO COPY-DONE
                   END-IF.
