End-of-File Label (EOF1)
         Except for character positions 1-3, which contain EOF, the EOF1 label has the same
         format as the HDR1 label. The values are the same, except for the Block count field,
         which is set to the number of physical data blocks since the previous HDR label group.

Second End-of-File Label (EOF2)
         Except for character positions 1-3, which contain EOF, the EOF2 label has the same
         format as the HDR2 label. This label is located on all tapes following the EOF1 label.

End-of-Volume Label (EOV1)
         Except for character positions 1-3, which contain EOV, the EOV1 label has the same
         format as the EOF1 label. This label is located at the end of a file section of a tape file
         that continues on another reel of tape.

Second End-of-Volume Label (EOV2)
         Except for character positions 1-3, which contain EOV, the EOV2 label has the same
         format as the EOF2 label. This label is located on all tapes following the EOV1 label.

E.2.2. INDEXED DISC Files
         For files that have DISC as implementor-name-1 in the ASSIGN clause and the
         ORGANIZATION IS INDEXED clause in the file-control entry, the labels are maintained
         by COBOL. Only HDR1 and EOF1 labels are recorded on the files. These labels are
         similar in format to the HDR1 and EOF1 labels of the TAPE or INTERCHANGE files
         except that these labels consist of 80 9-bit ASCII characters. Character positions 22-27
         of HDR1 contain UNISYS. Character positions 61-73 of HDR1 contain the file qualifier
         from the @ASG statement. The HDR1 and EOF1 labels are located at sector addresses
         0 and 2, respectively. In the remaining words of sector 2, additional information about
         the file is maintained.

         For a complete description of these words, see the PCIOS Administration and
         Programming Reference Manual.

E.2.3. RELATIVE and SEQUENTIAL DISC Files
         The labels recorded on files that have DISC as implementor-name-1 in the ASSIGN
         clause and the ORGANIZATION IS RELATIVE or SEQUENTIAL clause in the file-control
         entry are maintained by the Processor Common Input/Output System (PCIOS) as
         System Data Format (SDF) labels (see the PCIOS Administration and Programming
         Reference Manual). UCS COBOL uses the first seventeen 9-bit ASCII characters
         starting at word 14 in these SDF labels to contain the FILE-ID field.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                     EΓÇô5
Label Processing




E.3. The VALUE OF Clause
        The VALUE OF clause allows you to override system default values for certain fields
        within selected labels for unique label creation on output or validation on input.
        System default values generally originate on the @ASG statement for the file.

E.3.1. FILE-ACCESS
        The VALUE OF FILE-ACCESS clause is allowed only for files assigned to tape. The only
        allowable functioning characters are ASCII 1 through 7 and space (octal values 061
        through 067 and 040, respectively). The system treats any other character as a space.

        The function of the values of 061-067 correspond to the R, W, and F options on the
        @ASG statement; that is, if the R option is on the assignment when the file is created,
        the file is read only until it expires.


               Accessibility                    Assign Options
                Character
                                      F                W               R

             ΓÇ£ ΓÇ¥ or 040               X
             ΓÇ£1ΓÇ¥ or 061
             ΓÇ£2ΓÇ¥ or 062               X                X
             ΓÇ£3ΓÇ¥ or 063                                X
             ΓÇ£4ΓÇ¥ or 064               X                                X
             ΓÇ£5ΓÇ¥ or 065                                                X
             ΓÇ£6ΓÇ¥ or 066               X                X               X
             ΓÇ£7ΓÇ¥ or 067                                X               X

E.3.2. FILE-ID
        The contents of the literal or the data item referenced by the data name specified in
        the VALUE OF FILE-ID clause is used to override the qualifier*file-name specified on
        the @ASG statement for the file during label creation or validation.

E.3.3. PURGE-DATE
        The VALUE OF PURGE-DATE clause is allowed only for files assigned to tape. The
        contents of the literal or the data item referenced by the data name specified in the
        VALUE OF PURGE-DATE clause is used to override the purge date specified in field-4
        of the @ASG statement for the file during file creation. These contents must be of the
        form mmddyy, where mm is the number of the month (01-12), dd is the number of the
        day (01-31), and yy is the last two digits of the year. For example, July 4, 1991, would
        be indicated as 070491.




EΓÇô6                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                               Label Processing




E.4. Procedure Division I-O Statements
         This subsection explains the logical sequence of labeling operations that occurs
         implicitly during the execution of certain I-O statements. Since the labeling of files
         assigned as INTERCHANGE and TAPE files is under control of the system Executive
         Tape Labeling System, this logical sequence of operations often does not correspond
         directly to the physical sequence of operations performed on the file.

E.4.1. The CLOSE Statement
CLOSE File
         Output Files
         During the execution of a CLOSE statement without the REEL phrase for a file opened
         in the output mode, the following sequence of operations occurs:

         ∩é╖   The EOF1 label is created with the standard values.
         ∩é╖   If any VALUE OF clauses are specified for the file, the standard values in the EOF1
             label are replaced by the user-specified values.
         ∩é╖   The EOF1 label is written to the external media.

         In addition, for files assigned to tape, the following operations also occur:

         ∩é╖   The EOF1 label is preceded on the tape by a tape mark.
         ∩é╖   Following the EOF1 label, an EOF2 label and a double tape mark are also written on
             the tape.

         Input Files
         During the execution of a CLOSE statement without the REEL phrase for a file opened
         in the input mode, no label processing occurs if the file is positioned at a position
         other than its end. If the file is positioned at its end, the following sequence of
         operations occurs:

         ∩é╖   The EOF1 label is read from the external media and standard label values are
             verified.
         ∩é╖   If any VALUE OF clauses are specified for the file, the VALUE OF label entries are
             verified against the user-specified values.
         ∩é╖   For tape files, the EOF2 label is also read from the external media.

         I-O Files
         During the execution of a CLOSE statement without the REEL phrase for a file opened
         in the I-O mode, label processing is identical to that for a file opened in the input
         mode. Subsequent to the other operations, the EOF1 label is rewritten to the external
         media. This includes the supplementary information contained in words 20 through 27
         of sector 2 for indexed files.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                EΓÇô7
Label Processing




        Reversed Files
        Only tape files can be opened in the reverse mode.

        During the execution of a CLOSE statement for a file opened in the reverse mode,
        label processing occurs only if the beginning of file condition is encountered. If this
        condition has been encountered, label processing occurs similar to that stated for the
        CLOSE statement without the REEL phrase for a file opened in the input mode, except
        the HDR labels are treated as EOF labels.

CLOSE REEL
        The CLOSE statement with the REEL phrase applies only to tape files.

        Output Files
        During the execution of a CLOSE statement with the REEL phrase for a file opened in
        the output mode, the following sequence of operations occurs:

        ∩é╖   The EOV1 label is created with the standard values.
        ∩é╖   If any VALUE OF clauses are specified for the file, the standard values in the EOV1
            label are replaced by the user-specified values.
        ∩é╖   A tape mark and the EOV1 label are written on the tape.
        ∩é╖   The EOV2 label and a double tape mark are written on the tape.
        ∩é╖   The current reel is swapped to the next reel in the sequence specified on the
            @ASG statement for the file.
        ∩é╖   The labeling procedures continue on the new reel similar to those specified for an
            OPEN statement with the OUTPUT phrase. The file section field in the HDR1 label
            is updated to indicate the new section of the file.
        Input Files
        During the execution of a CLOSE statement with the REEL phrase for a file that is
        opened in the input mode, no end-of-volume label processing occurs for the current
        reel if the end of the file section has not been encountered. In this case, label
        processing resumes with the swap to the next reel in sequence below. If the end of
        the file section has been encountered, the following label processing occurs:

        ∩é╖   The EOV1 label is read from the tape and standard label values are verified.
        ∩é╖   If any VALUE OF clauses are specified for the file, the VALUE OF label entries are
            verified against the user-specified values.
        ∩é╖   The EOV2 label is also read from the tape.
        ∩é╖   The current reel is swapped to the next reel in the sequence specified on the
            @ASG statement for the file.
        ∩é╖   The labeling procedures continue on the new reel similar to those specified for an
            OPEN statement with the INPUT phrase (see E.4.2).




EΓÇô8                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                                                  Label Processing




E.4.2. The OPEN Statement
Output Files
         During the execution of an OPEN statement with the OUTPUT phrase, the following
         sequence of operations occurs:

         ∩é╖   The HDR1 label is created with the standard values.
         ∩é╖   If any VALUE OF clauses are specified for the file, the standard values in the HDR1
             label are replaced by the user-specified values.
         ∩é╖   The HDR1 label is written to the external media.

         In addition, for files assigned to tape, the following operations occur:

         ∩é╖   If the file being created is the first file on a tape or tape set, the HDR1 label is
             preceded on the tape by a VOL1 label.
         ∩é╖   Following the HDR1 label, a HDR2 label and a tape mark are also written on the
             tape.

Input or I-O Files
         During the execution of an OPEN statement with the INPUT or I-O phrase, the
         following sequence of operations occurs:

         ∩é╖   The HDR1 label is read from the external media and standard label values are
             verified.
         ∩é╖   If any VALUE OF clauses are specified for the file, the VALUE OF label entries are
             verified against the user-specified values.
         ∩é╖   For nonindexed disk files, the end-of-file address is extracted from the labels and
             made available to the program for subsequent end-of-file checks.
         ∩é╖   For sequential-access files, the file is logically positioned at the first available data
             record.
         ∩é╖   If the file being input is the first file on a tape or tape set, validation of the HDR1
             label is preceded by the system validation of the VOL1 label.

Reversed Files
         Only tape files can be opened in the reverse mode.

         During the execution of an OPEN statement for a file opened in the reverse mode,
         label processing occurs similar to that stated for the OPEN statement for a file opened
         in the input mode except the EOF labels are treated as HDR labels.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                       EΓÇô9
Label Processing




E.4.3. The READ Statement
        The READ statement can invoke label processing only in the case of a multiple reel
        tape file.

        If, during the execution of a READ statement, an end-of-file condition occurs, label
        processing occurs as stated in the execution of a CLOSE statement with the REEL
        clause for a file opened in the input mode.

E.4.4. The WRITE Statement
        The WRITE statement can invoke label processing only in the case of a multiple reel
        tape file.

        If, during the execution of a WRITE statement, an end-of-tape condition occurs, label
        processing occurs as stated in the execution of a CLOSE statement with the REEL
        clause for a file opened in the output mode (see E.4.1).




EΓÇô10                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
Appendix F
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL
Differences

         Universal Compiling System (UCS) COBOL is the Unisys implementation of the
         American National Standards (ANS) X3.23-1985 COBOL standard in the Universal
         Compiling System (UCS). UCS software for extended mode is available in addition to
         the current, familiar software for basic mode. UCS COBOL is available in addition to
         ASCII COBOL and not as a total replacement for it.

         UCS COBOL is the COBOL programmerΓÇÖs vehicle to take advantage of the Universal
         Compiling System and new COBOL developments as well as new system architecture
         developments.

         Although UCS is a new compiling system, compatibility with earlier compilers is a
         major goal. This appendix is an attempt to identify areas which might possibly need
         attention when upgrading from ASCII COBOL to UCS COBOL. This appendix is
         composed of four divisions. They are

         ∩é╖   Implementation Differences
             Those differences that occur primarily because UCS COBOL is a new
             implementation of COBOL.
         ∩é╖   Discontinued Extensions
             Features of ASCII COBOL that are not carried over into UCS COBOL. These are
             primarily features that are currently documented in the ASCII COBOL
             Supplementary Reference Manual.
         ∩é╖   Substantive Changes
             The changes in the 1985 COBOL standard issued in September, 1985, as well as
             the substantive changes made by the X3J4 technical committee as a result of the
             public review comments received during the public review period, which are
             identified as potentially affecting existing programs. For more complete
             information on the new standard, please refer to:
                X3.23-1985
                American National Standard
                Programming Language COBOL
             The changes in this section highlight the differences between the standard for
             ASCII COBOL (ANS X3.23-1974) and the standard for UCS COBOL (ANS X3.23-
             1985).



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  FΓÇô1
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




       ∩é╖   Obsolete Language Elements
           Features that are present in this level of the standard (COBOL 85), but will be
           removed from future revisions of the standard. These features are either obsolete
           or improperly specified, but it is felt their abrupt removal from the standard would
           be a disservice to COBOL users. It is strongly recommended that these features
           not be used when writing new programs.

       Note: This appendix contains some explanations and comments which are taken
       directly or paraphrased from the above-mentioned standard.

       Each subsection contains somewhat subjective evaluations of the listed differences.
       These judgments are based on the effect these differences have on your programs,
       how to deal with a required change, and the potential benefits of these changes.

       There is no requirement that you upgrade all ASCII COBOL programs to UCS COBOL.
       ASCII COBOL continues to be supported so that you can continue to execute your
       existing ASCII COBOL programs. The upgrade can be done over an extended period of
       time, with programs gradually switched to UCS COBOL when it makes good business
       sense for your organization. Therefore, as new programs are added to an existing
       application, you can write them in UCS COBOL. When existing programs require
       maintenance, it is a good time to upgrade them to UCS.

       This appendix will be updated as new information about the software implementation
       or about customer use of existing software becomes available. Comments or
       suggestions regarding this appendix or the software described herein are welcome
       and should be submitted on the enclosed Business Reply Mail Form.


F.1. Conversion Tools
       If you wish to migrate COBOL programs that are compatible with the ANSI-85
       standard to UCS, you only need to compile with UCS COBOL. However, you need to
       give special consideration to ASCII COBOL programs that

       ∩é╖   Are older than the ANSI-74 COBOL standard
       ∩é╖   Are not in conformance with the ANSI-74 or ANSI-85 COBOL standard
       ∩é╖   Have extensions not carried forward to UCS COBOL
       ∩é╖   Use data file structures that are not standard

       Since the UCS COBOL compiler only generates code for execution in extended mode,
       it is recommended that your ACOB programs are executed with Extended Instruction
       Set (EIS) enabled before migrating to UCOB. Enabling EIS instructions may help
       determine potential implementation differences. ACOB can generate EIS and non-EIS
       code through specific computer-names of the OBJECT-COMPUTER clause. Refer to
       the Environment Division in OS 2200 ASCII COBOL Programming Reference Manual
       for recommended computer-names and details.




FΓÇô2                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                              UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




         You must rewrite extensions that are not supported by UCS COBOL (see F.2.33)
         before you compile the ASCII COBOL source programs that use them. Also,
         incompatibilities between the ANSI-74 and ANSI-85 standards must be resolved (see
         F.4).

         The following tools are available to automate the upgrading of your programs to
         COBOL 85 and UCS COBOL:

         COMPAT compiler keyword option
         Using this option reduces the amount of changes your traditional program requires to
         execute. For example, the ASCII COBOL data allocation rules and ASCII
         COBOL-compatible implementation rules override UCS COBOL rules when you use
         the COMPAT keyword option to compile an upgraded COBOL program (see 2.2.7 for
         more information about the COMPAT option).

         COMP-BIN compiler keyword option
         Using this option causes an item declared as USAGE COMP to be treated as though it
         was declared USAGE BINARY. The COMPAT option automatically sets this option.

         D$WORK-WS compiler keyword option
         It is recommended that a COBOL program containing DMS statements where the
         DMCA is placed into COMMON using the INVOKE clause, be compiled with the
         D$WORK-WS keyword option. In ASCII COBOL, the ADMLP processor generates a
         relocatable holding the D$WORK data structure. In UCS COBOL this data structure is
         in the compiled OM element and by default is placed at the end of COMMON-
         STORAGE section when the INVOKE clause places the DMCA into COMMON. This can
         cause problems if the size of COMMON-STORAGE varies between the COBOL
         programs in an executable. The D$WORK-WS keyword option forces the D$WORK
         data structure to be placed into WORKING-STORAGE section instead, thereby
         bypassing any potential problems. Refer to Section 2.2.7, ΓÇ£Compiler Call Keyword
         Options for Program Control,ΓÇ¥ for a description of this keyword option.

         IR-DIFF compiler keyword option
         Using this option causes the compiler to issue a message whenever the result of a
         UCS COBOL calculation may differ. This difference occurs because the intermediate
         result in a UCS COBOL arithmetic expression assumes maximum precision. Thus, the
         higher accuracy of UCS COBOL may produce results that differ from the results of the
         same calculation in ASCII COBOL.

         The following subsections refer to these tools.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                              FΓÇô3
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.2. Implementation Differences
       The following identifies those differences that occur primarily because UCS COBOL is
       a new implementation of COBOL.

F.2.1. COMPUTATIONAL Fields Data Representation
       Description
       The default for the internal representation of COMP fields in UCS COBOL is ASCII
       digits. On option, COMPUTATIONAL fields are represented in binary.

       ASCII COBOL has two ways of representing data that is declared as
       COMPUTATIONAL. COMPUTATIONAL data is represented as either binary or ASCII.
       The ASCII COBOL default is binary. (When binary is used, the results of arithmetic
       operations do not conform to the American National Standards requirements; when
       ASCII is used, the results of arithmetic operations do conform.) UCS COBOL also
       supports these two ways of representing COMPUTATIONAL data. Arithmetic
       operations performed on both the ASCII representation and binary representation
       conform to the American National Standards.

       Changes
       You can take one of two courses of action. First, COMPUTATIONAL data that is
       represented in binary can be changed to USAGE BINARY manually. Truncation of
       BINARY fields is by decimal digit rather than number of bits allocated as in ASCII
       COBOL. The second option is to use the compatibility option (COMPAT) to get binary
       representation which is also decimal truncated.

F.2.2. COMPUTATIONAL-3 Deleted
       Description
       COMP-3 has been removed and replaced by PACKED-DECIMAL. The extra ΓÇ¥BΓÇ¥ option
       made COMP-3 the same as DISP for compatibility with old levels of ASCII COBOL.

       Changes
       Change COMP-3 syntax to PACKED-DECIMAL manually. You can also use the
       compatibility option (COMPAT) or COMP-BIN to have COMP-3 allocated as
       PACKED-DECIMAL.

F.2.3. SYNCHRONIZED Field Alignment
       Description
       In ASCII COBOL, SYNC meant ΓÇ£word align this field.ΓÇ¥ In UCS COBOL, SYNC has no
       effect on alignment. This change reduces problems resulting from the implicit
       insertion of slack bits. You need to insert slack explicitly in cases where slack bits are
       needed.

       Changes
       Use the compatibility option (COMPAT) to get ASCII COBOL style data alignment.



FΓÇô4                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                               UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.2.4. INDEX, COMP-1, COMP-2 Alignment
         Description
         These data types were automatically word aligned in ASCII COBOL. This is no longer
         true. Fewer problems result from the insertion of slack bytes.

         Changes
         Use the compatibility option (COMPAT) to get ASCII COBOL-style data alignment.

F.2.5. Data Allocation in IBM Records
         Description
         The extra A option forced data allocation in IBM records. This is no longer available.
         This option was used solely for the purpose of being compatible with ASCII COBOL
         level 3Rx and earlier.

         Changes
         Unisys does not know of any requirement for this capability in UCS COBOL.

F.2.6. IBM Data Allocation for Programs
         Description
         The extra C option could be used to force IBM data allocation throughout the program.

         Changes
         Unisys does not anticipate that this will be a problem since it only affects low usage
         binary fields in the IBM environment. UCS COBOL data allocation is compatible with
         recent IBM implementations.

F.2.7. Intermediate Operands
         Description
         The size of intermediate operands retained in calculations is different in UCS COBOL
         than in ASCII COBOL. This could lead to different program results. ASCII COBOL
         diagnosed the conditions in which an intermediate operand would exceed 21 digits.

         Changes
         UCS COBOL uses a single consistent algorithm. While some differences in precision
         can result, UCS COBOL is as precise or more precise than ASCII COBOL. An area that
         has created considerable confusion for customers is now eliminated.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                 FΓÇô5
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.2.8. Floating-Point Computations
       Description
       The extra T option could be used to force computations to use double precision
       floating point for intermediate results. This could possibly cause different results to be
       obtained if the feature was used.

       Changes
       UCS COBOL has gone to a single consistent algorithm. While some differences in
       precision can result, UCS COBOL is as precise or more precise than ASCII COBOL. This
       change also eliminates an area that has created considerable confusion for ASCII
       COBOL customers.

F.2.9. HIGH-VALUES
       Description
       HIGH-VALUES in ASCII COBOL had an octal value of 0177 unless the extra D option
       was used, in which case HIGH-VALUES meant 0377. In UCS COBOL, HIGH-VALUES is
       0377.

       Changes
       Use the compatibility option (COMPAT or COMPAT/HV177) to get ASCII COBOL
       HIGH-VALUES (0177).

F.2.10. Undefined Results
       Description
       There are possible program execution differences in cases where a program relies on
       undefined values to be something predictable. An example is the assumption that an
       ASCII COBOL binary field (USAGE COMP) in WORKING-STORAGE with no VALUE
       clause has zero as its initial value. Reliance on these situations could lead to portability
       problems and is a bad programming practice.

       Changes
       For the specific case mentioned above, add a VALUE clause with the appropriate
       values to the data description in the program. You also could use the INITIALIZE verb
       to get the initial values desired. The keyword option CLEAR also can be used.




FΓÇô6                                                                                7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                   UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.2.11. Calling Sequence
         Description
         The UCS COBOL calling sequence is common for all UCS languages and therefore
         cannot be the same as for ASCII COBOL. Non-UCS language subprograms and
         assembler subprograms are affected. The current formats for the CALL/ENTER
         common calling sequence are as follows:

                X9       Dedicated register
                X10      Dedicated register
                R12-15   Dedicated registers
                X3       Link vector of called routine
                X11      Link register
                A0       Contains the number of parameters in Q4, Q1-Q3 = 0
                A1       Parameter list pointer (virtual address)

         Each parameter is a three-word packet, where:
            Word 0 contains the bit offset in S6.
            Word 1 contains the virtual address.
            Word 2 contains the length in bits.

         Changes
         Only call programs written in one of the UCS languages.

F.2.12. Register Conventions
         Description
         The UCS COBOL register conventions is common for all UCS languages and therefore
         cannot be the same as for ASCII COBOL.

         Changes
         Only call programs written in one of the UCS languages.

F.2.13. ASCII COBOL Level 3R1 Calling Sequence
         Description
         The extra G option was available to generate ASCII COBOL level 3R1 compatible calling
         sequences. This was documented only in the ASCII COBOL Supplementary Reference
         Manual. This change affects old assembler subprograms that have never been
         modified to use ASCII COBOL level 3R2 or higher calling sequences.

         Changes
         The subprogram must be modified.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                             FΓÇô7
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.2.14. Segmentation Map Symbolic
       Description
       The map symbolic element produced by ASCII COBOL is no longer produced if
       segmentation was specified in the source program. This change is interrelated with
       the switch to dynamic linking and the Linking System.

       Changes
       Modify the runstreams to conform to Linking System requirements.

F.2.15. CALL Identifier
       Description
       The CALL identifier implementation in UCS COBOL is different from that in ASCII
       COBOL. There is no need to assemble an element such as C$S333. The changes also
       are related to the change to dynamic linking and the Linking System.

       Changes
       Program creation runstreams are different and linking is simplified by the Linking
       System.

F.2.16. Extra Options Deleted
       Description
       The following options for sequence number checking and frequency table generation
       are not available in UCS COBOL.

           0       Sequence of procedure file
                   searching
           2&3     Sequence number checking
           7       Frequency table generation

       Changes
       Unisys does not see a requirement to carry the sequence number checking or the
       frequency table generation forward into UCS COBOL. The UCS COBOL options
       SEARCH-PF-SI and SEARCH-SI-PF control the sequence of procedure file searching.

F.2.17. Referencing Record Areas before OPEN
       Description
       Action in ASCII COBOL programs depends on whether the file was move-mode or
       locate-mode. UCS COBOL allocates record areas at OPEN time, so no record area is
       available prior to the OPEN.




FΓÇô8                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




         Changes
         In some cases, the ASCII COBOL implementation permitted the invalid use of record
         areas before the OPEN. This invalid use is not permitted within UCS COBOL. The UCS
         Runtime System issues errors during execution time when attempting to do this.

F.2.18. Index-Name Formats
         Description
         Problems could occur if an index was used with a table other than the table defining
         the index. If the referenced table had a format identical to the defining table, correct
         results were obtained.

         Changes
         Delete this illegal programming construct. It is not allowed in UCS COBOL.

F.2.19. INDEX Data Items
         Description
         Index data items might have different internal formats in UCS COBOL.

         Changes
         This only causes problems when the program uses index data items in a nonstandard
         manner.

F.2.20. SEARCH ALL
         Description
         A slightly different binary search algorithm might be used, possibly yielding different
         results if the keys of the searched table are duplicated, out of order, or contrary to the
         specifications in the standard.

         Changes
         There is no change. No known instance exists where this illegal construct was used.

F.2.21. Overpunched Signed Numeric Fields
         Description
         UCS COBOL, in some cases, is inconsistent with the way ASCII COBOL decides to
         overpunch or not overpunch sign-included signed numeric fields, when the SIGN IS
         SEPARATE clause was not specified. This should not cause major problems, since the
         numeric values are valid whether or not an overpunch is present. The potential for a
         difference arises when a user program treats signed data as an alphanumeric bit
         string.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                   FΓÇô9
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




       For a data item described as signed (S in the PICTURE clause), which does not have
       the SIGN clause, the internal representation of the operational sign is implementor
       defined (ANS X3.23-1974). Unsigned values, positive-signed values, and negative-
       signed values are all legal in a data item described as signed. Each possibility must be
       allowed since the incoming data, possibly from foreign systems, should be treated
       correctly, regardless of whether or not an overpunched sign is present.

       Numeric comparisons are done with respect to the algebraic value of the operands
       and must work correctly whether overpunched or not. Non-numeric comparisons are
       done with respect to the collating sequence of the associated characters. It is possible
       that nonnumeric comparisons of the data items which can contain overpunched
       numeric data will give an unequal result, even though the contained numeric values
       are algebraically equal. See the ASCII COBOL Programming Reference Manual.

       This situation (presence or lack of overpunches) exists within ASCII COBOL as well as
       between ASCII COBOL and UCS COBOL.

       Changes
       Programs should not be coded to use only one of several legal internal forms of
       signed numeric data representation. There is no problem where the numeric data is
       treated as numeric.

F.2.22. Class Names
       Description
       Class name specifications in the SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph must be in the format
       ΓÇ£CLASS class-name IS ...ΓÇ¥ according to the COBOL 85 standard. The ASCII COBOL
       extension which allowed class name definitions required the format ΓÇ£CLASS-NAME IS
       mnemonic-name ... .ΓÇ¥

       Changes
       Restructure the class name specification manually.

F.2.23. Subscript Checking
       Description
       In ASCII COBOL, extensions were available to do subscript range checking on all table
       references. Either the X extra option or the USE FOR TABLE ERROR syntax in the
       DECLARATIVES could be used. UCS COBOL has an option which does consistent
       run-time error checking for all UCS languages.

       Changes
       Use the UCS COBOL keyword option RUNCHECK to perform the subscript verification.




FΓÇô10                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                               UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.2.24. Numeric PROGRAM-ID Name
         Description
         The program name in the program-id paragraph in the Identification Division in ASCII
         COBOL could be numeric; for example, 1234. In UCS COBOL this is not allowed. The
         standard does not allow numeric program names. It is felt that this causes very little
         impact on existing programs.

         Changes
         Change the program name manually. An alternative is to use the COMPAT option,
         which allows a numeric PROGRAM-ID.

F.2.25. Paragraph Followed by a GO TO Statement
         Description
         If any unaltered paragraph name is immediately followed by a GO TO statement, the
         address of the paragraph name is equated to the address of the target of the GO TO
         statement. For example:

           P1.
                 .
                 .
                 .
           P2.
           GO TO P1

         In this example, both P1 and P2 are assigned to the same code location.

         Changes
         In a PADS session, all PADS commands should refer to the target of the GO TO
         statement.

F.2.26. FILE STATUS with APPLY EXDEF and APPLY EXREF
        Clause
         Description
         The UCS COBOL use of the FILE STATUS variable in conjunction with the APPLY EXDEF
         and APPLY EXREF clauses is different from the ASCII COBOL use. In ASCII COBOL,
         when a program contains a file with a FILE STATUS item, and both the file and the FILE
         STATUS item are the object of an APPLY EXDEF clause, you do not need to specify the
         FILE STATUS item in the SELECT statement of the subprogram that contains the FILE
         STATUS item in an APPLY EXREF clause. This results in the FILE STATUS variable being
         updated in the subprogram even though the subprogram does not explicitly specify
         the FILE STATUS item in its SELECT statement. The subprogram FILE STATUS item,
         used in this way, is not updated in UCS COBOL.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                FΓÇô11
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




       Solution
       You must specify the FILE STATUS item in the SELECT statement of both programs,
       even if it uses the APPLY EXDEF and APPLY EXREF clauses. UCS COBOL does not
       update the value of the FILE STATUS item unless it is present in the SELECT statement
       of the program that requires the value of FILE STATUS to be updated.

F.2.27. Duplicate Data Names from Schema
       Description
       User-defined names such as record names, area names, and set names that are
       initially defined in the schema elements must not duplicate any other name in the UCS
       COBOL program. Every user-defined name that is used within the UCS COBOL
       program must be uniquely definable. Data names can be duplicated if they can be
       uniquely identified in the program through the use of qualification.

       ADMLP did not check for uniqueness of reference in names that were defined in the
       schema and duplicated in the ASCII COBOL program.

       Changes
       The compiler must be able to uniquely define all user-defined names. Ensure that no
       duplicate data names are defined in the schema and UCS COBOL program.

F.2.28. Report Format for Nonprint Files
       Description
       If a file designated for a report is assigned to a device other than the printer, UCS
       COBOL appends to the beginning of each record a 1-word field that contains carriage
       control information (see the UCS COBOL Programming Reference Manual Volume 1).

       The meaning of this 1-word field, called the carriage control field (the cc field), is
       different in UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL regarding page advancement. In UCS
       COBOL, if the cc field is negative, the printer advances to the specified line on the
       next page. For example, -5 in the cc field means advance to line 5 on the next page. In
       ASCII COBOL, page advancement is done with a value of -0 in the cc field, followed by
       another record that contains a positive value in the cc field that signifies the number of
       lines to advance.

       Changes
       A user-written program is required to extract individual records from a report file
       written to a nonprint file. This extraction program for ASCII COBOL must be modified
       to process page advancing for a nonprint report file created by UCS COBOL. However,
       once this extraction program has been modified for UCS COBOL, it can still process
       report writer records written to nonprint files for ASCII COBOL programs.




FΓÇô12                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                             UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.2.29. Communications Module Not Implemented
         Description
         The communications module that was implemented in ASCII COBOL is not
         implemented in UCS COBOL.

         Changes
         All DISABLE, ENABLE, RECEIVE, and SEND statements are invalid.

F.2.30. Data Allocation
         Description
         ASCII COBOL allocates all static variables in one bank. These variables are allocated
         even if they are never referenced in the program. UCS COBOL only allocates variables
         that are referenced in the program. In addition, the variables allocated by UCS COBOL
         are placed in multiple banks.

         Changes
         Use the keyword option COMPAT/FULL to ensure that all variables are allocated and
         placed in one bank.

F.2.31. Record Key/Alternate Key Alignment
         Description
         ASCII COBOL allowed data items specified in the RECORD KEY clause and ALTERNATE
         RECORD KEY clause to begin with the same leftmost character position in the record.
         This violates the COBOL 74 and COBOL 85 Standards and should not have been
         allowed. ASCII COBOL has been changed to flag this situation with a warning
         message.

         Changes
         The user must change the source program such that any RECORD KEY and
         ALTERNATE RECORD KEY data items specified do not start on the same leftmost
         character position in the record.

F.2.32. IBM Labeled Tapes
         Description
         In ASCII COBOL, IBM labeled tapes are handled by the ASCII COBOL runtime library
         when the tapes are assigned as unlabeled or with the Exec when the tapes are
         assigned as labeled. UCS COBOL does not handle the IBM labels itself and relies on
         PCIOS and the EXEC's use of the TLEBCDIC feature.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                             FΓÇô13
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




       Changes
       In UCS COBOL, if the IBM tape is labeled, the system must be set up for EBCDIC tape
       labeling and labeled tapes must not be assigned with the J option. The absence of the
       J option in the file's assignment will cause the Exec (level 40R3 and higher) to process
       the file's labels. For the Exec to process the labels, Exec configuration tag TLEBCDIC
       must be set to 1 or 2. TLEBCDIC set to 1 is preferred (required if IBM labeled tapes are
       being used with ASCII COBOL assigned as unlabelled and UCS COBOL). For more
       information, see the Exec System Software Installation and Configuration Guide.

        The following table illustrates the tape labels that will be produced by ACOB and
       UCOB based upon the tape assignment as well as the setting of the Label Records
       clause.


        User Specifications     Tape Produced from ACOB          Tape Produced from UCOB

        @asg,t with 'Label               Labeled                          Labeled
        Records Omitted'
        @asg,t with 'Label               Labeled                          Labeled
        Records Standard'
        @asg,tj with 'Label             Unlabeled                        Unlabeled
        Records Omitted'
        @asg,tj with 'Label              Labeled                   URTS error 19002/108
        Records Standa`rd'

F.2.33. Blocking Size
       Description
       In ASCII COBOL, the default block size for a file (no BLOCK CONTAINS clause
       specified) is 224. For UCS COBOL, the default block size is 1792.

        Changes
       For additional information, see Section 4.4 UCS Runtime I/O. This should not cause any
       problem when using the file with a default block size within the UCS environment. If
       the file needs to be used outside the UCS environment, the default block size can be
       altered by performing one of the following:

       1.   Change default block and prep factor in URTS$TABLES and re-link the programs.
       2.   Use DFP to alter the block size.
       3.   Use Sort to copy the resulting file and change the blocking factor.




FΓÇô14                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                              UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.3. Discontinued Extensions
         This subsection identifies features of ASCII COBOL that are not carried over into UCS
         COBOL. These are primarily features that are currently documented in the ASCII
         COBOL Supplementary Reference Manual.

F.3.1. IOS Files
         Description
         Non-PCIOS files in ASCII COBOL (MASS-STORAGE, UNISERVO and SEQUENTIAL-FILE)
         are discontinued. All of these formats were defined in the ASCII COBOL
         Supplementary Reference Manual.

         Changes
         Upgrade non-PCIOS files to their PCIOS equivalents. To do this, write an ASCII COBOL
         program that reads in the old file type and outputs a supported file type.

F.3.2. Compatible Files
         Description
         Support for CFH, LION, FORM01, FORM02, and FORM03 files is discontinued. All were
         defined only in the ASCII COBOL Supplementary Reference Manual.

         Changes
         Upgrade non-PCIOS files to their PCIOS equivalents. To do this, write an ASCII COBOL
         program that reads in the old file type and outputs a supported file type.

F.3.3. 770-PRINTER Deleted
         Description
         770-PRINTER as the implementor name in a SELECT statement is no longer necessary.

         Changes
         Change the syntax manually.

F.3.4. ALPHABET SECTION Deleted
         Description
         The ALPHABET SECTION feature is used for extending the source character set of
         ASCII COBOL, used especially for katakana characters.

         Changes
         Remove ALPHABET SECTION and CONTROL DIVISION from your programs. (UCS
         COBOL allows an extended character set.)




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                              FΓÇô15
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.3.5. Asynchronous Processing Module Deleted
       Description
       The Asynchronous Processing module was rarely used and has been deleted.

       Changes
       Remove the syntax from the programs. This change affects all HOLD, LOCK, and
       PROCESS statements.

F.3.6. APPLY INLINE Deleted
       Description
       The function of APPLY INLINE is not required. Remove the APPLY INLINE syntax and
       CONTROL DIVISION from your programs.

       Changes
       Remove the APPLY INLINE syntax and CONTROL DIVISION from the programs.

F.3.7. POINT LOCATION Clause Deleted
       Description
       The POINT LOCATION clause was used to specify the binary point location in PIC 1
       items and is defined in the ASCII COBOL Supplementary Reference Manual.

       Changes
       Remove the POINT LOCATION clause syntax manually.

F.3.8. REMARKS Deleted
       Description
       The REMARKS paragraph, defined in the ASCII COBOL Supplementary Reference
       Manual, has been deleted.

       Changes
       Change programs to use the asterisk to comment out all lines in the REMARKS
       paragraph manually.

F.3.9. MONITOR Deleted
       Description
       Newer facilities are provided for program debugging. This should not affect existing
       production programs.




FΓÇô16                                                                           7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                              UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




         Changes
         PADS is the primary debugging tool for future development. The keyword options
         MONITOR and MONITOR/LABEL provide a feature similar to the MONITOR verb within
         UCS COBOL. See 2.2.7 for more information on how to use MONITOR and
         MONITOR/LABEL.

F.3.10. Special Registers
         Description
         TALLY and MCFLAG were implicitly defined for use with EXAMINE and MONITOR, but
         could be used in any context. TALLY is not implicitly defined in UCS COBOL. MCFLAG
         is implicitly defined only if you specify the keyword options MONITOR or
         MONITOR/LABEL. See 2.2.7 for more information about MCFLAG.

         Changes
         Add definitions of TALLY and MCFLAG to the WORKING-STORAGE section manually.

F.3.11. ACCEPT and DISPLAY
         Description
            ACCEPT ..          FROM CARD-READER.
            DISPLAY ..         UPON PRINTER.
         Mnemonic names, defined in the SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph, must be used in
         conjunction with ACCEPT and DISPLAY. The extension which allows PRINTER and
         CARD-READER in ASCII COBOL is documented in the ASCII COBOL Supplementary
         Reference Manual.

         Changes
         Add mnemonic names manually to the SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph for PRINTER,
         CARD-READER, and CONSOLE and change ACCEPT/DISPLAY to refer to the mnemonic
         names.

F.3.12. EXAMINE, EXHIBIT, TRANSFORM Deleted
         Description
         The EXAMINE, EXHIBIT, and TRANSFORM verbs, defined in the ASCII COBOL
         Supplementary Reference Manual, have been deleted.

         Changes
         Change the deleted verbs to equivalent, legal syntax manually.

F.3.13. TRAILING Option of INSPECT Deleted
         Description
         This extension to the INSPECT statement, defined in the ASCII COBOL Supplementary
         Reference Manual, has been deleted.



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                          FΓÇô17
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




       Changes
       Delete the TRAILING option from programs manually.

F.3.14. NOTE Statement Deleted
       Description
       The NOTE statement is no longer legal.

       Changes
       Use the asterisk (*) for all types of comments.

F.3.15. ON Integer Deleted
       Description
       The ON statement, defined in the ASCII COBOL Supplementary Reference Manual,
       has been deleted.

       Changes
       The ON statement was used infrequently. Programs using the ON statement must be
       changed manually.

F.3.16. COBOL 68 Format COPY Statements
       Description
       The extra ΓÇ£EΓÇ¥ option, provided in ASCII COBOL to allow processing of unconverted
       COBOL 68 format COPY statements and procedures, is not available in UCS COBOL.

       Changes
       Convert procedures to the current UCS COBOL format.

F.3.17. Old ENTER Statements Deleted
       Description
       ENTER statements, defined in the ASCII COBOL Supplementary Reference Manual,
       have been deleted. UCS COBOL continues to support the ENTER MASM statement.

       Changes
       Unisys supports the extended mode MASM usage (assembler directive $OBJ) only in
       software written by Unisys or in interfaces written by the customer that explicitly
       require assembler-produced object modules according to the documentation written
       by Unisys.




FΓÇô18                                                                        7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                               UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.3.18. Mnemonic Name in CODE Clause
         Description
         The mnemonic name in the CODE clause allowed a mnemonic name (defined in
         SPECIAL-NAMES) to be used in place of a literal in a report description (RD).

         Changes
         Change the mnemonic to a two-character literal in the CODE clause of the report
         description manually.

F.3.19. COBOL 68 CODE Clause Deleted
         Description
         The extra O option allowed the code in a report file record to be put at the end of a
         record instead of at the beginning. This is a COBOL 68 carryover that has been
         deleted.

F.3.20. EQUALS, EXCEEDS, UNEQUAL
         Description
         These relational operators, which are defined in the ASCII COBOL Supplementary
         Reference Manual, are not allowed in UCS COBOL.

         Changes
         Modify programs to use EQUAL, GREATER, or NOT EQUAL as appropriate.

F.3.21. Fieldata
         Description
         The Fieldata character set and sixth-word aligned data is not supported in UCS COBOL.

         Changes
         Fieldata to ASCII migration is the subject of separate documents. Please check with
         Field Marketing branches for more detail.


F.4. Substantive Changes from the American
     National Standard (ANS)
         This subsection contains the analysis by Unisys of

         ∩é╖   The changes in the 1985 COBOL standard issued in September, 1985
         ∩é╖   The substantive changes made by the X3J4 technical committee as a result of the
             public review comments received during the public review period

         Existing ASCII COBOL programs which use the ANS 1974 COBOL standard may be
         affected by the following changes.



7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                FΓÇô19
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.1. Length of ALL Literal
       Description
       Delete the word ALL manually.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No expected impact.

       ALL is not allowed in statements such as

         DISPLAY ALL ΓÇÖABCΓÇÖ UPON PRINTER.

       Changes
       Delete the word ΓÇ£ALLΓÇ¥.

F.4.2. Alphabet-Name Clause
       Description
       The word ΓÇ£ALPHABETΓÇ¥ must be specified in the ALPHABET-NAME clause in
       SPECIAL-NAMES.

       This change is necessary to resolve an ambiguity, since system-names and user-
       defined words can intersect, which was not possible in COBOL 74.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       Illegal usage is flagged at compilation time.

       Changes
       Add the word ΓÇ£ALPHABETΓÇ¥ before any ALPHABET-NAME clauses in the
       SPECIAL-NAMES SECTION.

F.4.3. Collating Sequence
       Description
       The collating sequence used to access an indexed file is the native character set.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated because this is how ASCII COBOL currently works.

       Changes
       None.




FΓÇô20                                                                           7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                 UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.4. CURRENCY SIGN Clause
         Description
         The literal specified by the CURRENCY SIGN clause must not be a figurative constant.

         HIGH-VALUES, LOW-VALUES, and so forth, should not be allowed as currency signs.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated. Illegal usage is flagged at compilation time.

         Changes
         Insert a literal with the appropriate value.

F.4.5. RELATIVE KEY Phrase
         Description
         A RELATIVE KEY must not contain the PICTURE symbol P.

         A RELATIVE KEY with a P in the PICTURE clause could not be used to access all the
         records in a file.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated. Illegal usage is flagged at compilation time.

         Changes
         Remove the ΓÇ£PΓÇ¥ from the PICTURE clause.

F.4.6. MULTIPLE FILE TAPE Clause
         Description
         1.   All files on a multiple file tape must have the same labeling conventions. Problems
              occur if different files on one multiple file tape had differing labeling conventions.
         2.   SORT-MERGE files must not be specified. Scratch files on a multiple file tape have
              no reasonable application and could only cause problems.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated.

         Changes
         Modify the program, either manually or with a converter, as follows:
         1.   Use STANDARD labels in all files specified on a MULTIPLE FILE TAPE clause.
         2.   Remove SD names from the MULTIPLE FILE TAPE clause.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                   FΓÇô21
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.7. LINAGE Clause
       Description
       Files with the LINAGE clause specified must not be opened in the EXTEND mode.

       The size of the first logical page of a file opened in the EXTEND mode was undefined.
       The page number was set to one. There is not a good reason to allow this
       combination.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated.

F.4.8. FOOTING Phrase
       Description
       No END-OF-PAGE condition occurs if FOOTING is not specified in the FD.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated. ASCII COBOL currently works as specified in COBOL 85.

F.4.9. OCCURS Clause
       Description
       When a variable length receiving item contains the DEPENDING ON field, the
       maximum length of the field is used for the move.

       Contents of the receiving field in cases where COBOL 85 moves extra characters
       compared to COBOL 74 were, and are, undefined.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       Very little impact is anticipated.

       ASCII COBOL uses maximum length if the receiving field contains the DEPENDING ON
       field.

F.4.10. PICTURE Symbol P
       Description
       When a data item described by a PICTURE clause containing the symbol P is
       referenced, the digit positions specified by the P are considered to contain zeros in
       the following operations:

       ∩é╖   Any operation requiring a numeric sending operand
       ∩é╖   A MOVE statement where the sending operand is numeric and its PICTURE
           character string contains the symbol P




FΓÇô22                                                                            7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




         ∩é╖   A MOVE statement where the sending operand is numeric edited and its PICTURE
             character string contains the symbol P and the receiving operand is numeric or
             numeric edited
         ∩é╖   A comparison operation where both operands are numeric.

         This is a clearer, more intuitively correct approach. The cases where differences might
         occur are obscure and should not be very common.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         Very little impact is anticipated.

F.4.11. PROCEDURE DIVISION Header
         Description
         A data item specified on the USING phrase of the PROCEDURE DIVISION header must
         not be the subject of a REDEFINES clause.

         This restriction eliminates some problems which could occur if the same data area is
         passed as two separate parameters.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated. ASCII COBOL, while allowing the REDEFINES subject in the
         USING phrase, does not allow both the subject and object of the REDEFINES to be
         specified on the same USING.

F.4.12. Exponentiation
         Description
         The following special cases of exponentiation are defined in the 1985 COBOL
         standard:

         ∩é╖   If a value less than or equal to 0 is raised to a power of 0, the size error condition
             exists.
         ∩é╖   If the evaluation of the exponentiation yields both a positive and a negative real
             number, the positive number is returned.
         ∩é╖   If no real number exists as the result of the evaluation, the size error condition
             exists.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated. ASCII COBOL functions as specified in the COBOL 85
         standard.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  FΓÇô23
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.13. Order of Execution for a Conditional Expression
       Description
       Conditional expressions are evaluated from left to right within a hierarchical level, and
       the evaluation terminates as soon as a truth value is determined.

       Only debugging declaratives are affected in existing programs. Situations similar to the
       one shown below might not have worked in COBOL 74. These situations work with
       the COBOL 85 standard.

         01   SS PIC 999.
         01   LITTLE-TABLE.
              02 ABC PIC 9999 OCCURS 10.
         .
         .
              MOVE 100 TO SS.
              IF SS < 11 AND ABC (SS) = 0

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated.

F.4.14. Class Condition
       Description
       The ALPHABETIC class test is true for both uppercase and lowercase letters and
       space.

       The ALPHABETIC test makes more sense if it is true for lowercase and uppercase
       letters. Many compilers already work this way.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated, since ASCII COBOL currently accepts lowercase letters as
       alphabetic.

F.4.15. CANCEL Statement
       Description
       The CANCEL statement closes all files open in the CANCEL statement subprogram.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated.

       Change
       Change programs that call files that were open in a program that was canceled.
       Defining this previously undefined condition ensures that a program obtains a
       predictable result.




FΓÇô24                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                               UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.16. CLOSE Statement
         Description
         The NO REWIND phrase cannot be specified in a CLOSE statement having the
         REEL/UNIT phrase.

         The rules for the NO REWIND and REEL/UNIT phrases conflict in COBOL 74; both could
         not be processed.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated. Illegal usage is flagged at compilation time.

         Changes
         Remove the NO REWIND phrase from CLOSE statements that have a REEL/UNIT
         phrase.

F.4.17. COPY Statement in Comments
         Description
         If a COPY statement occurs within a comment-entry or in a place where a
         comment-entry can appear, it is treated as part of the comment-entry.

         This defines a previously undefined area and enhances program portability.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated. ASCII COBOL currently treats comment-entry COPY
         statements as part of the comment and does not copy any text from the procedure
         file.

F.4.18. COPY Statement on a Debugging Line
         Description
         If DEBUGGING MODE is not specified in the SOURCE-COMPUTER statement, a
         debugging line is considered to have all the characteristics of a comment line after all
         COPY statements have been processed.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated. ASCII COBOL currently does the REPLACING even if
         REPLACING is on a debug line and DEBUGGING MODE is not turned on. If DEBUGGING
         MODE is not on and the COPY statement begins on a debug line, ASCII COBOL treats
         the COPY statement itself as a comment line. UCS COBOL treats the copied text as a
         comment line. This should not cause a problem.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                FΓÇô25
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.19. DISPLAY Statement
       Description
       After displaying the last operand in a DISPLAY statement, the hardware device is
       positioned at the first character position of the next line.

       This rule is required so that the NO ADVANCING option can be fully specified.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       A program which intermixes DISPLAY statements with WRITE statements to the
       same output file could result in overprinting.

F.4.20. DIVIDE Statement
       Description
       Subscripts for identifier-4 in the remainder phrase of a DIVIDE statement are
       evaluated after the result of the DIVIDE statement is stored in identifier-3 of the
       GIVING phrase.

       The point at which the subscript for the remainder was determined was not defined in
       the COBOL 74 standard. Inconsistencies were likely.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated. ASCII COBOL functions as specified in the COBOL 85
       standard.

F.4.21. EXIT PROGRAM Statement Used Implicitly
       Description
       An implicit EXIT PROGRAM statement is executed if there is no next executable
       statement in a subprogram. This situation is undefined in COBOL 74.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated since ASCII COBOL currently works this way.

F.4.22. EXIT PROGRAM Statement Used with the PERFORM
        Statement
       Description
       When an EXIT PROGRAM statement is executed, all active PERFORM statements are
       assumed to have reached termination.

       An ambiguity is resolved. Program portability is enhanced.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated. An application that relies on this undefined situation in
       COBOL 74 could cause a problem.



FΓÇô26                                                                              7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                               UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.23. INSPECT Statement
         Description
         The order of execution for evaluating subscripts in the INSPECT statement is
         specified.

         The time of subscript evaluation should be defined in the standards, but was not in
         COBOL 74.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated.

F.4.24. MERGE Statement
         No two files in a MERGE statement can be specified in a SAME AREA or SAME
         SORT-MERGE AREA clause. Also, only the GIVING files in a MERGE can be specified in
         a SAME RECORD AREA clause.

         Description
         If this rule (not in COBOL 74) had been violated in a COBOL 74 program, the MERGE
         would probably not have worked correctly.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated.

         Changes
         Change any illegal usages that are flagged at compilation time.

F.4.25. PERFORM Statement ΓÇö Initialization of Variables
         Description
         The order of initialization of multiple varying identifiers in a PERFORM statement is
         defined.

         This situation was undefined in COBOL 74 and improves program portability. The
         chance of an incompatibility in an existing program is small.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         Very little impact is anticipated. To be affected, one VARYING identifier must depend
         on the other.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                FΓÇô27
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.26. PERFORM Statement ΓÇö Setting and Augmenting
        Variables
       Description
       In a PERFORM ... VARYING ... AFTER statement, identifier-2 is augmented before
       identifier-5 is set.

       The COBOL 74 rules for this condition do not make sense, so the change is needed.
       Very few programs are likely to be affected since there is no logic to the COBOL 74
       definition.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       Some problems could occur due to different increments of PERFORM statement
       variables.

       Change
       Modify PERFORM statement variables to reflect the COBOL 85 definition.

F.4.27. PERFORM Statement ΓÇö Evaluation of Subscripts
       Description
       The order of execution for evaluating subscripts in the PERFORM VARYING statement
       is specified in COBOL 85.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated. ASCII COBOL functions as specified in the COBOL 85
       standard.

F.4.28. READ Statement
       Description
       A READ ... INTO statement can be specified only if

       ∩é╖   Only one record description is subordinate to the file description
       ∩é╖   All associated records as well as the INTO record are group items or elementary
           alphanumeric items

       Conversion of multiple elementary records was not defined in COBOL 74. Various
       implementations can produce different results.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       Very little impact is anticipated. Illegal usage is flagged at compilation time.




FΓÇô28                                                                               7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                                UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.29. RETURN Statement
         Description
         A RETURN ... INTO statement can be specified only if all associated records as well as
         the ΓÇ£INTOΓÇ¥ record are group items or elementary alphanumeric items.

         Conversion of multiple elementary records was not defined in COBOL 74. Various
         implementations can produce different results.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         Very little impact is anticipated. Illegal usage is flagged at compilation time.

F.4.30. STOP RUN Statement/Program Termination ΓÇö File
        Closure
         Description
         The termination of a program with an explicit STOP RUN statement, an implicit STOP
         RUN statement, or an abnormal program termination causes all open files to be
         closed.

         Leaving files in an open mode at program termination can lead to invalid files. This
         leads to errors, since it is possible to leave a file open. This change does not affect
         correct operational programs.

         Expected Impact on OS 2200 ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated. In the past it has been quite common for files to be left in an
         open state, either by programmer error or program-user error. Sometimes such
         conditions were not noticed immediately and were often quite hard to explain.

         Changes
         None. The definition of the STOP RUN statement in the COBOL 85 standard requires
         the statement to close all open files. If a STOP RUN statement is not executed, all
         open files will be closed via URTS runtime termination routines.

F.4.31. STOP RUN Statement ΓÇö Message Queue Management
         Description
         The STOP RUN statement causes any messages partially received by the run unit from
         the message control system to be eliminated from the queue.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated.




7831 0455ΓÇô022                                                                                  FΓÇô29
UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




F.4.32. STRING Statement
       Description
       The order of execution for evaluating subscripts in the STRING statement is specified
       in COBOL 85. The order of subscript evaluation in COBOL 74 was not defined.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated.

F.4.33. UNSTRING Statement
       Description
       The order of execution for evaluating subscripts in the UNSTRING statement is
       specified in COBOL 85. The order of subscript evaluation in COBOL 74 was not
       defined.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated.

F.4.34. WRITE Statement
       Description
       The AFTER PAGE and END-OF-PAGE phrases must not be specified in the same WRITE
       statement. It is not logical to have both of these phrases in one statement.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       No impact is anticipated. Illegal usage is flagged at compilation time.

       Changes
       Change any WRITE statements that specify both the AFTER PAGE and END-OF-PAGE
       phrases.

F.4.35. File Position Indicator ΓÇö Record Pointer Replacement
       Description
       The current record pointer concept of COBOL 74 is replaced by a file position indicator
       in COBOL 85.

       Certain READ/WRITE/DELETE combinations could give undefined or surprising results.
       The current record pointer could point to a nonexistent record in some circumstances.
       The file position indicator is more specifically defined with a finite set of values.

       Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
       Very little impact is anticipated.




FΓÇô30                                                                             7831 0455ΓÇô022
                                               UCS COBOL and ASCII COBOL Differences




         Changes
         The two cases that are affected by this change are described in F.4.36 and F.4.37.

F.4.36. File Position Indicator ΓÇö Effect on READ/WRITE
        Statements
         Description
         The following sequence causes the low-key record to be read according to COBOL 85:

           OPEN I-O filename.
           WRITE record-with-a-low-key.
           READ filename NEXT ...

         In COBOL 74, the previous first record would have been read.

         Since the WRITE statement does not affect the file position indicator or current record
         pointer, it follows logically that the first READ NEXT statement for a file should give
         the first record in the file.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         Some problems could occur.

F.4.37. File Position Indicator ΓÇö Effect of Rewrite Statement
         Description
         If an alternate key is the key of reference, and the alternate key is changed by a
         REWRITE statement to a value between the previous value and the previous next key
         value, a READ NEXT statement would make the record that had just been written
         available.

         This is logical since the record that will be read is not the ΓÇ£sameΓÇ¥ record because its
         alternate key value has changed.

         Expected Impact on ASCII COBOL Programs
         No impact is anticipated since ASCII COBOL uses the current READ statement to read
         the rewritten record.
